blacktail.review: Checked by an independent skeptic; 25 corrections applied
review_points: Misread source. In the garrick thread, 'If from a rocky point, even a bung will do, no sinker' describes live-baiting GARRICK. Blacktail appear only as the live bait ('easier to ambush than shad or mullet'). The thread says nothing about catching blacktail on a float and names no Cape blacktail spot

These months are the dates the threads were posted, not the dates of the catches. The Kogelbaai post says blacktail are plentiful there in general, the Quarry post is general advice ('Dassies on low tide'), and Enigma's Clovelly catch has no date. Only Jacita May 2025, Jacita June 2025 and the Stran

This contradicts the profile's own Cape evidence: Jacita June 2025 'calm seas and some blacktail'; Kogelbaai 'Preekstoel is good when the swell is low'; the Glencairn drift line, which the profile itself rates for flat to small seas; and the shallow-flat fly tactic. The 'favours turbulent seas' basi

The only Cape source on water colour that the profile cites (Kogelbaai, 'needs a bit of colour') points the other way, and the profile's own coloured-water tactic presents coloured water as productive. No cited source says clear water is better for blacktail.

The Jacita report says nothing about water colour. It mentions cold water and high tide only, so it supports the high-tide and bloodworm parts but not the coloured-water trigger. 'Kogelbaai regulars ... rate wonderworm' overstates the source: wonderworm is 'worth trying', and 'best from Hangklip' re
The cited Quarry thread says nothing about shelter from swell. Its only conditions advice is low tide and that a drift line fails in moving water. The claim is unsupported.
Walt's 'moving water' means current or flow, not wave height. Gating the tactic on sea state is a stretch of the source.

The specific numbers (40 cm water, 750 mm, 5 s, figure-of-eight, 15 to 20 m, leader specs) all come from an Eastern Cape author, Gary Grobler of the Port Elizabeth Fly Tyers Guild. The page does not name where the fish were caught. The 5 to 7 weight comes from The Mission's wildeperd article and is
unverified: All temperature numbers are estimates (min 10, ideal 15 to 21, max 25 C). The minimum was lowered from 12 to 10 because fish are reported at Melkbosstrand in cold Atlantic water. FishBase has no temperature data, and the Springer below-20 C spawning claim was seen only in a search snippet.

peak_months 3 to 6 is low confidence. It rests on three late-autumn and winter catch reports (Strand Jun 2012, Jacita May and Jun 2025). The other thread months are posting dates, not catch dates, and blacktail are resident all year.
spawn_months 9 to 12 for the Cape is extrapolated from the Eastern Cape peak (Sep to Dec, Wikipedia, not re-checked). Cape spawning timing is not documented.

Every condition weight (light, sea, tide, flow, range, trend, clarity, wind) is an estimate. sea.flat was raised to 0.72 on Cape calm-sea reports (Jacita Jun 2025; Kogelbaai 'good when swell is low'). 'Favours turbulent seas' is from a search snippet only.

Tide weights: low draws on the Glencairn 'dassies on low tide' post, high on Jacita May 2025 ('especially on high tide') and pushing on the Botes fly article. tide.dropping 0.65 has no source. The Rooi-Els tourism page is not used as tide evidence.
clarity.coloured 0.85 is an estimate. No cited source says clear water is better for blacktail, and the Kogelbaai 'needs a bit of colour' remark is not blacktail-specific.
Typical weights (200 to 500 g; 1.5 to 2 kg for a big fish) are estimates. Only the lengths come from FishBase, and the 2 kg figure is a 1971 Eastern Cape/KZN quotation.
Float tactic: no cited source describes float-fishing for blacktail around Cape Town. The method is a low-confidence estimate.
Coloured-water scent tactic: the idea that blacktail hunt by scent in coloured water is an inference. Jacita supports only the high-tide timing and bloodworm.

Sight-cast fly tactic: the leader, retrieve and stand-off numbers are Port Elizabeth (Eastern Cape) technique. The rod weight and fly hook sizes are estimates. Tailing blacktail on Peninsula or False Bay flats are not documented in the cited sources.
Weighted fly tactic: the rod weight, line type and Clouser/Fritz alternatives are estimates. The Fish The Fly support is a search snippet only.
Night feeding by big blacktail rests on one 1971 Eastern Cape/KZN quotation. No Cape source supports it.
Shelter from swell at the Glencairn Quarry is not documented, so it is not offered as a rough-sea spot.
Lower abundance on the Atlantic side (west of Cape Point) is inferred from the published distribution; blacktail are nonetheless reported at Melkbosstrand.
The 1992 Rhodes MSc snippet and the Wikipedia spawning dates were not re-checked by the reviewer, and the Mann 2013 ORI/SAAMBR linefish profile could not be opened.

bronze-bream.name: Bronze bream
bronze-bream.season_note: Uncommon around Cape Town, because False Bay is the western edge of its range (southern Mozambique to False Bay). Adults are sedentary reef residents, so where the fish occurs it is there all year. The water temperature decides when it bites. Expect it mainly on the warmer False Bay rocks and around Cape Point and Buffels Bay. The best chance is in late summer and autumn, when the water is warmest (the peak months are an estimate). Atlantic-side reports of 'bronze bream' are probably hottentot, which is far commoner in that cold water: three fish at Blouberg in February 2024 and a boat fish at Langebaan in March 2025. In Cape fishing reports 'bronzie' usually means the bronze whaler shark, not this fish. Spawning data come from the Eastern Cape (January to June) and KwaZulu-Natal (winter). There are no Western Cape data.

temp.basis: Estimate, built from judgement, not measurements. The fish is a warm-temperate endemic at its western range limit in False Bay (Wikipedia, citing Iwatsuki & Heemstra 2022). Eastern Cape anglers caught bronze bream at Mazeppa Bay in clear water of '24C plus' (Sealine 2008). Another Eastern Cape angler says bronzies want water with a bit of colour that is not too warm (Sealine 2009). A Blouberg angler had no bites of any species at 12 C (April 2024), which says nothing specific about this fish.

bronze-bream.habitat: A sedentary resident of shallow rocky reef, usually less than 25 m deep and often in 1 to 5 m of foamy wash right against the rocks. It holds on reef tops, gully mouths and drop-offs, and grazes the reef as the tide floods it. An Eastern Cape angler rates spots with better drop-offs and deeper water as better for bronze bream. Around Cape Town, look mainly on the warmer False Bay rocks and at Cape Point and Buffels Bay (informal reports only). Several stretches are no-take: St James, Boulders, Castle Rock (Miller's Point to Partridge Point), Paulsberg, and Cape of Good Hope (Scarborough to Hoek van die Bobbejaan). Parts of the Cape Point coast are no-take, so check the Table Mountain National Park MPA zone map before fishing there.
bronze-bream.diet: Omnivore. It grazes algae and eats ascidians (redbait), crustaceans, worms and molluscs. Juveniles take more crustaceans than adults. Anglers' best baits are redbait and prawn.
bronze-bream.typical_size: Shore fish are usually 30 to 40 cm (0.7 to 1.5 kg). A big one is 50 cm or more and 3 to 4 kg: a Sealine angler took one of 3 to 4 kg at Ystervarkfontein, on the southern Cape coast. Maximum 65 cm TL, typical 35 cm (FishBase). It matures at about 5.5 years. A maturity length of about 30 cm is an estimate; it matches the legal minimum.
bronze-bream.handling: Minimum size 30 cm, bag limit 2 per person per day (check the current DFFE regulations). IUCN Near Threatened (2014). It is slow-growing and late-maturing (about 5.5 years), long-lived and sedentary, so local reefs are easily fished out, and numbers have declined markedly (Mann et al. 2014). Release big fish. Watch the sharp dorsal spines and gill-cover edges: wet your hands, support the body and unhook in the water when you can. A circle hook keeps most fish lip-hooked for a clean release.

tactics.title: Float-fished redbait in the wash
tactics.lure_or_bait: Redbait or prawn cut into a thin, longish strip, tied on gently with bait cotton, leaving the hook gape clear
tactics.rig: 1/0 circle hook under a small red float on a 0.35 mm trace, with no sinker or one small split shot. Use a light rock rod or a long spinning rod (about 3 m, rated 1 to 3 oz). The rod and trace are estimates; the source names only the hook and float.
tactics.retrieve: Let the float drift through the white water along the reef edge. With a circle hook, do not strike; when the float goes, wind steadily into the weight.
tactics.depth: 1 to 3 m, in the foam over reef edges and gully mouths
tactics.stand: On a safe ledge beside a gully or reef edge where the wash pushes across, never with your back to the sea
tactics.why: A Sealine bronze bream angler (Nov 2019) uses a small red float above a 1/0 circle hook, with a thin, longish bait cottoned on gently and the gape kept proud. The thread gives no location, trace or rod. Bronze bream feed in the wash over shallow reef.

tactics.title: Drift bait into the gully on the push
tactics.lure_or_bait: Redbait, or a redbait and prawn combination
tactics.rig: 1/0 to 2/0 hook on a 0.40 mm trace with a free-running 1/4 to 1/2 oz ball sinker, or no sinker at all
tactics.retrieve: Lob it into the head of the gully on the back of a surge and let the wash carry it in and out. Keep in touch, and wind into a steady pull.
tactics.depth: Bottom to mid-water in 1 to 3 m of foam
tactics.stand: On a high, safe ledge above the gully mouth, only where waves are not washing over the rock
tactics.why: The one detailed Sealine bronze bream catch (1.6 and 2.4 kg, Mazeppa Bay) came on redbait two hours into an incoming tide. An Eastern Cape angler advises fishing bronze bream water only when the swell is no bigger than 2.5 m. Both are Eastern Cape evidence.

tactics.title: Prawn when the water has colour
tactics.lure_or_bait: Sand prawn or bought prawn, or a redbait and prawn combination
tactics.rig: 1/0 hook on a 0.40 mm, 30 cm snood, with a 1 to 2 oz sinker on a lighter rotten-bottom strop
tactics.retrieve: Cast to the edge of the white water and hold it there. Wind into a steady pull.
tactics.depth: On the bottom at the reef edge, 1 to 4 m
tactics.stand: On a safe ledge at a reef point where onshore wind or swell has brought colour and wash
tactics.why: An Eastern Cape angler says bronze bream want water with a bit of colour. At Twini ledges the fish took prawn but ignored redbait on its own.

tactics.title: Finesse the deep gullies when it is flat and clear
tactics.lure_or_bait: A small, thin redbait or prawn strip
tactics.rig: Size 1 to 1/0 hook on a lighter trace than usual, about 0.35 to 0.45 mm. Use a 1 oz sinker on a 30 cm strop of lighter line than the main line. 0.45 mm comes from hottentot advice; anything lighter is an estimate.
tactics.retrieve: Cast into the deepest gully or drop-off and keep the bait still on the bottom. Strike late.
tactics.depth: On the bottom in the deepest water within casting range, 3 to 6 m
tactics.stand: On the ledge edge above a deep drop-off. Fish at first light or under cloud.
tactics.why: Estimate: with no wash, the fish probably sit deeper and get shy. In a hottentot thread, Cape rock anglers drop to a 0.45 mm trace on 'clear, shy-fish days', applied here by analogy. Eastern Cape advice points to drop-offs and deeper water for bronze bream.

tactics.title: First-light or overcast float session close in
tactics.lure_or_bait: Redbait strip
tactics.rig: 1/0 circle hook under a small float on a 0.35 mm trace, on a light rock rod or a long spinning rod (about 3 m)
tactics.retrieve: Work the float through every pocket of foam within 10 m of the rocks
tactics.depth: 1 to 2 m
tactics.stand: On a safe ledge close to the foam line. Move often to find feeding fish, and stay higher up when sets are running.
tactics.why: Estimate: grazing reef sparids feed most confidently in low light, and bronze bream are reported to spawn in the mornings and evenings.

tactics.title: Expect little in cold water
tactics.lure_or_bait: Prawn (a soft bait)
tactics.rig: 1/0 hook on 0.35 mm, small sinker
tactics.retrieve: Fish slowly in the sunniest, shallowest gullies around midday
tactics.depth: 1 to 3 m
tactics.stand: In sun-warmed gullies on the False Bay side rather than the Atlantic side, away from the no-take zones
tactics.why: Estimate. Bronze bream are at their cold range limit here. A Blouberg angler had no bites of any species at 12 C (April 2024), and a white musselcracker thread notes that 'in cooler waters fish may prefer a softer bait'. When the water is below this fish's range, consider targeting hottentot instead.

legal.bag_note: 2 per day. Counts toward the aggregate of 10.
legal.note: A and B agree and both match R.959. No closed season.
legal.quote: Bronze bream (bluefish) | Pachymetopon grande | 30 cm | 2

bronze-bream.review: Checked by an independent skeptic; 17 corrections applied
review_points: The profile's own handling text, citing Mann et al. 2014 via Wikipedia, says the fish is sedentary and resident on its home reef. A resident fish does not leave False Bay from June to October. What drops in winter is how often it gets caught, and the temp weighting already handles that. Limiting pre
In Cape Town reports 'bronzie' usually means the bronze whaler shark (Sealine: Strandfontein 'bronzies (bronze whaler sharks)'). Using it as an alias will match shark reports to bronze bream.

The text never gives the IUCN status, which is Near Threatened (2014), on the same Wikipedia page it cites. It also states 'Matures at about 30 cm' (in typical_size) with no source; Wikipedia gives only the age (5.5 years).

A 4 to 5 oz rock rod is standard rock-and-surf tackle, not the light tackle this page is about, and the cited float thread mentions neither a rod nor a trace. Both come from a search snippet about galjoen, bronze bream and blacktail rods.
The rig contradicts its own source. The cited post (a hottentot thread) gives 0.45 mm as the lightest trace on shy days; 0.30 to 0.35 mm is unsourced.

Worded as if it were bronze bream evidence. The April post is a no-bite report for every species at Blouberg, and the February 'bronze bream' from that cold Atlantic beach are probably hottentot. Neither is evidence of bronze bream's lower temperature limit.

The Hout Bay advice is invented; the profile's own unverified list says 'No Cape source covers Hout Bay harbour'. Hout Bay and Blouberg are both cold Atlantic side, where this species is at best a vagrant. The habitat text states these as fact, and species-level text will show at every spot.

'rough' means waves over 1.8 m reaching the spot. Telling a light-tackle angler to lob baits into gullies from rock ledges in that sea is a safety problem. The only cited support is an Eastern Cape rule of thumb ('swell not bigger than 2.5 m').
unverified: Peak months [1,2,3,4] are an estimate. No Cape Town source gives catch timing for this species.

Every Atlantic-side 'bronze bream' record found (Blouberg Feb 2024, Langebaan boat Mar 2025) is probably a misidentified hottentot (Pachymetopon blochii). The Cape Town evidence comes down to informal reports from False Bay, Cape Point and Buffels Bay.
Temperature min, ideal band and max are estimates. The 12 C Blouberg no-bite report covers all species, not this one.
All condition weights are estimates. The condition evidence (colour, swell under 2.5 m, incoming tide) comes from the Eastern Cape and Transkei, not Cape Town.
Spawning months come from the Eastern Cape (January to June). No Western Cape spawning data were found.
Maturity at about 30 cm is an estimate. Wikipedia gives only the age at maturity (about 5.5 years).
The rod (about 3 m, 1 to 3 oz) and 0.35 mm trace on the float rigs are estimates. The float thread names only a 1/0 circle hook and a small red float.
The lighter trace in the flat, clear finesse tactic is hottentot advice applied by analogy. Anything below 0.45 mm is an estimate.
The dawn/overcast float rule rests on general sparid behaviour, not on a bronze bream source.
The reviewer could not re-check the ideal-wind-directions thread, the Mazeppa Bay and Twini snippets, or the Ystervarkfontein report. All are Eastern Cape or southern Cape.

This session did not check the exact Table Mountain National Park MPA restricted-zone boundaries around Cape Point (Paulsberg, Cape of Good Hope). Check the zone map before fishing near Buffels Bay or Cape Point.
The size and bag limits come from a table posted on Sealine. Confirm them against the current DFFE recreational regulations.
The ORI/Mann 2013 profile was unreachable (DNS failure), and no Cape-specific magazine article on bronze bream was found. The Mission lists bronze bream only in a 'next up' list.

cape-kurper.name: Cape kurper
aka: Cape kurper (indigenous, do not target: release)
kurper (but note: 'kurper' in SA angling usually means tilapia)
cape-kurper.season_note: A year-round resident wherever it occurs. It breeds in the southern summer, when males defend a breeding territory and guard the eggs (FishBase, Wikipedia). The October to January spawn window and the October to March activity peak are estimates, and so is the idea that cold winter water slows it down. It is unconfirmed whether it lives in the Liesbeek. No fetched source puts it there: Wikipedia gives its range as the coastal rivers from the Coega to the Verlorevlei, plus the Cape Flats, and the government pages list only carp and sharptooth catfish for the lower Liesbeek. Summer water abstraction on the Bishopscourt slopes does cut the Liesbeek's flow (Wikipedia), so any kurper there would be left in the remaining pools.

temp.basis: Only 18 to 22 C is sourced (FishBase Ref. 2060, repeated by Seriously Fish), and that is an aquarium-style range. min 11, ideal 16 to 23 and max 27 C are estimates. They widen the sourced range on an unsourced assumption that wild Cape lowland streams run at about 10 to 12 C in winter and 22 to 25 C in summer. FishBase notes that it breathes air facultatively, which may help it cope with warm, low-oxygen summer pools (estimate).

cape-kurper.habitat: Quiet, slow water with cover. It prefers quieter edges with rocks, roots or plants (Wikipedia) and 'favors quiet or slow-flowing water and plant or root cover' (FishBase). In summer, males defend a breeding territory and guard the eggs (FishBase). Its recorded range is the coastal rivers from the Coega to the Verlorevlei, plus the Cape Flats (Wikipedia). A snorkel account found about seven at a dead trout in the Lourens River (Poroderma). Liesbeek: unconfirmed, and within its historical range only. No fetched source places it in the Liesbeek. The Liesbeek's lower reaches are carp and sharptooth catfish water (Western Cape Government / CapeNature), and large sections are canalised from Rondebosch down (Wikipedia). If it is there, the likeliest places are the less-canalised pools with overhanging plants, root tangles and undercut banks (estimate). Don't treat it as verified at the Liesbeek until CapeNature or a survey confirms it.
cape-kurper.diet: An ambush predator of 'insects and other invertebrates and small fish' (FishBase), and of crabs (Wikipedia). About seven Cape kurpers were seen gathered at a dead trout in the Lourens River (Poroderma snorkel account), so it also scavenges and is drawn to flesh.
cape-kurper.typical_size: Usually about 8 to 15 cm (estimate). Wikipedia gives a maximum of about 25 cm TL and 200 g, and FishBase gives 20 cm SL. LeRoy Botha reports a 19 cm fish that was 'easily three times the weight of any other Cape Kurper' (The Mission; the reviewer did not re-check this).
cape-kurper.handling: An indigenous, declining fish. Bass predation and habitat loss are the main threats, and IUCN lists it as Data Deficient (assessed 2017, via FishBase). The fetched sources don't establish that it is legally protected, but this page treats it as never a target, so always release it. CapeNature and the City ask anglers to return indigenous fish; their examples are yellowfish, sawfin and whitefish, and they don't name the Cape kurper. Don't confuse it with tilapia, which SA anglers also call 'kurper'. The Cape kurper is golden-brown with black spots and wavy bars. It has black stripes radiating from the eye and black-membraned dorsal and anal fins, and breeding males turn almost black. Its dorsal and anal fins carry spines (from general anabantid anatomy, not checked), so hold it gently from below with wet hands and never squeeze it. It 'occasionally plays dead when caught by anglers' (Wikipedia). A fish that is playing dead may come round and wriggle free suddenly (estimate), so unhook it over or in the water, keep it out of the water for seconds only, and let it swim off into quiet cover at the edge. Use barbless or crushed-barb hooks, and cut the line if it is deep-hooked. Never move live fish between waters: that needs a permit (CapeNature). Fishing public rivers such as the Liesbeek needs a CapeNature recreational angling licence (City of Cape Town).

tactics.title: Summer nest guards: keep small flies off the roots
tactics.lure_or_bait: When fly fishing kurper-range streams for carp, use #8 to #10 carp patterns (Lalu Bug, red squirmy) rather than #12 to #16 woolly buggers, nymphs or small streamers
tactics.rig: Barbless or crushed-barb hook; 3X to 4X tippet so any kurper that does take is landed in seconds
tactics.retrieve: Cast only to carp you can see. Do not blind-strip small streamers past root tangles, undercut banks and weed beds.
tactics.depth: Keep the fly away from the bottom of cover along the edge
tactics.stand: Fish the open runs and the middle of pools, casting away from overhanging roots, willows and weed beds along the bank
tactics.why: Males defend a breeding territory in summer and guard the eggs (FishBase, Wikipedia), so a small fly stripped past their cover invites a strike. LeRoy Botha reports a 19 cm Cape kurper taking a woolly bugger under a willow near the end of the day (The Mission; not re-checked). The spawning months and the low-light timing are estimates.

tactics.title: Bait for carp, not for kurper
tactics.lure_or_bait: Sweetcorn, bread flake or a small 8 to 10 mm boilie. Don't use earthworms, maggots, or flesh baits such as fish strips and chicken liver.
tactics.rig: #8 to #6 barbless hook, baited directly or on a short hair; 10 to 20 g running sinker; 3 to 5 kg line (the line strength is an estimate)
tactics.retrieve: Leave it static on the bottom. Keep the rod in hand or watch a bite alarm, so that a fish never swallows the bait unattended.
tactics.depth: On the bottom in open water
tactics.stand: Open pools away from the roots and plants along the edge, for example the lower Liesbeek, which is carp and sharptooth catfish water (it is unconfirmed whether kurper live there)
tactics.why: The kurper eats insects, other invertebrates, small fish and crabs (FishBase, Wikipedia), so plant baits rarely interest it. Worms and maggots on small hooks are the baits most likely to hook it (reasoned from its diet). Flesh baits can draw it too: about seven gathered at a dead trout in the Lourens River (Poroderma). The lower Liesbeek holds large numbers of carp and sharptooth catfish (Western Cape Government / CapeNature).

tactics.title: Spinning in kurper water: bigger lures, away from cover
tactics.lure_or_bait: A 7 to 10 cm paddle-tail on a light jighead or a weedless single hook, or a 7 cm minnow plug, rather than #0 to #2 inline spinners or 1 to 3 g micro jigs
tactics.rig: A single barbless hook in place of trebles; 6 to 8 lb fluorocarbon leader on a light spinning rod
tactics.retrieve: Retrieve steadily through open water at mid-depth. Do not crawl small lures along the bank under the roots.
tactics.depth: Mid-water in the open channel
tactics.stand: Cast up or across the open channel, not parallel to the undercut bank
tactics.why: This is an estimate, not a sourced finding: bigger lures fished away from cover may reduce kurper hits but will not prevent them. The kurper ambushes small prey from cover, and adults reach 20 cm SL (FishBase) or 25 cm TL (Wikipedia), so a 7 cm lure is still within an adult's prey size. Release any kurper you hook, following the release tactic.

tactics.title: Warm, low summer pools: land fast, release in the shade
tactics.lure_or_bait: Whatever you are using, with the barb crushed
tactics.rig: A barbless or crushed-barb #8 to #6 hook on 3 to 5 kg line (estimate). A fish this small comes in within seconds on light line, so heavy line isn't needed.
tactics.retrieve: Bring it straight in. Do not play it out.
tactics.depth: Unhook it in the water
tactics.stand: Release it into shaded, quiet water with cover at the edge, not onto a warm, shallow, sunlit flat
tactics.why: Summer water abstraction lowers stream flow (on the Liesbeek, from the Bishopscourt slopes: Wikipedia), and pools heat up (estimate). A short fight and a release in the water leave the fish less exhausted. It can breathe air facultatively (FishBase), but a quick release still matters.

tactics.title: Hooked a Cape kurper? Release it in the water
tactics.lure_or_bait: Any bait. Use barbless or crushed-barb hooks and keep forceps ready.
tactics.rig: Barbless hook; forceps; cut the line if it is deep-hooked
tactics.retrieve: Bring it in quickly. Do not lift it by the line.
tactics.depth: Keep it under the water, or over it, while you unhook it
tactics.stand: Release it beside quiet cover (roots or plants) at the edge, out of the current
tactics.why: It is an indigenous, declining fish (threatened by bass predation and habitat loss; IUCN Data Deficient), and this page treats it as never a target. It 'occasionally plays dead when caught by anglers' (Wikipedia), so keep it in or over the water until it swims off. CapeNature and the City ask anglers to return indigenous fish.

legal.bag_note: Protected indigenous fish: may not be caught or kept.
legal.quote: Ordinance s52: "no person shall without a permit-- (a) catch any fish which is an endangered wild animal or have in his or her possession any such fish or the carcase or spawn thereof". CapeNature policy (13 Nov 2025) 2.2.2: "When caught, no indigenous fish may be killed, and all such fish must be released alive." Policy Table 1: "#Sandelia capensis Cape kurper DD".

cape-kurper.review: Checked by an independent skeptic; 14 corrections applied
review_points: No fetched or cached source puts Sandelia capensis in the Liesbeek at all. Wikipedia gives only its range (coastal rivers from the Coega to the Verlorevlei, the Cape Flats), and the government pages list only carp and sharptooth catfish for the Liesbeek. 'That is when anglers run into them most' is

None of the sources shows legal protection. It is IUCN Data Deficient (FishBase, 2017). Wikipedia lists no legal status, and the CapeNature and City release lists name yellowfish, sawfin and whitefish, not Cape kurper. 'Protected' states a legal status that has not been established.

The engine ranks species by these weights and shows the 'top species right now'. On a summer dusk the page would rate a declining indigenous fish as excellent fishing, which encourages people to target it, even though the tactics are written as avoidance advice. The dusk = 1.0 weight also rests on a
These stream temperatures have no source, yet they are written as fact to justify widening FishBase's 18-22 C. Only 18-22 C (Ref. 2060) is sourced.

This contradicts the profile itself: kurper eat small fish and were seen gathered at a dead trout (Poroderma), so flesh bait is exactly what attracts them. 'Sits tight and feeds little in winter' is unsourced. 40-60 g sinkers and 10 kg line for sharptooth catfish is heavy tackle, not light tackle.

Unsupported, as the profile admits. This is an ambush predator of small fish that reaches 20 cm SL (25 cm TL), and Botha's 19 cm fish took a woolly bugger. A 7 cm soft plastic is within the prey size of an adult kurper. Telling anglers that a lure 'rarely gets hit' gives false assurance.
This is specialist carp tackle, not the brief's 'light bait fishing with small hooks'. The 8 kg minimum has no source and is presented as a rule.
The fetched Wikipedia text supports only 'occasionally plays dead when caught by anglers'. The slipping claim was not found.
unverified: Whether it lives in the Liesbeek is unconfirmed. No fetched or cached source places Sandelia capensis there; only its historical range (Cape Flats) covers it. The page must not show it as verified at the Liesbeek until CapeNature or a survey confirms it.

Legal protected status is not established in the fetched sources (IUCN Data Deficient only; the CapeNature and City release lists don't name it). It is treated as never a target because the brief lists it as protected. If the engine sets legal.protected for it, the label 'may not be caught or kept' asserts a legal status the reviewer could not source.
Spawning months 10 to 1 and peak months 10 to 3 are estimates: the sources say only 'summer'.
Temperature min 11, ideal 16 to 23 and max 27 C are estimates, and so are the stream temperatures used to justify them. Only 18 to 22 C (FishBase Ref. 2060, aquarium-style) is sourced.
All light weights are estimates, now with dawn and dusk level. The only angling data point is one fish caught 'near the end of the day' (Botha), which the reviewer did not re-check.
Flow 0.2 and the trend, clarity and wind weights are estimates
The Mission pages (Botha's 19 cm fish on a woolly bugger; Flemming's 1-weight account) were not in the reviewer's cache and were not re-checked
Typical size of 8 to 15 cm is an estimate
Fin spines come from general anabantid anatomy and were not checked in a fetched source
The idea that a fish playing dead may come round and wriggle free is an estimate. Wikipedia supports only 'occasionally plays dead when caught by anglers'.
The spinning tactic (bigger lures away from cover reduce hits) is reasoned from its ambush habit, not from angling reports
The 3 to 5 kg line and 10 to 20 g sinker for the carp-bait and warm-pool tactics are light-tackle estimates

cape-stumpnose.name: Cape stumpnose
cape-stumpnose.season_note: Present all year in Zandvlei, where the Zandvlei Trust reports Cape stumpnose as common. Juveniles enter estuaries as tiny post-larvae (6 to 10 mm per ORI, unverified), even over a closed mouth on overwash. Wikipedia says they generally spend their first year there; ORI's figure of 12 to 23 months is unverified. They leave for the sea at about 14 cm SL (about 19 cm TL) and do not return (ORI, unverified). Spawning is at sea near estuary mouths, Jul to Feb in the SE Cape (Whitfield 1998 via ORI, unverified). Cape Town is near the cold western end of the range, so the warm months (Nov to Apr) should fish best; that peak is an estimate. Zandvlei's mouth is open through winter. In summer it is closed and opened for a few days around each full moon, so the tide-stage estuary tactics here are limited to May to Oct and the default bank tactic covers summer. With the mouth closed, fish the weed edges and banks early and late. Release every Cape stumpnose caught at Zandvlei (Zandvlei Trust: catch-and-release of indigenous fish is required by law). Van der Elst inferred a summer migration into Cape waters, but ORI says this is unsubstantiated.

temp.basis: estimate: endemic warm-temperate/subtropical sparid, mainly on the eastern South African coast (Wikipedia), with ORI/Mann 2013 giving a range from St Helena Bay to Maputo (ORI not verified by the reviewer). Juveniles survive Cape estuary winters. Larvae were reared at 23 to 25 C (SAIAB larvae page). KZN reports have stumpies biting at 18.5 C and in 27 C summer water. Blaber's 1973 lethal-limit paper (J Fish Biol 5:593) could not be opened.

cape-stumpnose.habitat: Zandvlei: the lower reaches near the mouth, on sand banks, submerged weed beds and channel drop-offs. The usual vlei casting spots are the channel off the yacht club and the bends below and after the footbridge; these come from leervis, elf and carp threads, not stumpnose reports. Juveniles move in small groups over weed and seagrass, which they use for food and cover. A KZN estuary guide found most fish within 20 m of the bank. Every Cape stumpnose caught at Zandvlei must be released. At sea, adults are an inshore species over sand and shallow reef in under 50 m. Along False Bay that means harbours (Kalk Bay, Gordon's Bay) and small river mouths such as the Sir Lowry's Pass River at Gordon's Bay. At the Lourens River mouth, fish only from the shore on the east (Strand / Gordon's Bay) side: the shore west of the mouth to the Eerste River mouth is the Helderberg MPA, a no-take zone. In Cape Town they are mainly a False Bay fish.
cape-stumpnose.diet: Adults eat small bivalves, shrimps and prawns, crabs, echinoderms, barnacles, bryozoans and polychaete worms. Juveniles graze weed and eelgrass (Zostera) but digest only the diatoms and small invertebrates on it; diatoms are about half of what they eat. They feed by day.
cape-stumpnose.typical_size: Zandvlei: mostly 10 to 20 cm juveniles and sub-adults, most under the 20 cm legal size, and all must be released there whatever their size. At sea, legal fish are 20 to 28 cm (about 180 to 350 g, from the ORI length-weight relationship). A big one is 35 to 40 cm and 0.9 to 1.3 kg; 40 cm is the recorded maximum length (Wikipedia). Adults seldom exceed 1 kg; the SA shore record is reportedly 2.4 kg (unverified).
cape-stumpnose.handling: Not protected, but regulated. You need a recreational fishing permit. At sea, and in estuaries without a stricter rule, the bag limit is 5 per person per day, minimum size 20 cm TL, with no closed season. It is a no-sale species (SASSI red, 'don't buy'). At Zandvlei (a nature reserve that needs a permit) the Zandvlei Trust says catch-and-release of indigenous species is required by law, with leervis as its example: release every Cape stumpnose there, of any size, and never use one as livebait. Do not fish the Helderberg MPA (the shore between the Eerste and Lourens river mouths), which is no-take. Use small hooks, strike early to avoid deep hooking, and unhook in the water with wet hands or a dehooker. An undersize fish may not be kept anywhere, so it cannot be used as livebait either. Sharp dorsal and anal spines; small incisor teeth. Do not confuse with white stumpnose: the Cape has a gold stripe from head to tail, and the two have different limits.

tactics.title: Prawn on the flooding banks
tactics.lure_or_bait: Live sand prawn or mud prawn, threaded whole (pump your own: 50 per day on a recreational permit). A piece of white mussel or a small bloodworm as a backup (check the current DFFE bait limits).
tactics.rig: #4 to #2 baitholder hook on a 40 cm snood of 0.30 mm mono. 1/8 to 1/2 oz ball sinker running above a small swivel. 7 ft light rod with 4 kg line.
tactics.retrieve: Lob it out, let it settle and keep the line just tight. Every minute or two, ease it a turn closer along the weed edge. Strike on the first firm knock.
tactics.depth: on the bottom, 0.5 to 1.5 m, on the bank just off the weed
tactics.stand: At Zandvlei only while the mouth is open (through winter, and a few days around summer full moons): the bank beside sand banks and weed beds near the mouth, e.g. the first bend after the footbridge or opposite the yacht club (general vlei spots, not stumpnose-specific). Cast no more than 20 m out. Release every stumpnose at Zandvlei.
tactics.why: Fish push onto banks they cannot reach at low water. A KZN estuary guide (Sealine, 2010, Richards Bay) found two hours before to two hours after high tide best for estuary fish, with most within 20 m of the bank; it does not name the stumpnose species, and the window is untested at Zandvlei.

tactics.title: Dropshot the channel drop-off
tactics.lure_or_bait: 1.5 to 2 inch scented shrimp or worm soft plastic (Gulp-type shrimp, natural, tan or pink)
tactics.rig: #6 to #4 dropshot hook tied 25 to 30 cm above a 1/8 to 1/4 oz dropshot weight. 3 kg fluorocarbon leader on 4 to 6 lb braid. Ultralight 1 to 7 g rod.
tactics.retrieve: Cast across the channel and drag the weight a few centimetres at a time down the slope. Shake the slack line so the plastic quivers in place, and pause for long spells.
tactics.depth: bottom of the channel edge, 1 to 2.5 m
tactics.stand: At Zandvlei only while the mouth is open: the outside of bends where the channel runs close to the bank, e.g. the channel off the yacht club (a general vlei spot, not stumpnose-specific). Cast across and work down the slope. Release every stumpnose at Zandvlei.
tactics.why: Inferred, not sourced, and a secondary option behind the bait tactics. Falling water drains the banks and should push food and fish back to the drop-off, and the fish eats small shrimps and worms. The only drop-off advice found is Fish The Fly's tip to strip a mantis-shrimp fly near drop-offs 'for Springer and Stumpnose', which names no species or region and says nothing about dropshot.

tactics.title: Swing a small prawn fly with the tide
tactics.lure_or_bait: Small prawn or mantis-shrimp pattern, about #8 to #10 (size is an estimate), tan, white or pink, with bead-chain eyes
tactics.rig: 9 ft 5 to 7 weight rod, floating or intermediate line, 9 ft leader to a 3 kg fluorocarbon tippet
tactics.retrieve: Cast across the current and let the tide swing the fly over the drop-off. Then strip back slowly in short 5 cm strips with pauses, near the bottom.
tactics.depth: just off the bottom, 0.5 to 1.5 m
tactics.stand: Where the tide runs along a weed edge or drop-off, only while the estuary mouth is open. Cast from the {upwind} bank so the wind helps the cast. Release every stumpnose at Zandvlei.
tactics.why: Sean Mills (Sealine, 2014) swung prawn flies on a floating line with the tide at Knysna and found they worked for moonies and stumpnose but 'did not work so well in other estuaries'. He did not say whether the stumpnose were Cape or white, Knysna is a big open lagoon unlike Zandvlei, and the method is untested in Cape Town vleis. Fish The Fly says to strip its mantis shrimp close to drop-offs for stumpnose (species not named).

tactics.title: Big sea: retreat to sheltered water
tactics.lure_or_bait: Sand prawn, mud prawn or bloodworm
tactics.rig: #2 baitholder hook on a 40 cm snood, 1 to 2 oz running sinker, 6 kg line on a 9 to 10 ft light rod
tactics.retrieve: Cast into the calm water and hold. Move the bait occasionally to find fish.
tactics.depth: bottom, 1.5 to 4 m
tactics.stand: Inside the harbour basin (Kalk Bay, Gordon's Bay) on the side sheltered from the swell, well back from any wall that waves wash over, or a sheltered river mouth (Sir Lowry's Pass River; the Lourens only from its east side, as the shore west of it is the Helderberg MPA). Never fish the outer wall, breakwater or open rocks in a big sea; if swell is reaching the wall, go to the estuary or go home.
tactics.why: Inference: adults are small inshore fish of sand and shallow reef that spawn near estuary mouths, so churned surf is poor for them and sheltered water is the only sensible option in a big sea.

tactics.title: Cold water: small bait, slow, midday
tactics.lure_or_bait: Half a sand prawn or a small piece of bloodworm
tactics.rig: #6 to #4 hook on a 40 cm snood, lightest ball sinker that holds (1/8 to 1/4 oz), 3 to 4 kg line on a 7 ft light rod
tactics.retrieve: Leave it still and watch the line for small taps
tactics.depth: deepest water near the mouth, 1.5 to 2.5 m
tactics.stand: In the estuary, the deepest water near an open mouth where sea water pushes in (release every stumpnose at Zandvlei); at sea, a sheltered harbour basin. Fish the warmest part of the day (late morning to mid-afternoon).
tactics.why: Inference: a warm-temperate fish at the cold end of its range here, so feeding should slow in cold water. Small, still baits and the warmest hours give the best chance.

tactics.title: Light running sinker with prawn
tactics.lure_or_bait: Sand prawn or mud prawn (pumped, 50 per day), white mussel or bloodworm (check the current DFFE bait limits)
tactics.rig: #4 to #2 baitholder hook, 40 cm snood, 1/8 to 1/2 oz running ball sinker, 4 kg line on a 7 ft light rod
tactics.retrieve: Cast close, keep the line just tight, and ease the bait along every minute or two
tactics.depth: on the bottom, 0.5 to 2 m
tactics.stand: Near sand banks, weed-bed edges and channel drop-offs close to the mouth, within 20 m of the bank; at Zandvlei this is the summer tactic when the mouth is closed, and every stumpnose there must be released. In the sea, in calm or small seas only: a harbour wall (Kalk Bay, Gordon's Bay) or a river mouth, with the Lourens fished only from its east side (west of it is the Helderberg MPA).
tactics.why: ORI reports it is caught mainly on light tackle by shore and estuary anglers (ORI not verified by the reviewer). Prawn on a light running sinker is the standard estuary bait rig in a KZN estuary guide (Sealine, 2010).

legal.bag_note: 5 per day. Counts toward the aggregate of 10.
legal.note: A and B agree. The gazette and the brochure both give 20 cm. The acts.co.za consolidation leaves the size cell blank (transcription gap).
legal.quote: Cape stumpnose | Rhabdosargus holubi | 20 cm | 5

cape-stumpnose.review: Checked by an independent skeptic; 21 corrections applied
review_points: The Zandvlei Trust's wording is 'Catch and release of indigenous species such as Leervis is required by law.' That covers indigenous species in general, with leervis given only as an example. Cape stumpnose is indigenous, so at Zandvlei it should be released whatever its size, and none may be kept o

The Lourens River mouth is the eastern boundary of the Helderberg MPA. It is a no-take zone from the Eerste mouth to the Lourens mouth, extending 500 m seaward. From the Lourens mouth to the Gordon's Bay eastern breakwater only shore angling is allowed. Sending anglers to 'the Lourens mouth' without

In the same thread the fish was identified as a WHITE stumpnose; only another member's fish 'looked like a cape stumpnose'. The white-mussel anecdote is evidence about white stumpnose, not Cape stumpnose. The tactic is also set for dusk and night, which contradicts the profile's own biology ('They f

The whole tactic rests on one passing mention of a single fish, on the Kromme in the Eastern Cape. Nothing in the source supports the dawn/dusk, calm, flat and clear conditions; they are invented. The slow retrieve was the poster's general method for grunter. The 'when' block has no water:['estuary'

Neither source mentions grubs, soft plastics, jigheads, lift-and-drop retrieves or how the fish behaves in bright sun. Wikipedia says only that it feeds by day on bivalves, crustaceans and Zostera epiphytes. Every detail of this tactic is inference, yet it is cited as if it were sourced.

Fish The Fly's line is about stripping a mantis-shrimp FLY near drop-offs for 'Springer and Stumpnose'. It names no species and no region and says nothing about dropshot rigs. The other source cited is a Zandvlei leervis and carp spot thread that never mentions stumpnose. Neither source supports dro

The quote leaves out Mills's caveat that the method 'did not work so well in other estuaries'. He does not say whether these were Cape or white stumpnose, and he gives no fly size. Knysna is a large tidal lagoon and does not stand in well for Zandvlei, whose mouth is usually closed in summer.

The quotes are accurate, but the author fishes in KZN (Richards Bay), where 'stumpnose' (silvers) are a different setting from the Cape. The Zandvlei spots come from a leervis, elf and carp thread. The tide-stage 'when' will also fire at Zandvlei in Nov to Apr, the profile's own peak months, when th
unverified: Temperature band (min 12, ideal 16 to 24, max 28 C) is an estimate; Blaber 1973 lethal limits could not be opened

Every condition weight (light, sea, tide, flow, range, trend, clarity, wind) is an estimate from biology (day feeder, shallow inshore, estuary-dependent) and general estuary-angling practice. Only the pushing/high-tide preference has an angling source, a KZN estuary guide that does not name the stumpnose species.
Peak months Nov to Apr for Cape Town are an estimate (warm-water species near the cold end of its range); no Cape catch-by-month data was found

ORI-credited biology could not be checked because the reviewer could not open the ORI PDF: juvenile entry size 6 to 10 mm, 12 to 23 month estuary residence (Wikipedia says generally the first year), leaving at 14 cm SL, Jul to Feb spawning (Whitfield 1998), the St Helena Bay range limit, and 'caught mainly on light tackle by shore and estuary anglers'
Bait limits other than sand/mud prawn (white mussel 50 per day, bloodworm 5 per day) and the daylight-only rule for white mussel are unchecked; the DFFE brochure could not be opened
The SA shore record of 2.4 kg has no source in the profile
The May to Oct month limit on tide-keyed estuary tactics is an approximation of when Zandvlei's mouth is open; it misses the short summer full-moon openings
Dropshot tactic has no Cape-specific source for Cape stumpnose; it is inferred from diet and from drop-off advice for a fly that names no species
Prawn-fly tactic comes from Knysna and an unnamed stumpnose species; fly rod weight 5 to 7 and fly sizes #8 to #10 are estimates
Zandvlei casting spots (yacht club channel, bends after the footbridge) come from threads about leervis, elf and carp and general vlei fishing, not stumpnose specifically
Cape stumpnose at Kalk Bay harbour rests on one fish that 'looked like a cape stumpnose'; most Kalk Bay 'stumpies' reported are white stumpnose
That Cape stumpnose are scarce on the cold Atlantic side of the Peninsula is an inference from range and water temperature
Weights in typical_size come from the ORI length-weight equation, not measured Cape fish

carp.name: Carp
aka: golden ghosts / sludge suckers (Mission fly-mag slang)
carp.season_note: An alien species that lives year-round in every listed water. The Western Cape Government's 'Fishing in the Western Cape' page (quoting CapeNature) lists carp as common in the middle and lower Eerste and Lourens, present in large numbers in the lower Liesbeek, and found in Rietvlei and Sandvlei/Zandvlei; a CapeNature quote there places carp, with smallmouth bass, in the Berg above Paarl. Sealine places carp at Door De Kraal Dam (Durbanville), but the City allows only limited, controlled fishing there from October to April, with permits. Other City dams have been under an angling moratorium since 2005, and Zeekoevlei is closed to fishing. For Western Cape carp on fly, Leonard Flemming (The Mission, 2015) says stillwaters only warm up from mid-October and the season usually ends after the first big cold fronts. He names no month; late April or May is an estimate. He also finds winter fly fishing generally not worth the effort. In winter carp are sluggish and sit deeper, but sunny spells between fronts bring fish into the shallows (Flemming, 'The Pancake Jol', June 2021, at a Swartland dam). Spawning was seen at Voelvlei in October 2019, and anglers said the fish still bite while spawning. Bait anglers catch carp all year, but slowly in the cold months.

temp.basis: Partly sourced. FishBase gives a tolerance of 3 to 35 C and a breeding range of 15 to 20 C. Flemming (Mission 2015) says Cape stillwaters warm from mid-October, that river carp move onto tail-outs and pool heads once the water reaches about 20 C, and that winter fish are sluggish. The feeding cut-offs (10 C min, 27 C ideal top, 32 C max) are estimates.

carp.habitat: Soft-bottomed, slow or still water (FishBase: lowland rivers and well-vegetated lakes, also brackish). In the vleis and dams they hold along reed and weed-bed edges, in shallow bays, on flooded grassy banks, in scum lines and at stream inlets. They feed in under 1 m of water on warm days and drop into deeper water in winter. In rivers (Berg above Paarl, lower Eerste, Lourens, Liesbeek) they use the deeper slow pools, pool heads and tail-outs, and feed under undercut banks and overhanging brush. Some feed in strong current about 10 m out. In estuarine vleis such as Zandvlei and Rietvlei they are thought to keep to the fresher, weedier water (an estimate). Zandvlei's mouth is often closed in summer, so tide makes little difference there then; the tide ratings apply only while the mouth is open.
carp.diet: Bottom invertebrates (midge larvae and bloodworm, nymphs including dragonfly nymphs, snails) plus plant material and seeds. They also take tadpoles in early summer and suck floating insects off the surface. Urban fish learn to eat bread. Flemming finds Western Cape carp warier than carp elsewhere in South Africa: they graze small invertebrates in the silt and are best taken on small black-and-red patterns. A crayfish fly landed near them sent them tailing off into deep water.
carp.typical_size: Usually 30 to 60 cm and 0.5 to 4 kg (an estimate from Cape reports). A Stellenbosch farm dam gave 25 to 35 cm fish, and Theewaterskloof fish are 'typically 30 to 40 cm'. Winter fish caught on fly between cold fronts are seldom over 3 kg (Flemming, Pancake Jol). Big fish run 6 to 10 kg: 7 kg at Theewaterskloof, a disputed 6 to 8 kg at Rietvlei, a reported 10 kg night fish at Zandvlei (another regular there never saw one over 6 kg), 26-inch (about 66 cm) Berg River fish, and a 21 lb (about 9.5 kg) carp Flemming landed on fly with a 6 wt (2020).
carp.handling: No teeth. The hard, serrated leading ray of the dorsal and anal fins can nick hands and fray line, and carp are very strong and tippet-shy. Use a net and keep fish off rocks. Carp are an invasive alien: Rietvlei's rules say exotic carp and barbel must be removed, not returned, and indigenous fish must be returned. Never move live carp between waters (CapeNature requires a permit to transport live fish). Public waters need a CapeNature freshwater angling licence. Rietvlei allows rod and reel only, 2 rods with up to 2 hooks each, line no stronger than 4.5 kg, and fishing only 07:30 to 17:00. Door De Kraal Dam allows limited, controlled fishing October to April only, with permits; other City dams are under an angling moratorium. Zeekoevlei is closed to fishing. Recreational fishing there was suspended from 28 Aug 2023, and later all fishing except organised competitions (GroundUp, Oct 2023; check current City notices). Zeekoevlei fish carried mercury and lead far above safe limits, so don't eat carp from it. As a precaution, treat carp from the Lotus River canal that feeds it the same way. The Berg River at Paarl has had stormwater and E. coli pollution, so wash your hands after handling fish. Bycatch: witvis (endangered) may be in the Berg after reported stockings, and Cape kurper live in the Lourens. At Zandvlei the Zandvlei Trust asks that indigenous fish be released. Never target witvis, Berg River redfin, Cape kurper or Cape galaxias. If one takes, release it unharmed: keep it in the water, unhook it quickly (a small or barbless hook helps) and let it swim off.

tactics.title: Midday sight-fishing to tailing carp
tactics.lure_or_bait: Small black fly: an unweighted Black Zulu variant with a red wool tail (#12 to #14) or a small girdle bug for cruising fish. For fish nosing the bottom, a #14 black tungsten-bead carp jig with black CDC and a red tail.
tactics.retrieve: No stripping. Land the fly 10 to 20 cm in front of a feeding fish's head and let it sink into its path. Lift when you see the mouth flare or the fish tip down onto it. Carp rarely move more than a metre to a fly. If one spooks, wait for a fresh feeding fish rather than recasting.
tactics.depth: Shallows under 1 m, fly on or just off the bottom
tactics.stand: Walk slowly along shallow bays, flooded grass and weed edges with the sun behind you. Stay back from the edge so your shadow and the rod's shadow stay off the water. When several fish feed around you, stand still and let them come to you.
tactics.rig: 6 wt rod, floating line, leader 2 m or shorter ending in about 70 cm of 3X fluorocarbon (nothing lighter than 3X), no strike indicator
tactics.why: Cape carp are wary and usually take small patterns. Seeing the fish is everything, and the best window is roughly 11:00 to 16:00 once the water has warmed. Fish become warier as the sun drops (Flemming).

tactics.title: Dip a jig fly on windless days
tactics.lure_or_bait: #14 black tungsten-bead carp jig (black CDC, black dubbing, fluorescent red tail) or a collar-hackled weighted Black Zulu on a #12 wet-fly hook
tactics.retrieve: No cast. Lower the fly in front of the feeding fish and let it touch bottom, then lift it less than 5 cm and drop it again, wiggling it in one spot. Keep a finger on the line and lift at the soft suck or any tightening.
tactics.depth: On the bottom, with the fly hanging about 1 m below the rod tip
tactics.stand: Tight against reed beds, undercut banks and overhanging brush (Berg River), or over fish tailing in dam shallows. Feel each footstep, keep off loose rock and stay off the bank lip; heavy tramping sends fish into deeper water.
tactics.rig: 10 ft rod, the top end for this page (Flemming dips with 10 ft and 14 ft rods). Run 3X fluorocarbon tippet down the length of the rod, with the jig fly hanging about 1 m below the tip and no fly line in the water.
tactics.why: Flemming calls dipping ideal for carp in shallow, windless conditions; Berg River carp often feed under undercut banks and brush where you can't cast.

tactics.title: Berg River: heavy fly sunk into the current
tactics.lure_or_bait: Heavily weighted Lalu Bug (tadpole imitation), red squirmy worm, or a Flexpole / dragonfly nymph; drop to a smaller fly if fish refuse
tactics.retrieve: Short roll cast upstream of the fish so the current carries the fly down and sinks it into the feeding lane. Strike on the mouth flare, not before. A plop near the fish spooks the whole group, so land it softly and well upstream.
tactics.depth: Bottom of pool heads, inlets and tail-outs; some fish feed about 10 m out in current and quite deep
tactics.stand: From sandbank edges and the far bank at the head of pools and shallow sandy inlets above Paarl (a CapeNature quote on westerncape.gov.za puts carp and smallmouth bass above Paarl). Pools rearrange after every winter flood, so walk and re-scout.
tactics.rig: 5 to 6 wt, 3X fluorocarbon; check for fraying after each fish
tactics.why: Mission writers call the Berg at Paarl 'arguably the coolest carp-on-fly venue south of the equator' and describe its carp as hyper-spooky and picky. Wind makes spotting fish hard, so go when it's sunny and still. Witvis (endangered) may be present after reported stockings; if one takes, keep it in the water and release it at once.

tactics.title: Ledger mielies on the windward bank
tactics.lure_or_bait: 2 to 3 sweetcorn (mielie) kernels, or a thumbnail of dough (cake flour and water with cake colouring and a pinch of curry powder); a mielie 'bomb' (groundbait packed round the sinker) with a flavour dip
tactics.retrieve: Cast short to the first drop-off or weed edge, tighten up and leave it. Loose-feed a handful of kernels. Strike when the line runs or the rod tip pulls steadily round.
tactics.depth: On the bottom, 1 to 3 m, close in
tactics.stand: {downwind}; wind pushes food and warmer surface water onto it. Fish the margin first, as long casts aren't needed.
tactics.rig: Running ball or bomb sinker of 10 to 30 g above a swivel, 30 to 50 cm trace, size 8 to 10 hook (kernels can go on a hair). Main line 0.25 to 0.30 mm, under 4.5 kg breaking strain wherever Rietvlei-style line limits apply. Sizes are general carp practice (estimate).
tactics.why: Flemming finds the windward bank usually the most productive. Western Cape bait anglers use corn and mielie bombs and say you don't need to cast deep.

tactics.title: Night and first-light bait for the big ones
tactics.lure_or_bait: Flavoured mielies (2 to 3 kernels) or a firm dough ball the size of a marble
tactics.retrieve: Bait a spot at dusk with a few handfuls of corn, cast to it and sit it out with the line fairly slack (bail open or a light drag) so a running fish doesn't feel resistance. Lift into a steady run.
tactics.depth: On the bottom, margins to 3 m
tactics.stand: Beside reed beds or a channel edge you baited in daylight, and only at waters where night or early-morning fishing is confirmed to be allowed. Not Rietvlei (fishing 07:30 to 17:00 only, so no night or true dawn sessions), not Zeekoevlei (closed), and not Door De Kraal outside its October to April permit rules. Night access at Zandvlei is unverified, so check before you go, and go with company.
tactics.rig: Running sinker 15 to 30 g, swivel, 40 cm trace, size 8 hook, 0.28 to 0.30 mm line (general carp practice, estimate)
tactics.why: A Sealine member reported a 10 kg Zandvlei carp caught at night. The same angler fishes TCP-dipped mielies, but the thread doesn't say which bait took that fish, and others there say fish over 6 kg are rare. Treat this as a big-fish option, and only where access is allowed.

tactics.title: Bread crust for surface cruisers
tactics.lure_or_bait: Thumbnail of bread crust or a pinch of flake folded over the hook, or a bread fly (white foam) on fly tackle
tactics.retrieve: Throw a few free crusts first. Once fish are slurping, flick the hookbait among them and leave it. Wait until the crust disappears and the line moves off before lifting.
tactics.depth: Surface
tactics.stand: The bank where floating scum and loose crusts collect, or under overhanging trees in shade; stay low and still. At Rietvlei fishing ends at 17:00, so there are no dusk sessions there.
tactics.rig: Size 8 to 10 hook free-lined, or a small controller float 1 m up the line; 0.22 to 0.25 mm line (hook and line sizes are estimates)
tactics.why: A Sealine regular suggests crust for sighted carp at Zandvlei; Mission's Bread Hatch shows bread-trained golf-course koi taking a bread fly. Hook and line sizes are general practice, not from a Cape source.

tactics.title: Winter warm spell: hunt pancakes and mud boils
tactics.lure_or_bait: Small black weighted CDC nymph on a carp hook (#12 to #14 is an estimate; the source gives no size)
tactics.retrieve: Find feeding fish by 'pancakes' (small circles of flat water in the wind ripple) and mud boils. Place the fly accurately just ahead, let it sink to the bottom and lift on any movement. Lead each hooked fish well away from the group (Flemming played them about 50 m off), then return for the next.
tactics.depth: Slightly deeper water just off the bank (Flemming); about 1 to 2 m is an estimate. Fly on the bottom.
tactics.stand: Get height first (a dam wall or high bank) to spot the feeding group, then tiptoe along the bank to the water's edge beside them
tactics.rig: 10 ft 6 in 3 wt rod (the top end of light tackle for this page), long 4X fluorocarbon tippet. 4X was Flemming's winter choice for spooky fish; use 3X otherwise.
tactics.why: Carp fishing slows right down in a Cape winter, but sunny spells between cold fronts bring carp into the shallows and the margins. It worked even in fairly murky water ('The Pancake Jol', June). The source venue is a Swartland dam, so treat this as a pattern to try on the page's waters.

tactics.title: Coloured water: scented bait at inflows
tactics.lure_or_bait: Strong-smelling dough or flavour-dipped mielies (2 to 3 kernels)
tactics.retrieve: Ledger it still near where fresh water and food wash in; loose-feed little and often. Strike on a steady pull.
tactics.depth: Bottom, 0.5 to 2 m
tactics.stand: Near stream mouths, stormwater inflows and the edges of the coloured plume, on whichever bank you can reach safely
tactics.rig: Running sinker 10 to 20 g, 30 to 40 cm trace, size 8 to 10 hook, 0.25 to 0.30 mm line (general carp practice, estimate)
tactics.why: Sight-fishing fails in dirty water, so scent does the work. Inlets are carp feeding spots in Cape dams (Flemming). Avoid worms where witvis, redfin or Cape kurper live, since they take worms readily; corn and dough are more carp-selective (estimate).

tactics.title: Float-fished mielies or dough in the margins
tactics.lure_or_bait: 2 sweetcorn (mielie) kernels or a pea-sized ball of dough or bread paste
tactics.retrieve: Set the float so the bait just touches the bottom. Loose-feed a few kernels every few minutes over the float. Strike when the float slides away, or when it lifts and lies flat.
tactics.depth: Bait just touching bottom, usually 0.5 to 2 m
tactics.stand: Margins beside reed beds, weed edges and overhanging trees on the open vleis. In rivers, the slow deep pools of the lower Eerste, Lourens and Liesbeek, and the Berg above Paarl.
tactics.rig: Small stick float or waggler, a couple of split shot, size 10 hook on 0.20 to 0.25 mm line (sizes are estimates). At Rietvlei: no more than 2 rods with 2 hooks each, line under 4.5 kg, 07:30 to 17:00 only.
tactics.why: A simple, low-cost general carp method (an estimate: no Cape source describes float-fishing for carp) that suits the vleis and slow river pools where carp are the main resident fish. The light float shows the shy bites Cape carp give. Only the Rietvlei rod, hook and line limits are sourced.

legal.bag_note: No bag or size limit (an alien species).
legal.release: Putting it straight back where you caught it is allowed where it already occurs, but not in national parks or nature reserves; never move live fish to another water. Rietvlei's rules say to remove every carp you catch.
