review_points: The quote comes from Grumpy's fishing report in Republikein, which covers the Namibian coast (Henties Bay, Solitude, Zeila Wreck). It is not about the Cape and should not support a Cape tactic or the sea weights. The Cape sources say the same thing in their own words, so the Namibian source is not n

Safety and scope. The only Cape source for 'the rougher the better' says in the same sentence 'please be very careful here as the waves can get pretty hectic onto the rocks'. As a headline it pushes rock anglers onto ledges in seas over 1.8 m, the conditions in which anglers drown on this coast. The

This is heavier than both the Cape sources and the page's light-tackle scope. baldrick uses a 7 ft graphite rod in normal conditions and a 10 ft rod only when the surf is bigger, and District Mail says galjoen can be fished 'fairly light'. Rod length and lead weight are not sourced to any Cape galjo

The handling text names only Oudekraal, and gets that zone slightly wrong: Oudekraal is the northern boundary of the Karbonkelberg no-take zone, which runs from Oudekraal to Hout Bay. Bakoven itself lies outside it. More importantly, it leaves out the Cape of Good Hope restricted (no-take) zone, whi

These posts describe galjoen caught or targeted during the closed season. In the Gifkommetjie case it was also apparently inside a no-take zone. They are fine as evidence that the fish are present, but the temperature basis and tactic notes should not rest on them, and nothing should present them as

This quote is in neither of the two cited threads I opened. Captain Sparrow in 76420 says only 'I like fishing from low to high tide, so I can check for those gullies while still lowish'. Thread 5869 never mentions a pushing tide. It may be in thread 30031, which the cache could not show because the

The direction of each weight has qualitative support (bigger seas help, clear and cold water with 'not much movement' is poor, high tide fishes well at Macassar). The numbers themselves are estimates, yet unlike the light, trend and wind weights they are not listed under unverified. No source at all

The minimum size is 35 cm, so by the profile's own source most Macassar fish are at or under the limit and must be released. The handling text does not say so, and the tactics panel could imply that a typical fish can be kept.
unverified: The water temperature band (min 11, ideal 13 to 17, max 20 C) is an estimate. The only figures found are the FishBase/AquaMaps modelled range for the whole species range and Cape anecdotes that cold water is poor.

The tide, sea and clarity weights are estimates with only directional support: bigger seas help (District Mail), clear and cold water with little movement is poor (Sealine 5869), high tide fishes well at Macassar (Jacita), and one angler fishes low to high (Sealine 76420). No source covers a dropping tide. sea.rough is set low on purpose for safety, not because the fish stop biting.
The 'rolling water, pushing tide' quote was not found in Sealine 76420 or 5869. It may be in thread 30031, which could not be checked, so it has been dropped.
The light weights are an estimate. No source covers day versus night feeding, and all reported sessions were in daylight (08:00, midday to 16:00, late afternoon).
The pressure-trend weights are an estimate with no source.
The wind-strength weights are an estimate, inferred from the north-westerly rough-sea anecdotes.
The springs and neaps weights rest on two 2010 Sealine anecdotes only ('full moon' and 'spring high produces the best'). Their month was not recorded, so they may be closed-season posts.

Rod lengths and sinker weights are general practice. Only baldrick's 7 ft rod (10 ft in a bigger surf) is sourced, and no Cape galjoen article gives lead weights. Hook sizes (1/0 to 2/0 short-shank, size 2 circle) and line classes beyond the 15 lb mentioned on Sealine are also general practice.

The water depths in the tactics (1 to 4 m) and the 10 to 20 m casting distances are estimates. The sources say only 'Short casts only' and 'not even 7m from the shoreline' (Sealine), and Wikipedia gives shallow depths of around 10 m near the shore.
The exact position of the Macassar ledges relative to the Eerste River mouth (the western edge of the Helderberg no-take MPA) was not checked. The profile tells anglers to stay west of the mouth.
No source was found for catching galjoen on lures, soft plastics or fly. Every tactic is bait fishing, and no lure or fly rule is given on purpose.
Spawn months are approximated from the closed season, which is set for spawning. Britannica extends spawning to March.
1 to 14 October is legal but is left out of present_months because the engine works in whole months.
Weight equivalents for typical sizes (3 to 4 kg for a 50 cm-plus fish) are estimates.

The ORI/SAAMBR galjoen fact sheet (Mann 2013), https://saambr.org.za/wp-content/uploads/2023/03/ORI-Fish-Fact-Sheet-Galjoen.pdf, could not be read. WebFetch returned an API request-body error, and curl failed a certificate revocation check that was not bypassed. Its depth, temperature and residency details are therefore not cross-checked.
The DSAE '1955 account' that old red bait was the standard galjoen bait came from a search summary only and was not opened.

geelbek.name: Geelbek (Cape salmon)
geelbek.season_note: A summer visitor to False Bay. Sub-adults of 50 to 85 cm live mainly in the south-western Cape (ORI). They feed there and on the Agulhas Bank in summer, coming inshore in summer and moving offshore in winter. Ski-Boat/Angler Publications gives the False Bay geelbek season as November to March, and several local guides give October to April. Adults migrate east to spawn over offshore reefs of 40 to 60 m off KwaZulu-Natal. Spawning runs from August to November and peaks in September and October (ORI, citing Griffiths and Hecht 1995). The eggs and larvae then drift back south-west on the Agulhas Current. The South African stock runs from Cape Point eastward, which is why the Atlantic side (Melkbos) gives very few. A Sealine poster reports big fish in mid-December and again in February and March from the Betty's Bay harbour breakwater, which he said may be closed to fishing. The Kleinmond beach gives the odd Cape salmon in November. A Fishingbooker guide says geelbek come inshore from May to July, and a Ski-Boat article ties them to the winter sardine run. Both match the KZN season, not Cape shore catches, so the engine should not use them for Cape spots. From the shore around Cape Town geelbek is an occasional catch, usually taken by kob or bottom anglers.

temp.basis: The ideal of 18 to 21 C is the 'geelbek water temperature' in the Angler Publications/Ski-Boat False Bay species guide (https://www.anglerpublications.co.za/?p=5014, opened 29 Oct 2026). It comes from boat fishing, so it is a False Bay figure but not a measured shore threshold. The min of 15 C and max of 24 C are estimates within FishBase/AquaMaps' global modelled preferred range of 14 to 26.5 C. Geelbek are rare on the upwelling-cooled Atlantic side.

geelbek.habitat: Mainly a deep-water, shoaling, benthopelagic fish of 15 to 200 m (FishBase), found over reefs, wrecks, pinnacles and sand next to reef. From the Cape shore it turns up only where deep water, reef and kelp come close in: ledges and rocky points with gullies, sand holes and clearings among kelp, quiet bays next to points, and river mouths such as the Steenbras mouth. It comes into the shallows at night to feed on baitfish. After strong wind it sits on the edge of the kelp or in the shallow clearings inside it (Ski-Boat). The main False Bay areas are Cape Point, Buffels Bay, Whittle Rock, Millers Point, Swartklip to Macassar, Strand, Gordon's Bay, the Steenbras River mouth, Pringle Bay and Rooi-Els, and most of these are boat marks. Shore records come from Boskloof near the Steenbras mouth, Kogel Bay (the odd fish), Rooi-Els, Macassar Beach after a south-easter, and further east from Maasbaai, Dawidskraal and the Kleinmond beach. The Betty's Bay fish came from the harbour breakwater, which may be closed to fishing. An old forum post reports Diaz Beach in a big south-westerly sea, but that shore is in or beside the Cape of Good Hope no-take zone, so it is not a spot to send anglers. The South African stock runs from Cape Point eastward (ORI), and Melkbos has only hearsay of occasional fish. No source names geelbek at Glencairn Quarry or from the Monwabisi shore. For Glencairn, the nearest evidence is the boat marks at Millers Point and Whittle Rock. For Monwabisi, it is the boat shoal from Swartklip to Macassar.
geelbek.diet: Piscivore that feeds mainly at night on small pelagic shoaling fish: pilchard (sardine), anchovy, Cape horse mackerel (maasbanker) and mackerel, plus chokka (squid). Juveniles start on mysids, then switch to anchovy and pilchard. Sub-adults in the south-western Cape eat mainly anchovy.
geelbek.typical_size: Mostly sub-adults of about 60 to 85 cm (roughly 3 to 6 kg). ORI says sub-adults of 50 to 85 cm live mainly in the south-western Cape, and the legal minimum is 60 cm. Half are mature only at about 90 cm FL (ORI) or 95 cm TL (Boyd 2018). A big shore fish is over 95 cm and roughly 8 to 10 kg. The South African angling record is 14.9 kg (SADSAA, via ORI), and the published maximum is 130 cm and 25 kg (FishBase).
geelbek.handling: Recreational limits are 2 fish per person per day at a minimum of 60 cm TL, with no closed season, and you need a recreational fishing permit. The stock has collapsed. ORI (2013) puts spawner biomass per recruit at about 7%, and Boyd (2018) estimates about 10% of pristine spawner biomass. WWF-SASSI lists line-caught geelbek as orange, and IUCN lists the species as Near Threatened. Half are mature only at 90 to 95 cm, so most shore fish are juveniles; release anything under about 95 cm if you can. The mouth is soft and hooks pull out if you horse the fish, so play it gently. If you are releasing it, land it by hand or with a net on a wave, not with a gaff. Keep it in the water, support the belly and revive it head into the current. It has no dangerous spines or teeth. Where you can fish: Glencairn Quarry is in the Table Mountain National Park MPA's controlled area, where fishing needs a valid permit, and the Boulders and Castle Rock (Miller's Point to Partridge Point) no-take zones are off limits. At Macassar, fish only west of the Eerste River mouth, because the Helderberg MPA no-take zone runs from the Eerste to the Lourens River mouth. Diaz Beach and the Atlantic shore of the Cape Point reserve are in or beside the Cape of Good Hope no-take zone (Scarborough to Hoek van die Bobbejaan); check the MPA map and never fish inside it.

tactics.title: Night bait in the kelp holes
tactics.lure_or_bait: Fresh sardine (pilchard) half or fillet, or a 10 cm chokka strip. A sardine-and-chokka cocktail stays on the hook better when you cast. Use a fresh maasbanker fillet if you jigged some at dusk.
tactics.rig: 4/0 to 5/0 circle hook on 60 to 80 cm of 0.50 to 0.60 mm mono trace. Running sinker of 2 to 3 oz (56 to 85 g) on a slider, or a small grapnel of up to 3 oz over foul ground. Mainline of 0.35 to 0.40 mm mono or 20 to 30 lb braid, on a 9 to 10 ft rod. These sizes are estimates scaled down from published boat rigs (8/0 to 10/0 hooks), and 3 oz is the top end of light tackle.
tactics.retrieve: Cast to the edge of a sand hole or gully between kelp, let the bait settle and keep the line just tight. The bite is fast and aggressive: wind steadily so the circle hook sets itself, and do not strike hard. Play the fish gently, because the soft mouth tears.
tactics.depth: On the bottom, in 3 to 10 m of water at the foot of the ledge or in sand holes beside reef
tactics.stand: A ledge or point with deep water, kelp and sand holes close in. Shore spots with geelbek records within reach are Boskloof beside the Steenbras mouth, Kogel Bay (the odd fish) and the Rooi-Els rocks. Never fish alone after dark.
tactics.why: Geelbek are mainly nocturnal and come into the shallows at night to feed on baitfish. Overberg and False Bay shore reports put them in the evening or at night, on sardine, mackerel and chokka.

tactics.title: Slow-rolled paddle-tail at dusk
tactics.lure_or_bait: 5 to 6 inch (125 to 150 mm) paddle-tail on a 3/4 to 1 oz (21 to 28 g) jighead with a 4/0 to 5/0 hook. Rig it weedless over kelp.
tactics.colour: White, pearl or sardine (blue back, silver belly) in clear water. Chartreuse, pink-and-white or glow in coloured water or once the light has gone.
tactics.rig: 20 to 30 lb braid with 1 to 1.5 m of 0.50 mm (about 40 lb) fluorocarbon leader. The sizes are estimates.
tactics.retrieve: Count the lure to the bottom, then slow-roll it a metre or so above the bottom, just fast enough to keep the tail kicking, with an occasional lift and drop. If in doubt, slow down. The fish hit hard, so keep the drag moderate.
tactics.depth: Lower half of the water column, close to the bottom along the reef edges
tactics.stand: A rock point or ledge where you can cast along the edge of the reef or kelp into deeper sand. Work the down-current side of the point.
tactics.why: No Cape source records a shore geelbek on a soft plastic, so this tactic is extrapolated. Rock-and-surf anglers on the Strand reefs work paddle-tails for kob (Cole). Geelbek hunt baitfish over the same reefs in low light, and Mission Fly calls the eastern False Bay reefs traditionally known for geelbek. Jacita recommends paddle-tails around reefs and gullies.

tactics.title: Brown water after the south-easter
tactics.lure_or_bait: A chokka strip and sardine fillet cocktail, or a fresh elf or maasbanker fillet. In brown water, scent counts for more than looks.
tactics.rig: 4/0 to 5/0 circle hook on 0.50 to 0.60 mm trace, with a running sinker of 2 to 3 oz (56 to 85 g). The sizes are estimates, and 3 oz is the top end of light tackle.
tactics.retrieve: Cast into the gutters and along the line where brown water meets cleaner water. Leave the bait on the bottom, and check and rebait every 15 to 20 minutes.
tactics.depth: On the bottom of the gutters and holes off the beach
tactics.stand: Macassar Beach after a south-easter, on the stretch west of the Eerste River mouth: fish the gutters where brown water meets cleaner water. Stay west of the river mouth, because the shore from the Eerste to the Lourens River mouth is the Helderberg MPA no-take zone.
tactics.why: South-easterly winds push milky brown 'kob water' inshore along northern False Bay (Cole). Seaside Cottages calls Macassar Beach, near the estuary mouth, a hot summer spot for kob and geelbek after south-easterly winds. Boat kob anglers in the same water catch geelbek incidentally (Cole), and Cape fly writers prefer murky water to clear water for these fish.

tactics.title: Late-evening fly in a kelp gully
tactics.lure_or_bait: A large baitfish streamer of 10 to 15 cm on a 3/0 to 4/0 hook, such as a DMA or a big clouser. This is an estimate: no published geelbek catch names a fly, and Botes uses the DMA for kob and garrick.
tactics.colour: A dark silhouette (black or olive) at night; white or chartreuse at dusk
tactics.rig: Estimate: a 9 to 10 weight rod, intermediate or fast-sinking line, and 1.5 to 2 m of 0.45 to 0.50 mm fluorocarbon leader. Bring a stripping basket, as Eagleton used.
tactics.retrieve: Estimate: let the fly sink, then make long, steady strips with short pauses. Play the fish off the line rather than the reel, as Eagleton did, and do not bully it, because the soft mouth tears.
tactics.depth: Below the surface, from mid-water down to near the bottom of the gully
tactics.stand: A point beside a gully or channel between kelp beds, casting across it. Eagleton's fish came from a gully at dead low tide, after the wind had dropped.
tactics.why: Eagleton took a geelbek on fly from a gully in the late evening at dead low tide, after the wind had dropped (The Mission). He has also posted photos of two geelbek caught on fly at night on the West Coast, with no conditions given. Both are West Coast fish from outside this area, so treat them only as a pointer.

tactics.title: After the blow: unweighted drift bait into the kelp clearings
tactics.lure_or_bait: A sardine fillet or a chokka strip, or the two together
tactics.rig: 4/0 to 5/0 circle hook on 60 to 80 cm of 0.50 mm trace, with no sinker or a single split shot. 20 to 30 lb braid or 0.35 mm mono, on a 9 to 10 ft rod. The hook and line sizes are estimates.
tactics.retrieve: Lob the bait up-current of a clearing in the kelp and let it drift and sink naturally into the clearing or along its edge, paying out line so it does not drag. Stay in touch with the bait and wind steadily into the bite instead of striking.
tactics.depth: Sinking slowly to the bottom of shallow clearings in the kelp
tactics.stand: A rock ledge or point overlooking kelp with open clearings, in the day or two after a strong blow once the sea has dropped. Fish only from ledges the waves are not reaching, and leave if they start to.
tactics.why: Ski-Boat's False Bay guide says that after strong wind geelbek sit just on the edge of the kelp or in the shallow clearings inside it, and are fished on a drift line with no sinker. Sealine posters also report geelbek moving close inshore with strong wind. The guide is written for boats, so this shore version is adapted from it.

tactics.title: Dusk into dark: bait off a deep ledge
tactics.lure_or_bait: Fresh sardine fillet or chokka strip, or the two together
tactics.rig: 4/0 to 5/0 circle hook on 60 to 80 cm of 0.50 to 0.60 mm trace, with a running sinker of 2 to 3 oz (56 to 85 g), on a 9 to 10 ft rod. The sizes are estimates, and 3 oz is the top end of light tackle. In calm water after a blow, leave the sinker off and drift the bait instead.
tactics.retrieve: Cast to the sand beside the reef or kelp, leave the bait on the bottom on a just-tight line, and wind steadily into the bite instead of striking. Play the fish gently.
tactics.depth: On the bottom, at the foot of the ledge or in a gully
tactics.stand: A rocky ledge or point with deep water close in and kelp and sand holes nearby, such as Boskloof by the Steenbras mouth, Kogel Bay or the Rooi-Els rocks. Fish from last light into the first hours of dark, and never alone.
tactics.why: Geelbek are mainly nocturnal and feed on baitfish over structure. From the Cape shore they are usually an incidental catch on fish or chokka bait in the evening and at night.

legal.bag_note: 2 per day. Counts toward the aggregate of 10.

The DMA comes from Botes (?p=62491), who calls it his fly of choice for kob and garrick, not for geelbek. The rod, line and leader specifications are unsourced estimates presented a

Two sources are conflated. In Cole (?p=4082) the incidental geelbek were caught by anchored BOAT kob anglers. The Strand-reef paddle-tail line is only about shore kob anglers, and no source shows a geelbek on a paddle-tail from the Cape shore. The Ski-Boat first-light and late-afternoon advice (Beuk

The profile's own unverified list says no source names geelbek at Glencairn Quarry (the quarry thread lists roman, hottentot and yellowtail only) or from the Monwabisi shore, and that Melkbos rests on one hearsay post. The stand text still sends anglers to all three at night as if they were geelbek

The tidal-pool wall in the source (Cole ?p=4082) is at Strandfontein Pavilion, where BOATS anchor behind it. The profile turned it into a shore stand at Monwabisi. Cole does not mention Monwabisi or Macassar. The geelbek shore evidence for this stretch is Seaside Cottages: Macassar Beach near the es

This contradicts the profile's own best source and is heavy, risky tackle. Angler Publications ?p=5014 says that AFTER strong wind geelbek sit 'just on the edge or in the shallow little clearings' of the kelp and are fished on 'a drift line with no sinker', which is a genuinely light-tackle method.
unverified: Temperature: the ideal of 18 to 21 C is a boat-fishing figure from the Ski-Boat False Bay guide, not a measured shore threshold. The min of 15 C and max of 24 C are estimates within FishBase's global modelled range of 14 to 26.5 C.

The dawn and daytime light weights are estimates. Night and dusk are well supported. day_bright was raised to 0.25 because Beukes says geelbek are also regularly caught by day. No Cape source supports dawn specifically: the Ski-Boat first-light advice was a Covid-curfew workaround.
Tide weights are estimates. The only geelbek-specific tide is one fly catch at dead low tide; the other tide advice found is generic or about kob.
Spring versus neap weights are estimates; no source addresses them.
Pressure-trend weights are estimates, inferred from the strong-wind and big-sea reports and from south-easter (ridging high) brown water.

Wind and sea weights are moderate-confidence estimates resting on a few anecdotes. Sea.rough was cut to 0.4 for shore safety, and the Ski-Boat guide puts the fish in the kelp clearings after strong wind rather than during it.
flow (0.5) is an estimate.
Light-tackle hook, jighead, leader and sinker sizes are extrapolated from published boat rigs (8/0 to 10/0 hooks, 40 to 60 kg traces), and sinkers are capped at 3 oz.
No Cape source records a shore geelbek on a soft plastic; the paddle-tail tactic is extrapolated from Strand-reef kob paddle-tailing.
The fly tactic's fly, rod, line, leader and retrieve are estimates. The only fly catch with stated conditions (Eagleton's gully fish) is from the West Coast, outside the 1-hour area.
The unweighted drift-line tactic adapts a method from a boat-oriented False Bay guide to the shore.
The 8 to 10 kg weight for a big shore fish of over 95 cm is a length-based estimate.
No source names geelbek at Glencairn Quarry; the nearest geelbek marks are Millers Point and Whittle Rock, both boat marks.
No source names geelbek caught from the shore at Monwabisi; the nearest evidence is the boat shoal from Swartklip to Macassar.
Melkbos geelbek rests on one forum post repeating hearsay ('heard of occasional ... geelbek towards Melkbos').
The exact position of Diaz Beach relative to the Cape of Good Hope no-take boundary was not checked. Treat it as closed.
Fishingbooker's May to July inshore claim and Beukes's winter sardine-run remark conflict with every Cape source (October to April) and were not used.

gurnard.name: Gurnard
gurnard.season_note: Present all year. No Cape Town shore source shows a peak season, so none is set and the temperature weight carries the season. The only shore report with a water temperature (St Francis, Eastern Cape, May 2010) had steady bites at 14°C, and those anglers said gurnard like very cold, clean water. On the Atlantic side of the Peninsula the coldest water comes with summer south-east upwelling, so cold, clean spells there may suit them, but that is an estimate. Spawns November to January and March to April, with peaks in January and April.

temp.basis: Estimate. One sourced data point: St Francis (Eastern Cape) shore anglers, May 2010, report steady bites at 14°C and say gurnard like 'very cold, clean water'. The species ranges from Namibia to Mozambique on bottoms 10 to 390 m deep. All band edges are estimates.

gurnard.habitat: A bottom fish of sand and mud, usually in 10 m of water or deeper. It perches on its three free pectoral-fin 'finger' rays. Most are caught offshore. Shore fish come where deep, clean sand is within casting range, near drop-offs or beside structure. The shore catches in the sources are all outside Cape Town: the St Francis platform, St Helena Bay and the Hermanus harbour wall. One Sealine thread mentions the Cape Town harbour breakwater as a past mark (not re-checked). Hout Bay harbour is unconfirmed: one 2011 forum line has an angler 'mostly catching gurnard' at Kalk Bay, Hermanus and Hout Bay, but it does not say the fish came from shore.
gurnard.diet: Mainly crustaceans (crabs, prawns), cephalopods (chokka) and small fish.
gurnard.typical_size: Shore fish in the reports average 0.5 to 1.5 kg (roughly 30 to 45 cm). A big one is 60 to 70 cm and 3 to 4 kg (the species maximum is 75 cm). Females mature at about 35 cm and 4 years, males at about 37 cm and 5 years.
gurnard.handling: Bony head with sharp spines on the gill covers and the first dorsal fin, and tough, slimy skin. Grip it across the back with a cloth. No species-specific recreational bag or size limit was found, so the general limit for unlisted species probably applies (check DFFE). A recreational angling permit is required. Fish under about 35 cm are immature, so release them. If you try Hout Bay (unconfirmed for shore gurnard), it lies in the Table Mountain National Park MPA and the Karbonkelberg restricted (no-take) zone runs from Oudekraal to Hout Bay, so fish only from inside the harbour.

tactics.title: Running sinker on the sand
tactics.lure_or_bait: Chokka strip, or a chokka and pilchard 'mixed grill', about thumb-sized
tactics.rig: Light rod up to 10 ft. Running trace, 1/0 to 2/0 hook, 40 to 60 g sinker and about 0.35 mm (12 to 15 lb) line. The sinker and line sizes are estimates.
tactics.retrieve: Cast onto clean sand and leave it still. Every few minutes, inch it back half a metre to cover ground.
tactics.depth: On the bottom
tactics.stand: A harbour wall or platform with deep (about 10 m), clean sand within a light-tackle cast. Cast onto the sand and along any channel edge, clear of moored boats. This stand is an estimate, and no source confirms shore gurnard at Hout Bay harbour.
tactics.why: Shore anglers who target gurnard (St Francis, St Helena Bay, Hermanus) use a running trace with 1/0 or 2/0 hooks and a chokka and pilchard 'mixed grill'. Their catches came on long surf casts of about 100 m, with 0.57 mm line mentioned. That is heavy surf gear, beyond light tackle, so this only works where deep sand comes close in.

tactics.title: Afternoon bait for the bigger fish
tactics.lure_or_bait: Fresh chokka head or tentacles with a pilchard fillet
tactics.rig: Light rod up to 10 ft. Running trace, 2/0 hook, 40 to 60 g sinker (sizes are estimates).
tactics.retrieve: Static, with an occasional slow drag
tactics.depth: On the bottom
tactics.stand: The deepest sand within reach from a harbour wall or platform (estimate)
tactics.why: On the St Francis platform in May, fish bit on and off all day, but the bigger ones came 'after 3', about 2.5 hours before sunset. That is daylight, not dusk. The engine has no afternoon state, so this tactic is gated on daylight.

tactics.title: Soft plastic hopped on the sand
tactics.lure_or_bait: 3 to 4 inch curly-tail grub or shrimp-profile soft plastic, natural or pink, on a 10 to 14 g jighead (sizes and colours are estimates)
tactics.rig: Light spinning rod, 10 to 15 lb braid, 15 to 20 lb fluorocarbon leader
tactics.retrieve: Bump and drag it along the sand with short hops and long pauses. Lift it off the bottom now and then.
tactics.depth: On the bottom
tactics.stand: A harbour wall or platform, fanning casts over the sand beside any channel (estimate)
tactics.why: Shore anglers report gurnard taken 'with plastic' and on drop shot. A fly angler's gurnard took a sparse Clouser on a slow, jerky retrieve, though that fish came from a boat. Lure sizes and colours are estimates.

tactics.title: Dropshot on the sand edge
tactics.lure_or_bait: 3 inch shad or shrimp soft plastic, or a small chokka strip
tactics.rig: Dropshot: #1 to 1/0 hook 30 to 40 cm above a 20 to 30 g weight, 15 lb fluorocarbon. All sizes are estimates.
tactics.retrieve: Hold it on the bottom with small twitches, then drag it a metre and pause again
tactics.depth: 30 to 40 cm off the bottom
tactics.stand: A harbour wall or platform over deep sand, dropping near the foot of the wall or making a short cast onto the sand (estimate)
tactics.why: Shore anglers who target gurnard name drop shot and plastics. The source gives no rig sizes.

tactics.title: Fly: weighted crab pattern on the sand
tactics.lure_or_bait: Weighted crab or crustacean pattern, about #2 to 1/0. Second choice: a sparse Clouser Minnow.
tactics.rig: 5 to 9 weight rod, intermediate line from shore, tippet 15 lb or lighter
tactics.retrieve: Let the crab sink to the sand and crawl it back with short, slow strips. A Clouser is fished with a slow, jerky retrieve and can be worked a few metres above the bottom.
tactics.depth: On the bottom for the crab. Bottom to mid-water for the Clouser.
tactics.stand: A sandy beach or harbour wall with deep sand in fly range and a clear backcast (estimate)
tactics.why: The Mission recommends a crustacean imitation or Clouser on an intermediate line from shore, over sand in deepish water near drop-offs or structure. The shore fly fish it reports came off a West Coast beach on crab patterns. The sparse Clouser fish came from a boat in 8 m of water, about 4 m down.

tactics.title: Coloured water: scent baits
tactics.lure_or_bait: Pilchard fillet with a chokka strip, for a strong scent trail
tactics.rig: Light rod up to 10 ft. Running trace, 2/0 hook, 50 to 60 g sinker (estimate).
tactics.retrieve: Static, so the scent trail builds
tactics.depth: On the bottom
tactics.stand: The sheltered side of a harbour wall, away from breaking water. Do not fish exposed rocks when the sea is rough.
tactics.why: Estimate: scent baits should out-fish lures in coloured water. No source ties gurnard to water clarity. The bait itself (chokka and pilchard) is what shore gurnard anglers use.

legal.bag_note: Default of 10 per day for unlisted species. Counts toward the aggregate of 10. This is not a species-specific figure.
legal.note: Reconciled: A and B agree on the default 10 with no size limit. I checked the full R.959 Annexure 7 lists myself: no gurnard and no Triglidae entry. Confidence is medium because the figure comes from an absence, with the same reg 22(6) caveat as katonkel.
legal.quote: '(7) Species not mentioned in either of these lists have a bag limit of ten provided that sharks, rays, skates or chimaeras (Class Chondrichthyes) have a bag limit of one and rockcods (Family Serranidae) have a bag limit of five.'

gurnard.review: Checked by an independent skeptic; 22 corrections applied
review_points: No Cape Town shore source supports it. The basis is one St Francis shore report from May (Eastern Cape) and Knysna offshore boat fishing at 70 to 80 m. On the Atlantic side of the Peninsula the coldest water comes with summer south-east upwelling, so 'cold water means winter' contradicts the profile
In May at St Francis, 3 pm is about 2.5 hours before sunset, so it is day, not dusk. The source does not support a dusk peak, and the tactic is gated on the wrong light state.

The only source is one reader comment. 'Blakes Beach' is not identified as a Cape Town location, the fish came while catching maasbanker, and no lights are mentioned. 'Under the harbour lights' is invented, and a 0.7 night weight from one anecdote is presented as if it had backing.

The thread never mentions dirty or coloured water. The 'only took on the pike' report (St Helena Bay) is about bait choice in a session of unstated clarity, so the link to dirty water is fabricated. Glossing 'pike' as cut fish bait is also unverified.

The sourced shore method is surf tackle: casts of 'around 100m', with 0.57 mm line mentioned. The source gives no sinker sizes. Presenting it as a 40 to 60 g, 0.35 mm light-tackle method, and putting it on the Hout Bay wall, is unsupported. No source places gurnard ground within light-tackle range o
Neither Wikipedia nor the Mission wish-list article says this; the wish-list fetch explicitly lists thermocline and zooplankton as not covered. No cited source supports it.

The sparse Clouser fish came from a boat in 8 m of water, retrieved about 4 m deep (mid-water, not along the sand). The shore fly catch in the same article was on crab patterns from a West Coast beach. The harbour-wall stand is not sourced.
The harbour thread does not mention gurnard at all. The search hit is one passing 2011 line that does not say the fish were caught from shore. Neither supports a Hout Bay shore gurnard spot.
unverified: temp band 9/11-16/20: one sourced data point from St Francis (good bites at 14°C, 'likes very cold, clean water'); the band edges are estimates
no peak months are set: no Cape Town shore source shows a season; the idea that summer upwelling suits them on the Atlantic side is an estimate

all light weights are estimates; the only light evidence is bigger fish 'after 3' in daylight (St Francis) and one reader's night fly catch from a jetty at an unlocated 'Blakes Beach' (The Mission comment, 2017)
all sea, tide, range, trend, wind and flow weights are estimates
clarity: 'cold, clean water' is sourced; the coloured-water weight of 0.55 and the scent-bait tactic are estimates
sinker weights, line diameters, soft plastic and jighead sizes, and the dropshot rig details are estimates; the sources name dropshot and plastics but give no sizes
the sourced shore catches used long surf casts (about 100 m, 0.57 mm line); success on light tackle depends on deep sand close in and is unconfirmed
no source confirms shore-caught gurnard at Hout Bay harbour or any other mark within an hour of Cape Town; all tactic stands are estimates
the Cape Town breakwater thread, the WWF-SASSI rating and the FishBase summary were not re-checked by the reviewer
no species-specific recreational bag or size limit was found; the general limit for unlisted species is assumed
typical shore size 30 to 45 cm is converted from the reported 0.5 to 1.5 kg average (St Francis, St Helena Bay, Hermanus)

harders.name: Harders (mullet)
harders.latin: Chelon richardsonii (formerly Liza richardsonii); also Mugil cephalus (flathead mullet)
harders.season_note: Present all year around Cape Town: in harbours (Hout Bay), tidal pools (Monwabisi), along the Blouberg-Melkbos beaches and rocks, and as the most abundant fish in Rietvlei and a resident of Zandvlei and Milnerton Lagoon/Diep River. ORI (Lamberth, in Mann 2013) says harders live in the surf zone most of the year but form large shoals in autumn and spring before moving. The peak months here (March to May and September to December) are an estimate based on that note, because no Cape catch-by-month data was found. Harders spawn in spring and summer (September to March, with early and late summer peaks) in the nearshore surf zone of the Western Cape (ORI). Flathead mullet spawn at a different time: May to November, near estuary mouths (ORI, Whitfield). Zandvlei's mouth is often closed in summer, and Milnerton Lagoon's water quality swings after sewage spills and rain. Harders are WWF-SASSI Red because the stock west of Cape Point is overfished.

temp.basis: Estimate. The band is set low so that normal Atlantic-side upwelling (about 10 to 13 C at Blouberg and Melkbos) is not rated cold. ORI (Lamberth, in Mann 2013) says C. richardsonii makes up 99% of mullet biomass on the cool-temperate west coast and lives in the surf zone most of the year. Kruger (The Mission, 2014) says southern mullet prefer cooler, temperate water but gives no figures. FishBase/AquaMaps models a preferred range of 14.8 to 27 C for C. richardsonii and lists M. cephalus at 8 to 24 C; neither was re-checked. No measured feeding thresholds were found.

harders.habitat: Dense shoals in the top 0 to 3 m. ORI says southern mullet live in the surf zone most of the year. On beaches they sit just behind the shore break over sand, sometimes in a few cm of water on a pushing tide (Blouberg, Melkbos, Monwabisi). They also hold along rocky points and gullies, in harbours and on slipways (Hout Bay harbour, Kleinbaai), and in tidal pools. In estuaries and vleis they gather at mouth channels, bridges and weed-bed edges (Zandvlei near the footbridge and mouth, the Marina da Gama channels, the Milnerton Lagoon wooden bridge, the Rietvlei angling section). Estuaries are their nursery areas. Flathead mullet tolerate fresh water and push far up vleis and rivers; a southern mullet was reported far up the Diep River in 2026. When food is drifting they feed at the surface along scum and foam lines, facing into the current.
harders.diet: Grazers. They eat diatoms, micro-algae and detritus, swallow fine sand grains as grit for a gizzard-like crop, and take some planktonic crustaceans. Flathead mullet also eat foraminifera and plant debris. They feed on the small organisms that onshore winds and pushing tides pile into scum lines. Anglers catch them on bread and tiny scraps of sardine fed into a chum trail, or on small flies, not on spinners.
harders.typical_size: From the shore, harders are usually 20 to 30 cm (about 100 to 300 g). A big one is 38 to 40 cm (about 0.6 to 0.7 kg). The largest recorded is 45 cm TL and 1.1 kg, a Saldanha fish (ORI, Mann 2013). Kruger (The Mission) says most mullet weigh under a pound (about 0.5 kg) and calls 0.5 to 1 kg a good fish. Flathead mullet in Zandvlei and Rietvlei are estimated at 35 to 50 cm, with a big one 60 cm or more at 2 to 3 kg. ORI gives 44 to 48 cm TL as their size at maturity (KwaZulu-Natal data) and says they are seldom caught on line.
harders.handling: No spines or teeth. The mouth is soft but the lips are tough, so play fish gently on light line and use a landing net for bigger fish. Wet your hands and unhook in the water when releasing, because they shed scales and slime easily. Permits: harders are a marine and estuarine fish, so fishing for them from the sea, a harbour, a tidal pool or an estuary (including Milnerton Lagoon) needs a DFFE recreational permit endorsed for angling. Zandvlei (Sandvlei) and Rietvlei also need a CapeNature angling licence; carry both at Zandvlei and confirm with the reserve. Limits: 50 mullet per person per day, all species combined (Family Mugilidae), with no minimum size and no closed season (R1111 Annexure 7, DFFE brochure Table 1, ORI). Harders are WWF-SASSI Red (overfished west of Cape Point), so keep only a few from the sea for the pan or for bait and release the rest. At Rietvlei all indigenous fish, harders included, must be released; only carp and barbel may be removed. At Zandvlei the Zandvlei Trust asks that indigenous fish be released. Rietvlei rules: rod and reel only, 2 rods with 2 hooks each, line no stronger than 4.5 kg, fishing 07:30 to 17:00 only, in the marked angling section. Cast-netting needs a DFFE recreational permit endorsed for cast-netting, and no netting is allowed between sunset and sunrise. The DFFE brochure gives conflicting net limits (6 m diameter in reg 5; 4 m diameter, 2 m length and 13 mm mesh in the Table 1 note), so check with DFFE before netting. Before cast-netting at Strand or Gordon's Bay, check R1111 reg 10(f)(v), which defines a closed area from the Lourens River to the Gordon's Bay eastern breakwater. The Helderberg MPA, between the Eerste and Lourens river mouths, is no-take. Milnerton Lagoon and the Diep River have a history of sewage spills and high E. coli, so do not eat fish from there after rain or a spill. At Hout Bay, fish inside the harbour. The coast from the Sentinel north to Oudekraal (the Karbonkelberg restricted zone) is no-take.

tactics.title: Bread flake under a float in the harbour
tactics.lure_or_bait: A thumbnail-size pinch of fresh white bread flake (or a small cube of crust) on the hook, or a tiny sliver of sardine. Chum with stale bread crumbs soaked in seawater, with a few drops of anchovy or pilchard oil.
tactics.retrieve: Fish it static and let the float drift through the chum cloud. Ignore the nibbles and strike only when the float slides away, because harders mouth bread and drop it if they feel resistance. Chum little and often to hold the shoal.
tactics.depth: 0.3 to 1.5 m below the surface, inside the chum cloud. Go deeper in bright sun.
tactics.rig: 2 to 3 kg (4 to 6 lb) mono, a small cone or pencil float with a red or orange tip, one or two split shot so the flake sinks slowly, and a #10 to #12 fine-wire hook. Use a 2 to 2.4 m ultra-light rod or a 7 ft light spinning rod with a 2500 reel.
tactics.stand: Harbour walls, slipway ends and calm corners out of the surge where harders already shoal: the inner walls and slipway at Hout Bay harbour, Kleinbaai at Blouberg, the Monwabisi tidal-pool wall.
tactics.why: SA forum anglers on Sealine advise very light tackle in sheltered water with chum, and bread or sardine on a small hook. That thread names no Cape venue, and one poster recalls East London. The District Mail column (Strand / False Bay) gives an ultra-light rod, a #12 hook and sardine at jetties, harbours and tidal pools. The Cape spots come from local harder-spot threads.

tactics.title: Sardine skin on a drag float in the wash
tactics.lure_or_bait: A fingernail-size sliver of sardine skin with a little flesh on a #12 to #14 hook. Chum with mashed sardine, stale white bread crumbs and anchovy oil.
tactics.retrieve: Cast to the edge of the foam and let the white water push the float about. The sinker sits well below the float, so it drags in the wash and the bait moves naturally. Keep the line just tight and lift into any run.
tactics.depth: About 30 to 40 cm under the float, in the top of the wash.
tactics.rig: A cheap cone-shaped polystyrene float with a red or orange top, a small ball sinker set well below it, a swivel, a 30 to 60 cm trace of 0.20 to 0.25 mm mono and a single #12 hook, on a light 7 to 9 ft rod.
tactics.stand: A gully, slipway or the sheltered side of a point, not open beach: the Kleinbaai slipway at Blouberg, the Monwabisi pool wall, gullies at Blouberg and Melkbos fished from the sand. Cast into the edge of the foam line. Do not stand on wave-washed rocks; in a moderate sea, fish only from the sand, a slipway or a harbour wall.
tactics.why: On the Sealine forum (general SA advice that names no Cape venue), Jigger says sardine works best in the waves on a float rig whose sinker sits low enough to drag in the white water. Dr Halibut Hoffman adds that chumming is the key and that a gully or slipway beats open beach.

tactics.title: Sand-flea dry fly on the push behind the shore break
tactics.lure_or_bait: Leonard Flemming's floating Sand Flea on a #14 light-wire hook (a Grip hook in his article; white foam back, white or chartreuse dubbing, grizzly hackle). Or a #12 chartreuse foam indicator fly with a #14 to #16 shrimp or midge on a dropper.
tactics.retrieve: Dead-drift it among the visible fish, or give tiny figure-of-eight twitches with pauses. Lift on any swirl at the fly.
tactics.depth: The surface film.
tactics.rig: A 6 wt rod (Flemming's choice; a 5 wt is enough in light wind) with a floating line, and a leader of 9 ft or more down to 3X to 6X tippet.
tactics.stand: Stand ankle- to knee-deep on the sand just behind the shore break, where shoals show on the pushing tide (Blouberg, Melkbos, Monwabisi beach). Cast along the beach to fish you can see.
tactics.why: Flemming landed about 60 southern mullet in two hours of pushing tide, just behind the shore break on an unnamed south-western Cape beach, with this fly. The beaches named here come from local spot lists. The clear-water condition is an estimate, because you need to see the fish; Flemming does not mention clarity. Kruger (Eastern Cape, Gamtoos River) found mullet took a chartreuse floating indicator fly over the subsurface fly.

tactics.title: Scum-line fly after an onshore blow
tactics.lure_or_bait: A #12 chartreuse indicator-style dry fly with a #14 to #16 chartreuse nymph, shrimp or midge on a dropper. A small black fly or a #14 hare's ear nymph also works.
tactics.retrieve: Very slow strip, or dead-drift along the foam and scum line. Strike on a swirl at the indicator fly.
tactics.depth: Surface down to 30 cm.
tactics.rig: A 5 to 6 wt rod (Kruger suggests 4 to 6 wt in wind or surf) with a floating line and a standard tapered leader, plus 3 to 5 ft of 4X to 5X tippet.
tactics.stand: The beach corner where the onshore breeze piles foam and scum against the shore: the sheltered corners at Blouberg and Melkbos, or the Monwabisi pool corner. Stay on the sand. Cast across the scum line and let it drift.
tactics.why: Kruger saw mullet feeding on small food organisms in surf-zone scum lines after strong onshore winds. That was in the Eastern Cape (Gamtoos River), not the Cape. The only Cape support is the District Mail column (Strand / False Bay), which mentions mullet feeding in the 'skuim kolle' (foam patches) in the surf in spring.

tactics.title: Bread fly over a bread chum line in the vlei
tactics.lure_or_bait: A bread fly (white foam, deer hair or white yarn) on a #4 to #8 stainless hook, fished among loose floating bread. Or a #12 chartreuse yarn indicator fly with a #14 to #16 point fly.
tactics.retrieve: Dead-drift it among the floating chum without moving it. Wait for a mouth to close on the fly, then lift.
tactics.depth: Surface.
tactics.rig: A 3 to 6 wt rod with a floating line, a 9 ft leader and 3 to 5 ft of 4X to 5X tippet.
tactics.stand: Stand on {downwind}, so the floating bread drifts to you and the shoal follows it. At Zandvlei, use the channel near the footbridge and mouth or the Marina da Gama channels. At Rietvlei, use the marked angling section, which is open 07:30 to 17:00 only. Release the harders you catch at both vleis.
tactics.why: Philip Meyer's tips (via Flemming's 'Mullet mania') are to chum with large pieces of bread and anchovy oil, keep gulls off the chum, and fish a stainless bread fly, which makes mullet boil at the surface. Kruger warns that wind breaks up chum in closed estuaries, so this works only in calm or light wind. It is limited to daytime light because of Rietvlei's 07:30 to 17:00 hours.

tactics.title: Hare's ear nymph and white streamer at Zandvlei
tactics.lure_or_bait: A #14 hare's ear nymph for average harders. For the big mullet, a large white streamer worked near the weed beds (the #2 to #1/0 hook size is an estimate).
tactics.retrieve: Fish the nymph near shoals with a slow figure-of-eight or a dead drift, with long pauses. Swim the streamer slowly past weed edges.
tactics.depth: 0.3 to 1 m, just over the tops of the weed.
tactics.rig: A 5 to 6 wt rod with a floating or slow intermediate line and a 9 ft leader: 4X to 5X tippet for the nymph, or 3 to 4 kg tippet for the streamer.
tactics.stand: At Zandvlei, fish close to the mouth around the footbridge at sunrise, or the weed-bed edges along the Marina da Gama channels that you can reach from the bank (Mills fished them from a float tube). The channels are sheltered from wind. Release indigenous fish, as the Zandvlei Trust asks.
tactics.why: Sean Mills (2009) describes this approach for Sandvlei: the mouth and footbridge area at sunrise, a #14 hare's ear for average mullet, and large white streamers near weed beds for big mullet. Mills says sunrise; dull daylight is an estimated extension. He does not say which species the big mullet are, and ORI notes flathead mullet are seldom caught on line.

tactics.title: Trot the run-out at the lagoon bridge
tactics.lure_or_bait: Bread flake, or a tiny sliver of sardine skin, on a #12 hook.
tactics.retrieve: Trot the float down the edge of the outgoing current, holding back now and then so the bait rises. Strike on a positive slide.
tactics.rig: 2 to 3 kg mono, a small stick or cone float, a little split shot spread down the line and a #12 hook, on a light 7 ft rod.
tactics.stand: The Milnerton Lagoon wooden bridge and the channel edges below it (only when the water is clean), or the Zandvlei mouth channel only when the mouth is open (it is often closed in summer; release indigenous fish there). Fish the seam between fast and slack water.
tactics.why: The spring-ebb trigger is an estimate. Its only basis is one Sealine poster's childhood memory that outgoing spring tides at Milnerton produced springers and mullet, caught with a milk crate rather than on rod and line. Other posters caught harders off the wooden bridge in the 1980s and around 2011. Skip this after sewage spills or heavy rain.

tactics.title: Bread flake and bread chum in calm water
tactics.lure_or_bait: Fresh white bread flake, or a tiny sliver of sardine, on a #10 to #12 hook. Chum with soaked stale bread crumbs (and a splash of anchovy oil in salt water).
tactics.retrieve: Fish it static in the chum cloud, and strike when the float slides away, not on the nibbles. Chum little and often.
tactics.depth: 0.3 to 1.5 m below the surface.
tactics.rig: 2 to 3 kg mono, a small cone or pencil float, one or two split shot and a fine-wire #10 to #12 hook, on an ultra-light rod or a light 7 ft spinning rod.
tactics.stand: The calmest water where harders show: harbour walls and slipways, tidal-pool walls, and vlei banks near channels. On a vlei, stand on {downwind}, where floating food collects.
tactics.why: SA forum anglers on Sealine (no Cape venue named) advise very light tackle in sheltered water with chum, and bread or sardine on a small hook. The District Mail column (Strand / False Bay) gives an ultra-light rod, a #12 hook and sardine at jetties, harbours and tidal pools.

legal.bag_note: 50 per day for all mullet species combined, since the listing is family-level. Excluded from the aggregate of 10 because
legal.note: A and B agree and both match R.959. Cast-netting harders needs a cast-net endorsement and is banned between sunset and sunrise (reg 22(17)); net-size limits are under general.
legal.quote: Mullets / harders | Family Mugilidae | None | 50

harders.review: Checked by an independent skeptic; 23 corrections applied
review_points: The ORI linefish profile records a larger maximum for C. richardsonii from Cape (Saldanha) fish: 450 mm TL and 1100 g (female, 11 years). The 40.5 cm figure understates it.

A Cape-relevant source exists. ORI gives C. richardsonii spawning in 'spring and summer with early and late summer peaks', in the nearshore surf zone in the Western Cape, so Sep to Mar holds for harders. The single array also covers flathead mullet, but ORI gives M. cephalus 'an extended spawning se

ORI says harders are resident in the surf zone most of the year 'but form large shoals in autumn and spring prior to movement'. That points to autumn as well as spring shoaling, not a summer-only peak. The current array misses the autumn shoals. It is still an estimate, because no Cape catch data ex

This is resolved. R1111 Annexure 7, the DFFE brochure Table 1 and both ORI profiles give the recreational and subsistence bag as 50 per person per day, with no minimum size and no closed season. 'Unlimited' is the commercial limit. The 50 applies to Family Mugilidae as a whole, so all mullet species

Partly confirmed. Mullet/harders are on Annexure 8, and the sunset-to-sunrise ban is brochure reg (18) and ORI. The brochure contradicts itself on size: reg (5) says 'not exceeding 6 m in diameter', but the Table 1 header says the net may not have mesh over 13 mm 'or which measures more than 2 m in

The profile never mentions that a DFFE recreational fishing permit endorsed for angling is required to catch harders, a marine and estuarine species, from the sea, harbours, tidal pools and estuaries such as Milnerton Lagoon. The westerncape.gov.za page does list Sandvlei under the CapeNature licenc

The Rietvlei rules say 'Carp and barbel must be removed from the water. Indigenous species must be returned.' Harders are indigenous, so at Rietvlei every harder must be released, and none can be kept for the pan or for live bait.

Rietvlei fishing is limited to the reserve's hours, 07:30 to 17:00. For most of the year the engine's dawn and dusk windows fall outside those hours, so the tactic would send people to fish there when it is not permitted.
unverified: The temperature band (min 9, ideal 12 to 20, max 26 C) is an estimate. It rests on the Cape distribution in cold upwelling water (ORI) and Kruger's qualitative 'prefer cooler water'. The FishBase/AquaMaps ranges were not re-checked, and no measured feeding thresholds were found.
All light weights are estimates, based on the FishBase note that M. cephalus is 'mainly diurnal', the night cast-net ban and the daytime fishing in the sources.

The sea, wind, tide, range, flow, trend and clarity weights are estimates. They are derived qualitatively from Flemming (pushing tide, behind the shore break), Kruger (Eastern Cape: onshore-wind scum lines; wind breaks up chum in closed estuaries), Sealine posters (gullies and calm water beat open beach; one rules out dirty water) and the Milnerton thread. The clarity weights have no basis in Flemming's Sand Flea article, which does not mention water clarity, and the trend weights have no source at all.
peak_months (March to May, September to December) is an estimate from ORI's note that harders form large shoals in autumn and spring before moving. No Cape Town catch-by-month data was found.

Not re-checked by the reviewer: the WWF-SASSI Red listing, the FishBase/AquaMaps temperature ranges, Flemming's 'Mullet mania' (?p=59333, the bread fly and Philip Meyer's tips) and the Two Oceans Aquarium page.

Cast-net size: the DFFE brochure contradicts itself (6 m diameter in reg 5; 4 m diameter, 2 m length and 13 mm mesh in the Table 1 note). The exact prohibition in R1111 reg 10(f)(v) (Strand to Gordon's Bay) was not re-read.
Hout Bay harbour: the cached Hout Bay harbour thread mentions only hottentot and snoek. Harders there rest on the spot list and general harbour advice, not on a Hout Bay source.
The spring-ebb trigger for the lagoon-bridge tactic is an estimate. Its only basis is a childhood memory of milk-crate catches at Milnerton, not rod-and-line fishing.
The sand-flea tactic's clear-water condition and named beaches (Blouberg, Melkbos, Monwabisi) are estimates or come from spot lists; Flemming names only an unnamed south-western Cape beach.
The scum-line tactic is Kruger's Eastern Cape (Gamtoos) observation. Its only Cape support is the District Mail's 'skuim kolle' remark, made in a kob-fishing context.
In the Zandvlei hare's ear tactic, the day_dull light condition is an estimate; Mills says sunrise.

Flathead mullet sizes in Zandvlei and Rietvlei (35 to 50 cm, big 60 cm or more at 2 to 3 kg) are estimates. Mills mentions 'big mullet' at Sandvlei without species or sizes, and ORI's maturity size of 44 to 48 cm TL is from KwaZulu-Natal.
The streamer hook size (#2 to #1/0) and the float-rig line strengths (2 to 3 kg) are estimates. The sources give only 'large white streamers', 'VERY light tackle', a #12 hook and 4X to 5X tippet.

hottentot.name: Hottentot
hottentot.season_note: Hottentot are resident and live in a small area all their lives (WWF-SASSI), so they can be caught all year. Villagevoice lists them as 'All year'. Anglers on the West Coast (Tietiesbaai, Dwarskersbos), beyond this page's one-hour area, call them thick all year. Around Cape Town, shore anglers fish for them mostly from late spring to autumn. On the Atlantic seaboard (Saunders Rock, Maidens Cove, Bakoven, Camps Bay) they are the summer target and galjoen the winter one (zeeQo, Sealine 2010). A search snippet says Silwerstroom shore angling is 'particularly hottentot in January and February'. The peak months here are an estimate that reflects angler effort, not availability. Part of the summer 'peak' is anglers switching from galjoen, which is closed from 15 October to the end of February, so peak and off-peak should score only slightly differently. Kalk Bay harbour in general fishes best from October to April (Walt), but that advice is not specific to hottentot. They are caught in winter too. One hottentot took a 4/0 Clouser from a boat over very deep water off the Cape Peninsula in mid-winter, suspended and probably feeding on shrimp (Flemming 2015). The Oceana Cape Bream Challenge, fished from boats around Robben Island in May, targeted fish over 2 kg. Neither is evidence for a shore method. Spawning goes on all year with peaks in summer and winter (IUCN/Wikipedia), and De Villiers 1977 found no distinct spawning season. The spawn_months are those summer and winter peaks put into calendar months, which is an estimate.

temp.basis: Estimate. The species lives in the cool Benguela current from Angola to Cape Agulhas (Wikipedia/IUCN; FishBase). A Reef Life Survey search snippet (the page returned 403 and was never opened) gives a survey sea temperature range of 14.8 to 19.3 C, which puts the observed lower bound above the ideal_lo used here. Hotties are caught all year on the Atlantic seaboard, where the sea typically runs about 10 to 15 C. That range is an estimate from typical seaboard temperatures, not from a cited catch record. Sealine spearo Jacquesdw (2012) says that in cold water hotties sit high in the kelp fronds, a green tinge makes them active, and 'ice cold blue water shut them down'. Jo-Jo (2011) says sardine bait works 'better when water is cold'. The min, ideal and max values are estimates fitted to these points.

hottentot.habitat:
Kelp beds (Ecklonia maxima) on shallow rocky reef. Adults also use subtidal reefs, blinders and pinnacles down to about 55 m, and juveniles stay inside the kelp. They hold in small shoals, have a small home range and seldom move far (WWF-SASSI, Two Oceans Aquarium, Wikipedia/IUCN). From the shore they are caught in the gaps and sand patches beside kelp, fishing off rock ledges and harbour walls. Known spots:
- The kelp near the middle of the Kalk Bay wall. Fish the harbour wall only: the rocks north of the harbour are in the St James no-take zone.
- Saunders Rock, 'behind the pool or to the left in the little bay'.
- The rocks and kelp at Blouberg.
- Hout Bay harbour's far side, before the sewage works. Do not go past the works towards the Sentinel, where the Karbonkelberg no-take zone begins.
- The Glencairn/Simon's Town quarry, north of Simon's Town and outside the Boulders zone, which runs from the east end of Simon's Town harbour to Oatlands.
Cast short, because the deep water is out of casting range (Jacquesdw). Divers say the bigger fish sit in the denser kelp (DJP).
hottentot.diet: A generalist omnivore. In Western Cape stomach samples (Pulfrich 1987), amphipods and red seaweeds dominate. They also eat other crustaceans, polychaete worms, molluscs (mussels), sea urchins and occasionally small fish. Larger fish eat more seaweed, and their molar-like teeth crush shells. One fish caught from a boat in winter was suspended over deep water and was probably feeding on shoals of shrimp (Flemming, The Mission, 2015). Anglers say they 'will go for just about anything': white mussel, redbait, chokka, sardine, prawn and worm.
hottentot.typical_size: From the shore, mostly 20 to 30 cm (0.2 to 0.5 kg). Many are under the 22 cm limit at Kalk Bay, Saunders Rock and Blouberg. A good one is 1 to 1.5 kg, and a big one is 2 to 2.4 kg: a 2.4 kg fish was caught and released off the Hout Bay shore (Sealine 2010). The species reaches about 46 to 54 cm and 2.7 kg and matures at about 22 to 25 cm. Most live to about 12 years, and the maximum recorded age is about 19 years.
hottentot.handling:
The fish has sharp dorsal and anal fin spines and strong crushing teeth. Hold it firmly behind the head and keep your fingers out of its mouth.

The rules: you need a recreational fishing permit, the minimum size is 22 cm and the bag limit is 10 per person per day (WWF-SASSI; check the current DFFE regulations). WWF-SASSI rates it green (Best Choice). Many shore fish are undersize. Circle hooks reduce deep hooking, and long-shank hooks make a swallowed hook easier to remove. Unhook with wet hands and release quickly. The fish louse Anilocra capensis often rides on hotties and is harmless to anglers.

Never fish the no-take zones near hottentot ground:
- Karbonkelberg: Oudekraal to Hout Bay (the Sentinel). At Hout Bay, stay on the harbour side of the sewage works.
- St James: St James tidal pool to Kalk Bay tidal pool. Fish only the Kalk Bay harbour wall, not the rocks north of it.
- Boulders: the east end of Simon's Town harbour to Oatlands.
- Castle Rock: Miller's Point to Partridge Point.
- Paulsberg: Smitswinkel Point to Venus Pool.
- Cape of Good Hope: Scarborough to Hoek van die Bobbejaan.
- The Helderberg MPA between the Eerste and Lourens river mouths.

The Cape Point section of the national park also needs a SANParks activity permit. Collecting white mussel, redbait or worm bait falls under the same fishing permit and its daily limits.

tactics.title: Small bait in the kelp gaps
tactics.lure_or_bait: Fresh white mussel (salt it to firm it up and use half a mussel per bait), fresh redbait, or a long thin chokka strip. Cut baits long and thin so a hottie can swallow them.
tactics.rig: A #1 to 2/0 circle or long-shank hook (1/0 to 2/0 is plenty) on a hook trace of 0.45 to 0.6 mm, about 45 cm long. Run the sinker on a short (about 30 cm) weak trace at least a third lighter than the main line, so it breaks off in the reef. Use a 1 to 3 oz sinker on a light 9 to 10 ft rod.
tactics.retrieve: No retrieve. Cast, let it settle and hold a tight line. Hotties peck repeatedly, so wait for the steady weight, then lift. Rebait often, because mussel gets stripped fast.
tactics.depth: On the bottom beside the kelp, 1 to 5 m
tactics.stand: On a rock ledge or harbour wall beside a kelp bed, outside the no-take zones. Make a short cast into the gaps and sand patches right next to the kelp, not far out. Baits on sand are safer from crabs.
tactics.why: This is the standard local method in Sealine threads: subaruseun's rig and kelp-edge advice, plus white mussel or chokka from several posters. Hotties live in the kelp, and the deep water is out of casting range.

tactics.title: Cold upwelled water: lift the bait off the bottom with a floatie
tactics.lure_or_bait: Sardine or a chokka strip, with white mussel as the back-up. Sardine is said to fish better in cold water.
tactics.rig: A 1/0 circle or long-shank hook on a stiff 0.5 to 0.6 mm hook trace about 30 to 50 cm long. Thread a small piece of foam (a 'floatie') onto the trace about two finger-widths from the hook. A 1 to 2 oz running sinker on a weak trace anchors the rig on the bottom, and the foam lifts the bait off it. Size the foam so the bait just lifts but does not drag the sinker.
tactics.retrieve: Let it sit and swing in the surge beside the kelp. Check it often and recast to a new gap.
tactics.depth: Lifted 20 to 50 cm off the bottom beside the kelp by the floatie, which keeps the bait out of the crabs and the weed
tactics.stand: From a ledge or harbour wall overlooking a kelp bed. Cast into the calm pockets between the kelp heads.
tactics.why: Jacquesdw, a Sealine spearo, saw hotties sitting higher in the kelp fronds in cold water and says ice-cold blue water shuts them down. The floatie lifts the bait a little way towards them. Jo-Jo says sardine fishes better in cold water. The floatie rig comes from a Sealine thread, where it is used for galjoen and rock fish and Tappit lists hotties among them. A true suspended float rig for hotties is not documented.

tactics.title: Green water and a bit of swell: redbait on the wash side
tactics.lure_or_bait: Fresh or slightly 'ripe' redbait, or white mussel
tactics.rig: A 1/0 to 2/0 hook on a 0.5 to 0.6 mm trace. Use a 2 to 3 oz sinker on a weak 30 cm sinker trace. In deeper water, use a longer sinker trace (about 60 cm) and a short hook trace (about 20 cm).
tactics.retrieve: Static. Keep the line tight through the surge and strike on the steady pull.
tactics.depth: On the bottom in the gullies and at the kelp edge, 2 to 6 m
tactics.stand: On a high, dry ledge or a harbour wall where the swell pushes through a kelp gully below you. Fish the foamy wash side of the gully. Never stand on wet, wave-washed rock. If the sets reach your ledge, move to a harbour.
tactics.why: Jacquesdw says 'dirty water but not rough water', and that a green tinge makes them active. Stinkmossel says to use redbait when the water looks like galjoen water. One uncached post (WillemduToit) claims they feed better in bigger water, but that is unverified and conflicts with Jacquesdw.

tactics.title: Flat calm: drift-line at the harbour wall
tactics.lure_or_bait: Chokka tentacle or sliced chokka, white mussel, or a pilchard strip. Try two hooks with a different bait on each.
tactics.rig: No sinker, or a single small split shot. Use a #1 to 1/0 hook on a 0.4 to 0.45 mm trace, going lighter on clear days when the fish are shy. Let the bait's own weight carry it down.
tactics.retrieve: Let it sink slowly down the kelp line, then lift and let it fall again.
tactics.depth: Sinking from mid-water to the bottom along the kelp, 1 to 4 m
tactics.stand: Along the kelp near the middle of the Kalk Bay harbour wall (the wall only, not the rocks north of the harbour), on the harbour side at Hout Bay, or on the rocks at the Glencairn/Simon's Town quarry. Drop the bait straight down beside the kelp.
tactics.why: Walt (Sealine) recommends a sinkerless drift line at the Simon's Town quarry but says it won't work well in moving water. Kalk Bay hotties hold at the kelp near the middle of the wall. A 0.45 mm trace is advised for shy fish in clear water.

tactics.title: Hout Bay harbour side: fish bait at the outer kelp edge
tactics.lure_or_bait: Fish bait such as sardine or a chokka strip, about 6 to 8 cm long and thin
tactics.rig: A 2/0 to 3/0 long-shank hook (3/0 to 4/0 for big fish) on a 0.6 mm trace, with a 2 to 3 oz sinker on a weak sinker trace. A 50 to 60 m cast is at the top end of light tackle, so use a 10 ft rod and a 3 oz sinker.
tactics.retrieve: Static. Hold a tight line and lift on the steady weight.
tactics.depth: On the bottom at the outer kelp or reef edge, 3 to 8 m
tactics.stand: Hout Bay harbour side, just before the sewage works at the far end of the harbour. Do not go past the works towards the Sentinel, which is the Karbonkelberg no-take zone. Cast about 50 to 60 m to the kelp edge by the round rock that shows as the tide drops.
tactics.why: Speartackle (Sealine, 2011) recommends the shore just before the sewage works, casting about 60 m. In the same thread he notes that the Sentinel to Oudekraal is no-take. The round rock that shows about 2 hours after high tide is a casting marker. The tide trigger is an estimate: no source says the fish bite better on the drop. Roper says the big Hout Bay hottentot usually take fish bait. Subaruseun's 3/0 to 4/0 hooks are for big fish.

tactics.title: Rough sea: stay off the rocks, fish inside a harbour or not at all
tactics.lure_or_bait: Redbait or white mussel, which stay on the hook
tactics.rig: A 1/0 to 2/0 hook on a short 20 to 30 cm hook trace, with a 2 to 3 oz sinker on a weak trace
tactics.retrieve: Static, with a short cast. Hold the rod high to keep the line off the wall and the rocks.
tactics.depth: On the bottom in the sheltered harbour basin, 2 to 5 m
tactics.stand: Only from inside a harbour basin, well back from any outer wall that waves can wash over. Stay off open rocks and exposed ledges completely in a rough sea, because freak waves kill rock anglers on this coast. If no sheltered harbour spot is available, do not fish.
tactics.why: This is a safety fallback, not an opportunity: rough water is a poor day for hotties and a dangerous one for rock anglers. Jacquesdw says they want 'dirty water but not rough water'. The Rooi-Els safety warnings apply to every exposed ledge. The claim that hotties feed in big water comes from one uncached post and is unverified.

tactics.title: Dropshot a scented worm in the gullies (experimental)
tactics.lure_or_bait: A scented 2 to 3 inch worm or shrimp soft plastic (for example a 2-inch Gulp sandworm), or a soft plastic tipped with a sliver of chokka
tactics.rig: A #2 to #1 dropshot hook, nose-hooked, on a 20 to 30 cm dropper above a 7 to 14 g weight. Use 6 to 8 lb braid with a 0.3 mm fluorocarbon leader.
tactics.retrieve: Hold it still beside the kelp, give small shakes and lift-drops, and pause for long periods. Hotties peck, so give the fish time.
tactics.depth: On the bottom or up to 30 cm above it, in the gullies and at the kelp edge
tactics.stand: Stand above a kelp gully or by a harbour wall, outside the no-take zones, and work the gaps right at your feet.
tactics.why: A Sealine poster (Reefman) suggests dropshotting the gullies at Cape Point, though not for hotties specifically. Hotties eat amphipods and worms. Local anglers say unscented plastics struggle (zeeQo) and that lures are not worth the bother (Zeebo, saltysouti). This is an experimental tactic and should work less well than bait.

legal.bag_note: 10 per day. A bag of 10 does not exceed 10, so it counts toward the aggregate of 10 and on its own fills it.
legal.note: A and B agree and both match R.959. No closed season.
legal.quote: Hottentot | Pachymetopon blochii | 22 cm | 10

hottentot.review: Checked by an independent skeptic; 21 corrections applied
review_points: This list is incomplete in a way that matters for this species. It leaves out the St James restricted (no-take) zone, which runs between the St James tidal pool and the Kalk Bay tidal pool. That is right next to Kalk Bay harbour, which the profile recommends, and the rocks north of the harbour are n

This merges two different spots. In the 2010 thread (hout-bay.44419), the 2.4 kg fish and the dome rock 80 m out are 'PAST the sewage treatment plant', which is towards the Sentinel. In July 2011 (52668), speartackle himself pointed out that 'the entire area from the Sentinel Point to Oudekraal is a

Speartackle's 'round rock visible about 2 hours after high tide' is a casting marker, not a statement that the fish bite better on the drop. The only tide advice in the sources is Walt's 'low tide' at the Simon's Town quarry, given for a sinkerless drift line, and the quarry thread links low tide to

In the cited foam-floaties thread, the foam goes 'two fingers from the hook' on a stiff trace for galjoen and rock fish. It is a floatie that lifts the bait off the bottom above the sinker, so the bait rises at most about one trace length (roughly 0.2 to 0.5 m). A rig with a sinker on the bottom can

Walt's 'Best times are from about October to April' refers to Kalk Bay harbour fishing in general: kob, elf and stumpnose in summer south-easter weather. That thread says nothing about when hottentot are best.

Flemming's 2015 article in The Mission names only the 'Cape Peninsula', not Buffels Bay. The fish was taken under a rubber duck over water 'probably a 100 yards deep', far deeper than the 55 m the profile itself gives as the habitat. It says nothing about shore fishing or kelp-edge fly fishing.

In the cache, the Steve Austin step-by-step appears only under The Mission's wildeperd, garrick and Garden Route tags, and nothing links it to hottentot or to Cape Town shore fishing. Every fly size, rod weight and colour is invented. The single data point (a 4/0 Clouser from a boat over deep water)

A 5 oz (about 140 g) sinker is beyond the light tackle this page covers; the profile's own base rig is 1 to 3 oz on a light 9 to 11 ft rod. The 'bigger water' claim rests on WillemduToit in hotties.102565, which is not in the cache and was not verified. It also conflicts with Jacquesdw's 'dirty wate
unverified: Temperature min/ideal/max (10/12-17/21 C) are estimates. They are fitted to the Benguela distribution, an unopened Reef Life Survey snippet (14.8-19.3 C, whose lower bound is above ideal_lo) and forum remarks about cold blue water. The 10 to 15 C Atlantic catch range is an estimate from typical seaboard sea temperatures.
All light weights (no source on time of day; daytime feeding assumed for a kelp-grazing sparid)

Tide weights, and the dropping/low tide trigger on the Hout Bay tactic. These are estimates: the Hout Bay rock that shows about 2 h after high is a casting marker, not evidence of a better bite, and Walt's low-tide advice is for the quarry drift line.
Range weights set to 1/1 (no evidence of a spring/neap effect)
Pressure-trend and wind-strength weights (estimates)

Sea-state and clarity weights are taken from conflicting forum anecdotes ('dirty but not rough', 'can't be any swell'). The claim that they feed better in bigger water comes only from the uncached hotties.102565 thread (WillemduToit) and is unverified.

Peak months (Nov-Apr) are an estimate that reflects angler effort, not availability: anglers switch to hottentot while galjoen is closed (15 Oct to end Feb). Keep the gap between peak and off-peak weights small.
Spawn months: 'peaks in summer and winter' converted to Dec-Feb and Jun-Aug by the researcher
Silwerstroom 'particularly hottentot in January and February' comes from a search snippet, not an angling article
Floatie rig: the foam-floaties thread describes it for galjoen and rock fish, not specifically for hotties. A true suspended float rig for hotties is undocumented.
Dropshot tactic: no documented Cape Town shore catches, and local anglers say plain lures do poorly
Bag limit of 10 and size limit of 22 cm are from WWF-SASSI (confirmed there). Current DFFE regulations were not checked directly, and Sealine posts quote other bag figures.
Local names not checked against a source

katonkel.name: Katonkel (bonito)
katonkel.season_note: From the shore this is a summer-to-autumn fish that the south-easters bring in. In Sep 2024 a Sealine moderator wrote that 'summer conditions, lots of south east winds push them into the bay and into casting range'. He named Fish Hoek Bay, the rocks between Glencairn and Fish Hoek, and Simon's Town, and in early September 2024 he advised waiting for them to return. At Glencairn Quarry a regular spun on January to March mornings for 'Tail' and 'landed a few bonnies' (Sealine, 2010). In mid-March 2012, katonkel were caught in beach nets and sold at Kalk Bay, though the thread disputes the ID. Boat lists put them in False Bay in both summer and winter (Angler Publications; seasidecottages). From the shore, chances outside about November to May are slim. Stocks crashed for over a decade and have 'recovered strongly in recent years' (Sealine, May 2021). In the Cape, katonkel means Sarda sarda, not king mackerel or skipjack.

temp.basis: Estimate. FishBase gives a subtropical tolerance of 12 to 27 C. The Cape shore band (14 / 17 to 21 / 24 C) is an estimate tied to the warm, clean water that summer south-easters push onto the western side of False Bay.

katonkel.habitat: A fast, schooling, open-water hunter (FishBase: epipelagic, neritic). From the shore it is a deep-water ledge fish on the western side of False Bay: the rocks below the railway line at Glencairn Quarry, the rocks between Glencairn and Fish Hoek, Fish Hoek Bay, and Simon's Town (stay out of the Boulders no-take zone). It usually runs with yellowtail and follows bait shoals into casting range. At Glencairn the bottom is foul, and the ledges are low and get wave-washed in any real swell. Reach the rocks only through the official gate over the railway line, never across the tracks elsewhere. The quarry itself was in use as a shooting range in 2010. The Cape Point cliff spots (Rooikrans) are left out on purpose: they are cliff-gaff, heavy-tackle ground for experienced anglers only, not light-tackle spots.
katonkel.diet: Small schooling fish (sardine, anchovy, mackerel, maasbanker), squid and shrimp. Adults are cannibalistic and take relatively large prey (FishBase).
katonkel.typical_size: Usually 45 to 60 cm fork length (1.5 to 3 kg). A big one is 70 cm plus, about 5 kg (FishBase common length 50 cm FL, max 91 cm; Wikipedia about 75 cm and 5 to 6 kg).
katonkel.handling: Sharp teeth. The Mission says a wire trace is 'quite advisable when going after bonito' and captions a fish 'check those teeth!'. Lip-grip or tail it and keep your fingers away from the mouth. If you keep it, bleed it (pull the heart through the gill or break the neck), then ike-jime it and ice it at once, because poorly handled fish eat badly (Sealine). Law: katonkel is not listed by name in the DFFE recreational regulations (Annexure 7), so it counts toward the overall cumulative daily bag of 10 fish per person. No species-specific size limit is listed, and you need a recreational fishing permit (DFFE 2024 brochure).

tactics.title: First-light tin spoon off the ledges
tactics.lure_or_bait: Chrome or silver tin spoon (Secret 70 or Abu Lucas-mould type). The source names the models but not the weights; about 40 to 70 g is an estimate.
tactics.retrieve: Cast long, count 3 to 5, then wind fast and steady. If fish follow, speed up rather than stop.
tactics.depth: Top 3 m
tactics.stand: The quarry ledges below the railway line at Glencairn, or the rocks toward Fish Hoek, casting out over deep water. Reach the rocks only through the official gate over the railway line, never across the tracks elsewhere. Stay off any ledge that waves are washing.
tactics.rig: Medium-heavy rock spinning, at the top end of light tackle: a 2.7 to 3 m (9 to 10 ft) rod casting up to about 80 g, a 4000 to 5000 reel, 10 to 15 kg braid and 1 m of 0.6 mm mono leader. All of these are estimates; no cited source gives a rod, reel or line. A short wire trace is optional (The Mission advises wire for bonito).
tactics.why: A Sealine moderator (Sep 2024) recommends tin spoons such as the Secret 70 and Abu Lucas mould for False Bay katonkel and yellowtail. A Glencairn regular spun on January to March mornings for 'Tail' and 'landed a few bonnies' (Sealine, 2010). The dusk trigger is an estimate.

tactics.title: South-easter push: plugs into the chop
tactics.lure_or_bait: Wayne Stanley-style casting plug, 'white 2oz for cape fish' (about 57 g), then pink or green, with 4/0 to 5/0 Mustad trebles
tactics.retrieve: Fast retrieve with long sweeps of the rod so the plug darts and splashes (estimate)
tactics.depth: Surface to 1 m
tactics.stand: The highest safe, dry ledge at Glencairn Quarry or toward Fish Hoek, with the wind in your face. Stay well back from the wash, and do not fish if waves are reaching the ledges. Reach the rocks only through the official gate over the railway line, never across the tracks elsewhere.
tactics.rig: As for the spoon, with 1 m of 0.6 to 0.7 mm leader. A rod rated to about 80 g handles 2 oz plugs. This is the top end of light tackle.
tactics.colour: white first, then pink or green
tactics.why: The Sealine moderator (Sep 2024) wrote: 'Summer conditions, lots of south east winds push them into the bay and into casting range.' He names Wayne Stanley plugs in white, pink and green with 4/0 to 5/0 Mustad trebles. It is the wind that brings the fish in, not the swell, so this tactic is limited to a flat or small sea: the low quarry ledges get wave-washed in anything bigger.

tactics.title: Fish showing close: keel spinner or slow spoon
tactics.lure_or_bait: 2.5 oz (about 70 g) keel spinner, or a Secret 70 / Abu Lucas-mould tin spoon
tactics.retrieve: Shorter casts and a slower, wobbling retrieve just under the surface
tactics.depth: Top 2 m
tactics.stand: A dry ledge on the rocks closest to where the fish or bait are showing, between Glencairn and Fish Hoek or at Simon's Town (never inside the Boulders no-take zone). At Glencairn, reach the rocks only through the official gate over the railway line.
tactics.rig: As for the spoon: wire or 0.6 mm leader. At the top end of light tackle.
tactics.why: The Sealine moderator recommends tin spoons and a '2.5 oz keel spinner for closer casting and slower retrieve'. The calm, daytime trigger is an estimate.

tactics.title: Baitfish fly when they're in range
tactics.lure_or_bait: Sardine or anchovy pattern, or a Clouser, size 1/0 to 2/0, white with a grey or blue back (estimate)
tactics.retrieve: Strip fast with both hands (rod under the arm) as soon as the fly lands
tactics.depth: Top 2 m on an intermediate line
