tactics.stand: Flat, dry ledges at Glencairn Quarry with room behind you for a backcast. Reach the rocks only through the official gate over the railway line, never across the tracks elsewhere.
tactics.rig: 9 ft, 8 to 9 weight rod (estimate), intermediate line, 15 cm of 10 to 15 kg wire or a 0.5 mm bite tippet
tactics.why: The Mission, a fly-fishing magazine, says that around the Peninsula the fish is 'most commonly known as Katonkel' and that a wire trace 'is quite advisable when going after bonito'. It gives no flies, rod weight or shore spots, so the pattern, rod and stand are estimates.

tactics.title: Off-colour water: bright plug, cleanest edge
tactics.lure_or_bait: 2 oz (about 57 g) pink or green casting plug
tactics.retrieve: Slower and noisier than usual. Concentrate your casts along the line where clean water meets dirty.
tactics.depth: Surface to 1 m
tactics.stand: Whichever safe, dry ledge is closest to a clean-water edge. At Glencairn, reach the rocks only through the official gate over the railway line.
tactics.rig: As for the plugs. At the top end of light tackle.
tactics.why: The Sealine moderator (Sep 2024) names pink and green plugs for False Bay katonkel. Using them in coloured water is an estimate. Katonkel are clear-water hunters, so the odds are poor.

tactics.title: Drift a sardine when the lure bite dies
tactics.lure_or_bait: A half or whole small sardine (or a sardine strip) on a 2/0 to 3/0 hook under a small float or balloon
tactics.retrieve: Let the wind and current carry it out along the ledge. Free-spool when it runs.
tactics.depth: 1 to 3 m
tactics.stand: A dry, deep-water ledge at Glencairn Quarry, drifting the bait out with the current. Do not try it in a south-easter, which blows the float back onto the rocks. Reach the rocks only through the official gate over the railway line, never across the tracks elsewhere.
tactics.rig: 15 to 20 kg wire or 0.6 mm mono trace, 2/0 to 3/0 hook, small float, no sinker (estimate)
tactics.why: Estimate. Katonkel eat small schooling fish such as sardine (FishBase), so a drifted sardine is a reasonable fallback. A south-easter blows floats at the quarry 'onto the bricks' (Sealine, 2010), so this only works in an offshore or cross wind. The bottom is foul, so keep the bait up off it.

tactics.title: Silver spoon, fast
tactics.lure_or_bait: Silver tin spoon (Secret 70 / Abu Lucas-mould type; about 40 to 70 g is an estimate) or a casting jig
tactics.retrieve: Long cast, short count, fast steady retrieve
tactics.depth: Top 3 m
tactics.stand: A dry ledge on the quarry rocks below the railway line at Glencairn, casting to deep water. Reach the rocks only through the official gate over the railway line, never across the tracks elsewhere.
tactics.rig: Medium-heavy rock spinning, at the top end of light tackle: 2.7 to 3 m rod, 10 to 15 kg braid, 0.6 mm mono leader or a short wire trace (all estimates)
tactics.why: The Sealine moderator names tin spoons for False Bay katonkel, and Glencairn regulars spin the quarry ledges for them.

legal.bag_note: Default of 10 per day for unlisted species. Counts toward the aggregate of 10. This is not a species-specific figure.
legal.note: Reconciled: A (Gazette) found the species absent from Annexure 7; B (brochure) asked the Gazette reader to confirm. I read the full R.959 Annexure 7 Prohibited and Permitted lists myself. Neither lists Sarda or bonito. 'Tunas (tunny)' is Thunnus spp. only, and the mackerels listed are Scomber and Scomberomorus. The default therefore applies: 10 per day and no size limit, from DFFE permit condition
legal.quote: '(7) Species not mentioned in either of these lists have a bag limit of ten provided that sharks, rays, skates or chimaeras (Class Chondrichthyes) have a bag limit of one and rockcods (Family Serranidae) have a bag limit of five.'

katonkel.review: Checked by an independent skeptic; 19 corrections applied
review_points: Sarda sarda is not listed by name in Annexure 7, so a katonkel counts toward the overall cumulative recreational daily bag limit of ten fish (DFFE brochure reg. 9/10(b)). It is not a no-limit species like chub mackerel.

The source gives heavier gear: 2 oz (57 g) plugs with 4/0 to 5/0 trebles, and a 2.5 oz (about 70 g) keel spinner. The spoon weights were shrunk without a source. The rod, reel, braid and wire spec is not in any cited source; the thread mentions none of them. This is yellowtail-grade rock spinning, p

In the thread, 'plenty of katonkel' were bought from the Kalk Bay harbour slab. The fish 'trekked at Fish Hoek all day' were tuna. Katonkel in beach nets are mentioned, but the identification was disputed ('Thats no boni, check the lekker tanne!').
The thread only implies it ('wait for the yellowtail and katonkel to return'). It does not say so.

Rooikrans comes from a holiday-cottage blog that calls it a cliff spot needing a cliff gaff and 'Only for confident, experienced anglers'. It is heavy-tackle yellowtail fishing, sits in Table Mountain National Park near MPA restricted zones (Cape of Good Hope, Paulsberg), and is at the edge of the o

This is an unsourced estimate with safety effects. The only shore spots are low quarry and railway ledges, described as 'Pretty rough water' with fish lost 'waiting for a wave to lift it up onto the ledges'. Rating 1 to 1.8 m seas as best sends anglers onto wave-washed ledges. The source says the so
Access is through a gate over the active Metrorail line, and in 2010 the quarry was a shooting range. Neither point is given as a caution.
unverified: The temperature min, max and ideal band (14 / 17 to 21 / 24 C) are estimates. The only sourced figure is FishBase's 12 to 27 C tolerance.
All light, tide, range, trend, clarity and wind weights are estimates, as is flow 0.7. Only the south-easter push and the morning fishing are sourced.
The sea weights (flat 0.75, small 1, moderate 0.6, rough 0.1) are an estimate capped for safety on low, wave-washed ledges. The source says the wind brings the fish in; it says nothing about swell.
The present and peak months (November to May, peak January to April) are inferred from 'summer' and south-easter reports plus the January to March quarry mornings.
No South African spawning months were found, so spawn_months is left out.

Every rod, reel, braid and leader spec is an estimate; no cited source gives tackle beyond the lures. Spoon weights (about 40 to 70 g) are estimates: the source names the Secret 70 and Abu Lucas models only.
The retrieve styles, the dusk trigger, the fly pattern and rod, the coloured-water tactic and the sardine drift are estimates.
It is not known whether Glencairn Quarry is still a shooting range (reported in 2010), or what the current rules are for the railway-line gate.
The seasidecottages page was cited at two different URLs (researcher and reviewer). The content matches, but the live URL was not re-checked.
The bag-limit reading comes from the reviewer's cached copy of the DFFE 2024 brochure and Annexure 7. No live URL is recorded, and the regulations can change.

klipvis.name: Klipvis
klipvis.latin: Clinidae (mainly Clinus spp., e.g. super klipfish Clinus superciliosus)
klipvis.season_note: A resident rock-pool and kelp family, present all year. The super klipfish ranges from northern Namibia to the Kei River (FishBase). There is only weak angling evidence. In a 2011 Sealine post, an angler who fished Kalk Bay, Hermanus and Hout Bay said he was 'mostly catching gurnard, maasbanker, shy sharks, and klipvis', but did not say which fish came from the shore. In Feb 2024, Sealine anglers reported 'plenty of rockfish' off the Blouberg beach and rocks, species unconfirmed. Peak months are an estimate: the calmer summer months with offshore winds make the Atlantic-side rocks fishable. Hout Bay harbour is sheltered all year.

temp.basis: Estimate. The super klipfish range (northern Namibia to the Kei River, FishBase) spans the cold Benguela west coast and the warm-temperate south coast, so summer False Bay water near 20 C should still count as ideal. No thermal study found.

klipvis.habitat: Intertidal and subtidal rocky shore, from rock pools to at least 50 m. Found among weed and kelp, under ledges and in the gaps between harbour-wall blocks. Colour matches habitat: pale fish favour sand, green fish Caulerpa or Codium weed, and red fish red algae (Zsilavecz 2005, via Wikipedia). At Blouberg, look in the rocks, kelp gaps and pools along the beachfront. At Hout Bay harbour, fish the foot of the quay and breakwater walls.
klipvis.diet: Bottom crustaceans (amphipods, isopods, crabs), plus sea urchins, small gastropods, polychaete worms and small fishes (FishBase via Wikipedia).
klipvis.typical_size: Usually 8 to 15 cm. A big super klipfish is 25 to 30 cm; the maximum is 30 cm TL (FishBase).
klipvis.handling: No species-specific rules. Klipfish are on neither the permitted-species list (Table 4) nor the prohibited list (Table 3). The general bag limit of 10 per person per day applies, and you need a recreational fishing permit (DFFE regulations brochure). Most fish are tiny, so release them in the water. Use small, ideally barbless, hooks (#10 to #14) to avoid deep hooking. Wet your hands, and mind the spiny dorsal fin. The super klipfish (Clinus superciliosus) gives birth to live young (Veith 1979), so release gravid fish. The Bot River klipfish (Clinus spatulatus) is Endangered but lives only in the Bot River and Kleinmond estuaries, not at these spots. Hout Bay: the Karbonkelberg restricted (no-take) zone runs from Oudekraal to the Sentinel / Hout Bay, up to about 3.3 nautical miles offshore. Fish only inside Hout Bay harbour, and check the SANParks MPA zone maps. Kalk Bay harbour is fishable, but neighbouring St James and Boulders are no-take zones, so don't fish their rocks or tidal pools. Never collect bait (mussel, red bait) in a no-take zone. Blouberg rocks: watch for sets on the outer rocks.

tactics.title: Tiny hook straight down beside the rocks
tactics.lure_or_bait: A pea-sized piece of worm, prawn, black mussel, sardine or chokka
tactics.rig: Ultra-light rod, 1 to 3 kg line, #10 to #14 hook on a 20 to 30 cm dropper of 0.20 mm line, with a split shot or 5 to 15 g sinker below
tactics.retrieve: Drop it straight down at the foot of the wall or into a gap in the kelp and hold it still. Strike on the first sharp rattle, then lift steadily so the fish can't dive back into a hole.
tactics.depth: On the bottom among rocks and weed, 0.5 to 4 m
tactics.stand: On the harbour wall or flat rocks, fishing vertically against the structure rather than casting out. Stay outside the no-take zones (St James, Boulders, Karbonkelberg).
tactics.why: Adapted from the District Mail's ultra-light #12-hook harbour and tidal-pool method for strepies and mullet; no Cape source covers klipfish specifically. In 2011 a Sealine angler reported klipvis among his catches at Kalk Bay, Hermanus and Hout Bay, without saying whether from shore. In 2024 Sealine anglers reported 'plenty of rockfish' off the Blouberg rocks, species unconfirmed. Klipfish live among rocks and weed and eat small crustaceans (FishBase).

tactics.title: Low-tide pools and gullies
tactics.lure_or_bait: Small piece of black mussel or red bait (collected within permit limits, never in a no-take zone) or worm
tactics.rig: #12 hook, one split shot 20 cm up, 1 to 2 kg line, short ultra-light rod
tactics.retrieve: Lower it into the deepest pools and the gully mouths and let it sit by the weed edge. Move on after a few minutes without a bite.
tactics.depth: Bottom of pools and gullies, 0.3 to 2 m
tactics.stand: On flat rocks at low tide, working the deeper pools and gullies first and backing off as the push comes in. Never turn your back on the swell. Not in the St James or Boulders tidal pools: both are no-take zones.
tactics.why: Klipfish live in rock pools and the intertidal zone (FishBase, Zsilavecz 2005). At Blouberg, Sealine anglers caught plenty of 'rockfish' off the rocks (species unconfirmed) and noted black mussel and red bait on the small rock formations.

tactics.title: Micro soft plastic dropped along the wall
tactics.lure_or_bait: 1.5 to 2 inch grub, nymph or worm soft plastic in natural brown, olive or red, scented
tactics.rig: #8 to #10 dropshot hook nose-hooked, 3 to 7 g dropshot weight on a 10 to 20 cm tag, 0.15 to 0.20 mm fluorocarbon, ultra-light rod
tactics.retrieve: Drop it to the bottom against the wall, shake it in place for 10 to 20 seconds, then lift and move it a metre along the wall
tactics.depth: Bottom, tight to the wall or weed
tactics.stand: Along the harbour quay or breakwater, working the base of the wall block by block
tactics.why: Klipfish ambush small crustaceans and fish and blend in with the weed, so a tiny lure jiggled at their doorstep should draw strikes in clear water. This is inferred from diet and habitat; no Cape source covers it.

tactics.title: Big swell: fish inside the harbour
tactics.lure_or_bait: Small piece of sardine or worm
tactics.rig: #10 to #12 hook, 10 to 20 g sinker to hold against surge, 1 to 3 kg line
tactics.retrieve: Vertical drop at the foot of the inner quay; hold still
tactics.depth: Bottom, 1 to 4 m
tactics.stand: Inside the harbour basin, on the sheltered inner quay or slipway side. Stay off the exposed rocks and the outer breakwater. If waves are breaking over any part of the wall, don't fish.
tactics.why: This is a fallback, not an opportunity: the exposed rocks are dangerous in a big sea. A sheltered harbour wall has the same rock-and-weed habitat. That klipfish hole up during surge is an estimate. The rig adapts the District Mail's ultra-light harbour method for strepies and mullet.

tactics.title: Coloured water: smelly bait right on the structure
tactics.lure_or_bait: Small strip of sardine or chokka, or a piece of worm
tactics.rig: #10 to #12 hook, split shot, 1 to 3 kg line
tactics.retrieve: Hold it dead still in the gaps at the base of the rocks; give bites a second to develop
tactics.depth: Bottom, in the gaps
tactics.stand: On the rocks or wall in small seas only, fishing the nearest holes and gaps rather than open sand
tactics.why: In murky water a visual ambush predator struggles to see a lure, so scent bait placed in its hide-outs should work better (estimate). Sardine on a #12 hook adapts the District Mail's harbour method for strepies and mullet; it is not a klipfish-specific source.

legal.bag_note: Default of 10 per day for unlisted species. Counts toward the aggregate of 10. This is not a species-specific figure.
legal.note: Reconciled: A rated this medium and B rated it low, because B could not check the Annexure. I read the full R.959 Annexure 7 Prohibited and Permitted lists myself. Clinidae (klipfish) appears on neither, and no family-level entry covers them. The default therefore applies: 10 per day and no size limit (DFFE permit condition (7), capped by reg 22(7)(f)). I set confidence to medium because the figur
legal.quote: '(7) Species not mentioned in either of these lists have a bag limit of ten provided that sharks, rays, skates or chimaeras (Class Chondrichthyes) have a bag limit of one and rockcods (Family Serranidae) have a bag limit of five.'

sources: Sealine thread 'Fishing from Houtbay Harbour', 2011 (MPA no-take note), opened 29 Oct 2026
klipvis.review: Checked by an independent skeptic; 15 corrections applied
review_points: The cited range, northern Namibia to the Kei River, includes the whole warm-temperate south coast, where inshore water regularly tops 20 C. Calling it a cold-temperate family contradicts the profile's own source. A 21 C max and 17 C ideal top would mark ordinary summer False Bay water (Kalk Bay, abo
The article gives this method for catching strepies and mullet (for bait). It does not mention klipfish. Using it is a reasonable adaptation, but the wording suggests a klipfish-specific source.

The cached snippet says 'mostly catching ... klipvis' alongside gurnard, maasbanker and shy sharks, and does not say these were shore catches. Gurnard and maasbanker suggest at least partly boat or harbour fishing.
This is a minor imprecision: the forum source says 3.3 nm at its widest point. The substance (Karbonkelberg restricted zone, Oudekraal to Hout Bay) is supported by Wikipedia.
This is not wrong: viviparity in Clinus superciliosus is well documented (Veith 1979). It can be moved out of 'unverified' with that citation.
unverified: No Cape angling source covers klipvis tactics specifically. The tactics adapt the District Mail's ultra-light harbour and tidal-pool method (written for strepies and mullet) plus biology.
Micro soft-plastic dropshot tactic: no source; inferred from diet and habitat
Every condition weight is an estimate; no study found on feeding by light, tide or sea state
Temperature band (10 / 12 to 20 / 24 C) is an estimate based on the species' range from cold to warm-temperate water
Peak months are an estimate based on the calmer summer seas on the Atlantic side
That klipfish hole up during surge (big-swell tactic) is an inference, not a sourced fact
The Sealine 2011 klipvis report does not say whether the fish were caught from shore or at which of Kalk Bay, Hermanus or Hout Bay
Whether the 'rockfish' reported at Blouberg (Sealine 2024) were klipfish rather than other small reef fish
Veith 1979 (viviparity) was cited by the reviewer from general literature and was not opened
Exact current Karbonkelberg zone boundaries and offshore extent; check SANParks zone maps

kob.name: Kob (kabeljou)
kob.season_note: Kob are in False Bay all year ('present year-round', District Mail, 25 Sep 2025), but the shore season really starts in early October, when the first south-easters stir up the brown 'kob water' (the 'Kobtober' column, Sep 2022; Cole, Mar 2020). It stays good until at least the end of April (District Mail, Jan 2025), and Naysmith gives October to April. Winter can still produce big fish. Winter kob of up to 15 kg were reported at Strand in 2022, after a strong easterly and a lot of colour in the water (District Mail, Sep 2022). Rain-coloured 'ginger beer' water pushed into the Strand to Gordon's Bay corner by a north-westerly is good kob water (District Mail, Jul 2023). On the Muizenberg to Strandfontein beaches, kob run from late August to March, mostly at night. On the Atlantic side (Blouberg, Derdesteen, Haakgat, Bontkop, Melkbos, Clifton), kob are a summer and autumn fish. They come in when warm, coloured water carrying mullet lies inshore and the swell drops to 1 to 1.5 m. A long south-easter brings up cold, clear upwelled water and empties those beaches. Both species occur in False Bay. Silver kob dominate the reefs and gullies, and local writers also identify surf and shorebreak kob as dusky kob. Anglers cannot reliably tell them apart. The spawn months follow silver kob, which spawn in South Africa all year but mainly from August to December, peaking from September to November.

temp.basis: ideal_hi 21 and the core ideal of 18 to 21 C come from Rob Naysmith's False Bay silver kob notes ('Where to fish part 3', Ski-Boat Nov 2021, Angler Publications). ideal_lo 16 comes from a West Coast forum remark about Tietiesbaai and Dwarskersbos ('when the water warms up above 16/17deg', Sealine, Oct 2014). That is outside this page's area, so it is used only as an analogue and is an estimate. max 24 is an estimate. A District Mail column (29 Jan 2025) called 20 to 24 C False Bay water 'extremely warm', said it made fish lethargic and fishing very difficult, but the same column reports a 16 kg kob from Macassar that week. So the warm penalty is kept mild. min 13 is an estimate. Clean, cold upwelled water is described as poor for kob (District Mail, Jul 2023; Sealine Melkbos thread, Feb 2024), and the natural range of SA dusky kob is given as 12 to 28 C (Rhodes thesis, seen only as a search summary).

kob.habitat: Sandy surf beaches with gutters, holes and troughs just behind the shorebreak. Also the edges of inshore reefs and gullies where sand meets rock (False Bay 'bricks' and the Strand reefs), harbour mouths and walls over sand (Kalk Bay, Hout Bay; harbour kob are occasional, so fish there only in small seas and never on an outer wall the swell washes over), and estuary or river mouths. From the shore they are caught in 1 to 4 m of water. Naysmith gives 3 to 30 m from a boat. They come shallower on the rising tide and at night ('Kob come in really close sometimes'). In False Bay they follow the murky 'kob water' the south-easter stirs up between Muizenberg and Gordon's Bay, and the wind decides where it lies. A true south-easter puts them from Kalk Bay to Strandfontein, a southerly from Strandfontein to Macassar, and a westerly or north-westerly at Strand and Gordon's Bay (Naysmith 2021; District Mail, Jul 2023). Two closed areas lie inside that stretch. The St James no-take zone lies between Kalk Bay and Muizenberg. The Helderberg MPA runs from the Eerste River mouth at Macassar to the Lourens River mouth at Strand, so fish Macassar west of the Eerste mouth and Strand east of the Lourens mouth. Silver kob dominate the reefs and gullies west of Cape Agulhas and are common in the surf zone of the cool Atlantic coast. Dusky kob are commoner east of Agulhas, where the juveniles grow up in turbid estuaries. Local writers identify False Bay surf and shorebreak kob as dusky too.
kob.diet: Fish and squid. Mullet (harders) are the main prey in the surf. Kob also take anchovy, maasbanker and mackerel, streepies (karanteen), round herring, small hake, chokka (squid) and octopus. Juveniles take shrimp and mysids, plus prawns and worms. Kob hunt with the lateral line in discoloured water and 'seldom chase fast-moving prey' (District Mail, Sep 2025; Wikipedia/IUCN for silver kob diet; Filmalter 2020 for dusky kob juveniles).
kob.typical_size: Most shore kob around Cape Town are 35 to 70 cm (about 0.5 to 4 kg). Many are juveniles of 35 to 45 cm, caught at night on the Strand reefs (District Mail, Jan 2025), and Monwabisi reports are mostly undersized and near-legal fish. A big one is 10 to 16 kg. A 16 kg kob came from Macassar in Jan 2025, and winter kob of up to 15 kg were reported in Sep 2022. Large surf kob may be dusky kob (see handling). Silver kob reach 145 cm and 36 kg; dusky kob reach about 2 m and 80 kg.
kob.handling: No dangerous spines or teeth. A recreational permit is required. West of Cape Agulhas, which covers every spot on this page, the minimum is 50 cm and the bag is 5 per person per day for all kob (Argyrosomus) species, with no closed season (MLRA Annexure 7 as amended Nov 2012). The 60 cm, 1-fish shore and estuary rule applies east of Cape Agulhas only. Local columns still quote 60 cm (Mattheys, Sep 2025), so check the current DFFE brochure. Silver kob are IUCN Vulnerable, with all stocks overfished. Dusky kob adult biomass is estimated at 1 to 4.5% of pristine. Both species occur here and anglers cannot reliably tell them apart. Treat any big surf kob as possibly dusky and release it, and release anything under about 60 cm. Use circle hooks, wet your hands, and support the fish horizontally. Never drag it over dry sand, keep it out of the water only briefly, and cut the line on a deep-hooked fish. Tag through the ORI tagging programme. Never fish the St James no-take zone (between Kalk Bay and Muizenberg) or the Helderberg MPA (between the Eerste River mouth at Macassar and the Lourens River mouth at Strand). Stay off exposed rocks in big swell, and don't fish alone after dark.

tactics.title: Night bait in the deepest gutter
tactics.lure_or_bait: Chokka strip and sardine fillet combo, or a fresh streepie or mullet fillet (Mattheys: 'a strepie fillet can be deadly' in False Bay), 10 to 12 cm long. Use a 4/0 to 6/0 circle hook with a small piece of foam or a 'dingle dangle' float to lift the bait off the sand. A strepie kept for bait must be at least 15 cm and counts toward the 10-strepie bag.
tactics.rig: Running (sliding) sinker: a 2 to 3 oz (56 to 85 g) grapnel on a sinker slide, then a swivel and 60 to 80 cm of 0.5 to 0.6 mm mono or fluorocarbon trace to the circle hook. Main line 0.35 mm mono or 20 to 30 lb braid on a 9 to 10 ft rod. This is the top end of light tackle and suits the 35 to 60 cm kob most nights produce. Local writers use 14 kg line and heavier for big kob, which is beyond this page's light-tackle scope.
tactics.retrieve: Cast and leave it. Let the circle hook set itself: just wind tight and lift when the rod loads. Rebait every 20 to 30 minutes, because fresh bait matters.
tactics.depth: On the bottom, in 1 to 3 m of water at the back of the gutter or hole behind the shorebreak
tactics.stand: On the sand opposite the deepest, most coloured gutter or hole. At reef-edge spots, cast onto the sand patch beside the rock, not into it. Kob come in very close at night, so don't overcast. Fish with company after dark. Locals warn against fishing Muizenberg and Sunrise beaches alone at night.
tactics.why: Most shore kob in the Cape are caught after dark on fresh fish or chokka baits. Muizenberg kob come 'mostly at night', the small Strand reef kob 'especially at night', and kob 'often feed after dark' even in clean water.
sources: District Mail ?p=66200, 14 Sep 2022 (4/0 to 6/0 hooks, dingle dangle, chokka and sardine)
District Mail ?p=72637, 29 Jan 2025 (6/0 with flotation; night kob on Strand reefs)
District Mail ?p=65894, 30 Sep 2022 (heavier line for big reef kob)
Sealine 'Simon's Town to Kalk Bay', Jan 2008 ('Kob come in really close sometimes')
Cole, Angler Publications, Mar 2020 (circle hooks; feed after dark)

tactics.title: Low-light paddle-tail in coloured water
tactics.lure_or_bait: 5 to 6 inch (12 to 15 cm) paddle-tail or fluke on a 3/4 to 1 1/2 oz (20 to 40 g) jighead. Rig it weedless on an EWG hook over reef.
tactics.rig: 30 lb braid with 1 m of 50 to 60 lb fluorocarbon leader (80 lb over foul reef), joined with an FG knot. A 9 to 10 ft spinning rod casting 1 to 3 oz and a 4000 to 5000 reel.
tactics.retrieve: Low and slow. Let it hit bottom, then slow-roll it just above the sand, with rod-tip lifts and a pause on every drop. Most takes come as it falls.
tactics.depth: The bottom third of the water, 1 to 4 m
tactics.stand: On the beach, or on stable rocks the swell does not wash over, beside a gutter where white water rolls into deeper water. Cast across the gutter and work the lure back along the edge of the sandbank, or through the shallow water just behind the shorebreak.
tactics.colour: Pearl white or silver to imitate mullet. In very brown water, try a chartreuse or darker tail for silhouette (colour is an estimate).
tactics.why: Kob hunt by lateral line in murky water at low light and 'seldom chase fast-moving prey'. Cape lure anglers fish 'shallow water behind the shorebreak on beaches and on the bricks, specifically at dusk and dawn'. Botes ties that to dusky kob; silver kob hold more on the reefs and gullies.
sources: District Mail ?p=268986, 25 Sep 2025 (low and slow; paddle tails)
The Mission 'It's only rock & surf but I like it', 9 Aug 2020
Cole, Angler Publications, Mar 2020 (paddle-tails off the Strand reefs)

tactics.title: Pushing-tide bucktail on the surf beaches
tactics.lure_or_bait: 1 to 2 oz (28 to 56 g) bucktail jig with a 4 inch soft-plastic trailer, or a 20 to 40 g slow-pitch jig
tactics.rig: 30 lb braid, 1 m of 50 lb fluorocarbon leader, 9 to 10 ft rod casting 1 to 3 oz
tactics.retrieve: Cast beyond the gutter and let it sink to the sand. Then lift and drop: two slow turns of the handle, a rod lift, and let it flutter back down. Stay in touch with the bottom.
tactics.depth: Hopping along the bottom, 1 to 3 m
tactics.stand: On an open sand beach, opposite a rip or a deep trough between banks. Move up the beach as the water rises. The last two hours of the push and the first hour of high tide are the prime window, and spring tides are better.
tactics.colour: White or pearl bucktail with a white or pink trailer (estimate)
tactics.why: 'The last two hours of the pushing tide and first hour of high are prime feeding windows.' Kob move shallower as the tide rises. Strandfontein and Macassar are named as excellent for bucktails, jigs and stickbaits.
sources: Naysmith, 'Where to fish part 3', Angler Publications (Ski-Boat Nov 2021)
Jacita 'Mastering rock and surf fishing', 12 Aug 2025 ('on the push or turn of the tide')

tactics.title: Fly in the low-tide reef gullies
tactics.lure_or_bait: Light grey or white DMA (Jimmy Eagleton pattern), Clouser or silicone mullet, 2/0 to 4/0, 10 to 15 cm long
tactics.rig: 9 to 10 weight rod, intermediate or sink-tip line, 1.5 to 2 m of 30 to 40 lb fluorocarbon tippet
tactics.retrieve: Let the fly sink into the gully, then strip slowly with long pauses. If nothing takes in about 15 minutes, move to the next gully.
tactics.depth: Near the bottom of the gully, 1 to 3 m
tactics.stand: On a dry, stable rock well above a gully where foam rolls over shallow reef into a deeper pocket. Cast into the foam and let the wash carry the fly into the deep water. Only in flat or small surf, and in daylight or twilight. Never fish it alone, and never stand on a ledge the swell washes over.
tactics.why: False Bay fly anglers find silver kob in inshore reef gullies and foamy holes at low tide, with 'a take within the first five to ten casts' when kob are about. Botes, fishing the eastern False Bay reefs, found 'much of the action came during daylight', and a late-morning low tide fished well in 'Shark bait and silver kob'. Most of these reports come from float tubes and SUPs, so this rule adapts them for anglers on shore rocks, in calm water and daylight only.
sources: The Mission 'Shark bait and silver kob', 21 Apr 2020
The Mission ?p=62491 (Botes, eastern False Bay reefs, DMA, daylight action)
The Mission 'It's only rock & surf but I like it', 9 Aug 2020

tactics.title: Spin the south-easter kob water
tactics.lure_or_bait: Sinking stickbait of 90 to 120 mm (20 to 40 g), or a 30 to 60 g spoon
tactics.rig: 30 lb braid with 1 m of 50 lb fluorocarbon leader on a 9 to 10 ft rod. The heavier lure helps cast into the onshore wind.
tactics.retrieve: Slow, steady wind through the brown water and foam lines, with an occasional twitch. Let it sink close to the bottom before winding.
tactics.depth: Mid-water to bottom, 1 to 3 m
tactics.stand: On a beach the wind is blowing onto, where brown 'kob water', foam patches ('skuim kolle') and mullet shoals sit in the surf zone. In False Bay the wind direction picks the stretch. A south-easter puts kob from Kalk Bay to Strandfontein; skip the St James no-take zone between Kalk Bay and Muizenberg. A southerly puts them from Strandfontein to Macassar; stay west of the Eerste River mouth, because the shore from there to the Lourens River mouth is the Helderberg MPA, closed to fishing. A westerly or north-westerly puts them at Strand (east of the Lourens River mouth) and Gordon's Bay.
tactics.why: A south-easter blowing onshore along False Bay is called 'perfect Kob conditions'. Kob feed in the surf among mullet in the 'skuim kolle'. 'The prime fishing time for kob in False Bay is during or just after the south easterly gales slow down.' Bait is still the main Cape kob method. Cole notes that 'lures are not commonly used to target kob in False Bay', so treat spinning as the minority approach.
sources: Jacita 'Fishing report Cape Town October 2025' (20 to 26 Oct 2025)
District Mail, 11 Oct 2023 'Gearing up for the Cape spinning season'
District Mail ?p=268986, 25 Sep 2025 (stickbaits named for Strandfontein and Macassar)
District Mail ?p=85480 'Kob like the ginger beer water', 3 Jul 2023

tactics.title: Clear water: fish deep or wait for dark
tactics.lure_or_bait: A whole fresh maasbanker, mullet (harder) or streepie, or a chokka head 'guts and all', on a 4/0 to 6/0 circle hook. Catch the baitfish first on a sabiki or a size 12 hook. Maasbanker have no size or bag limit, and harders have no minimum size and a bag of 50. A strepie must be at least 15 cm and counts toward the 10-strepie bag, so release the small ones.
tactics.rig: Running sinker with the lightest lead that holds (1 to 3 oz), 60 cm of 0.5 to 0.6 mm fluorocarbon trace, 9 to 10 ft rod
tactics.retrieve: Leave it static in the deepest water
tactics.depth: On the bottom in the deepest water you can reach
tactics.stand: At the inner end of a harbour wall or a channel over sand, or a high, dry rock ledge above deep sand. Only when the swell is small: never on an outer wall or a ledge the swell washes over. On open beaches in clear, cold water, come back at dusk.
tactics.why: Clean, cold water is poor for kob, and anglers prefer 'murky water from an onshore wind' over clear water from an offshore wind. But clean water 'is not a reason to give up, since kob often feed after dark'. Harbours supply maasbanker and mackerel as kob bait.
sources: The Mission 'It's only rock & surf but I like it', 9 Aug 2020
District Mail ?p=53409, 17 Nov 2023 (sabiki for maasbanker in harbours)
MLRA Annexure 7 (strepie 15 cm and bag 10; harders bag 50; maasbanker no limit)

tactics.title: Off-temperature water: short night and first-light sessions
tactics.lure_or_bait: 4 to 5 inch paddle-tail on a 1/2 to 1 oz (14 to 28 g) jighead, or a strip of fresh chokka if bait fishing
tactics.rig: 20 to 30 lb braid with 1 m of 40 to 50 lb fluorocarbon leader on a 9 to 10 ft rod. For bait, a 1 to 3 oz running sinker.
tactics.retrieve: Dead slow along the bottom with long pauses, because kob are sluggish in water that is too warm or too cold
tactics.depth: Hard on the bottom in the deepest part of the gutter
tactics.stand: The deepest gutter or the harbour mouth, fished in the last hour of dark and at first light only. On the Atlantic side, after a long south-easter has upwelled cold, clear water, look for any brown patch with mullet in it.
tactics.why: In Jan 2025, 20 to 24 C water made fish 'lethargic' and fishing 'extremely' difficult, though the same week produced a 16 kg kob at Macassar. Clean, cold water is poor. West-coast anglers wait for warm surface water and look for 'a brown patch in otherwise clear water'.

tactics.title: Fresh bait or a slow paddle-tail in the nearest gutter
tactics.lure_or_bait: Chokka and sardine combo, or a fresh fish fillet (streepie of 15 cm or more, mullet, maasbanker), on a 4/0 to 5/0 circle hook with a small foam float
tactics.rig: Running sinker: a 2 to 3 oz grapnel on a slide, 60 to 80 cm of 0.5 to 0.6 mm trace, and a 9 to 10 ft rod with 0.35 mm mono or 20 to 30 lb braid. This is the top end of light tackle, suited to kob of 35 to 60 cm in calm gutters. Big kob need heavier surf gear.
tactics.retrieve: Cast to the back of the gutter and leave it, rebaiting often. If you prefer a lure, slow-roll a 5 inch paddle-tail along the bottom.
tactics.depth: On the bottom, 1 to 3 m
tactics.stand: On the beach opposite the deepest, most coloured hole or gutter, or on the sand beside a reef edge. Fish it hardest around high tide and at dusk, and with company after dark.
tactics.why: Chokka and sardine are the staple Cape kob baits, and kob hold in holes and gutters close to shore on sandy beaches.
sources: Jacita 'Mastering rock and surf fishing', 12 Aug 2025 (chokka and sardine for kob)

legal.bag_note: West of Cape Agulhas, which covers the whole Cape Town area: 5 per day, silver and dusky kob combined. Counts toward the
legal.note: A and B agree and both match R.959. The rules depend on area, so the page must say it shows the west-of-Agulhas row. East of Cape Agulhas, kob caught in estuaries and from the shore: 60 cm, 1 per day. From a boat at sea between Cape Agulhas and the Umtamvuna River: 50 cm, 5 per day, but only one kob over 110 cm. From a boat in KZN: 40 cm. The over-110 cm cap is not attached to the west-of-Agulhas
legal.quote: Kob [West of Cape Agulhas only] | Argyrosomus spp | 50 cm | 5  ;  Kob caught in estuaries & from the shore [East of Cape Agulhas only] | Argyrosomus spp. | 60 cm | 1  ;  Kob caught from a boat at sea [Cape Agulhas to Umtamvuna River] | Argyrosomus spp. | 50 cm | 5, but may only land or be in possession of one kob > 110 cm

kob.review: Checked by an independent skeptic; 25 corrections applied
review_points: The cited Annexure 7 page (fetched 2 Nov 2026) has no aggregate 10-fish limit. Ten appears there only as single-species bags, for example strepie. The 10-fish total is attributed to a source that does not contain it.

The profile's own sources contradict this. Mattheys (?p=268986, its main False Bay lure source) identifies False Bay shore kob as Argyrosomus japonicus (dusky kob). The Mission 'It's only rock & surf' links the quote 'shallow water behind the shorebreak on beaches and on the bricks, specifically at

The Cape shore and reef fly reports partly contradict this. Botes (The Mission ?p=62491), fishing the eastern False Bay reefs, reports that 'much of the action came during daylight'. In 'Shark bait and silver kob', Jannie found good catches at a late-morning low tide. Night is better (Cole; Strand r

Local reports tie the best kob bites to strong wind. 'Hello Kobtober' (?p=65894) says 'strong south-easterly winds and flat seas with coloured water are when kob bite best'. ?p=66200 says catches rose after 'a lot of colour and a strong easterly wind blowing'. Jacita calls the onshore south-easter '
'Hello Kobtober' says flat seas with coloured water are when kob bite best, at Strand and on the reefs. The profile lists sea.flat as unverified, but the one direct source contradicts a 0.5 penalty.

This is standard rock-and-surf (medium-heavy) tackle, not the page's 'light bait fishing with small hooks'. The Cape sources push heavier still: Mattheys advises 14 to 18 kg line, minimum 14 kg and up to 36 kg, with 6/0 to 10/0 hooks on the False Bay reefs (?p=65894), and Naysmith uses 5/0 to 10/0 h

The sources are float-tube and SUP sessions, and The Mission describes boulder fields in surf after dark as 'very demanding'. Sending a shore fly angler onto wet reef ledges at night in 1 to 1.8 m surf is unsafe, and the only shore-based fly report (Botes, ?p=62491) is from daylight, morning and eve

Legality. Under Annexure 7, strepie (Sarpa salpa) has a 15 cm minimum size and a bag of 10. The small strepies a size 12 hook or sabiki usually catches in harbours are often under 15 cm, and keeping them as bait is illegal. Strepies kept for bait also count toward the 10-fish bag.
unverified: temp.min 13 C is an estimate: no source gives the temperature at which Cape kob stop feeding
temp.ideal_lo 16 C comes from a West Coast (Tietiesbaai/Dwarskersbos) forum remark used as an analogue, not a Cape Town observation
temp.max 24 C is an estimate. The Jan 2025 column called 20 to 24 C water bad for fishing in general, but reported a 16 kg kob at Macassar in the same week, so the warm penalty is kept mild.
trend weights (falling 0.8, steady 0.8, rising 0.7) are estimates; no source links air-pressure trend to the kob bite

wind weights are estimates. strong was raised to 0.85 because local reports tie the best bites to strong onshore south-easters with coloured water ('Hello Kobtober', ?p=66200, Jacita Oct 2025). No source gives km/h thresholds.

light weights are numeric estimates. The ranking (night > dusk > dawn > overcast day > bright day) is sourced. day_bright was raised to 0.45 because Botes and 'Shark bait and silver kob' report daylight reef and gully catches.
flow 0.6 is an estimate (gutters, rips and the spring-tide note suggest moderate water movement helps)
sea weights are estimates. flat was raised to 0.75 because 'Hello Kobtober' names flat seas with coloured water as when kob bite best.

Details for Atlantic seaboard spots (Clifton, Camps Bay rocks, Bontkop, Haakgat, Hout Bay harbour) are extrapolated from the Melkbos and Blouberg reports and from general silver kob biology. Shore reports from those exact spots are sparse.

Lure sizes, jighead weights and lure colours are estimates within the lure types the sources name (paddle-tails, bucktails, stickbaits, spoons, 20 to 30 g slow-pitch jigs). Only the light grey DMA fly colour is sourced.
The fly gully tactic adapts float-tube and SUP reports to anglers standing on shore rocks

The light-tackle bait rigs (2 to 3 oz sinker, 9 to 10 ft rod, 0.35 mm line, 4/0 to 6/0 circle hook) were scaled down to fit this page. The Cape sources fish heavier gear (14 kg line and up, 6/0 to 10/0 hooks) for big kob.

Regulations (west of Cape Agulhas: 50 cm, 5 per day, no closed season) come from Annexure 7 as amended Nov 2012 and may be out of date. Local columns quote 60 cm (Mattheys, Sep 2025), and Mattheys (Feb 2026) gives about one fish and about 50 cm, so check the current DFFE brochure. The earlier 10-fish aggregate daily limit was dropped because Annexure 7 does not contain it.
Spawn months reflect silver kob (main August to December) from Wikipedia/IUCN and a search summary of Griffiths 1997; the Mann 2013 ORI profile text was not reached
Dusky kob spawning timing and location: the reviewer recalls Eastern Cape spring and summer spawning as well as KZN (Griffiths 1996), but this was not checked
The dusky kob adult biomass figure (1 to 4.5% of pristine) is not tied to a source re-checked in this revision
The 12 to 28 C dusky kob natural range and the 16 to 21.5 C juvenile silver kob gradient come from search summaries of theses, not full texts
The 15 kg winter kob location (Strand) is from the researcher's reading of ?p=66200; the reviewer confirmed the 15 kg figure but did not restate the place

largemouth-bass.name: Largemouth bass
largemouth-bass.season_note: Bass are a resident alien species, so they can be caught all year. FOSAF names spring and autumn as the best seasons and says summer is also good if you fish very early or very late in the day. Fish The Fly prefers spring and summer. Winter is slow: fish the warmest part of the day, slowly and near the bottom (FOSAF, Fish The Fly). Bass spawn in October, and the males guard nests and fry in shallow water (FOSAF). FishBase says spawning starts at about 15 C and that bass do not feed while spawning. The peak months are therefore an estimate: autumn (March to May) plus pre-spawn and early spawn (September and October). November and December to February are good but not peak. One spot has a limited season. Door De Kraal Dam is open October to April only, for 'limited and controlled fishing' with permits, and has been since 2007 (City of Cape Town Media Office, 18 Feb 2020). A 2025 Weekend Argus article still names it as a designated City fishing site. The engine should give that spot zero for May to September.

temp.basis: The min of 10 and max of 32 come from the FishBase temperature range (10 to 32 C). The IUCN GISD also says populations do not persist where the annual water temperature is below 10 C. FishBase says bass stop feeding below 5 C and above 37 C. The ideal band of 18 to 27 C is an estimate: it sits above the spawning trigger of 15 to 16 C (FishBase, Wikipedia) and below the summer surface temperatures of shallow Cape Flats vleis.

largemouth-bass.habitat: A freshwater ambush predator of still water and backwaters that hunts close to structure. FishBase lists it as freshwater only, with no brackish water. Look for weedbeds, lily pads, bulrush and reed edges, rocky reefs, submerged trees, drop-offs and inlets (FOSAF; Fish The Fly). FishBase lists lakes, ponds, swamps, backwaters and river pools, at 0 to 6 m deep. The IUCN GISD says it prefers clear, quiet water and overgrown banks. At the Cape spots, that means two kinds of water. The first is the shallow, reed-fringed Cape Flats vleis (Princess Vlei, Little Princess Vlei). The second is the small urban Door De Kraal Dam (Bellville/Durbanville), which needs a City permit and is open October to April only. Angling at other City dams has been banned since 2005 (City of Cape Town, 2020). Bass at Zandvlei are not confirmed. CapeNature's species list for Sandvlei and the reserve management plan do not name them, and the only mention found is one 2008 Sealine forum post. Sealine anglers report that bass in heavily fished waters near Cape Town are 'very cautious of any lures'.
largemouth-bass.diet: Adult bass eat fish, crayfish and frogs (FishBase). FOSAF adds aquatic insects, including dragonfly nymphs, and adult dragonflies taken at the surface. Juveniles eat crustaceans, insects and small fish (FishBase). Locally, likely prey includes tilapia and carp fry, mosquitofish and frogs (an estimate). In South Africa, bass have been recorded eating migrating estuarine fish (African Zoology 2006, seen as a title only).
largemouth-bass.typical_size: Fish from urban Cape vleis and dams are mostly 0.2 to 0.8 kg (25 to 35 cm), which is an estimate. A good fish is about 1 kg and 40 cm or more: FOSAF gives 40 cm and 1 kg after two years. The upper ends of 1.5 kg and 45 cm are estimates. A big fish is over 2.5 kg. For comparison, Eikenhof (Grabouw) fish are mostly under 1 kg during the day, with fish up to about 2.5 kg at dawn and in the evening (Sealine 2023). Some private Elgin and Grabouw farm dams hold fish over 3 to 4 kg (Sealine 2023). FOSAF gives the South African record as 4.5 kg.
largemouth-bass.handling: Bass have no teeth, only rough pads, but the dorsal fin is spiny. Land a bass by gripping its lower lip, and support the belly of a big fish. Bass are an invasive alien species: never move live bass between waters. CapeNature requires a permit to move live fish. You need a CapeNature recreational freshwater angling licence in public waters if you are over 6, but not on private farm dams. Door De Kraal Dam also needs a City permit and is open October to April only. The City has banned angling at its other dams since 2005. Under FOSAF's summary of the 2014 regulations, bass caught in rivers should be killed, and bass from recognised bass dams and farm dams may be released. Check the rule at each vlei and reserve before you release a fish. Zandvlei is not a confirmed bass water, and it is a nature reserve. If you fish there, you also need the national DFFE recreational angling permit (from the Post Office or tackle shops). The reserve plan says both provincial and national permits apply. The Zandvlei Trust says indigenous fish such as leervis must be released, by law. The estuary is a nursery for threatened juvenile white steenbras, and the indigenous Cape galaxias lives there. Bait collection is not allowed.

tactics.title: Dawn and dusk topwater on the reed line
tactics.lure_or_bait: 60 to 70 mm cupped popper or walk-the-dog stickbait (6 to 9 g), or a weedless hollow-body frog (8 to 12 g) over lily pads and weed. Fly anglers: deer-hair popper or slider, sizes 2 to 6, on a floating line.
tactics.rig: 10 to 15 lb braid with about 1 m of 6 to 8 kg mono leader (mono floats, which helps the popper). Use the lure's own trebles, or the frog's built-in double hook. On fly, use a 2.5 to 3 m leader for surface flies (FOSAF).
tactics.retrieve: Pop once, then wait until the rings die (3 to 5 seconds). Twitch and pause again. Strike only when you feel weight, not at the splash.
tactics.depth: Surface, over 0.3 to 1.5 m of water
tactics.stand: Walk the bank and cast parallel to the bulrush edge and into the gaps in the lily pads, not straight out into open water. In a light breeze, start on the {downwind} bank.
tactics.colour: Natural frog green or bone. Black on dark mornings.
tactics.why: FOSAF says the best times are early morning and late afternoon in summer, and that poppers work well in low light. At a Winelands farm dam in midsummer, The Mission found that poppers and sliders were taken as they landed on the bulrush and lily-pad edges.

tactics.title: Bright sun: dropshot the shade and the first drop-off
tactics.lure_or_bait: 3 to 4 inch finesse worm or small soft minnow, nose-hooked
tactics.rig: Size 1 or 2 dropshot hook. 3.5 to 5 g dropshot weight 30 to 45 cm below the hook. 8 to 10 lb fluorocarbon leader on light braid.
tactics.retrieve: Cast and let it settle. Shake the rod tip on a slack line without moving the weight. Drag it 30 cm, then pause 5 to 10 seconds.
tactics.depth: On the bottom, on the first drop-off (about 1 to 3 m)
tactics.stand: Shaded banks, overhanging trees, and the steepest or deepest bank you can reach (for example, near a dam wall). Cast along the bank, not across it.
tactics.colour: Green pumpkin, watermelon or natural brown
tactics.why: General bass practice (an estimate, not from a Cape source) is that bright light pushes bass into shade, cover and deeper water. On a sunny midsummer visit to a Winelands farm dam, The Mission found the surface bite 'wasn't really on'. Fish The Fly says to fish structure and drop-offs. Bass close to Cape Town are heavily fished and wary of lures (Sealine), which suits a slow finesse presentation.

tactics.title: Cold water: slow on the bottom in the warmest hours
tactics.lure_or_bait: 3 inch paddle-tail, or a small craw or creature bait, on a 3.5 to 5 g jighead. Or a 5 inch stick worm, wacky-rigged. On steep banks, a finesse worm on a slow dropshot also works.
tactics.rig: 3.5 to 5 g jighead with a 1/0 to 2/0 hook, or a size 1 wacky hook with an O-ring. 8 to 10 lb fluorocarbon leader.
tactics.retrieve: Drag and hop it slowly along the bottom with long pauses. Slow everything down.
tactics.depth: On the bottom, in the deepest water you can reach (2 to 4 m)
tactics.stand: The deepest bank: steep sides, or near the dam wall. Fish in the early afternoon, when the water is warmest.
tactics.why: FOSAF says big fish come in winter on a slow retrieve close to the bottom. Fish The Fly says winter is slow, so fish when the water is warmest. At Albert Falls (KwaZulu-Natal, so not a Cape source), ECR reports that cold snaps mean slow fishing, and that a drop-shot fished slowly on steeper banks kept producing.

tactics.title: Wind: fish the wind-blown bank
tactics.lure_or_bait: Size 2 to 3 inline spinner (5 to 7 g), a compact 7 to 10 g spinnerbait, or a 50 to 60 mm lipless crankbait (7 to 10 g)
tactics.rig: 10 to 15 lb braid with a 1 m fluorocarbon leader of 8 to 12 lb. Use a small snap so the lure can swing freely.
tactics.retrieve: Steady, just fast enough to feel the blade or rattle working. Stop it dead every few metres.
tactics.depth: The top 1 to 1.5 m
tactics.stand: {downwind}. Cast along the shoreline and the reed edge rather than straight out.
tactics.colour: White or silver in clear water, chartreuse in murky water
tactics.why: Wind piles baitfish and plankton onto the shore it blows towards, and the ripple hides the line from wary fish. This is standard bass-angling practice, but no Cape-specific source for it was found.
sources: estimate: no source found; general bass-angling practice

tactics.title: Coloured water after rain: vibration at the inflows
tactics.lure_or_bait: 7 to 10 g spinnerbait with a Colorado blade, or a 3 inch paddle-tail on a 5 g jighead
tactics.rig: 10 to 15 lb braid with a 1 m fluorocarbon leader of 10 to 12 lb
tactics.retrieve: Slow-roll so the blade thumps, close to reeds and other cover. Bump the lure into the cover.
tactics.depth: The top 1 m, along the edge
tactics.stand: Stream and stormwater inflows, and the line where coloured water meets clearer water. Work the reed edge next to them.
tactics.colour: Chartreuse and white, or black and blue
tactics.why: Fish The Fly says to always fish around structure, drop-offs and inlets. In murky water, bass hunt more by vibration than by sight. The lure colours and the vibration rule are estimates.

tactics.title: Spring shallows: pre-spawn and nest guarders
tactics.lure_or_bait: 4 to 5 inch stick worm, weightless or wacky-rigged, or a weedless creature bait
tactics.rig: Size 1 wacky hook, or a 3/0 offset worm hook (weedless). 8 to 10 lb fluorocarbon leader.
tactics.retrieve: Cast beyond the clear or sandy shallow patches by the reeds. Let it sink slowly on a slack line, twitch it, then leave it lying still.
tactics.depth: Shallows, 0.5 to 1.5 m
tactics.stand: Sheltered, sun-warmed shallow bays and reed margins
tactics.colour: Green pumpkin or watermelon in clear water, black in stained water
tactics.why: Bass spawn in October, and the males guard nests and fry in shallow water (FOSAF). Spawning starts at about 15 to 16 C (FishBase, Wikipedia). FishBase says bass do not feed while spawning. General bass practice (not from the cited sources) is that guarding males strike at anything near the nest to drive it off. CapeNature sets no closed season for bass.

tactics.title: Fly: dragonfly nymph on the drop
tactics.lure_or_bait: Size 6 beadhead dragonfly nymph or Strip Leech. Alternatives: Woolly Bugger, Mrs Simpson or Clouser, sizes 4 to 8.
tactics.rig: 6 to 7 weight rod: FOSAF calls a 7 weight about the lightest rod to consider, and Fish The Fly says a 6/7 weight does the job. Intermediate line. About 1 m of leader for subsurface flies. Tippet 3 to 5 kg, and not less than 5 kg near heavy cover.
tactics.retrieve: Cast to structure and let the fly sink while you watch the line, because takes often come on the drop. Then strip in short pulls, or use a slow figure-of-eight.
tactics.depth: 0.5 to 2 m, along the base of the weed edge
tactics.stand: Weedbeds, lily pads, reed edges and submerged branches. Cast parallel to the edge.
tactics.why: FOSAF says to start with an intermediate line and a size 6 beadhead dragonfly nymph or Strip Leech, and that takes come as the fly sinks. Fish The Fly gives the rod, tippet and line set-up.

tactics.title: Weedless fluke or paddle-tail along the edges
tactics.lure_or_bait: 4 to 5 inch soft jerkbait (fluke) rigged weightless, or a 3 inch paddle-tail on a 3.5 g jighead
tactics.rig: 3/0 offset worm hook for the fluke, or a 3.5 g jighead with a 1/0 hook. 10 to 15 lb braid with a 1 m fluorocarbon leader of 8 to 10 lb.
tactics.retrieve: Fluke: twitch twice, then pause, so it darts, glides, and sinks on the pause. Paddle-tail: slow-roll with pauses.
tactics.depth: The top 1 to 1.5 m, and the edge of the drop-off
tactics.stand: Walk the bank and work the reed edges, lily-pad gaps, inlets and drop-offs. Make a few casts at each piece of cover, then move on.
tactics.colour: White or pearl in clear water. Darker in stained water.
tactics.why: Writing about Eikenhof near Grabouw, a Cape angler advised: 'Go for soft plastics, especially smallish flukes'. On an overcast midsummer day, The Mission found that the surface bite came back. Fish The Fly says to always fish around structure, drop-offs, inlets and banks.

legal.bag_note: No bag or size limit (an alien species).
legal.release: Putting it straight back where you caught it is allowed where it already occurs, but not in national parks or nature reserves; never move live fish to another water.

The same page says a 2005 moratorium bans angling at all other City dams, which bears on whether other City-managed waters are

The Zandvlei Trust says 'A fishing permit is required which is obtainable from any Post Office or some fishing tackle shops', which is the national DFFE recreational angling permit. The IRMP says fishing there 'is regulated through the issuance o

None of the official or reserve sources lists bass at Zandvlei. CapeNature's species list for 'Sandvlei' is 'carp, Mozambique tilapia, sharptooth catfish and mullet'. The Zandvlei IRMP counts six alien fish but names only carp. The Zandvlei Trust fauna page names no bass. The FishBase summary fetche

Bass presence there is unsupported (see above). The tactic sends a juvenile-fish imitation into the reserve's recruitment area for leervis and steenbras. White steenbras is the reserve's 'only one threatened species' (IRMP), and leervis release is required by law. In practice the most likely catches

The ECR piece is a KwaZulu-Natal winter report about cold snaps. It says nothing about light or warm water. This is a cold-water observation from another region, moved onto a summer bright-sun condition. The why text also says 'The low light and wind weights are estimates', which does not belong in

This is a generic clarity tactic that will fire at every bass spot (Door De Kraal, Princess Vlei), but its stand text names the inflow at one water, and a water where bass presence is unverified. Users at other spots get directions that do not apply to them.

The cited Mission bass article (Buckets of Buckets) does not mention tadpoles. The only cached tadpole line is from a different Mission river article, where the author speculates 'tadpoles are plentiful in early summer?' about another fish. The FishBase summary says 'Adults feed on fishes, crayfish

FishBase says bass 'don't feed during spawning'. FOSAF says spring and autumn are best and 'summer is also good'. Fish The Fly prefers 'Spring and Summer'. Peak months that include the core spawning month but leave out September (pre-spawn) and all of summer are weakly supported. They are labelled a
unverified: The ideal temperature band of 18 to 27 C is an estimate. Only the 10 to 32 C range and the 5 C and 37 C feeding limits are sourced, from FishBase.
Light weights: dawn and dusk are backed by FOSAF. Day-bright 0.4 and day-dull 0.7 are estimates; The Mission's sunny versus overcast visits partly support day-dull being higher than day-bright.

Night is set to 0 because night shore access at Door De Kraal, Princess Vlei and Little Princess Vlei (all City-managed) was not checked. Biologically, bass do feed at night (the earlier estimate was 0.25). Raise it only for a spot where night angling is confirmed as allowed.
The pressure-trend weights (falling 0.8, steady 1, rising 0.5) are estimates from common bass-angling belief about cold fronts. No source was found.
The wind weights (calm 0.8, breeze 1, strong 0.5) are estimates.
The clarity weight for coloured water (0.55) is an estimate, based only on GISD's 'prefers clear, quiet water'.
flow 0.2 is an estimate from habitat descriptions (FishBase: lakes, ponds, backwaters).
Tide and range are set to a neutral 1 because the species is treated as freshwater only.

Peak months [3, 4, 5, 9, 10] are an estimate. FOSAF names only seasons, and FishBase says bass do not feed while spawning. Spawn months October to November are an estimate built from FOSAF's 'October'.

Typical sizes for Cape urban vleis are estimates. The only local size data comes from Eikenhof and farm dams (Sealine). The good-fish upper ends of 1.5 kg and 45 cm are estimates; FOSAF gives 40 cm and 1 kg at two years.

These are general bass practice, not Cape-sourced: the bright-sun shade and dropshot tactic, the wind-blown-bank tactic, the lure colours and vibration rule for coloured water, and the claim that nest-guarding males strike at lures.
The Afrikaans name 'grootbekbaars' is not confirmed against a source.
Bass at Princess Vlei and Little Princess Vlei rest on the page's own spot verification. The only external hint is a second-hand 2020 Sealine post about fish from 'Little Prinsses Vlei'.

Bass at Zandvlei: low confidence. The only evidence is one 2008 Sealine forum mention. They are absent from CapeNature's species list for Sandvlei (carp, Mozambique tilapia, sharptooth catfish, mullet), and the reserve management plan names only carp among its six alien fish. Do not treat Zandvlei as a bass spot unless the spot verification has better evidence.
Not checked: whether the City's 2005 moratorium on angling at City dams affects Princess Vlei or Little Princess Vlei, and what fishing rules apply at each of them.

The Door De Kraal October to April season comes from a City media page dated 18 Feb 2020. The 2025 Weekend Argus article confirms it is still a designated site but does not restate the season.
The African Zoology 2006 record of bass eating estuarine fish was seen only as a search-result title; the abstract was not read (nisc.com returned 404).
The web search budget ran out partway through, so no SA Bass magazine, Stream X or SA Bass club tactical articles were reviewed.

leervis.name: Leervis (garrick)
leervis.season_note: Zandvlei has a resident population of good-sized leervis (Wale, The Mission 2023). In the Breede Estuary in the Western Cape, tagged adults were present all year, and presence was 'largely unaffected by month of the year' (Kilian et al. 2025). The best Cape fishing is on warm summer days (Sealine 2009 names February; a December catch was six fish of 50 to 80 cm). The Cape spinning season opens around October, when the south-easter arrives and the sea warms (Mattheys, District Mail, Oct 2023). Surface flies work in early summer (Killick 2025). A June 2009 post says the fish are less active in winter. So May to September stay in the season, but cold water scores them down; they are not marked absent (estimate). Many mature fish are thought to migrate up the east coast to spawn off KwaZulu-Natal from September to November (general knowledge, not checked here). Zandvlei's mouth stays open in winter. In summer it is kept closed except for a few days around the full-moon spring tide, so tide tactics there apply only while it is open. Zandvlei is reported closed to angling from sunset to sunrise, so at Zandvlei 'dawn' and 'dusk' mean the first and last hour of legal daylight. Reports from Milnerton Lagoon are thin: sizeable fish in the 1980s and a juvenile near the wooden bridge around 2011. Rietvlei is historic only (1980s), and its 07:30 to 17:00 fishing hours rule out dawn and dusk there.

temp.basis: Estimate. FishBase/AquaMaps gives a modelled preferred temperature of 16.2 to 29 °C (mean 26.3, from 478 cells; not rechecked). Cape anglers favour 'really warm days in summer', and a June 2009 post says the fish are less active then (Sealine). The 15/18/25/28 cut-offs are estimates placed inside the modelled range to suit Cape inshore and vlei water. Winter fish score lower in this band but are not treated as absent. No measured Cape thermal threshold was found.

leervis.habitat: A coastal pelagic predator of the surf zone, backline, rocky points and estuaries, in water from 0 to 50 m deep. Juveniles grow up in Cape estuaries, and Zandvlei is a recognised recruitment area for the species. In the Breede Estuary, tagged adults stayed mostly in the lower reaches (Kilian et al. 2025). In Zandvlei the fish hold on channel drop-offs, shallow banks and weed-bed edges. Named spots are the stretch from the yacht club to the bridge near the mouth, the first bend after the footbridge, the bowling-green (first big) bend, Uitsig Point and the first channel, the main island, and up into the Marina da Gama channels. At Milnerton Lagoon the named spots are the old wooden bridge and the old pump station. In the surf, look for a hole or gutter with a bank behind it and a channel out to sea. Garrick feed close in.
leervis.diet: A fish-eater that hunts near the surface. In Cape estuaries it eats harders (mullet) and Gilchrist's round herring (Gilchristella aestuaria), a small shoaling baitfish. The Stella fly was developed for Zandvlei leervis feeding on round herring (Wale). It also takes blacktail, small stumpnose and shad. Juveniles eat mainly crustaceans (FishBase).
leervis.typical_size: Most Zandvlei fish are 50 to 80 cm (about 2 to 5 kg), and a 70 cm fish on fly is a good catch. A big Cape fish is 10 to 12 kg (one angler's best was about 12 kg on a spinner). An anecdotal 24 kg leervis was taken on fly at Zandvlei in 2004. The SA angling record is reported as 32.2 kg, and the species can reach 2 m and 50 kg.
leervis.handling: Recreational species that may not be sold (listed as SASSI Red; not rechecked here). National limits: 70 cm minimum, measured as total length (in a straight line from the tip of the snout to the end of the tail), and 2 per person per day (DFFE recreational regulations, R1111 Annexure 7). At Zandvlei, the Zandvlei Trust says catch and release of indigenous species such as leervis is required by law. You need a fishing permit (from the Post Office or tackle shops), and angling is reported closed from sunset to sunrise. Rietvlei (Table Bay Nature Reserve) rules: a CapeNature freshwater permit, fishing hours 07:30 to 17:00, line including leader no heavier than 4.5 kg breaking strain, at most two hooks per rod, and indigenous fish must be returned. Milnerton Lagoon has recurring sewage contamination, so wash your hands and do not keep fish. Leervis are clean fighters, so keep the fight short with a leader of 7 kg or more (except at Rietvlei, where the 4.5 kg limit applies). Use single, barbless or circle hooks. Wet your hands, support the fish horizontally in the water, keep your fingers out of the gills, and revive it before letting go. Watch for the short, sharp free spines ahead of the dorsal and anal fins. Zandvlei regulars ask anglers not to tag Zandvlei fish, because the tags leave holes.

tactics.title: Low-light walk-the-dog over the banks
tactics.lure_or_bait: Walk-the-dog stickbait or popper, 7 to 11 cm and 8 to 15 g: Zara Spook or Super Spook Jr, Rapala Skitter Walk, Skitter V or Pencil 107, Skitter Pop or Chug Bug. Swap the trebles for a single or barbless hook.
tactics.colour: white, bone or light pink; silver or blue popper
tactics.retrieve: Steady walk-the-dog, fast enough that the lure skates. If a fish swirls behind it, speed up rather than stop. Expect follows and refusals: change the speed, not the lure, and work it right to your feet.
tactics.depth: surface, over 0.5 to 2 m of water
tactics.stand: A point or bend where a channel drop-off meets a shallow bank or weed bed. Cast across the shallows where baitfish dimple. At Zandvlei: the yacht club to the bridge near the mouth, the first bend after the footbridge, or the bowling-green bend. Fish only after sunrise and before sunset there, because night angling is reported closed. At Milnerton Lagoon: the old wooden bridge.
tactics.rig: 7 ft light-medium spinning rod, 2500 to 4000 reel, 10 to 20 lb braid, 1 m of 12 kg mono or fluorocarbon leader, small oval split ring on the lure
tactics.why: Leervis feed best in low light. Rush of Blue rates dawn and dusk best. Zandvlei regulars report early morning best and most strikes in the late afternoon (Sealine), and sunrise and sunset are named as garrick times (4x4community, via search). Killick gets a better hook-up rate in low light with a fast retrieve. Local spinners name the Zara Spook, Skitter Pop and Chug Bug. Mattheys says topwater is 'especially deadly for the smaller fish in the estuaries', so expect school-sized fish more often than the big ones.

tactics.title: Stella or crease fly at first light
tactics.lure_or_bait: Foam-capped topwater baitfish fly: the Stella (tied on Mustad stinger deer-hair 2XL hooks), a crease fly or a small popper. Size about 6 to 9 cm on a 1/0 hook (estimate).
tactics.retrieve: Constant short, sharp strips, fast enough to keep the fly popping and swimming. A fast retrieve in low light gives better hook-ups (Killick). When fish roll on bait, drop the fly just ahead of the swirl and start stripping at once (estimate).
tactics.depth: surface
tactics.stand: Wade knee to hip deep off a shallow bank beside a weed bed and fan casts in an arc. At Zandvlei, fish the shallow banks of the main vlei and the Marina channel edges, between sunrise and sunset only (night angling is reported closed).
tactics.rig: 8 to 9 weight rod, floating line, 3 m leader of 7 kg monofilament (Andy Killick's Zandvlei rig)
tactics.why: Killick, a Zandvlei regular, uses surface flies in early summer and hooks more fish in low light with a fast retrieve. The Stella was developed for Zandvlei leervis feeding on Gilchrist's round herring (Wale). On a crease fly for leeries, 'white is hard to beat' (Botha). The fly size, hook size and drop-ahead cast are estimates, because the Stella tying article gives only the hook model.

tactics.title: Clouser or Deceiver down the channel edge
tactics.lure_or_bait: Clouser Minnow or Lefty's Deceiver, 1/0 to 2/0 and 7 to 10 cm; brush flies; a silicone Flathead Mullet for bigger fish
tactics.colour: pink-and-white or chartreuse-and-white Clouser; all-white Deceiver
tactics.retrieve: Let the fly sink, roughly a count of 5 to 10 (estimate), then strip fast and stop-start in short, jerky pulls with brief pauses. Keep stripping to the rod tip.
tactics.depth: mid-water down to just above the weed, 1 to 2.5 m along drop-offs
tactics.stand: Where a channel runs past a bank, cast across the drop-off and strip up the slope. One example is the channel that runs out from the Zandvlei yacht club.
tactics.rig: 8 to 9 weight rod, intermediate line, or floating line with a weighted fly; 3 m leader of 7 kg mono
tactics.why: Zandvlei fly anglers found that subsurface Clousers and Deceivers stripped after they sink draw more strikes than poppers, and they advise fishing the drop-offs at the channels (FlyTalk, via search). Kennedy took a 70 cm fish on a silicone Flathead Mullet. Fish The Fly says garrick like a fast, short, jerky stop-start retrieve. That source gives no time of day, so using this when the light is bright, when surface flies slow down, is an estimate.

tactics.title: Paddle-tail with more thump in dirty water
tactics.lure_or_bait: 3 to 4 inch paddle-tail or fluke on a 5 to 10 g jighead, rigged weedless where the weed is thick. In the surf, a 4 to 5 inch paddle-tail on 14 to 21 g.
tactics.colour: white or pearl; chartreuse or pink for contrast
tactics.retrieve: Steady slow roll so the tail thumps, with an occasional twitch and drop at the channel edge
tactics.depth: mid-water to near the bottom along the channel edge, 1 to 3 m
tactics.stand: Move to cleaner water. After a mouth opening at Zandvlei, the footbridge side runs cleaner than the yacht club side. Elsewhere, fish the line where clean and dirty water meet.
tactics.rig: 7 ft spinning rod, 15 to 20 lb braid, 1 m of 12 kg leader
tactics.why: After the Zandvlei mouth is opened, the yacht club side goes discoloured with foam and silt, and fly anglers rate it poor. The water near the footbridge stays cleaner. Cape spinners use paddle-tails and flukes for garrick (Mattheys). Picking vibration and contrast for dirty water is an estimate.

tactics.title: Slow and deep in the warmest part of the day
tactics.lure_or_bait: 3 to 4 inch paddle-tail on a 7 to 10 g jighead, or a 10 to 14 g bucktail or lead-head
tactics.retrieve: Slow lift and drop through the deepest channel, ticking the weed tops, with a pause after each lift. Expect few fish.
tactics.depth: the deepest water, 2 to 4 m channels
tactics.stand: Deep channel bends and the lower reaches towards the mouth, in the afternoon after the sun has warmed the shallows
tactics.rig: 7 ft spinning rod, 10 to 20 lb braid, 1 m of 12 kg leader
tactics.why: Cape anglers rate warm summer days best, and a June post says the fish are less active then. In the Breede Estuary, tagged adults stayed mostly in the lower reaches. Working the fish slowly in the deepest, most stable water in the warmest part of the day is an estimate.

tactics.title: Ambush the drain on the dropping tide
tactics.lure_or_bait: 15 to 20 g spoon or a 9 to 11 cm white chisel-nose plug; a paddle-tail on a 7 to 10 g jighead where it is weedy
tactics.retrieve: Cast up-current and across, then retrieve fast with the flow so the lure swings past the drop-off like bait flushed off the bank
tactics.depth: top 1.5 m along the drop-off
tactics.stand: Where the lagoon drains off a bank into the main channel. At Milnerton Lagoon: the old wooden bridge and the old pump station. At Zandvlei, only while the mouth is open (it is open in winter, but in summer usually only for a few days around the full-moon spring tide): the channel from the yacht club to the mouth.
tactics.rig: 7 ft spinning rod, 2500 to 4000 reel, 15 to 20 lb braid, 1 m of 12 kg leader
tactics.why: As the tide falls, it exposes banks and drop-offs and forces baitfish into the strike zone (Rush of Blue, generic SA advice). Milnerton anglers caught mullet off the wooden bridge and 'sizer leeries' near the old pump station (1980s reports). A closed Zandvlei has little or no tidal movement, so this tactic applies there only when the mouth is open.

tactics.title: White plug through the gutter by the vlei mouth
tactics.lure_or_bait: White chisel-nose or needle-nose plug of 25 to 40 g, or a 20 to 30 g spoon or slow-pitch jig
tactics.retrieve: Fast, with rod sweeps and a couple of flat-out bursts. Keep the lure moving all the way into the shorebreak, where many hits come. Make about 10 casts per hole, then move.
tactics.depth: top 1 m
tactics.stand: On the bank in front of a hole or gutter that has a channel out to sea, within casting range. At Sunrise Beach and the Zandvlei mouth, fish the gutter where vlei water meets the surf, especially when the mouth is open. Stay off when the sea is rough.
tactics.rig: 7 ft medium-heavy spinning rod, 4000 reel, 20 lb braid (Mattheys's light Strand outfit). On an open beach like Sunrise, a 9 to 10 ft rod casting up to about 1.5 oz reaches further. That rod is an estimate and the top end of light tackle: Mattheys uses 11 to 12 ft rods on open beaches, which is beyond light tackle. 1 to 1.5 m of 12 to 15 kg leader (estimate).
tactics.why: Garrick hunt mullet in the surf zone and feed close in. Mattheys fishes 'very light' at Strand, with white chisel-nose and needle-nose plugs, spoons and 20 to 30 g slow-pitch jigs. Rush of Blue says the swell must not be too big. A 2008 Sealine poster had never heard of leeries caught in the Muizenberg surf, so treat this as a low-confidence bonus close to the vlei mouth.

tactics.title: Fast silver spoon or white plug along the drop-off
tactics.lure_or_bait: 10 to 20 g silver or copper spoon (Abu Toby, Koster, Hopkins Shorty) or a 9 to 11 cm perspex chisel-nose plug
tactics.colour: silver or copper spoon; white or light pink plug
tactics.retrieve: Fast and erratic like a fleeing baitfish, with a few flat-out bursts, fished right to your feet. Vary the speed from cast to cast. Make about 20 casts per spot, then move to the next bend.
tactics.depth: top 1 m
tactics.stand: Parallel to the nearest drop-off or weed edge. On a vlei, fish {downwind}, where the chop pushes baitfish together.
tactics.rig: 7 ft light-medium spinning rod, 2500 to 4000 reel, 15 to 20 lb braid, 1 m of 12 kg leader, single hooks for release. At Rietvlei, line and leader must be 4.5 kg breaking strain or less, with at most two hooks per rod.
tactics.why: Zandvlei regulars list small Toby and Koster spoons and chisel-nose plugs. Rush of Blue advises fishing parallel to drop-offs and weed beds, imitating an injured baitfish, and not being put off when the wind brings chop. One Zandvlei angler says you will catch them 'anywhere where you can cast a lure without catching weed'.

legal.bag_note: 2 per person per day. Counts toward the aggregate of 10.
legal.note: A and B agree and both match R.959. No national closed season. Local estuary bodies (for example the Zandvlei Trust) may encourage or require catch-and-release, but the national rule is 70 cm and 2 per day.
