The Sealine reply does not say which species 'them' refers to, and the thread is about chokka as well, which are fished at night under lights. Neither quote shows that maasbanker bite a

Re-fetching the FishBase summary page found no preferred-temperature or AquaMaps values; it gives only 'Subtropical; 14N - 37S'. The figure cannot be verified from the cited page. It may be on the separate AquaMaps or 'estimates based on models' section, but as cited it is unbacked. The inshore rang

The quote says 'baitfish', not maasbanker. The same harbours hold strepies, mullet and sardine/anchovy. It is a boat-fishing article (anchor and chum, tuna). It supports year-round presence only indirectly, and no June to August maasbanker catch was found

Kalk Bay and Simon's Town lie inside the Table Mountain National Park MPA. Whether its regulations restrict chumming or ground-baiting from the shore was not checked. The District Mail column says only 'optional sardine block' and does not say how it is used
unverified: Whole temp block (min 9, ideal 12 to 19, max 23 C): estimate. The modelled 9.2 to 15.2 C figure was not found on the FishBase summary page, and the AquaMaps page was not checked
spawn_months 9 to 3: estimate. The only sourced fact is that the spawner stock is on the Agulhas Bank east of 22 degrees E (Barange et al. 1998)
present_months June to August: estimate. No winter maasbanker catch was found, and the 'baitfish most of the time' source does not name maasbanker

peak_months 11 to 3: estimate from a few Sealine reports (a September run start in one year, none by mid-October in another, January 2015 and a boat report in February 2013). September and October are variable
Light weights: the night pattern rests on FishBase biology and the Strand Pavilion fly note. The numbers are estimates
Sea, tide, flow, range, trend, clarity and wind weights: all estimates. The strong-wind weight has only boat evidence (Simon's Town, Feb 2013)
Strong-wind lee-of-the-wall tactic: shore use unconfirmed
Hout Bay harbour as a shore maasbanker spot: plausible but unconfirmed
Typical shore size 15 to 25 cm and big fish 35 to 45 cm: estimate
Micro-metal spinning, float, and coloured-water tactics: no Cape source for the methods themselves; built from biology
Table Mountain National Park MPA rules on chumming or ground-baiting from the Kalk Bay and Simon's Town harbours: not checked
Current status of Betty's Bay harbour for fishing (closed at last report, 2016)
Current DFFE recreational bag limit for maasbanker: not checked
WWF-SASSI, ORI and Smith's Sea Fishes entries were not consulted

mozambique-tilapia.name: Mozambique tilapia
mozambique-tilapia.season_note: Around Cape Town this is a summer fish. Afrikaans Wikipedia says they only bite well, especially on lures, once the water is regularly above about 21 C. In the Cape vleis that means roughly November to April, best from December to March, with a few fish on warm spells in October and May (estimate). In winter (June to August) the vleis cool to roughly 11 to 14 C (estimate) and the fish go almost dormant, so expect next to nothing. They breed all summer and each female raises several broods. Waters with a source near Cape Town: Rietvlei in the Table Bay Nature Reserve (fish during reserve hours only, 07:30 to 17:00) and Zandvlei/Sandvlei (Western Cape government fishing page), and Wildevoelvlei (Imhoff's Gift). The lower Berg River and Misverstand Dam also hold them, but both are more than an hour from Cape Town. Zandvlei's mouth is often closed in summer, so tide timing there only matters while the mouth is open. Zeekoevlei holds the best-known Cape population but is closed to fishing: the City suspended recreational angling on 28 August 2023 because of mercury and lead in the fish, and news reports also mention a temporary closure after a sewage spill on 31 December 2025. Afrikaans Wikipedia also names Winelands farm dams. Those are private waters, and their fish may be Nile tilapia hybrids.

temp.basis: FishBase gives a natural range of 17 to 35 C and an extended range of 8 to 42 C. Afrikaans Wikipedia (Bloukurper) says they start dying at about 10 C, especially when water cools fast, and only bite well, especially on lures, once the water is regularly above 21 C. USGS NAS says they do not survive below about 10 C. ideal_lo 21 comes from af.wikipedia, and max 35 is FishBase's natural upper limit. min 16 (feeding largely stops) and ideal_hi 30 are estimates. The reviewer did not re-check the FishBase or af.wikipedia figures.

mozambique-tilapia.habitat: Still or slow water. FishBase says adults prefer standing water, are common in blind estuaries and coastal lakes, and are absent from fast-flowing water, at depths of 1 to 12 m. They tolerate a wide range of salinity: USGS reports growth and breeding at 35 per mille salinity and survival up to 120 per mille. That lets them live in brackish Zandvlei and in Rietvlei on the Diep River. To feed, they hold in warm shallows of about 0.5 to 4 m beside cover such as reed beds, waterlilies, submerged trees and grass, and over sandy bays (Sealine Kurper 101). Shoals often cruise just under the surface beside reed beds and leave visible wakes (Fish the Fly, The Mission). In summer, males dig circular sandy nest pits in the shallow margins. In Zandvlei, expect them mostly in the fresher, reedier upper reaches (estimate). Tide only matters there while the mouth is open.
mozambique-tilapia.diet: They eat both plants and animals, and also feed on decaying matter (detritus). The diet is mainly algae, phytoplankton, diatoms and detritus, plus zooplankton, insect larvae, shrimp, crabs, earthworms and plant matter. Large fish eat small fish and sometimes their own young. Juveniles eat more animal food than adults (FishBase, Wikipedia, USGS, af.wikipedia). That is why bread, worms, small nymphs and small lures all work. They often nip and mouth a bait rather than grab it hard.
mozambique-tilapia.typical_size: Estimate for Cape vleis: typically 20 to 30 cm and 200 to 500 g, and a good fish is about 35 cm and 1 kg. FishBase gives a common length of 35 cm TL, a maximum of 39 cm SL and a maximum published weight of 1.1 kg. On Sealine, northern anglers report fish of 4.4 kg from Roodekoppies, 3.5 kg from Hartbeespoort and 3.2 kg from Loskop. Fish that size are not expected around Cape Town.
mozambique-tilapia.handling: Mozambique tilapia are indigenous to South Africa, with a native range from the Eastern Cape (Bushman/Brak River) northwards. In Cape Town's vleis they were brought in from elsewhere, so the species is not protected here. Never move live fish between waters. The dorsal and anal fins are spiny, so smooth the dorsal fin back from the head before you grip the fish. Their small sharp teeth chew up flies. General catch-and-release practice (estimate): handle the fish with wet hands, support it under the belly, and do not lay it on grass or paving. Release big fish. PERMITS: Rietvlei needs a CapeNature freshwater angling licence (valid 12 months). Zandvlei is an estuary nature reserve, so carry a DFFE recreational angling permit (from the Post Office or tackle shops). If you fish the fresher upper reaches, carry a CapeNature freshwater licence as well. BAG LIMITS: CapeNature says alien species, tilapia included, generally have no bag or size limit in the Western Cape. RIETVLEI (Table Bay Nature Reserve): fish only during reserve hours. The gates are open 07:30 to 17:00, but the City's current page gives 07:30 to 16:00 with exit by 17:00, so confirm at the gate. Rod and reel only. At most 2 rods, each with at most 2 hooks. Line no stronger than 4.5 kg breaking strain. Ask the gate ranger which fishing sites are open. Rietvlei's rules say exotic fish must be removed and indigenous fish returned, but they name only carp and barbel as exotic, so ask the ranger how tilapia are treated. ZANDVLEI: the Zandvlei Trust says indigenous fish should be released, and the law requires you to release indigenous estuary fish such as leervis/garrick. Juvenile white steenbras and stumpnose also take small baits there, so unhook them gently in the water and let them go. ZEEKOEVLEI is closed to fishing, and its fish carry high levels of mercury and lead, so do not eat them. PROTECTED LOOKALIKES: do not confuse this fish with the Cape kurper (Sandelia capensis), a protected indigenous Cape fish that is brown and mottled with a large mouth. If you hook one, release it at once in the water. In the Berg River system, witvis and Berg River redfin are protected. Never target them, and release any you catch straight away.

tactics.title: Bread flake under a float, warm middle of the day
tactics.lure_or_bait: A pinch of fresh white bread flake, or a marble-sized ball of brown bread moulded round the hook
tactics.rig: Size 8 to 10 short-shank hook (up to size 6 for a bread ball) tied straight to 2 to 3 kg line (the limit at Rietvlei is 4.5 kg). Small pencil or quill float with one or two split shot about 15 cm above the hook. No swivel needed.
tactics.retrieve: Leave it still. Tilapia nip and mouth the bait, so ignore the first bobs. Wait for the float to slide away or lie flat, then strike with a short sideways flick. Re-bait often.
tactics.depth: 0.5 to 1.5 m, with the bait just off the bottom or in mid-water where shoals are cruising
tactics.stand: Gaps in the reeds, edges of lily pads and sandy bays within 10 to 15 m of the bank. In a breeze, fish {downwind}, where warm surface water and drifting food collect.
tactics.why: On Sealine (Kurper 101), Cobia333, who fishes Western Cape dams, says a small ball of white bread 'worked wonders for me in any dam that had them in'. He also uses brown bread on a no. 6 hook with no sinker. Sean Mills (The Mission) says tilapia are nippers that like warm water, so fishing towards midday is often better. The downwind-bank advice is an estimate.

tactics.title: Worms under a red-and-white float in coloured water
tactics.lure_or_bait: A small bunch of 2 or 3 garden earthworms, or one larger worm threaded on so the tail still wriggles
tactics.rig: Size 8 to 10 baitholder hook on 2 to 4 kg line (no stronger than 4.5 kg at Rietvlei), a small red-and-white bobber or quill float and one split shot
tactics.retrieve: Leave it still, but every minute or two lift the float 30 cm and let it settle so the worm moves and releases scent. Strike when the float moves off steadily.
tactics.depth: Worm just above the bottom, 0.5 to 1 m, near cover
tactics.stand: Inflows, drains and reed margins where coloured water meets clearer water, and the sheltered corners of the vlei
tactics.why: Afrikaans Wikipedia calls a bunch of earthworms under a red-and-white float the simplest kurper method. On Sealine (Kurper 101), Dr halibut fishes a 'little hook on float with worms'. The idea that scent works better than sight in coloured water is an estimate.

tactics.title: Windy day: bread dough on a light running sinker
tactics.lure_or_bait: Bread dough (white or brown bread kneaded with a little water) on one rod and earthworm on the second rod
tactics.rig: 5 to 10 g running ball sinker stopped by a small swivel, then a 30 to 40 cm trace of 2 to 3 kg line to a size 6 to 8 hook. At Rietvlei the limit is 2 rods with at most 2 hooks each.
tactics.retrieve: Leave it still with a slight belly in the line and watch the rod tip. Do not strike at the first rattles. Wait for a steady pull.
tactics.depth: On the bottom, 1 to 3 m, just off the reed edge
tactics.stand: The {downwind} bank. Make short 10 to 20 m casts into the chop along the reed line, where warm surface water and loose food pile up.
tactics.why: On Sealine (Kurper 101), Dr halibut fishes a float rod with worms beside a second rod with bread dough on a small running sinker on the bottom. Wind makes a float hard to read. It is an estimate that strong wind slows the bite and that the downwind bank holds the food.

tactics.title: Micro spinner worked slowly near the bottom
tactics.lure_or_bait: Mepps Black Fury inline spinner, size 0 or 1 (about 2.5 to 3.5 g)
tactics.colour: black blade with red or yellow dots
tactics.rig: Ultralight rod with a 1000-size reel. Either 3 to 4 kg mono, or 6 lb braid with 1 m of 3 to 4 kg fluorocarbon leader (no stronger than 4.5 kg at Rietvlei). Tie direct or use a small snap.
tactics.retrieve: Cast and let it sink close to the bottom. Reel just fast enough to keep the blade turning, and pause beside cover. Takes are often a tap or a slight extra weight. This slow retrieve is an estimate.
tactics.depth: Near the bottom, 1 to 3 m
tactics.stand: Cast parallel to reed lines and fan your casts across sandy bays and lily edges
tactics.why: Cobia333 (Sealine Kurper 101, Western Cape) recommends a Mepps Black Fury spinner for kurper. Afrikaans Wikipedia says kurper only bite well on lures once the water is regularly above 21 C. On Sealine, Herman Nel reports blue kurper of 2.7 and 3.2 kg taken on artificial lures (dam not named). The slow near-bottom retrieve is an estimate.

tactics.title: Brown bread ball with no sinker, crawled along the bottom
tactics.lure_or_bait: A marble-sized ball of brown bread moulded firmly round the hook
tactics.rig: Size 6 hook tied straight to 2 to 3 kg line on a light spinning rod. No sinker and no swivel: the weight of the bread ball carries the cast.
tactics.retrieve: Cast out, let it sink to the bottom, then crawl it back as slowly as you can along the bottom, pausing often. Watch the slack line for a twitch or a slow draw, then lift into steady weight.
tactics.depth: On the bottom, 1 to 2 m
tactics.stand: Sandy bays and reed edges close in. Calm conditions let you see and feel the light line.
tactics.why: On Sealine (Kurper 101, post #5), Cobia333 uses a brown bread ball on a no. 6 hook with no sinker or swivel: 'Cast in let it sink to bottom and retrieve it as slow as possible along the bottom.' Keeping it to calm days, so the light line can be read, is an estimate.

tactics.title: Soft nymph under a hopper to shoals near the surface
tactics.lure_or_bait: Size 14 soft-bodied nymph in the style of Sean Mills' chartreuse 'Tilapia Candy' (a stretchy soft-plastic body on a nymph hook)
tactics.rig: 3-weight rod (the setup in the source), floating line, a foam hopper as the indicator, and 30 to 40 cm of 4X tippet tied from the hopper's hook bend to the nymph
tactics.retrieve: Land the flies with a splat near the shoal, wait a few seconds, then give a short sharp jerk. Stripping and twitching with the rod tip also works. When the hopper moves cleanly away, set the hook with a short sideways flick.
tactics.depth: Top 30 to 50 cm
tactics.stand: Short casts to wakes and dimples beside reed beds. Keep low and quiet, because shoals spook easily, even at a bird flying over.
tactics.why: In a reed-choked Cape Town lake, Sean Mills (The Mission) found that other tilapia (dwarf, vlei and Nile tilapia) nip and drop ordinary nymphs but hold a soft chartreuse body long enough to be hooked. He expects the same from Mozambique tilapia, but he has not tested it on this species. He describes tilapia holding near the surface in shoals of similar-sized fish that spook at a bird flying over. Fish the Fly says blue kurper shoals can often be seen making wakes beside reed beds.

tactics.title: Summer heat: small streamer on a sharp pull
tactics.lure_or_bait: Small minnow or buggy streamer, size 10: white Sean's Minnow, Clouser Minnow or Woolly Bugger
tactics.rig: 4 to 6 weight rod with floating or intermediate line. Tippet about 0.20 to 0.25 mm: heavier near snags (Fish the Fly warns that fish run for cover), lighter if the fish are shy.
tactics.retrieve: A very sharp, snappy 'pull, pull, pull, pause', with a long pause so the fish can catch up and suck in the fly. Strike when the line moves.
tactics.depth: Top 1 m, letting the fly sink slowly on the pause
tactics.stand: Over warm sandy shallows next to reeds, casting to cruising fish. Leave the circular nest pits alone and cast to the fish moving around them.
tactics.why: The main support is Fish the Fly, which says a faster streamer retrieve draws a reaction from blue kurper. The exact retrieve comes from Nile tilapia at a private Winelands venue: on the Cape Fly Fishing blog, Sean Mills reports tilapia hitting a white size 10 minnow this way on a 34 C day at the Le Bonheur crocodile farm (probably air temperature). The Mission says Mozambique tilapia turn very aggressive when nesting, and the Sealine Kurper 101 thread asks anglers not to disturb nests.

tactics.title: Cold water: tiny bait in the warmest corner
tactics.lure_or_bait: Half an earthworm or a small pinch of bread
tactics.rig: Size 10 to 12 hook on 2 kg line, with either a 3 to 5 g running sinker or a very sensitive small float
tactics.retrieve: Leave it completely still and give it time. Bites are tiny.
tactics.depth: The deepest sun-warmed water you can reach close in, 1.5 to 3 m
tactics.stand: Sunny, sheltered shallow bays out of the wind, on the {upwind} bank. Go in the warmest hour of the afternoon after several warm, sunny days.
tactics.why: Afrikaans Wikipedia says blue kurper go dormant in winter in the colder parts of South Africa and begin dying near 10 C. Sean Mills (The Mission) advises avoiding winter and fishing towards midday. Expect very little. Whether Cape vleis have any cold-water bite at all is an estimate.

tactics.title: Bread or worm under a small float at the reeds
tactics.lure_or_bait: Bread flake or a small ball of bread. Switch to a small bunch of earthworms if bread draws no bites.
tactics.rig: Size 8 hook on 2 to 3 kg line, small float, one split shot
tactics.retrieve: Leave it still and wait for the float to slide away, then make a short sideways strike
tactics.depth: 0.5 to 1.5 m, near the bottom beside cover
tactics.stand: Reed edges, lily pads and sandy bays within 15 m of the bank. Approach quietly.
tactics.why: This is the most widely recommended simple kurper method: bread from Cobia333 and worms under a float from Dr halibut (Sealine Kurper 101), and earthworms under a red-and-white float in Afrikaans Wikipedia. It suits the shallow, reed-lined Cape vleis.

legal.bag_note: No bag or size limit in fresh water (alien in the Western Cape).
legal.release: Putting it straight back into the same water is allowed; never move live fish.
legal.quote: CapeNature permit page: "Popular alien angling fish include carp, largemouth bass, rainbow trout and Mozambique tilapia." NEMBA List 7: "22. Oreochromis species excluding Oreochromis mossambicus and Oreochromis placidus Tilapia a. 3". Notice 2 para 1: "e. All alien fresh-water fish, except for the release of alien freshwater fish into rivers, wetlands, natural lakes and estuaries."

mozambique-tilapia.review: Checked by an independent skeptic; 22 corrections applied
review_points: Wrong species. The Sealine 'Vleikurpers' thread is about vlei kurper, the banded tilapia (Tilapia sparrmanii), not the blue kurper (Mozambique tilapia). It names no water or province. It cannot be cited as evidence for O. mossambicus.

Misattributed quote. In post #5, the 'let it sink ... as slow as possible along the bottom' instruction belongs to Cobia333's brown bread ball (no. 6 hook, no sinker or swivel), not to the spinner. All he says about the spinner is 'Try the Mepps Black Furry spinner for them.' So the slow bottom craw

The two locations have been merged. The 2.7 and 3.2 kg fish caught 'op kunsaas' (on lures) were posted by Herman Nel from an unnamed dam. The 3.2 kg Loskop fish was a friend's catch, and the thread does not say how it was caught.

Overstated. Mills says he had NOT yet tested the soft-bodied fly on Mozambique tilapia ('I expect similar results'). His Cape Town reed-choked lake holds dwarf, vlei and Nile tilapia. He used a size 14 nymph on a 3-weight. The article does not mention a tungsten bead or size 12, as far as the fetch

No such advice appears in either Sealine thread cited. Neither Kurper 101 nor 'groot bloukurper fotos' gives handling guidance. The only related remark is 'that fish is being held next to his body'. It is fine as general good practice, but the Sealine attribution is invented.

The 07:30 to 17:00 hours come from the Friends of Rietvlei page, whose content is dated 2006 to 2014. The cached search on the City's current Table Bay Nature Reserve page gives hours of 07:30 to 16:00, with exit by 17:00.

Incomplete for an estuary. Zandvlei is an estuary nature reserve. The Zandvlei Trust says the permit comes 'from any Post Office or some fishing tackle shops', which is the DFFE recreational angling permit. CapeNature says estuaries and the sea need a marine angling licence. The Western Cape governm

This can now be answered from the cache. CapeNature's recreational fishing page says alien species (carp, bass, tilapia, catfish) generally have no bag or size limits. Separately, Rietvlei's rules say exotic fish must be removed and indigenous species returned, and they name only carp and barbel as
unverified: The Cape-area present_months, peak_months and spawn_months are inferred from the 21 C bite threshold (af.wikipedia) and from summer breeding (Fish the Fly, FishBase). No Cape catch log or seasonal report for tilapia was found.
The vlei water temperatures in season_note (about 11 to 14 C in winter) are an estimate, not a measured source.
temp.min 16 and temp.ideal_hi 30 are estimates. temp.ideal_lo 21 (af.wikipedia) and temp.max 35 (FishBase natural range) have sources, but the reviewer did not re-check them.

All condition weights (light, sea, tide, range, flow, trend, clarity, wind) are estimates. The only qualitative support: 'fishing towards midday is often better' (The Mission), 'they seem to follow a barometer more than seafish' (Sealine, with no direction given) and the preference for standing water (FishBase). sea is set to neutral because it does not apply to a vlei and estuary fish.
The tide and range weights assume Zandvlei's mouth is mostly closed in summer and that tilapia sit in the fresher upper parts of Rietvlei and Zandvlei. No tilapia-specific source confirms either.
Fishing the {downwind} bank because warm surface water and food pile up there is general stillwater reasoning, not a tilapia-specific Cape source.
The typical Cape shore-caught size (200 to 500 g, about 1 kg for a good fish) is an estimate.
Micro-spinner retrieve: Cobia333 only names the Mepps Black Fury spinner. The slow near-bottom retrieve is an estimate.
Soft-bodied nymph: Sean Mills tested it on dwarf, vlei and Nile tilapia, not on Mozambique tilapia, and only expects the same results.
The sharp-pull streamer retrieve comes from Nile tilapia at a Winelands farm venue (Le Bonheur), not from Mozambique tilapia in a Cape vlei. The 34 C was probably air temperature.

Rietvlei hours conflict: Friends of Rietvlei (content dated 2006 to 2014) gives 07:30 to 17:00, while the City's current Table Bay Nature Reserve page (cached search) gives 07:30 to 16:00 with exit by 17:00.

Zandvlei permit sources conflict: the Zandvlei Trust and CapeNature point to a DFFE recreational (marine/estuarine) permit, while the Western Cape government page lists Sandvlei under CapeNature freshwater.
Rietvlei's rules name only carp and barbel as exotic fish to be removed. Whether tilapia must be removed or returned there is not stated.
Whether selling tilapia is barred by a CapeNature licence condition was not confirmed, so the claim was removed from handling.
Wildevoelvlei rests on an Imhoff's Gift page cited by the reviewer whose URL was not recorded. Whether angling is allowed at Wildevoelvlei was not checked.
Tilapia in the Liesbeek River is unconfirmed: the Western Cape government page lists only carp and sharptooth catfish there, so the Liesbeek is no longer named.
Not confirmed whether translocated O. mossambicus in the Western Cape is listed under NEMBA as an alien invasive.
Winelands farm-dam fish may be hybrids with Nile tilapia (hybridisation is documented elsewhere in South Africa, per Wikipedia). Not checked for the Cape.

The reviewer could not check these, for lack of budget: the FishBase temperature ranges, af.wikipedia's 21 C threshold and red-and-white float method, the USGS salinity figures, the Fish the Fly blue-kurper page and the Le Bonheur blog post.

rainbow-trout.name: Rainbow trout
rainbow-trout.season_note: The CPS river beats (Smalblaar, Molenaars) are open 1 September to 31 May. That is a CPS club rule, and guides quote the same closed season (31 May to 1 September). No statutory provincial closed season was found. The winter closure covers the spawn (June to August according to Fish The Fly). The best months are in spring, September to November (Flyloops), when the water is cool. The Smalblaar has heavy Leptophlebiid and Baetis mayfly hatches, but the CPS doesn't say when they happen. Fishing picks up again in autumn as the nights cool. Flyloops gives March to May, but March can still be hot and hard on the shallow lower beats (lower Smalblaar, Molenaars Lower), so April and May are the better months. In February and March fish early, high up and in shaded kloofs. Trout in the Berg are now sparse after rotenone treatment (The Mission, 2019). A wild rainbow near Paarl was reported in late 2025.

temp.basis: max 21 C: Fish The Fly, 'ideally need the water temperature to be 21 degrees celsius or lower'. ideal_lo 10 C: estimate from general trout biology (FishBase's 10 to 24 C is the species' overall temperature range, not a feeding optimum, so it is loose context only). ideal_hi 17 C and min 5 C: estimates from general trout biology. Fish The Fly also says spawning needs water of 15 C or lower. In summer the Cape lower beats 'warm up very quickly' (CPS Molenaars page), and Fish The Fly's Slow Day article describes lethargic fish in the hotter months.

rainbow-trout.habitat: Clear, cold, well-oxygenated freestone mountain streams in the Boland: the Smalblaar and Molenaars in Du Toitskloof, the Berg above Franschhoek, the Lourens above Somerset West and the Eerste above Stellenbosch. Fish hold in pool heads, runs and glides, on current seams, in the pockets behind boulders, under undercut banks and in shaded kloofs. In summer they drop into the deepest, shaded, well-aerated water. Shallow lower beats warm fast in summer and become hard fishing, with spooky fish. The CPS notes that the lower Molenaars beat is seldom fished outside the early season. On the Smalblaar, the Hotel Beat still fishes well in higher water. Rotenone removed most of the Berg's trout (The Mission, 2019), but a wild rainbow near Paarl was reported in late 2025. CapeNature says trout are common in the upper Eerste and Lourens, but public bank access there (nature reserve and private land) is not verified. Get permission before you fish.
rainbow-trout.diet: Mainly aquatic insects: Leptophlebiid and Baetis mayflies, midges and caddis, eaten as nymphs, emergers and duns. Also land insects that blow onto the water (hoppers, beetles, ants), and crabs, frogs, platannas, tadpoles and small fish.
rainbow-trout.typical_size: Most Cape stream rainbows are 20 to 30 cm (estimate). A big one is 45 to 51 cm. Fish of 'up to 20 inches' are routinely taken on the lower Molenaars, and 'trophy fish of three pounds' (about 1.4 kg) are still caught on the Smalblaar every year.
rainbow-trout.handling: Rainbow trout is an alien species. On CPS beats (Smalblaar, Molenaars), barbless hooks and catch and release are mandatory, and 'even injured fish must be returned'. Book beats in advance with the CPS, and carry a CapeNature freshwater angling licence. Wet your hands, net the fish in the water and keep it submerged. To revive it, hold it facing into a gentle current, supporting it under the belly and at the wrist of the tail. Don't touch the gills. Hold it there until it swims off on its own, and don't pull it back and forth. When the water is warm (over about 20 C), keep fights and handling short. Protected indigenous fish share these streams: Berg and Breede River redfins, Cape kurper and Cape galaxias. Never target them. CapeNature requires catch and release of indigenous freshwater fish, so if you hook one, unhook it in the water and let it go.

tactics.title: Low-light dry fly on the glides
tactics.lure_or_bait: Size 14 to 16 RAB, Para-Adams or Elk Hair Caddis dry fly
tactics.rig: 2 to 3 weight rod, floating line, 9 to 12 ft leader tapered to 6X (about 2.5 lb) tippet, barbless hook
tactics.retrieve: Cast a metre upstream of the rise and let the fly drift with no drag. Lift into the fish when the fly disappears.
tactics.depth: Surface
tactics.stand: Below the fish at the tail of the pool, kneeling and back from the edge. Cast up into the glide and the bubble line at the pool head.
tactics.colour: Natural grey or brown. Go darker if small black mayflies are on the water.
tactics.why: Cool water and soft light bring trout up to feed in the open glides. This comes from general trout behaviour and Cape trip reports, not from a CPS rule. The CPS Smalblaar page notes that early mornings and late afternoons are cool at Ravens Crag. Cape trip reports took fish on the RAB (Davis, Smalblaar) and the Para-Adams (Kennedy).

tactics.title: Bright sun: dry-dropper in the pocket water
tactics.lure_or_bait: Size 12 to 14 hopper, Stimulator or DDD, with a size 16 to 18 beadhead PTN or Zak nymph on a 50 to 80 cm dropper
tactics.rig: 2 to 3 weight rod, 9 ft leader to 5X or 6X, dropper tied to the bend of the dry, all hooks barbless
tactics.retrieve: Make short upstream casts into each pocket and let the flies drift naturally, keeping the fly line off the water. Strike if the dry dips or stops.
tactics.depth: Surface to 60 cm
tactics.stand: Wade up the margins and cast into the seams behind boulders, the white water at pool heads and shaded undercut banks.
tactics.colour: Natural; black or olive nymphs in good light
tactics.why: In hard light trout hold under broken water and in shade. For the Smalblaar's boulder pockets (Cathedral Beat), the CPS says 'a tandem rig consisting of larger dries and small nymphs provides the most productive method'. On the Holsloot, Kennedy took a fish on a suspended Zak nymph.

tactics.title: Overcast: match the mayfly hatch
tactics.lure_or_bait: Size 16 to 18 parachute Baetis, CDC emerger, Para-RAB or small RAB
tactics.rig: 2 to 3 weight rod, 12 ft leader to 6X or 7X, barbless
tactics.retrieve: Drift the fly drag-free over fish that are rising steadily. Fish the emerger in the surface film.
tactics.depth: Surface film
tactics.stand: At the tails of long runs and pools where duns collect. Cast to the steadiest risers first.
tactics.why: The Smalblaar has 'heavy Leptophlebid and Baetis mayfly hatches', and on the Elandspad fish took 'little emergers, to RABs and hoppers'. The idea that small mayflies hatch best under cloud is general fly-fishing knowledge, not from a Cape source.

tactics.title: Warm water: fish high, small and early
tactics.lure_or_bait: Size 18 to 20 CDC dry, small parachute or midge
tactics.rig: 2 weight rod, long leader to 7X tippet, barbless; land fish fast
tactics.retrieve: Make long, fine, drag-free drifts to spooky fish. Land each fish quickly and release it without lifting it out of the water.
tactics.depth: Surface, or a tiny nymph through the deepest, most oxygenated pool heads
tactics.stand: Upper, shaded kloof beats (eg Ravens Crag on the Smalblaar) and the white water at pool heads. Skip shallow lower beats such as Molenaars Lower once they warm, and stop fishing when the water passes about 21 C.
tactics.why: On the Molenaars in summer, 'smaller CDC and parachute patterns fished off fine tippets become essential', and the lower beat 'warms up very quickly'. Davis found that 'February and March is always a tough time of the year for the lower beats', even with 'a 7x and #20 midge'. The shaded kloof on Ravens Crag 'provides the trout with cool water throughout summer'. Fish The Fly wants the water at 21 C or lower. Small redfins and kurper also rise in warm, low water. They are protected, so unhook any you catch in the water.

tactics.title: Cold water: slow nymph through the deep pools
tactics.lure_or_bait: Size 12 to 16 tungsten-bead GRHE, PTN or Zak nymph
tactics.rig: 3 to 4 weight rod, floating line, 9 ft leader to 5X, small yarn or dry-fly indicator, barbless
tactics.retrieve: Let the nymph drift naturally along the bottom through pool heads and the slow, deep water. Fish the warmest hours of the day.
tactics.depth: Near the bottom, roughly 0.5 to 1.5 m (estimate)
tactics.stand: Beside the deep pools, high-sticking the nymph down the seam, and in the large pools of early-season beats such as Picnic Beat.
tactics.colour: Natural brown or olive; orange hotspot in poor light
tactics.why: The CPS says 'indicator nymphing works well in the deeper pools' (Donkergat), and that Picnic Beat is 'best fished in the earlier part of the season'. Cold fish sit deep and won't move far for food, so the fly has to reach them. That midday is best in cold water, and the depth range, are estimates.

tactics.title: After rain: heavy nymph or bugger in the soft edges
tactics.lure_or_bait: Size 10 to 12 olive or black beadhead Woolly Bugger, red squirmy worm fly, or size 12 tungsten GRHE
tactics.rig: 4 to 5 weight rod, floating line with a 9 ft 4X to 5X leader (or a short sink-tip), barbless
tactics.retrieve: Let it drift naturally along the bottom, or swing it and strip it in short 10 to 20 cm pulls through the slack water.
tactics.depth: Near the bottom
tactics.stand: Along the soft inside edges, in eddies and in the slack water behind big rocks where fish shelter from the flow. The Smalblaar's Hotel Beat 'fishes well in higher water'. Fish only when the river is fishable and safe to wade. Stay out of fast, rising or flooding water, and never cross a swollen stream: Boland kloof streams rise fast after a front.
tactics.colour: Orange, white or red when it is murky (estimate; Fish The Fly gives orange and white for poor light); black or olive once it clears
tactics.why: High, coloured water pushes trout into the soft water and hides your leader (estimate). The fly choice comes from Fish The Fly's slow-day method: a beaded size 10 olive Woolly Bugger stripped fast for lethargic fish in the hotter months, in orange and white 'when the light is poor'. That article does not cover coloured water. The Mission (Nov 2025) reported a wild Berg River rainbow near Paarl that took a red squirmy.

tactics.title: Breezy day: hopper or beetle under the grassy banks
tactics.lure_or_bait: Size 10 to 14 foam hopper, beetle or flying ant, or a RAB
tactics.rig: 3 weight rod, 9 ft leader to 5X, barbless
tactics.retrieve: Land the fly with a soft plop near the bank, let it drift naturally, and twitch it now and then.
tactics.depth: Surface
tactics.stand: Under the overhanging fynbos and grass on the bank the wind is blowing off, where it knocks hoppers and beetles onto the water, and along the foam lines they drift into. A ripple on the water also lets you get closer to the fish.
tactics.why: Elandspad fish took 'RABs and hoppers', and on the lower Molenaars 'larger terrestrial insect imitations work well' early in the season. Rainbows also eat flying insects. That a ripple helps you get close is an estimate. A strong wind spoils dry-fly fishing (Botha, Eerste).

tactics.title: Upstream dry-dropper, stalking the clear water
tactics.lure_or_bait: Size 14 RAB or Para-Adams, with a size 16 to 18 beadhead PTN or Zak dropper
tactics.rig: 2 to 3 weight 7 to 8 ft rod, floating line, 9 to 12 ft leader to 6X tippet, barbless hooks
tactics.retrieve: Make short upstream casts and let the flies drift without drag. Strike at any check or dip of the dry.
tactics.depth: Surface to 60 cm
tactics.stand: Work upstream from the tail of each pool, keeping low and back from the edge. Cover the pool heads, seams and boulder pockets before moving on. Fish CPS beats only once they are booked, and other water only where access is permitted.
tactics.why: Cape freestone streams are small and usually clear, so the fish spook easily. The CPS describes the Smalblaar's Hotel Beat water as 'almost always crystal clear'. Fishing upstream on fine tippet is the standard method. On CPS beats you must book, barbless hooks and catch and release are mandatory, and the CPS river season runs 1 September to 31 May.

legal.bag_note: No provincial bag or size limit; club rules apply on Cape Piscatorial Society water (river season 1 September to 31 May, some beats catch and release only).
legal.release: You may keep or release it; never move live fish.
legal.quote: NEMBA List 7: "20. Oncorhynchus mykiss (Walbaum, 1792) Rainbow Trout 2 a. All persons are exempted from requiring a permit for restricted activities "b" and "j" in Notice 1." CapeNature: "in some rivers there are catch restrictions for trout imposed by angling clubs." CPS rules (club, not law): "The fishing on the rivers is only allowed from 1 September to 31 May."

rainbow-trout.review: Checked by an independent skeptic; 21 corrections applied
review_points: The quote is misattributed. The Mission's CPS article says 'quality fishing in the mornings and late afternoons' about booking the Lakenvlei hut in summer, and Lakenvlei is a stillwater above Ceres, not a stream. The CPS Smalblaar page says only to bring 'warm clothing for the early morning and late

The source has been moved out of its context. Fish The Fly's Slow Day article recommends the beaded olive Woolly Bugger for a fast-strip method aimed at lethargic fish in hotter months. It does not cover murky or coloured water, so 'when it is murky' is the profile's own extrapolation. The tactic al

No source supports it, and the one cited is contradicted. Jacita's 'fly rods or spinners' line is about Lakenvlei/Lakensvlei, and CPS rules for that water say 'Fly fishing only, no spinners or any conventional tackle'. The named example, the upper Berg, is where the profile itself (citing The Missio

The token and the reasoning disagree. The engine renders {downwind} as 'the bank the wind is blowing onto'. On a narrow stream, terrestrials are blown off the vegetation on the bank the wind comes FROM, so they land along the {upwind} bank. The title's 'windward' is ambiguous for the same reason. Th

Overstated. CPS says the lower Molenaars beat 'warms up very quickly' and is 'seldom fished outside of the early season', meaning anglers rarely fish it. It says nothing about fish leaving. Davis says February and March are 'tough' on the lower beats, with 'wisened trout' that were still rising. No

FishBase's 10 to 24 C is a climate or distribution descriptor, not a feeding-optimum range, so using its lower bound as the ideal lower bound misuses the field. The value is plausible, but its basis should be 'estimate', with FishBase as loose context only.

Unsafe advice. Standard catch-and-release guidance is never to touch the gills, which are easily damaged. I could not confirm that Fish The Fly's 'How To Handle Trout' says 'rub the gills'; if it does, it should not be repeated.

The CPS Smalblaar page confirms 'heavy Leptophlebid and Baetis mayfly hatches' but gives them no season, so tying them to spring is unsourced. The spring peak is supported by Flyloops ('Spring (September-November)'). The 1 Sep to 31 May season is a CPS club rule. CapeNature states no statutory close
unverified: temp.min 5 C, temp.ideal_lo 10 C and temp.ideal_hi 17 C are estimates from general trout biology. FishBase's 10 to 24 C is the species' range, not an optimum. Only max 21 C is sourced (Fish The Fly).

Every condition weight (light, clarity, wind, trend) is an estimate. Cape trip reports inform them (clear, windless days with fish moving; wind cancelling dry-fly fishing), but no source puts numbers on them.
flow 0.8 (how much the fish wants moving water) is an estimate. It reflects trout holding on current seams, runs and pool heads in freestone streams, but no source gives a number.
The trend (air pressure) weights have no source at all.
The typical size of 20 to 30 cm is an estimate. Only the big-fish figures (20 in on the Molenaars, 3 lb trophies on the Smalblaar) are sourced.
Spawn months 6 to 8 follow Fish The Fly (June to August in SA). FishBase gives August to November for the Southern Hemisphere.

The 1 September to 31 May season is a CPS club rule. CapeNature states no statutory closed season, and no statutory Western Cape trout rules (fly-only waters, bag or size limits) were found. Trout stay in the rivers all year; present_months leaves out June to August because CPS water is closed and the fish are spawning.

The CPS stream pages confirm barbless hooks and compulsory catch and release, but neither they nor the Rules page says the river beats are formally fly-only. The Rules page makes only Lakenvlei fly-only. This profile gives fly tactics only.
No stream within an hour of Cape Town was found where spinning for trout is both legal and publicly accessible, so this profile has no spinning tactic.
Public access to fish the upper Eerste and Lourens (nature reserve and private land) is not verified, and neither is access to the upper Berg.
Trout in the Liesbeek: no source found. The CapeNature and Jacita pages mention only carp and catfish in the lower Liesbeek.
Upper Berg: trout are described as sparse after rotenone treatment (The Mission, 2019). The only recent record found is one wild rainbow near Paarl, reported in Nov 2025 (trip date not given).

These are general fly-fishing knowledge with no Cape source: that Baetis hatches peak on overcast days, that midday is best in cold water, that ripple lets you approach closer, and that coloured water calls for orange, white or red flies. The CPS gives no season for the Smalblaar's mayfly hatches.
The cold-water nymph depth of 0.5 to 1.5 m is an estimate.
Fish The Fly 'How To Handle Trout', FishBase, Flemming's 'Cape Streams Catfish Run', Davis's 'EP 3 Report' and Botha's '7-Year-Itch' were not re-checked by the reviewer.

red-roman.name: Red roman
red-roman.season_note: Roman are caught from Cape rocks all year. The Kleinmond and Whale Coast guides list roman for 'all year, all rocky parts of the coast', and no Cape source gives a seasonal peak, so the season is rated flat and water temperature does the work. Cole 2020 is a boat-angling article about False Bay reefs, and its point is not specific to roman: bites slow below about 13 C and after sudden drops. Tracked roman in False Bay reportedly sheltered in caves during cold upwelling (Kerwath et al. 2007, abstract only). In summer the western False Bay shore (Kalk Bay, Glencairn, Miller's Point) is usually warmest, while south-easters bring cold upwelled water onto the Atlantic side (Soetwater). Spawning is a restricted summer season (Buxton 1990). The November to February months are an estimate. There is no closed season, but release the big fish in those months, because the big ones are the breeding males.

temp.basis: Estimate. The floor is inferred for roman, not measured: Cole 2020 (Ski-Boat, boat angling over False Bay reefs, all species, not roman-specific) says bites slow below 13 C and after rapid temperature drops. Kerwath et al. 2007 (abstract, not checked against the paper) reported roman sheltering in caves during upwelling. The ideal band and the upper limit are estimates from the species' range, Cape Point to about Port St Johns (WWF-SASSI), where the core reefs rarely run above 22 to 23 C.

red-roman.habitat: Rocky reef from 1 to 100 m (FishBase). Juveniles live in shallow seaweed and kelp beds. Adults stay on one reef patch for years. In the Castle Rock MPA next to Miller's Point, tracked fish held home ranges of only about 1000 to 3000 m2 (Kerwath et al. 2007, abstract only), and shore tag-recapture work in Tsitsikamma also found very high site fidelity. They hold near caves, overhangs and ledges. From the shore, look for deep water close in: the ledges opposite Glencairn quarry, the vertical outer wall of Kalk Bay harbour (the shore north of the harbour, from the Kalk Bay tidal pool to St James pool, is a no-take zone), the rocks by Wooley's Pool at Clovelly, and kelp-fringed reef edges at Soetwater, plus Miller's Point on the slipway side of the Castle Rock beacon only. They are most abundant from Cape Point eastwards, and the cold Atlantic side has fewer.
red-roman.diet: A bottom-feeding predator of crabs and other crustaceans, sea urchins, polychaete worms, molluscs, brittle stars and small fish. Juveniles eat minute crustaceans (FishBase, and Buxton's Rhodes work as summarised on Wikipedia). Smith's description, quoted on FishBase: 'voracious but sluggish, takes any bait'. Cape shore guides name chokka, redbait, and sardine or mullet strips. Octopus is a common tough alternative.
red-roman.typical_size: From Cape shores mostly 20 to 35 cm (about 0.2 to 0.8 kg), and many are under the 30 cm legal minimum. A big shore fish is 40 to 45 cm (about 1.5 to 2 kg). The species reaches 50 cm TL and 4.2 kg, with a common length of 32 cm (FishBase).
red-roman.handling: The minimum size is 30 cm TL. The bag limit is 2 per person per day, inside the 10-fish cumulative daily bag (MLRA recreational annexure, WWF-SASSI, Whale Coast guide). Roman are IUCN Near Threatened and WWF-SASSI orange ('Think twice'). They grow slowly, mature late and are protogynous (females turn into territorial males), so the big fish are the males and are worth releasing, especially in the November to February spawning months. Each fish stays on one small patch of reef, so one ledge is easily fished out: release most of what you catch. The dorsal spines are sharp and the strong jaws can crush, so hold the fish by the body with wet hands. Use circle hooks, which usually set in the corner of the mouth. On a deep-hooked fish, cut the trace close to the hook rather than ripping it out (Cole 2020). Shore fish come from shallow water and rarely suffer barotrauma, so release them quickly at the waterline. In rough seas (over about 1.8 m reaching the spot), don't fish exposed rock at all. No fishing in the Table Mountain National Park MPA restricted (no-take) zones, several of which border good roman ground. St James runs from the St James tidal pool to the Kalk Bay tidal pool, just north of Kalk Bay harbour. Boulders runs from Simon's Town harbour to Oatlands Point. Castle Rock runs from the Miller's Point beacon to Partridge Point, so at Miller's Point fish only on the slipway side of the beacon. Paulsberg runs from Smitswinkel Point to Venus Pool, on the False Bay side of Cape Point. Cape of Good Hope runs from the Scarborough fence to Hoek van die Bobbejaan. Karbonkelberg runs from Oudekraal to Hout Bay. Boundaries have been revised, so check the current SANParks MPA map before you go.

tactics.title: Chokka strip on the ledge drop-off
tactics.lure_or_bait: A chokka (squid) strip about 6 x 1.5 cm, a bunch of tentacles, or a piece of octopus leg. A sardine or mullet strip as backup.
tactics.rig: 1/0 to 2/0 circle hook on 30 to 40 cm of 0.35 to 0.40 mm (about 7 to 9 kg) trace, lighter than the main line so the trace breaks first. Running sinker of 2 to 3 oz (56 to 85 g) on a rotten-bottom weak link, so a snag costs only the sinker. 10 to 12 kg nylon or 25 to 30 lb braid on a 2.7 to 3 m rod.
tactics.retrieve: Cast along the edge of the drop-off, let it settle, take up the slack and hold still. Roman hit hard and bolt for a hole. Don't strike a circle hook: wind tight, lift steadily, and steer the fish away from the rock straight away.
tactics.depth: On the bottom at the base of the ledge or reef edge, usually 3 to 10 m of water
tactics.stand: A ledge or wall with deep water close in. Cast along the drop-off, not out over sand. Good spots are the ledges opposite Glencairn quarry, the outer side of Kalk Bay harbour wall, the rocks around Wooley's Pool at Clovelly, and the reef edges at Soetwater. At Kalk Bay, fish the harbour wall itself: the shore north of it, from the Kalk Bay tidal pool to St James pool, is a no-take zone. At Miller's Point, stay on the slipway side of the Castle Rock restricted-zone beacon.
tactics.why: Roman stay on small home ranges on the reef and take tough baits readily. Cape shore anglers name the Glencairn quarry ledges, the Kalk Bay wall and Soetwater for roman, with chokka as the bait. Circle hooks set in the corner of the mouth (Cole 2020), so the fish can be released.

tactics.title: Low tide: two baits off the quarry ledges
tactics.lure_or_bait: Chokka tentacles on one hook and a different bait on the other: a sardine or mullet strip, or redbait
tactics.rig: Two-hook paternoster with 1/0 circle hooks on 25 cm droppers of 0.35 to 0.40 mm, and a 2 oz (56 g) sinker on a weak link
tactics.retrieve: Cast to the foot of the ledge, let it settle and keep the line tight. Lift a few centimetres every minute or so to keep the hooks out of the crevices.
tactics.depth: Bottom, at the foot of the ledge or reef face
tactics.stand: The ledges opposite Glencairn quarry, or any ledge you can reach safely at low water that puts you close to the drop-off. Watch the push and move back before the tide floods your ledge.
tactics.why: At Glencairn quarry, a regular advised fishing for roman on the low tide (he said that afternoon's tide was too high), using two hooks with different baits, chokka tentacles among them. This is one angler's advice, so the tide effect itself is an estimate.

tactics.title: Cold water: small bait, dead still at the cave
tactics.lure_or_bait: A small chokka tentacle, or a piece of octopus or redbait, about half the usual size
tactics.rig: 1/0 circle hook on 0.35 to 0.40 mm trace, and the lightest sinker that holds (1.5 to 2 oz on a weak link)
tactics.retrieve: Dead still. Give each hole 10 to 15 minutes, then move to the next overhang. Bites are slow, so don't overwork it.
tactics.depth: Tight on the bottom under overhangs and in the deepest holes
tactics.stand: The deepest, most sheltered hole or overhang on the spot. If the whole area has upwelled cold (often the Atlantic side under summer south-easters), the western False Bay shore is usually warmer.
tactics.why: Cole 2020 is a boat-angling article, and his observation covers all False Bay reef fish, not roman alone: bites slow below about 13 C and after sudden drops. Tracked roman reportedly retreated into caves during upwelling (Kerwath et al. 2007, abstract only). The cold-water slowdown for roman from the shore is therefore an inference.

tactics.title: Coloured water: redbait and strips in the gullies
tactics.lure_or_bait: Redbait bound on with bait elastic and topped with a small chokka strip so it stays on, or a sardine or mullet strip
tactics.rig: 1/0 circle hook on 30 cm of 0.35 to 0.40 mm trace, 2 to 3 oz (56 to 85 g) sinker on a weak link
tactics.retrieve: Hold still and re-bait often so the scent keeps working. Wait for a solid pull, then wind tight without striking.
tactics.depth: Bottom, at the edge of the reef where the gully meets deeper water
tactics.stand: Reef-edge gullies with some wash but no breaking water, such as the rocks beside Wooley's Pool at Clovelly. Keep your back to the land and watch the sets.
tactics.why: A Fish Hoek guide suggests taking redbait to the rocks beside Wooley's Pool for red roman, and the Kleinmond guides name sardine or mullet strips and chokka for roman. The idea that smelly baits beat visual ones in dirty water is a general estimate, not a sourced roman finding.

tactics.title: Moderate sea: the sheltered side of the reef
tactics.lure_or_bait: Chokka strip or octopus leg. Both stay on the hook in surge.
tactics.rig: 2/0 circle hook on 0.40 mm trace, 3 oz (85 g) sinker on a rotten-bottom weak link. This is the top end of light tackle: if 3 oz won't hold, the spot is too rough to fish.
tactics.retrieve: Cast into the calmer pocket, hold firm and let the sinker grip. Re-cast if the surge rolls it into the kelp.
tactics.depth: Bottom, on the sheltered side of the reef
tactics.stand: The sheltered side of a point, or the inside of a harbour wall. Stay off exposed ledges and wave-washed walls: surges come over the Kalk Bay wall, and freak waves have killed anglers on Cape ledges. If the sea is rough, don't fish exposed rock at all.
tactics.why: Light shore tackle can't hold on an exposed ledge once the swell builds. Roman stay on their small patch of reef, so the sheltered edge of the same reef can still hold fish. That benefit is an estimate. The sources here back the safety warnings.

tactics.title: Night: chokka on the wall, low odds
tactics.lure_or_bait: Chokka strip or tentacles. A white mussel on a second hook catches the stumpnose that were biting on the same wall at night.
tactics.rig: Two-hook paternoster, 1/0 circle hooks, 0.35 to 0.40 mm droppers, 2 oz (56 g) sinker on a weak link
tactics.retrieve: Hold still, tight to the wall
tactics.depth: Bottom, against the wall or ledge face
tactics.stand: A lit harbour wall rather than open rock, and only when the sea is calm enough that nothing washes over it. At Kalk Bay, use the outer vertical face, casting towards the bell. The shore north of the harbour, from the Kalk Bay tidal pool to St James pool, is a no-take zone.
tactics.why: Tracked roman reportedly swim less at night (Kerwath et al. 2007, abstract only), so expect few. A Kalk Bay regular still names the vertical wall and chokka for roman on a night session.

legal.bag_note: 2 per day. Counts toward the aggregate of 10.
legal.note: A and B agree and both match R.959. No closed season. Listed simply as 'Roman'.
legal.quote: Roman | Chrysoblephus laticeps | 30 cm | 2

red-roman.review: Checked by an independent skeptic; 18 corrections applied
review_points: Misattributed. In Cole's ski-boat article the 13 C line and the rapid-drop line are general False Bay reef-fishing observations under 'Seasons and conditions' and are not tied to roman. The 12 to 13 C floor is therefore an inference for roman, not a sourced roman threshold. It is also a boat observa

Misrepresents the source. Cole says micro jigs are used as the BOTTOM WEIGHT on a baited trace, and that they snag often. He does not describe jigging them as lures for roman. No cached Cape source documents roman on jigs or paddle-tails from the shore, so this tactic has no support at all.

Neither source names roman. The Glencairn 'drop shot type fishing' is a sinkerless natural-bait drift ('using bait for weight'), not a soft-plastic dropshot. The Cape Point dropshot suggestion is generic, and much of the Cape Point reserve shoreline falls in the Cape of Good Hope and Paulsberg no-ta

In the Kalk Bay thread the 'many fish biting, especially on the high tide' remark refers to a night session that caught stumpnose. No roman was reported caught. The only roman-relevant tide advice in the cache, Walt at Glencairn quarry, recommends LOW tide and calls a high tide too high. The weights

Those hard knocks and the hook-up were a stumpnose (MrPenn500 fishing for stumpnose), not a roman. This is evidence for white mussel on stumpnose, not on roman. Rotten redbait is listed for galjoen in the Kleinmond guides, not roman. Seaside Cottages only says to buy redbait 'for luck' before going

Incomplete in a way that matters legally for the spots this profile names. The TMNP MPA also has no-take restricted zones at St James (St James tidal pool to Kalk Bay tidal pool, immediately north of the recommended Kalk Bay harbour), Cape of Good Hope (Hoek van die Bobbejaan to the Scarborough fenc

Internally inconsistent. 0.45 mm nylon breaks at about 11 to 13 kg, which is heavier than an 8 to 10 kg main line and about equal to 20 lb braid. The sacrificial-trace logic (trace breaks before the main line, as in Cole 2020) fails at the lighter end of the stated range.

Rough here means over 1.8 m reaching the spot. Recommending any rock fishing then is unsafe on this coastline: the cached Rooi-Els thread records anglers killed by freak waves, and Seaside Cottages warns of surges over the Kalk Bay wall. A 3 to 4 oz sinker with 0.50 mm trace is also beyond the page'
unverified: temp: all values are estimates. The roughly 13 C floor is inferred for roman from Cole 2020's general observation for all False Bay reef fish (boat angling), not from a roman-specific measurement.
peak_months: no Cape source gives a seasonal peak (the Kleinmond and Whale Coast guides say 'all year'), so the season is rated flat and water temperature drives the rating.
spawn_months: Buxton 1990 gives a 'restricted summer breeding season' (seen in a search listing only). November to February is an estimate.
Kerwath et al. 2007 (caves during upwelling, reduced night activity, home ranges of 1000 to 3000 m2) was summarised from an abstract or search listing and has not been checked against the paper.

Tsitsikamma tag-recapture: the '61% recaptured within 50 m' figure and its attribution (Kerwath et al. versus Cowley, Brouwer and Tilney 2002) are unconfirmed. The profile keeps only 'very high site fidelity'.
Light weights: only the low night weight has any backing (Kerwath et al. 2007, abstract). The dawn, day and dusk values are estimates.

Sea, tide, range, trend, clarity, wind and flow weights are estimates. Tide is near flat. The only roman-specific tide advice (one Glencairn quarry angler) favours low tide, and the low-tide tactic rests on that single post.
FishBase size and depth figures, the IUCN Near Threatened status and the WWF-SASSI orange rating were not re-checked by the reviewer.
typical_size for shore-caught fish around Cape Town is an estimate. Only the species maximum and common length come from FishBase.
Bag and size limits (30 cm, 2 per day) come from WWF-SASSI, the acts.co.za regulation annexure and the ShowMe Whale Coast table, not from a current DFFE notice.

Restricted-zone boundaries come from the SANParks brochure and acts.co.za as summarised in the project's legal notes. The Boulders boundary wording in particular should be checked against the current SANParks MPA map.
The benefit of fishing the sheltered side of the reef in a moderate sea, and the benefit of scent baits in coloured water, are estimates.

red-stumpnose.name: Red stumpnose
red-stumpnose.season_note: A resident, territorial reef fish that does not migrate. It is endemic from Cape Point to the Wild Coast, so False Bay is at the cold western edge of its range. It is listed here only as a release-only incidental catch, not as a target. There is only one possible shore record near Cape Town: a single January 2010 forum list of species caught at Glencairn Quarry, and that thread also covers boat fishing about 200 m out. Year-round presence and a December to March peak are estimates (the warmest months on the western side of False Bay). Boat anglers report adults moving onto shallower reefs in summer to spawn, but that is in the Eastern Cape.

temp.basis: estimate: no sourced temperature figures. Inferred from its warm-temperate endemic range (Cape Point to East London and the Wild Coast; FishBase 22 to 35°S, subtropical, not re-checked by the reviewer).

red-stumpnose.habitat: Rocky reef. Adults live on deeper, larger reefs (30 to 150 m, most often 50 to 70 m). Juveniles use shallower reef, so any fish met from shore would most likely be a juvenile (estimate). Solitary, territorial and non-migratory. Shore occurrence near Cape Town is unconfirmed. The only mention is one ambiguous Sealine post about Glencairn Quarry that may refer to boat catches, and the Quarry may lie inside a closed area (see handling).
red-stumpnose.diet: Octopus is its favourite; also crabs, crayfish, sea urchins, red bait, other molluscs, worms and small fish. Strong crushing teeth.
red-stumpnose.typical_size: Any shore fish is likely to be a juvenile under the 30 cm minimum (estimate). Adults reach 75 cm and 5.8 kg (FishBase). Matures at about 30 cm.
red-stumpnose.handling: Release-only incidental catch, never a target. If caught: Endangered, 1 per day, 30 cm minimum; release undersize fish in the water. Endangered on the IUCN Red List (year unconfirmed) and WWF-SASSI red. It matures at about 30 cm and is slow-growing; it reportedly lives up to about 50 years, so releasing every fish, legal-size ones included, is recommended. Keep it in the water or wet, unhook quickly with wet hands or a dehooker, never gaff it, and mind the sharp dorsal spines and crushing jaws. A circle hook helps it to be lip-hooked (estimate). A recreational angling permit is required. Legal: MLRA regulation 10(f)(ii) closes a 500 m strip from Jager's Walk (south end of Fish Hoek Beach) to the northern boundary of Glencairn Beach to fishing except under permit. The sources place the Glencairn Quarry ledges inside that strip ('just past Fish Hoek', with Glencairn station and its pool a separate spot further on). Do not fish the Quarry until DFFE or SANParks confirm whether that closure was replaced by the 2004 Table Mountain National Park MPA controlled zone.

tactics.title: Not a target: release-only incidental catch
tactics.lure_or_bait: None recommended. Do not fish for it. It may take chokka, octopus, red bait or prawn meant for other reef fish (estimate).
tactics.rig: No dedicated rig. If you are bait-fishing reef for other species, a circle hook makes any fish easier to release (estimate).
tactics.retrieve: If one is hooked, bring it in steadily, keep it in or over the water, unhook it quickly and release it. If caught: Endangered, 1 per day, 30 cm minimum; release undersize fish in the water.
tactics.depth: On the bottom near reef, where it would be hooked by chance
tactics.stand: No stand recommended. Do not use the Glencairn Quarry ledges until DFFE or SANParks confirm that the reg 10(f)(ii) closed strip (Jager's Walk to Glencairn Beach) no longer applies. Do not fish exposed ledges when a moderate or rough sea is running.
tactics.why: Endangered (IUCN) and SASSI red, with a bag of 1 and a 30 cm minimum. It matures at about 30 cm and lives up to about 50 years, so fish met from shore would mostly be undersize. Shore occurrence near Cape Town rests on one ambiguous, possibly boat-caught record.

legal.bag_note: 1 per person per day
legal.note: A and B agree and both match the recreational Annexure 7. No closed season. Ignore the commercial Annexure 4 row (different size, garbled in extraction); the recreational figure is 30 cm, 1 per day.
legal.quote: Red stumpnose (Miss Lucy) | Chtysoblephus gibbiceps | 30 cm | 1

red-stumpnose.review: Checked by an independent skeptic; 17 corrections applied
review_points: The source confirms the species is IUCN Endangered, with a bag of 1 and a 30 cm minimum. By the profile's own account, shore fish are mostly juveniles under 30 cm. Scaling hooks down specifically to catch them sets the page up to target undersize fish of an endangered, slow-maturing species (said to

The only evidence is one January 2010 list of species 'caught there'. The list also has geelbek and katonkel, which are unlikely from these ledges, and appears in a thread that includes boat fishing 200 m out. So it may not be a shore catch at all. 'January to March' shore reports are overstated: th

The sources place the Quarry between Fish Hoek and Glencairn: 'just past Fish Hoek', the view 'towards Simon's Town', and Glencairn station and its pool given as a separate nearby spot. That puts the ledges inside the reg 10(f)(ii) 500 m closed strip (Jager's Walk to the northern boundary of Glencai

It is unsafe: it directs anglers onto exposed rock ledges when the swell is 1 to 1.8 m or more. The source does not offer that water as a rough-sea refuge. Enigma suggested it simply as another spot (with large pyjama sharks), and Big Gray said the south-easter and sea would push a float onto the ro

The source says only 'a slightly longer sinker trace to prevent the hook being caught'. The weak link and the strike advice are not in it, and the 1/0 to 3/0 hook is scaled down from 7/0 for juveniles. All of this is presented as the recommended rig.
That advice was for roman, hottentot, wildeperd and dassies. Red stumpnose is not mentioned in that thread.
The profile itself calls the fish a resident, territorial and non-migratory reef fish, so it cannot be absent for four months. The gap is an artefact of having summer-only reports.
The source confirms Endangered but gives no assessment year, and no other source confirming '2024' was opened.

present_months (all year, inferred from resident non-migratory behaviour) and peak_months (December to March) are estimates

temp band 13/15-20/23 is an estimate from the species' range

IUCN Endangered assessment year not confirmed
FishBase figures (75 cm, 5.8 kg, 22 to 35°S) and the WWF-SASSI red listing were not re-checked by the reviewer

smallmouth-bass.name: Smallmouth bass
smallmouth-bass.season_note: The bass are in the river all year. CapeNature lists smallmouth bass and carp in the Berg River above Paarl. The Mission reports good, sizeable smallmouth in the sections below the Berg River Dam near Franschhoek. Fishing picks up once the winter flood water drops and warms in spring. In early October the Breede was 'quite cold' and 'flowing very strongly', and fishing was slow. Spawning starts at about 15 to 18°C, and Fish the Fly says breeding peaks at about 16°C. On the upper Gouritz (Karoo) a female with spawn-worn tail tips was caught during the spawn on 14 November. Mid-summer low flows give clear water and the best lure fishing. From June to August the river is cold and often high and coloured. The bass are still there, but they sit sluggish in deep pools. Numbers in the Berg fell after the 2017-18 drought.

temp.basis: Partly sourced. Wikipedia: below 16°C they move to deeper pools, semi-hibernate and feed very little, and they spawn at 15 to 18°C. Fish the Fly: breeding peaks at about 16°C. FishBase gives a tolerance range of 9 to 30°C. ideal_hi and max are estimates.

smallmouth-bass.habitat: Clear, rocky, flowing water: pool heads and tail-outs, the edges of sandbank drop-offs where a shallow inlet meets a deep pool, current seams, eddies behind boulders, weirs and shaded banks. In hot summer months they move to deeper, faster water. When the water is cold they retreat to deep, slow pools. On the Berg, fish the middle river from below the Berg River Dam (Franschhoek) down to Paarl. At Paarl, anglers report fish in the town stretch upstream of the police station, below the weir, around the footbridge and at Berg River Park. The Arboretum section is hard to reach from the bank. Water quality in the Paarl stretch can be poor (see handling).
smallmouth-bass.diet: Mainly small fish, plus insects, tadpoles, frogs and crustaceans. In Cape rivers the crustaceans are probably freshwater crabs, since there are no native crayfish. Young fish eat plankton and insect larvae.
smallmouth-bass.typical_size: Typically 25 to 40 cm (0.3 to 1 kg) in the Berg. A big one is about 45 to 50 cm (18 to 20 inches, 1.5 to 2 kg). The SA record is close to 3 kg.
smallmouth-bass.handling: An alien invasive in the Western Cape. It is the main predator blamed for the loss of witvis and the decline of the Berg River redfin. You need a CapeNature freshwater angling licence (valid 12 months). Moving live fish between waters needs a permit, so never transfer bass. It is not confirmed whether NEM:BA invasive-species rules say bass in the Berg must be kept rather than released, so check with CapeNature. Protected indigenous fish share this water: the Berg River redfin (Endangered) and witvis, which the Freshwater Research Centre has been reintroducing since March 2025. Neither is ever a target. To avoid them, use lures and flies of 5 cm or more with single barbless hooks, and do not use tiny baits or small nymphs. If you hook one, unhook it in the water with wet hands and release it straight away. Report witvis sightings to the Freshwater Research Centre. Water quality in the Paarl stretch can be poor because of sewage and stormwater. Avoid wading and swallowing the water, wash your hands afterwards, and do not eat fish from this stretch.

tactics.title: Hopped craw or grub on the seam
tactics.lure_or_bait: 2.5 to 3 inch craw, creature or curly-tail grub in green pumpkin, brown or brown-orange, on a 3.5 to 5 g ball jighead (or a 3 g Ned rig)
tactics.rig: #1 to 1/0 jighead hook with the barb crimped, 6 to 8 lb fluorocarbon leader on light braid, ultralight spinning rod
tactics.retrieve: Cast up and across and let it tumble down with the current, then make short hops along the bottom with pauses
tactics.depth: Bottom of pool heads, tail-outs and sandbank drop-offs
tactics.stand: The inside bank of a bend, casting up and across into the seam where fast water meets the pool
tactics.why: The spot comes from a fly catch: a Berg smallmouth taken on a sandbank drop-off. The craw and grub choice is general bass practice (estimate). Smallmouth eat crustaceans and small fish off the bottom.

tactics.title: Topwater at first and last light
tactics.lure_or_bait: 5 to 7 cm popper or small walk-the-dog lure in natural or frog colours (on fly: a deer-hair mouse, popper or Dahlberg diver)
tactics.rig: Single barbless hook, or trebles with the barbs crimped, 8 lb leader
tactics.retrieve: Pop and pause, letting it sit until the rings fade. Work it along shaded banks and slack water beside the current.
tactics.depth: Surface
tactics.stand: Downstream of a pool, casting up along the shaded bank and willow edges
tactics.why: Fish the Fly lists poppers and deer-hair mice for smallmouth. Limiting this to dawn and dusk is an estimate, because no source gives a time of day. In the Mission author's experience Dahlberg divers gave only modest results.

tactics.title: Fly: streamer on the drift
tactics.lure_or_bait: #2 to #4 streamers of 5 cm or more: Peacock Woolly Bugger, Clouser Minnow or Fritz bugger
tactics.rig: 5 to 6 weight rod, floating line (intermediate or sinking in deep holes), tapered leader to about 10 lb, barbless hook
tactics.retrieve: Dead-drift it along the drop-off and through the tail-out with short strips. Strip-strike on the slightest tap.
tactics.depth: Just off the bottom to mid-water
tactics.stand: Below the pool, casting up and across to the drop-off edge
tactics.why: The Mission author's favourite smallmouth fly is a Peacock Woolly Bugger. Fish the Fly lists Woolly Buggers and Clousers on a 6 weight with 10 lb tippet. An 18-inch Berg fish near Paarl took a Lalu Bug drifted along a sandbank drop-off. Small flies like that also hook Berg River redfin and witvis, so use streamers of 5 cm or more instead. Hook sizes are estimates.

tactics.title: Bright sun: finesse in the deepest shade
tactics.lure_or_bait: 2 to 3 inch finesse worm or minnow soft plastic, natural or green pumpkin
tactics.rig: Dropshot: #2 hook 20 to 30 cm above a 3 to 5 g weight, 6 lb fluorocarbon
tactics.retrieve: Hold it in place and shake gently, moving it slowly across the deepest part of the pool
tactics.depth: Near the bottom of the deepest pool
tactics.stand: Well back from the bank and low, making long casts into the shaded deep water under willows
tactics.why: Wikipedia: smallmouth move to deeper water in the hot summer months. The link to bright light, and the idea that fish in clear, low water spook easily, are estimates.

tactics.title: Coloured water: flash and vibration
tactics.lure_or_bait: Inline spinner #2 to 3 (gold or copper blade), or a small 7 g spinnerbait or bladed jig in chartreuse and white
tactics.rig: Single barbless hook where possible, 8 lb leader
tactics.retrieve: Slow-roll it through eddies and slack edges out of the main flow
tactics.depth: Mid-depth to just above the bottom
tactics.stand: Beside slack water and back-eddies on the inside of bends
tactics.why: An estimate: after rain the Berg runs high and coloured, and bass find a lure that flashes and vibrates more easily than a soft plastic. Lure choice is not sourced.

tactics.title: Cold water: dead-slow on the bottom of deep pools
tactics.lure_or_bait: 3 inch tube or craw on a 5 to 7 g jighead in brown or green pumpkin
tactics.rig: Barb crimped, 6 to 8 lb fluorocarbon leader, ultralight spinning rod
tactics.retrieve: Drag it along the bottom very slowly with long pauses, and fish the warmest part of the day
tactics.depth: Bottom of the deepest, slowest pool
tactics.stand: The head of the deepest pool, casting into the slow water
tactics.why: Below 16°C smallmouth hold in deep pools and feed very little. An early-October Breede trip in cold, strong water produced only a few bites.

tactics.title: Hot summer: the deep, fast run at the pool head
tactics.lure_or_bait: 5 to 7 cm diving crankbait in natural minnow colours, or a 3 inch paddle-tail on a 5 to 7 g jighead
tactics.rig: Barbs crimped, 6 to 8 lb fluorocarbon leader, ultralight to light spinning rod
tactics.retrieve: Cast up into the head of the run and bring it back slightly faster than the current, bumping the bottom, then let it swing through the deepest slot
tactics.depth: Near the bottom of the deeper, faster water where the run enters the pool
tactics.stand: Beside the run at the head of a pool, casting up and across into the deepest fast water
tactics.why: Wikipedia: smallmouth move to deeper, faster-moving water in the hot summer months. Lure choice is an estimate.

tactics.title: Overcast: cover water with a minnow plug
tactics.lure_or_bait: 6 to 7 cm suspending jerkbait or minnow plug in natural silver, olive or brown
tactics.rig: Hooks crimped barbless, 8 lb leader
tactics.retrieve: Jerk, jerk, pause, working the whole pool from head to tail
tactics.stand: Walk the bank, casting fan-wise across each pool
tactics.why: An estimate: under cloud, bass roam more, so a search lure covers more water. Fish the Fly confirms they eat mainly fish.

legal.bag_note: No bag or size limit (an alien species).
legal.release: Putting it straight back where you caught it is allowed where it already occurs, but not in national parks or nature reserves; never move live fish to another water.
