smallmouth-bass.review: Checked by an independent skeptic; 13 corrections applied
review_points: The cited source says deeper, faster water in hot months and never mentions riffles. A shallow 0.3 to 1 m riffle tactic contradicts the reason given for it.

This contradicts the profile's own handling rule (lures and flies of 5 cm or more, to avoid the Endangered Berg River redfin and reintroduced witvis). A #10 Woolly Bugger or a Lalu Bug is well under 5 cm and is exactly the small offering that hooks small indigenous minnows. Hook sizes are not source

CapeNature says 'above Paarl'. The pollution article's 'really good, sizeable smallmouth bass' were in 'lower sections near the current Berg River Dam', which is upstream of Paarl near Franschhoek, so this looks like a misreading of 'lower'. No source places smallmouth in the lower Berg.

The profile itself says fish are still in the river. Excluding winter double-counts what the temp=cold weight already does, and it means the profile's own 'Cold water: dead-slow on the bottom of deep pools' tactic can almost never fire.

The cited Mission article reports an inlet at the top of the Arboretum releasing 'filthy, dirty smelly water', with alleged high E. coli. The author's dog became seriously ill and he scrubbed his sons after they had been in the water. Another Mission piece mentions 'the odd turd and pollution'. The

Both fish were caught on flies (a Lalu Bug, and a small fly on a 3 weight), not on soft plastics. The tail-out is on the Gouritz (Karoo), well outside the one-hour area. This is fly evidence used to support a soft-plastic tactic.

The Dahlberg remark is the author's past experience and is not tied to Berg smallmouth. Fish the Fly gives no time-of-day guidance, so the dawn and dusk gating is an estimate presented without that label.
unverified: ideal_hi 25°C and max 28°C are estimates; no Berg River water-temperature series was found
Spawn months October to December for the Berg are inferred from a Gouritz spawn on 14 November and the 15 to 18°C trigger
All light, trend, wind and clarity weights and flow 0.6 are estimates. Only 'favours clear water', 'wind made sight fishing tough' and 'deeper, faster water in hot summer months' are sourced

These are general bass practice, not Cape-sourced: the coloured-water spinner, the bright-day dropshot, the hot-summer pool-head lure, the overcast jerkbait, and the craw and grub choice in the default tactic. Lure and fly hook sizes are estimates
Limiting the topwater tactic to dawn and dusk is an estimate; no source gives a time of day
Not confirmed whether NEM:BA invasive-species rules require bass in the Berg to be kept rather than released
Freshwater crabs in the Berg bass diet are an inference
The Paarl access points (upstream of the police station, below the weir, Berg River Park) come from 2009 forum posts and may have changed
The reviewer did not check the witvis reintroduction article (March 2025 start), the NEM:BA listing or the Berg River redfin's Endangered status

spotted-grunter.name: Spotted grunter
spotted-grunter.season_note: Cape Town is at the far south-western edge of its range (WWF-SASSI: 'South Western Cape up to Mozambique'). Here it is a rare straggler, not a regular target. Local anglers called it 'definitely not a common occurence', and one could 'only remember of one being landed on rod and reel' in False Bay (Sealine, 2010). The Cape-area records are: about 4.5 kg on prawn 'just past the palletjies at Strandfontein' (rod, January 1997); one off Gordon's Bay harbour wall caught 'during dredging' (March 1999); and one over 5 kg reported from the Muizenberg/Sunrise Beach area (catch date not given; mentioned in an August 2010 thread). There are also treknet fish from Strandfontein and the Zandvlei (Sandvlei) mouth. An angler who has fished Zandvlei since the 1950s never saw or heard of one there. Local anglers guess that warm, flat summer water brings them west, hence the Dec to Mar peak; the months are inferred from a handful of records. It is caught regularly only further east, from De Mond and Struisbaai to the Breede at Witsand. On the Breede, grunter stay all year but go into a 'hibernation state' and become gun-shy in winter (Krige). At Witsand, grunter and kob were taken while the wind was south-easterly, and fishing was poor while the north-wester blew (FOSAF report, 26 Oct 2026). Spawning happens at sea off KwaZulu-Natal, about Aug to Dec (Webb 2002, via abstract). They do not spawn in the Cape, so no spawn months are set here. A good rating at a Cape spot means conditions suit a stray, not that fish are there. Treat a False Bay grunter as a bonus while bait-fishing for steenbras or kob.

temp.basis: Estimate. Childs et al. 2008 (Great Fish estuary telemetry, AJMS 30:123-132) is reported to have recorded fish in about 16 to 30 C. It also reports that estuary numbers tracked sea temperature and that fish went back into the estuary when upwelling cooled the sea. These claims were read via a search abstract only (core.ac.uk returned 403), so they are unverified. Cape upwelling water (12 to 14 C) is too cold, and local anglers link Cape strays to warm summer water. The min, ideal and max cut-offs are estimates. Min was raised from 14 to 15 so cold water scores near zero at Cape spots.

spotted-grunter.habitat: Elsewhere in its range it lives over sand and mud in estuaries and the shallow surf next to them. It feeds on sand-prawn and mud-prawn banks, channel drop-offs and shallow flats, and often tails head-down in water under 1 m on the flood. Childs 2008 (abstract via search, unverified) reports fish coming into the estuary on the incoming tide by day and going out to sea on the ebb at night. Around Cape Town every record is from the False Bay coast, and every rod record is from the sea: the Strandfontein surf just past the palletjies (low flat reef shelves), the Muizenberg/Sunrise Beach area, and Gordon's Bay harbour wall. The Zandvlei mouth has a treknet record only. Its mouth is managed and is opened only about nine times a year for about five days, so tidal flow inside is weak or absent. The Zandvlei mouth is the nearest estuary to the record sites. No grunter records were found for the Eerste or Lourens mouths, and the coast between those two mouths is the Helderberg MPA no-take zone. No record was found from The Horses or Broken Road themselves. They sit on the same Muizenberg to Swartklip sand-and-low-reef surf. Fish for it on the open beach, not in the vlei.
spotted-grunter.diet: Burrowing crustaceans first. Larger fish prefer sand prawn (Callichirus/Callianassa kraussi) and mud prawn (Upogebia africana) (Webb 2002 thesis, via abstract). It also eats crabs (including marsh crabs), shrimps, amphipods, worms, small bivalves, gobies and silversides. It blows mud prawns out of their burrows with a jet of water ('tail, blow') and sucks sand prawns out ('tail, suck, bail'). It also eats prawns swimming in mid-water during 'prawn walks' (The Mission, Botha 2020 and 2021, Garden Route).
spotted-grunter.typical_size: The Cape records are few but large: about 4.5 kg (Strandfontein, 1997) and over 5 kg (Muizenberg/Sunrise Beach area, date not given). Elsewhere, shore fish in estuaries are typically 40 to 60 cm (about 1 to 3 kg; estimate). A big one is 70 cm+ and 5 to 6 kg. Maximum is about 80 to 91 cm and 9 to 9.5 kg, living up to 15 to 16 years.
spotted-grunter.handling: Listed as Vulnerable (National Biodiversity Assessment 2018) and SASSI red ('don't buy'): no sale, recreational only. Minimum size 40 cm, daily bag 5 per person, and a recreational permit is required. In the Cape it is a rare stray, so release it. It has sharp dorsal and anal spines and grunts when handled. Wet your hands, support the belly, keep it in the water where you can, and unhook quickly. Circle hooks reduce deep hooking. If it has swallowed the hook, cut the trace close rather than tearing it out. In the Zandvlei Estuary Nature Reserve, the Zandvlei Trust says catch and release of indigenous species is required by law, and a permit is needed. A 2012 forum thread, citing the Nature Conservation Ordinance 1974, says the vlei is closed to angling from sunset to sunrise. Check the current rules with the City of Cape Town or the Zandvlei Trust. Night sessions belong on the open beach, in a group.

tactics.title: Sand prawn on the pushing tide, first gutter
tactics.lure_or_bait: 2 or 3 whole sand prawns threaded on the hook, or one mud prawn. Bought, or pumped where collecting is allowed, under a recreational permit and within the daily bait limit.
tactics.rig: 1/0 to 2/0 circle hook on a 60 to 80 cm trace of 0.35 to 0.40 mm fluorocarbon. A 30 to 60 g ball or bean sinker running on the main line above a swivel. Main line 0.25 to 0.30 mm mono or 15 to 20 lb braid on a 2.7 to 3.0 m (9 to 10 ft) light rod.
tactics.retrieve: Cast, let it settle, then leave it still. Grunter pick the prawn up and swim off with it. Let the line come tight and lift steadily (circle hook); don't strike at the first taps.
tactics.depth: On the bottom, where the inner bank drops into the first gutter, 0.5 to 2 m
tactics.stand: On the open beach. At Strandfontein, just past the palletjies (the low flat reef shelves), cast to the lip of the first gutter and move back up the beach as the flood covers the bank. The same kind of gutter at Sunrise Beach (the open-beach side of the Zandvlei mouth, outside the reserve), The Horses or Broken Road also fits, but only Strandfontein has a rod-caught record. After dark, fish in a group.
tactics.why: Elsewhere, grunter move onto prawn banks on the incoming tide (Childs 2008, abstract via search, unverified). Garden Route estuary reports give the pushing tide as the grunter bite. Applying that to the False Bay surf is an extrapolation. The one Cape rod-caught grunter with a known bait (Strandfontein, 1997) took prawn in this surf.

tactics.title: Night surf gutter, long thin trace
tactics.lure_or_bait: A bundle of sand prawn, or prawn tipped with a small piece of bloodworm (within bait limits)
tactics.rig: Single 1/0 to 2/0 hook on a long, thin trace of 1 to 1.2 m of 0.35 mm, with a small bead of float foam to lift the bait just off the sand. A 40 to 60 g running sinker on a sliding clip, on a 2.7 to 3.0 m (9 to 10 ft) light rod. Use a small grapnel of up to about 85 g only if needed to hold in a south-easter; that is the top end for light tackle.
tactics.retrieve: Static. Lift and check the bait every 5 to 10 minutes and recast into the same gutter. Let a grunter run with the bait before you lift.
tactics.depth: Bottom of the first gutter behind the inner sandbank, 1 to 2 m
tactics.stand: Strandfontein just past the palletjies, in the first gutter, not the backline. Sunrise Beach, The Horses and Broken Road are the same kind of surf (no grunter record at the last two). Fish in a group, never alone at night.
tactics.why: The one Cape rod-caught grunter with a known bait came from this surf, on prawn. Sunrise Beach anglers use long, thin, lightly floated traces for steenbras ('keep it long and thin'). The same rig suits a stray grunter, but that is an extrapolation. Local anglers guess that warm, calm summer water brings strays west.

tactics.title: Soft plastic prawn worked along the gutter
tactics.lure_or_bait: A 2.5 to 3 inch prawn or shrimp soft plastic, or a small 2.5 to 3 inch paddle-tail, on a 7 to 14 g jighead with a 1/0 hook, just heavy enough to keep bottom contact in the gutter. A scented plastic helps.
tactics.rig: 15 to 20 lb braid to 1 to 1.5 m of 0.30 to 0.35 mm fluorocarbon leader, on a 2.4 to 2.7 m light spinning rod with a 2500 to 3000 size reel
tactics.retrieve: Drag it slowly along the bottom with short 10 to 20 cm hops and 2 to 3 second pauses, like a prawn flicking off the bank. Takes usually come on the pause. Lift into weight; don't strike at taps.
tactics.depth: On the bottom, 0.5 to 2 m
tactics.stand: On the open beach on a flat or small sea: Strandfontein just past the palletjies, or the first gutter at Sunrise Beach, The Horses or Broken Road. Cast along the gutter and work the lure back along the foot of the inner bank, where prawns wash off as the flood covers it.
tactics.colour: Natural tan, brown or olive in clear water. Root-beer or motor-oil in coloured water.
tactics.why: Grunter chase swimming prawns as well as digging them out (Botha, Garden Route). On the Breede, big fish are taken in deep channels on prawn or lures. Lure-caught grunter are documented in the Eastern Cape and Garden Route, not in Cape waters, so this is an extrapolation for a rare stray.

tactics.title: Coloured water after a blow
tactics.lure_or_bait: A bundle of sand prawn, or sand prawn tipped with bloodworm (within bait limits)
tactics.rig: 1/0 to 2/0 hook on an 80 cm trace of 0.35 to 0.40 mm, with a 40 to 60 g running sinker on a slider, on a 2.7 to 3.0 m (9 to 10 ft) light rod. Use a small grapnel of up to about 85 g only if the south-easter won't let the sinker hold; that is the top end for light tackle.
tactics.retrieve: Static on the bottom. Recast to stay in the coloured water as it shifts.
tactics.depth: Bottom of the nearest gutter, 1 to 2 m
tactics.stand: On the sand, where churned-up or coloured water runs along the beach. Fish the Strandfontein gutters after a south-easter, or Sunrise Beach where the Zandvlei plume runs out while the mouth is open. Stand on the beach, not out on the palletjies or other reef shelves. In a moderate sea, stay well back from the wash.
tactics.why: Elsewhere the species lives in highly turbid estuaries, and turbidity is reported to be one of the things that moves it (Childs 2008, abstract via search, unverified). The clearest Cape hint is the Gordon's Bay harbour-wall fish caught during dredging (1999). At Witsand, grunter and kob were taken while the wind was south-easterly (FOSAF). Coloured water also hides the line from a wary bottom feeder.

tactics.title: Prawn on a running sinker in the first gutter
tactics.lure_or_bait: 2 or 3 sand prawns threaded on the hook (or mud prawn)
tactics.rig: 1/0 to 2/0 circle hook, 60 to 80 cm of 0.35 mm fluorocarbon trace, and a 20 to 60 g running sinker (lighter on a flat sea), on a 2.7 to 3.0 m (9 to 10 ft) light rod
tactics.retrieve: Static on the bottom. Let the fish run, then lift steadily.
tactics.depth: On the bottom, 0.5 to 2 m
tactics.stand: The first gutter at Strandfontein just past the palletjies, where the one rod-caught grunter with a known bait was taken. The same kind of gutter at Sunrise Beach, The Horses or Broken Road also fits. Fish in a group after dark.
tactics.why: Prawn on the bottom is the one method with a Cape catch behind it. Grunter here are rare strays, so fish it as a bonus while targeting steenbras or kob.

legal.bag_note: 5 per day. Counts toward the aggregate of 10.
legal.note: A and B agree and both match R.959. No closed season.

spotted-grunter.review: Checked by an independent skeptic; 24 corrections applied
review_points: In Cape Town shore-angling slang, 'spotty' or 'spotties' is the spotted gully shark (Triakis megalopterus). The only cached Cape use (Platboom, Cape Point) describes 'spotties' teeth' wearing through leaders and calls the fish 'apparently common there'. A grunter has no such teeth and is not common

The thread only says Captain Sparrow reported 'a spotted grunter over 5 kg from the area', and that it was unusual there. August 2010 is when the thread was posted, not when the fish was caught. Nothing says it was the poster's first. The catch date is unknown, so it cannot be used as evidence of an

The source names a third, probably rod-caught fish: Gordon's Bay harbour wall, March 1999, caught 'during dredging'. The Sunrise Beach fish is only 'from the area', with no method given. The profile also leaves out the dredging context, which is the clearest Cape evidence for its coloured-water weig

The only Zandvlei evidence is one second-hand treknet fish 'a few years' before 2010. An angler who has fished Zandvlei since the 1950s 'never saw or heard of grunter or kob there'. The mouth is managed and is often closed (opened about nine times a year for five days). Six of eight tactics send ang

Other river mouths on the False Bay coast within the page's area, notably the Eerste River at Macassar and the Lourens River at Strand, are also estuaries. The claim is wrong as stated (reviewer's regional knowledge; not in cache).

The profile's own handling note says the vlei is closed to angling from sunset to sunrise (2012 report, Nature Conservation Ordinance 1974), and the stand is the Zandvlei mouth sandbank. As written, the engine could show an after-dark tactic inside a closed reserve. The same conflict affects the top

False Bay surf at Muizenberg and Strandfontein is often 18 to 22 C in summer, so on a calm, warm summer dawn on a pushing spring tide every factor scores at or near 1. The engine could then rank grunter as the 'top species' and show its tactics, for a fish with about three rod records near Cape Town

The Sunrise Beach thread gives 'keep it long and thin' with a small float as general advice for steenbras and other bait fishing, not for grunter. Using it for grunter is an extrapolation and should be labelled as such.
unverified: Rarity is not captured by any profile field. On a calm, warm summer dawn with a pushing spring tide, every factor can score near 1 at a False Bay spot, for a fish with about three rod records in 30 years. The reviewer suggests an engine-level abundance multiplier of about 0.1 for Cape spots (estimate), or barring grunter from being ranked top species.

Temperature cut-offs (min 15, ideal 18 to 25, max 29 C) are estimates. The 16 to 30 C range and the upwelling link come from the Childs 2008 abstract via search, which could not be checked (core.ac.uk 403).
All Childs 2008 claims (flood-by-day entry and ebb-by-night exit, and the correlations with temperature, pressure, upwelling and turbidity) were read via a search abstract only and are unverified.

Cape Town present months (Oct to May) and peak months (Dec to Mar) are inferred from a handful of records (Jan 1997, Mar 1999, an undated Sunrise Beach-area fish, Hermanus in December) and one angler's guess that warm, flat summer water brings them west.

No grunter record was found for The Horses or Broken Road specifically. Strandfontein has one dated rod-caught record (1997) plus treknet fish. The Muizenberg/Sunrise Beach area has one undated fish of unknown method. The Zandvlei mouth has a treknet record only.

Spawning (Aug to Dec, at sea) is for KwaZulu-Natal only, from the SANBI profile citing Webb 2002, read via a search snippet (page returned 403). spawn_months is left empty because they do not spawn in the Cape.

Light weights are partly estimated. Childs' day and night movement pattern is unverified, and the Garden Route report says big fish come onto the flats only in very low light. The exact values are judgement.
Sea-state weights (flat 0.85, small 1, moderate 0.6, rough 0.2) are estimates, with no sourced numbers.

Pressure trend weights (falling 1, steady 0.9, rising 0.6) are estimates. Falling is rated highest because Krige's best day is 'the last good day before a new front hits', but that is about Breede winter fish, so for Cape strays it is guesswork.
Clarity weights (coloured better than clear) are estimates, based on the turbid-estuary studies (unverified) and the Gordon's Bay fish caught during dredging.
Wind weights are estimates. The FOSAF Witsand note is about direction (south-easterly good, north-westerly poor), not strength.
Flow 0.5 is an estimate.

Neaps 0.55 rests on one Port Elizabeth fly report ('not a good grunter day because it's the neap tide') and the Mission's note that the spring flood flushes prawn holes on Garden Route mud flats. Applying either to the Cape surf is an extrapolation.
Typical shore size of 40 to 60 cm (1 to 3 kg) in estuaries is an estimate. The Cape records are both large fish of 4.5 to 5+ kg.

Pushing-tide, long-thin-trace and soft-plastic tactics are applied to the Cape surf by extrapolation. The pushing-tide bite is from Garden Route estuaries, the long thin trace is local steenbras advice, and lure catches are from the Eastern Cape and Garden Route. Soft-plastic sizes, jighead weights and rig details are standard light-tackle choices, not taken from a source.
The Zandvlei reserve closure from sunset to sunrise comes from a 2012 forum thread found in a cached search. Check the current rules with the City of Cape Town or the Zandvlei Trust.
Bait-collection rules on the Strandfontein and Sunrise Beach beaches were not confirmed. The tactics say to use bought bait, or bait pumped where collecting is allowed under a permit.

springer.name: Springer (ladyfish)
springer.season_note: Rare or doubtful at Zandvlei. Treat any springer as a bonus, not something to plan a trip around. Zandvlei lies west of the documented range: Mann 2013 says 'from the Breede River north-eastwards', and WWF-SASSI says 'along the South Western Cape up to Mozambique'. A Southern Cape fly writer said in 2022 that skippies are now 'very rarely' seen there. The only Zandvlei records are anecdotal. A 2008 Sealine post says springer are 'plenty' and sometimes large there, and a 1950s recollection lists springers alongside harders. Caution: in Cape slang 'springer' also means a large harder (mullet). A Sealine Milnerton post says 'springers (large harders)', and an estate page lists 'springer' with mullet in the closed Wildevoelvlei, so some local 'springer' reports are really mullet. The months are borrowed from the Eastern Cape, where the fish are more common in spring and summer and larvae enter estuaries then (Mann 2013). No peak month is set on purpose: the ranking should apply a strong presence penalty until local catches are confirmed. Zandvlei's mouth is open all winter. In summer it is closed and only opened for a few days at each full moon, so new fish can only come in from the sea while it is open. Breeding shoals gather off Mozambique in winter, and Mann gives the South African breeding season as essentially unknown, so no spawn months are set for Cape spots.

temp.basis: estimate. Tropical to subtropical species. Juveniles depend on 'warm, turbid estuaries', and adults are more common off the Eastern Cape in spring and summer (Mann 2013). No thermal data found.

springer.habitat: Shallow coastal water and estuaries, especially permanently open ones. It tolerates a wide range of salinity and turbid water, and juveniles use warm, turbid estuaries as nurseries (Mann 2013). Zandvlei is only open seasonally, which may help explain why the fish is scarce there. At Zandvlei, fish the open channel and bends rather than the weedy shallows. Garrick anglers name the bowling green and first big bend, the bridge, the water up to Marina da Gama, and 'anywhere where you can cast a lure without catching weed' (Sealine 2008 garrick thread). These are garrick spots, assumed to suit springer.
springer.diet: Small fish and crustaceans. Adults feed mainly in the early evening (Mann 2013) and take fish, squid and shrimp bait (FishBase). Most of the time they hunt very small prey such as tiny crustaceans and small baitfish, though they will chase a 20 cm mullet, and they love swimming prawns (The Mission, 2022).
springer.typical_size: Estimate for Zandvlei: 35 to 55 cm FL (about 0.5 to 1.5 kg); a big one is 3 kg plus. The SA angling record is 11.8 kg, and the maximum recorded length is 118 cm FL (Mann 2013).
springer.handling: No-sale recreational species. The national limits are a bag of 5 per person per day, no minimum size and no closed season (Mann 2013; DFFE recreational brochure Table 4). IUCN status is Least Concern (2012), and the stock has not been assessed (Mann 2013). WWF-SASSI lists it as red, the category for species that are illegal to sell; the reviewer did not check that listing. At Zandvlei you need a recreational fishing permit. The Zandvlei Trust says indigenous species must be released, so release every springer you catch there, and by law any leervis (garrick). It jumps repeatedly and throws hooks, so use single hooks, ideally barbless (circle hooks for bait), and keep the fish in the water to unhook it. It is slimy and thrashes, so handle it with wet hands and release it quickly. Buy bait rather than collecting it inside the nature reserve.

tactics.title: Small spoon through the channel
tactics.lure_or_bait: Small Abu Toby-style spoon, 7 to 12 g, silver or silver-blue
tactics.rig: Light spinning rod, 2 to 3 kg nylon or 10 lb braid, 60 cm of 0.30 mm fluorocarbon leader, single hook in place of the treble
tactics.retrieve: Cast across the channel, count it down 2 to 3 seconds, then retrieve fast and erratically with short pauses
tactics.depth: Top metre of the water column
tactics.stand: A point or bend where the channel runs close to the bank and is clear of weed, e.g. the first big bend near the bowling green (a garrick spot, assumed to suit springer). At Zandvlei release every springer, and any leervis by law (Zandvlei Trust).
tactics.why: Small Toby-style spoons are named in the 2008 Zandvlei thread that reports springer as 'plenty', though that poster mainly targeted leervis, so it is not springer-specific evidence. Mann 2013 says springer eat small fish.
sources: Mann BQ (ed.) 2013, ORI Special Publication 9, Elops machnata profile (J.Q. Maggs)

tactics.title: Popper or walk-the-dog at last light
tactics.lure_or_bait: Small popper (Skitterpop or Roosta style, 5 to 7 cm) or small walk-the-dog stickbait
tactics.rig: 2 to 3 kg line or 10 lb braid, 60 cm 0.30 mm fluorocarbon leader, loop knot
tactics.retrieve: Pop-pop-pause, or a steady walk-the-dog. If fish splash without connecting, slow down and leave longer pauses.
tactics.depth: Surface
tactics.stand: The {downwind} bank, where the wind pushes bait and shrimp, or a bend with surface activity. At Zandvlei release every springer, and any leervis by law (Zandvlei Trust).
tactics.why: Springer feed mainly in the early evening (Mann 2013). Roosta and Skitterpop poppers are named in the 2008 Zandvlei thread, though that poster mainly targeted leervis. Ed Truter (The Mission) says surface chuggers work in low light and walk-the-dog for hardware.
sources: Mann BQ (ed.) 2013, ORI Special Publication 9, Elops machnata profile

tactics.title: Drift a shrimp fly in the current (mouth open only)
tactics.lure_or_bait: Shrimp pattern (glass shrimp to swimming-prawn size), sparse bucktail Clouser or Charlie, size 6 to 2, natural colours
tactics.rig: 6 to 7 weight rod (estimate), intermediate or slow-intermediate line, 2 to 2.5 m leader to 0.25 to 0.30 mm tippet
tactics.retrieve: Cast up and across the current and let the fly drift like a loose shrimp with occasional short strips
tactics.depth: Mid-water to just under the surface
tactics.stand: Only when Zandvlei's mouth is open: all winter, but in summer only for the few days around each full moon when it is opened. Check the mouth before you go. Then fish the channel towards the mouth and the bridge, from the bank the current sweeps. At Zandvlei release every springer, and any leervis by law (Zandvlei Trust).
tactics.why: Truter says a drifting shrimp in the current is an easy target and to 'drift the fly rather than strip it'. Botha says 'skippies love swimming prawns'. Zandvlei only has tidal flow while the mouth is open. Springs stands in for the summer full-moon openings, but a closed mouth means no current and this tactic does not apply.
sources: Wikipedia, Zandvlei Estuary Nature Reserve (mouth management), cached 29 Oct 2026

tactics.title: Bigger baitfish fly in low light
tactics.lure_or_bait: Finger Mullet, Whistler or Andino-style baitfish fly, size 2 to 1/0, or a small surface chugger fly
tactics.rig: 6 to 8 weight rod (estimate), floating or intermediate line, 0.30 mm tippet
tactics.retrieve: Fast, steady strips; with a chugger, short pops and pauses
tactics.depth: Surface to 0.5 m
tactics.stand: The {downwind} bank or a channel edge where fish are seen chasing. At Zandvlei release every springer, and any leervis by law (Zandvlei Trust).
tactics.why: Truter: in low light, or when fish are chasing hard, go bigger and chunkier (Finger Mullets, Whistlers, Andinos, surface chuggers).

tactics.title: Small chiselnose plug along the weed edge
tactics.lure_or_bait: Small chiselnose perspex plug, 6 to 9 cm, clear or silver
tactics.rig: 2 to 3 kg line or 10 lb braid, 60 cm 0.30 mm leader, loop knot
tactics.retrieve: Twitch and pause just under the surface, working the lure parallel to the weed edge
tactics.depth: Subsurface, 0 to 0.5 m
tactics.stand: Parallel to a weed edge where the channel drops off, from a bank you can cast along. At Zandvlei release every springer, and any leervis by law (Zandvlei Trust).
tactics.why: Small chiselnose perspex plugs are among the lures named in the 2008 Zandvlei thread. That poster mainly targeted leervis, so this is a leervis lure assumed to suit springer.

tactics.title: Prawn or sardine strip under a float
tactics.lure_or_bait: A whole small prawn, or a 4 to 5 cm strip of sardine or chokka
tactics.rig: Small pencil float set 0.5 to 1 m deep, 60 cm 0.30 mm leader, No. 2 to 1/0 circle hook so the fish is lip-hooked and can be released unharmed
tactics.retrieve: Let it drift along the channel edge with the current or wind, with an occasional slow twitch
tactics.depth: 0.5 to 1 m
tactics.stand: The {downwind} bank, letting the float drift along the channel edge. At Zandvlei release every springer, and any leervis by law (Zandvlei Trust).
tactics.why: Springer tolerate turbid water and eat small fish and crustaceans (Mann 2013), and take fish, squid and shrimp bait (FishBase). Scent helps in coloured water. A circle hook avoids deep hooking, since every fish goes back at Zandvlei.
sources: Mann BQ (ed.) 2013, ORI Special Publication 9, Elops machnata profile

tactics.title: Cold water: scale down and fish slow
tactics.lure_or_bait: Small sparse shrimp or Gotcha-style fly, size 8 to 6, natural tan or olive
tactics.rig: 6 to 7 weight rod (estimate), slow-intermediate line, long 2.5 m leader to 0.22 to 0.25 mm tippet
tactics.retrieve: Very slow figure-of-eight or dead drift; change casting angle if fish ignore it
tactics.depth: Mid-water in the deepest part of the channel
tactics.stand: The deepest channel bend, which holds the most stable water. At Zandvlei release every springer, and any leervis by law (Zandvlei Trust).
tactics.why: Truter's advice when fish do not react: scale down, get more subtle, fish slower, drift the fly, change the angle. The species prefers warm water (Mann 2013), so cold water is a poor bet.
sources: Mann BQ (ed.) 2013, ORI Special Publication 9, Elops machnata profile

legal.bag_note: 5 per day. Counts toward the aggregate of 10.
legal.note: A and B agree and both match R.959. No closed season.
legal.quote: Springer (ten pounder) | Elops machnata | none | 5

sources: Wikipedia, Zandvlei Estuary Nature Reserve (mouth management), cached 29 Oct 2026
springer.review: Checked by an independent skeptic; 17 corrections applied
review_points: Mann 2013 gives the IUCN Red List status as Least Concern (2012, Adams et al. 2012c), not Data Deficient. The 'Data Deficient' label is unsourced or confused with another listing.

Zandvlei lies west of the documented range (Breede River eastwards), and the only Cape records are one 2008 forum post and a 1950s recollection. In Cape slang 'springer' also means a large harder: an estate page lists 'springer' with mullet in closed Wildevoelvlei, and Sealine 2014 says 'springers (

The bowling-green and first-big-bend locations come from the Garrick thread and are garrick spots. The 2008 thread's lure list is not clearly tied to springer; that poster's main target was leervis. The springer tactics are in effect leervis tactics at Zandvlei, where leervis must be released by law

Zandvlei only has tidal flow while the mouth is open. In the profile's own peak months (Dec-Mar) the mouth is closed except for a few days at each full moon. Without a mouth-state input, the engine will fire tide-current tactics on summer days when there is no current.
This is Mozambique offshore spawning (breeding shoals off Mozambique in winter). Mann gives reproductive style and season as essentially unknown for South Africa, so it has no bearing on the Cape.
unverified: Whether Elops machnata is a regular Zandvlei fish at all: Mann 2013 puts its range from the Breede River eastwards, the only Zandvlei reports are anecdotal (2008, 1950s), and some Cape 'springer' reports mean large harders (mullet). The ranking should apply a strong presence penalty; the profile has no field for that, so peak_months is left empty instead.
Present months for Zandvlei are an estimate borrowed from Eastern Cape seasonality (Mann 2013). There is no Cape catch data, and Zandvlei's mouth is closed for most of the summer.
Temperature band (16 / 20 to 27 / 31 C) is an estimate
Light weights are partly sourced (early-evening feeding, Mann 2013); the dawn, day and night values are estimates

Tide, range, flow, trend, wind and clarity weights are estimates. Tide and range are flattened towards neutral because the engine has no mouth-state input and Zandvlei has no tidal flow while the mouth is closed.

The drift-fly tactic uses springs as a stand-in for the summer full-moon openings. It will also fire on new-moon springs, when the mouth is normally closed, so its text tells anglers to check the mouth first.
Lures and stands come from Zandvlei garrick/leervis anglers and are assumed to suit springer
The WWF-SASSI red rating and 'South Western Cape' range wording, The Mission articles and the FishBase summary were cited by the researcher but not independently checked by the reviewer
The Zandvlei Trust page says indigenous species 'such as Leervis' must be released. Applying that to springer is a reading of 'indigenous species', not a named rule.
Fly rod and line weights are estimates; the source names intermediate lines but no rod weight
Typical Zandvlei size is an estimate
Advice to buy bait rather than collect it in the reserve is precautionary; no Zandvlei bait-collection rule was found

steentjie.name: Steentjie
steentjie.season_note: Lives in False Bay all year. A Sealine search snippet reports one caught off the Strand in October 2009. The November to April peak is an estimate, and no dated catch supports it. In the coldest water it goes quiet: in August 2011 a Langebaan angler on Sealine wrote 'not even a Steentjie is biting' at 11 C, and anglers there waited for the general fishing season to start again from September. It spawns July to October in the Western Cape, when males dig and guard nests on sand beside reef.

temp.basis: Estimate. The only direct anchor is one Langebaan post on Sealine (August 2011) reporting no steentjie bites at 11 C. The species ranges from Saldanha Bay to KwaZulu-Natal (Iwatsuki & Heemstra 2022, via Wikipedia), so Cape Town sits mid-range, not at a warm edge, and the fish is common in upwelled Atlantic water of 12 to 15 C. The ideal band and the max are estimates. No published survey or lab thresholds were found.

steentjie.habitat: Shoals over rocky reef, ledges and kelp edges, from the shallows down to about 60 m. Common around harbour walls and jetties. It also enters estuaries and lives among the weed there. From the shore, fish the line where reef or kelp meets sand, anywhere from mid-water to the bottom. In spawning season (July to October) males guard nests dug in sand next to reef. It is small and abundant, so it is often bycatch and a bait-stealer when you are after bigger reef fish.
steentjie.diet: Omnivore: eats algae and small crustaceans such as amphipods, isopods and small shrimps. Juveniles eat zooplankton. It pecks and strips baits quickly. Anglers report steentjies 'cleaning' baits and taking black mussel before stumpnose can reach it.
steentjie.typical_size: Shore fish are usually about 18 to 28 cm (roughly 150 to 300 g, an estimate). A big one is 35 to 40 cm and close to 1 kg (estimate). FishBase gives a maximum length of 45 cm TL, with 25 cm typical. Females mature at about 23.5 cm fork length and males at about 24.9 cm.
steentjie.handling: No minimum size. Bag limit 10 per person per day (from a 2009 regulations list on Sealine; check current DFFE rules). The dorsal fin is spiny: hold the fish from the head end with the spines folded flat. It is a robust little fish: unhook it quickly with pliers and return unwanted fish head-first into the water. You may use it as bait only if it was caught on rod and line, and it counts toward the bag limit. IUCN Least Concern. It changes sex from female to male as it grows, so the big dark fish guarding nests from July to October are males. Consider releasing them in spawning season.

tactics.title: Small bait on a short running trace along the reef edge
tactics.lure_or_bait: A thin 1 to 2 cm strip of chokka (squid), a piece of prawn, a sardine strip or white mussel
tactics.rig: Size 6 to 2 short-shank hook on a 0.30 to 0.35 mm snood. In rocky ground keep the hook and sinker traces no longer than 30 cm. Use a 1 to 2 oz sinker on a lighter weak-link strop (rotten-bottom), so a snagged sinker breaks off and the fish does not.
tactics.retrieve: Cast to the edge where reef or kelp meets sand and keep the line just tight. Steentjies peck, so wait for a firm pull or for the line to move off before lifting. Re-bait often.
tactics.depth: On or just off the bottom, about 2 to 8 m down
tactics.stand: On a ledge, pier or harbour wall, casting along the line where reef or kelp meets sand rather than straight into thick kelp
tactics.why: Steentjies are small-mouthed shoaling omnivores that pick at small baits. Small hooks and short traces suit them and lose less tackle on the reef. The short weak-link sinker strop is hottentot advice, applied here by analogy to a similar small reef sparid.

tactics.title: Float a small bait down the kelp edge on calm days
tactics.lure_or_bait: A tiny strip of chokka or a piece of prawn
tactics.rig: Small pencil or bubble float set 1 to 3 m deep. Size 6 to 4 hook on 0.25 to 0.30 mm line, with one or two split shot to cock the float.
tactics.retrieve: Let the float drift slowly along the kelp line or ledge face. When it dips twice or slides away, wind down and lift.
tactics.depth: Mid-water, 1 to 3 m down
tactics.stand: On a ledge or harbour wall above deeper water, letting any current carry the float along the kelp edge
tactics.why: Estimate. Steentjies are shoaling daytime feeders that pick at small food. In calm, settled water a float keeps the bait above the snags and in front of the shoal. No Cape source describes float fishing for steentjie.

tactics.title: Sabiki bait-jig off the ledge
tactics.lure_or_bait: Sabiki bait-jig with small feathered or flasher hooks (sizes 8 to 10). Tip each hook with a sliver of chokka for more bites.
tactics.rig: Sabiki string with a 1 oz sinker clipped to the bottom loop, on a light 2 to 4 kg spinning outfit
tactics.retrieve: Drop to the bottom, lift slowly about 1 m and let it flutter back. If fish hit in mid-water, stop a few turns up and jig there.
tactics.depth: From the bottom up to mid-water off the ledge face
tactics.stand: On a ledge, pier or harbour wall with deep water straight below, so you can drop vertically without snagging the kelp
tactics.why: Sealine anglers report that 'all I ever seem to catch on a sabiki is Steentjies'. The shoals take small flashing hooks readily.

tactics.title: Dropshot a small shrimp plastic in clear water
tactics.lure_or_bait: 2 inch scented shrimp or sandworm soft plastic (e.g. Berkley Gulp! 2 in Shrimp or Sandworm) in natural or camo
tactics.rig: Size 6 to 4 dropshot hook, nose-hooked, on a 0.25 mm fluorocarbon leader, with a 7 to 10 g dropshot sinker 30 to 40 cm below
tactics.retrieve: Lower it onto the reef-sand edge, hold it still and give tiny twitches. Let the shoal peck, and lift when weight comes on.
tactics.depth: 30 to 40 cm off the bottom
tactics.stand: On a ledge, pier or harbour wall above a sand patch or a channel in the reef
tactics.why: Estimate. The fish eats small crustaceans and feeds by sight in daylight, so a scented shrimp imitation held still in clear water should draw it. No Cape source describes this method for steentjie.

tactics.title: Scent bait on the bottom in coloured water
tactics.lure_or_bait: Sardine (pilchard) fillet strip, or chokka with a little sardine
tactics.rig: Size 4 to 2 hook on 0.30 to 0.35 mm line, 30 cm snood, 1 to 3 oz sinker on a rotten-bottom strop. 3 oz is the top end for light tackle, so use only as much weight as holds bottom.
tactics.retrieve: Cast to the reef edge and leave it. Check and re-bait every few minutes.
tactics.depth: On the bottom, 2 to 6 m
tactics.stand: On the sheltered side of a ledge or harbour wall, out of the surge
tactics.why: Estimate. In coloured water, scent should matter more than sight, and sardine is a standard Cape bottom bait. No source describes this tactic for steentjie.

tactics.title: Fish slowly on the bottom when the water is cold
tactics.lure_or_bait: Sardine strip or prawn
tactics.rig: Size 4 hook on 0.30 mm line, 1 to 2 oz sinker on a short strop
tactics.retrieve: Fish slowly or dead still on the bottom, and give bites time to develop
tactics.depth: Hard on the bottom
tactics.stand: A sheltered ledge or harbour wall out of the surge; fish slowly on the bottom.
tactics.why: Estimate. One Langebaan report says steentjies stopped biting at 11 C. The advice that sardine works 'better when water is cold' comes from hottentot anglers at Sea Point.

legal.bag_note: 10 per day. It counts toward the aggregate of 10 and on its own fills it.
legal.note: A and B agree and both match R.959. No closed season.
legal.quote: Steentjie | Spondyliosoma emarginatum | None | 10

steentjie.review: Checked by an independent skeptic; 16 corrections applied
review_points: The cited Langebaan thread (53295) holds no 17 C reading, no November 2011 post and no steentjie-fillet comment, and no other source in the profile carries it. Also, a steentjie fillet working well means steentjie used as BAIT for other fish, so even if the post exists it says nothing about when ste

The species ranges west to Saldanha Bay (Wikipedia, Iwatsuki & Heemstra 2022), so Cape Town is mid-range, not a warm edge, and the fish is abundant in cold upwelled Atlantic and West Coast water that sits at 12 to 15 C for much of the year. A 15 C ideal floor will mark Atlantic-side steentjie as 'co

On Cape coasts cold spells are usually upwelling events, which bring cold bottom water inshore. Deeper water is then colder, not warmer, so the claim gets the physics backwards and no source supports it. The cited 'sardine better when cold' quote is about hottentot at Sea Point, not steentjie.

This text names one spot, but it sits in the unconditional tactic (when {}), so the engine will show 'below the quarry' at every steentjie spot (Kalk Bay harbour, Strand, Blouberg). The only source for the quarry ledges names roman, not steentjie.

The 'new season' post is a general Langebaan lagoon remark, not about steentjie. Neither it nor the October 2009 Strand catch supports Nov-Apr as peak months; the only dated catch cited is in October.
Both cached threads (hotties.61809, white-mussel.58422) are hottentot threads. The advice transfers fairly to small reef sparids, but the 'why' text should say it is borrowed.
unverified: All condition weights (light, sea, tide, flow, range, trend, clarity, wind) are estimates based on general reef-sparid behaviour plus Sealine anecdotes. No source measures steentjie bite rates against these conditions.

Temperature min, ideal band and max are estimates. Only the single 11 C 'no bite' post from Langebaan (Aug 2011) is sourced. The earlier '17 C in November 2011' anchor was not in the cited thread and has been removed.
Peak months (November to April) are an estimate, and no dated catch supports them. Spawning July to October is sourced (Mann et al. 2014 via Wikipedia).
No source places steentjie at a particular Cape shore spot. The only Glencairn quarry-ledge report names roman, so Glencairn detail belongs in the spot record, not here.
The float, dropshot and coloured-water scent tactics have no steentjie-specific source.
The short weak-link sinker strop and the 'sardine better in cold water' advice are hottentot advice, applied by analogy.

The reviewer could not re-check these: the livebait-steentjies sabiki quote, the kob.23405 Strand October 2009 snippet, and the 2009 bag-limit list. From memory, the reviewer says bag 10 with no minimum size matches current DFFE recreational rules. Check current DFFE regulations, including the rule on using it as bait.
The shore size and weight ranges (18 to 28 cm, 150 to 300 g; big fish 35 to 40 cm near 1 kg) are estimates. Only the 45 cm maximum, the 25 cm typical length and the maturity lengths are sourced.
The ORI/Mann 2013 linefish profiles could not be opened (oceanographicresearchinstitute.org did not resolve), so the biology numbers come from FishBase and the IUCN data cited on Wikipedia.

strepie.name: Strepie
strepie.season_note: Strepie are caught all year but are 'not so plentiful in winter' (Sealine, May 2016). Holiday catches are reported for December, Easter and the school holidays (Sealine, 2018). The April to September spawning months are for South Africa as a whole (Wikipedia), which does not say where spawning happens. The species makes an annual migration between nursery areas in the Eastern and Western Cape and KwaZulu-Natal, so these are reference months only: they are not a local Cape spawning aggregation and do not raise Cape winter scores. That migration may be why bigger fish thin out of Cape waters in winter while small fish stay in pools and harbours, but this is an inference.

temp.basis: Estimate. FishBase classifies the species as subtropical but gives no numbers, and the Wikipedia article gives no temperature. The band is set against False Bay summer water, when the fish are most plentiful.

strepie.habitat: Shoals over rocky reef and sand with weed growth, from the shallows to about 70 m (FishBase). Around Cape Town: harbour walls and jetties, tidal pools, weedy gullies and rock ledges such as the quarry rocks at Glencairn, usually in calm, sheltered water. Juveniles crowd tidal pools and harbours, and many of them are under the 15 cm legal minimum.
strepie.diet: Juveniles mainly eat crustaceans. Adults are almost entirely herbivorous, grazing seaweed (FishBase). They still take small baits of sardine, redbait, mussel worm and prawn readily.
strepie.typical_size: Usually 15 to 25 cm in harbours and pools, and many pool fish are smaller; a first catch of 17 cm is typical (Sealine). The legal minimum is 15 cm. A big one is 35 to 40 cm. Males are 15 to 30 cm and females run larger, 31 to 45 cm (Wikipedia); the maximum is 51 cm (FishBase, Wikipedia).
strepie.handling: Legal limits (DFFE recreational regulations): 15 cm minimum size and 10 per person per day. Fish kept for bait count towards both. Measure every fish and release anything under 15 cm quickly in the water. Sharp dorsal and anal spines, so smooth the dorsal fin down before gripping. Widely used as live or fillet bait for kob and other gamefish, and the size and bag limits apply there too. If eating, gut the fish at once and avoid the head and viscera: rare hallucinogenic poisoning has been reported from Mediterranean fish, possibly from the algae they eat (Wikipedia). Not a protected species. Check the current DFFE limits before keeping fish.

tactics.title: Chum and a matchhead hook
tactics.lure_or_bait: Small pieces of firm sardine on a size 12 to 14 hook; mashed sardine as chum
tactics.retrieve: No retrieve. Hold the line, lift gently on any tap, and keep a little chum going in. Measure each fish: keep only 15 cm and over, 10 a day at most.
tactics.depth: 1 to 3 m, near weed and rock
tactics.stand: Sheltered side of the harbour wall, or a calm pool or gully off the rocks. Pools are full of undersized fish, so expect to release most. Make sure the pool is open to fishing and outside the no-take zones such as St James and Boulders.
tactics.rig: Ultralight rod, 2 to 4 kg line, tiny split shot 15 cm above the hook, no float needed
tactics.why: 'Very small hook, about the size of a matchhead', firm sardine pieces, and 'throw in a bit of chum' (Sealine, Jan 2018). The District Mail column suggests a jetty, harbour or tidal pool with an ultralight rod, a number-12 hook and sardine. Small hooks catch many fish under the 15 cm legal minimum (DFFE), which must go back.

tactics.title: Redbait on a light rod off the Glencairn ledges
tactics.lure_or_bait: Pea-sized piece of redbait (rooiaas) on a size 10 to 12 hook
tactics.retrieve: Lob it into the gully or the weed edge and let it settle. Lift and drop now and then. Keep only fish of 15 cm and over.
tactics.depth: 1 to 3 m in the gullies
tactics.stand: Rocky outcrop below the railway line at Glencairn Quarry, fishing the gullies in front of you. The ledges are low: in a moderate sea near high tide, stay well back from the wash and leave if sets reach your feet.
tactics.rig: 8 ft 6 in fly rod with a small spinning reel or an ultralight spinning rod, 3 kg (6 lb) line, small hook and the smallest sinker that holds; the bottom is foul
tactics.why: At Glencairn Quarry one regular fished redbait for hottentot on 'an 8 ft 6 fly rod, 6 lb line, small hooks and small sinkers', and another, on a fly rod with a light spinning reel, found that 'even the odd strepie can give a half decent pull on ultra light tackle' (Sealine, Jan 2010). Redbait for strepie and the pushing-tide timing are estimates.

tactics.title: Pencil float in a flat calm
tactics.lure_or_bait: Pinch of bread flake or a strip of sardine skin on a size 12 hook
tactics.retrieve: Let the float sit in the chum line and strike when it dips or slides. Measure each fish and release anything under 15 cm.
tactics.depth: Float set 1 to 2 m
tactics.stand: Harbour wall or jetty corner out of the current, or a protected pool that is open to fishing
tactics.rig: Small pencil or quill float, 2 to 3 kg line, one shot below the float, size 12 hook
tactics.why: Floats work only in calm conditions. At Glencairn 'the south-easter pushes the float onto the bricks' (Sealine, Jan 2010). The bread bait is an estimate.

tactics.title: Bread or weed fly down the chum line
tactics.lure_or_bait: Bread fly (white foam or deer-hair puff) or a small green weed fly, size 12 to 10
tactics.retrieve: Dead-drift it in the chum slick and watch the leader for the take
tactics.depth: Surface film to 1 m
tactics.stand: Harbour wall or the sheltered side of rocks, with bread or sardine chum drifting past
tactics.rig: 4 to 5 weight rod, floating line, 2 to 3 kg tippet
tactics.why: On Sealine, bread flies after chumming work for mullet, which share harbour chum lines with strepie. Using them for strepie, and the weed fly, are estimates based on the strepie's grazing diet.

tactics.title: Prawn or mussel worm as the tide floods the gullies
tactics.lure_or_bait: Small piece of sand prawn or mussel worm on a size 10 hook
tactics.retrieve: Let it wash naturally into the gully on each surge. Keep only fish of 15 cm and over.
tactics.depth: 0.5 to 2 m
tactics.stand: Edge of weedy gullies the rising tide is flooding, from a ledge well above the wash. Keep your way back dry as the tide comes in, and back off if sets reach your feet.
tactics.rig: Ultralight rod, 3 kg line, small sinker or split shot
tactics.why: Prawn 'works well' for strepie (Sealine, Plettenberg Bay, Jun 2024), and mussel worm was used to catch them (Sealine, May 2016). The pushing-tide timing is an estimate.

tactics.title: Big swell: harbour basin only, stay off the rocks
tactics.lure_or_bait: Sardine pieces on a size 12 hook, with chum
tactics.retrieve: Still-fish and lift on taps. Release anything under 15 cm.
tactics.depth: 1 to 2 m
tactics.stand: Inside a sheltered harbour basin, well back from any wash. Do not fish the rocks, ledges or open tidal pools that the swell washes over; in a rough sea it is better not to fish at all than to go onto the rocks.
tactics.rig: Ultralight rod, 2 to 4 kg line, tiny split shot
tactics.why: Strepie are fished in calm, sheltered spots, and 'most places are dangerous for children' (Sealine, 2018). The District Mail column also points to jetties and harbours. Rough water on rocks is dangerous, and a big swell lowers the score.

tactics.title: Dirty water: heavier chum, smellier bait
tactics.lure_or_bait: Sardine pieces on a size 12 hook; chum of mashed sardine or mackerel with sand and anchovy oil
tactics.retrieve: Still-fish in the chum and lift gently on taps. Measure each fish and release anything under 15 cm.
tactics.depth: 1 to 2 m
tactics.stand: Sheltered harbour wall, or a gully mouth only when the sea is small, with the chum drifting along it
tactics.rig: Ultralight rod, 3 kg line, tiny split shot
tactics.why: Chum of mashed sardine or old mackerel with sea sand and anchovy oil sent fish 'into a frenzy' (Sealine, May 2016). Using it in coloured water is an estimate.

tactics.title: Size 12 hook, sardine and chum
tactics.lure_or_bait: Small firm sardine pieces on a size 12 hook, with mashed sardine chum
tactics.retrieve: Still-fish and lift on taps. Keep only fish of 15 cm and over, 10 a day at most, including any kept for bait.
tactics.depth: 1 to 3 m near weed or rock
tactics.stand: Sheltered harbour wall, calm gully or a tidal pool that is open to fishing and outside the no-take zones
tactics.rig: Ultralight rod, 2 to 4 kg line, tiny split shot
tactics.why: Matchhead hook, sardine and chum in calm, sheltered spots (Sealine, 2018; District Mail, 2023). Many small fish caught this way are under the 15 cm legal minimum (DFFE).

legal.bag_note: 10 per day. It counts toward the aggregate of 10 and on its own fills it.
legal.note: A and B agree and both match R.959. The cast-net list gives the same 15 cm and 10. 'Karanteen' means strepie.
legal.quote: Strepie (karanteen) | Sarpa salpa | 15 cm | 10

strepie.review: Checked by an independent skeptic; 13 corrections applied
review_points: Bag 10 is confirmed, but the profile leaves out the legal 15 cm minimum size. The tidal-pool and harbour tactics with tiny hooks will mostly hook fish under 15 cm, and the profile also promotes strepie as kob livebait, where the size limit applies too. As written, it encourages keeping undersized fi

Wikipedia gives April to September 'off South Africa' but not where, and describes an annual migration from Cape nursery areas to KwaZulu-Natal. Spawning is therefore not shown to happen in Cape Town waters. If the engine treats spawn months as a local aggregation boost, it would raise Cape winter s
unverified: The temperature band (12 / 15 to 20 / 24 C) is an estimate, since no numeric source was found. The ORI/SAAMBR strepie fact sheet (https://saambr.org.za/wp-content/uploads/2023/03/ORI-Fish-Fact-Strepie-ZC-LB.pdf) could not be read.
All light, sea, tide, range, trend, clarity and wind weights are estimates, as is flow 0.3, though calm and sheltered water is sourced.
Peak months (November to April) are inferred from 'not so plentiful in winter' and holiday-season reports.
Spawn months (April to September) cover South Africa as a whole; where spawning happens is not given, so they are not a local Cape aggregation and are kept for reference only.
The idea that bigger fish leave Cape waters in winter while small fish stay is an inference from the migration and the 'not so plentiful in winter' report.
A 35 to 40 cm 'big one' for Cape shore fishing is an estimate.
Redbait for strepie at Glencairn is inferred: the redbait rig in the source was used for hottentot, and the strepie remark came from another angler on a similar light setup.
The bread-fly and weed-fly tactic is an estimate built from a mullet source and the strepie's diet.
The bread bait on a float, and the pushing-tide timing for redbait and prawn, are estimates.

white-musselcracker.name: White musselcracker
white-musselcracker.season_note: Scarce around Cape Town. Expect only the occasional small fish on False Bay reefs; most of what anglers know about this fish comes from the southern and Eastern Cape. The fish live on the reefs all year. In False Bay the best chance is probably autumn and winter, when south-westerly swell 'opens' gullies and reef gaps. A Valsbaai angler took a small white musselcracker in April 2019 as the SW swell started 'working' the spots again. That peak is an estimate from one report. It spawns August to January. It is scarce on sandy stretches: at Strandfontein, locals say there is 'not a lot of cracker there' compared with kob, and one Cape regular says Cape waters have 'no crackers' at all.

temp.basis: Estimate. This is a warm-temperate fish found only in South Africa, from the Cape to KwaZulu-Natal (FishBase; Mann et al. 2014 via Wikipedia), and juveniles stay on shallow reefs all year. No source gives temperature thresholds, so all four values are estimates.

white-musselcracker.habitat: Shallow rocky coast. Juveniles stay on reefs no deeper than about 12 m. Adults range down to 80 m but come into the wash to feed on reef covered with mussels, redbait and urchins, and they work gullies and the edges where reef meets sand. Big ones often follow groups of galjoen. Around Cape Town most shore fish are juveniles below the 60 cm legal size. Many False Bay reefs lie inside the Table Mountain National Park MPA. Check the zone before you fish, and never fish a no-take area such as St James, Boulders or Castle Rock (Miller's Point to Partridge Point).
white-musselcracker.diet: Crushes hard-shelled prey with powerful jaws and molar teeth: mussels, sea urchins, crabs, gastropods, redbait and bristle worms, and sometimes green algae. Anglers catch it on white mussel, sand prawn, redbait, crab, octopus and chokka, and occasionally on sardine at night.
white-musselcracker.typical_size: Around Cape Town expect juveniles, mostly under the 60 cm legal size (that size range is an estimate). Further along the southern Cape, a big shore fish is 70 to 90 cm and 8 to 15 kg: a 78 cm, 9.3 kg fish was taken at Kanon near Gouritz, and Sealine reports shore fish of 15 to 18 kg. Maximum 120 cm TL and about 22 kg.
white-musselcracker.handling: Minimum size 60 cm, bag limit 2 per person per day. Expect undersize fish and release them fast. IUCN Near Threatened and declining. It matures at about 5.5 years and lives to about 31. Big crackers often die after a long fight and time out of the water: one Sealine angler released three of 15 to 18 kg, and two of them died. This page is for light tackle, which is not meant for big crackers. Land fish quickly, keep them in the water, support the belly, and revive them facing into clean wash. The crushing jaws can break fingers, so never put a hand near the mouth: use long-nose pliers or a dehooker. ORI runs a tagging programme. Use only legal bait: white mussel, redbait and prawn within permit limits. Venus ear is illegal. Crackers often move with galjoen. Galjoen are closed from 15 October to the end of February, so release any galjoen at once in that window. Outside it, galjoen have a 35 cm minimum and a bag of 2.

tactics.title: Running sinker on the reef-sand edge
tactics.lure_or_bait: White mussel (salted to firm it), sand prawn or redbait. A small crab or an octopus leg also works where legally obtained.
tactics.rig: 1/0 to 2/0 circle or bait-holder hook on a 0.40 to 0.45 mm abrasion-resistant leader. Keep hook and sinker traces no longer than 30 cm. Use a 1 to 2 oz sinker on a lighter weak-link strop; 3 oz is the top end, for surge only.
tactics.retrieve: Cast to the sand edge beside the reef or into a gully mouth and keep the line tight. Let the fish load the rod, then lift it away from the rocks straight away. Expect undersize fish and release them fast.
tactics.depth: On the bottom, 1 to 4 m
tactics.stand: On a dry rock or ledge above a gully mouth, or above the line where reef meets sand
tactics.why: Crackers forage reef edges for shellfish. Short traces and weak-link sinkers cut losses in rock. False Bay anglers call white mussel 'one of the most universal baits', and a 78 cm cracker at Kanon took prawn on a light leader and a small hook.

tactics.title: Drift bait in the wash at first and last light
tactics.lure_or_bait: Crab, white mussel or prawn
tactics.rig: 1/0 to 2/0 hook on 0.40 to 0.45 mm, with no sinker or a pea-sized ball sinker so the bait tumbles naturally. Thread two hooks through a crab.
tactics.retrieve: Lob it into the wash and let the surge carry it over the reef edge. Feed slack as it moves, then wind into a solid take.
tactics.depth: Bottom to mid-water, in 1 to 3 m of foam
tactics.stand: On a ledge well above the wash line, beside the foam. Move back as the tide pushes, and never turn your back on the sea.
tactics.why: Sealine reports put crackers at 'early morning or late afternoon'. One was taken 'early in the morning on my drift bait technique' on a 6 ft 6 bass rod, and another at Kanon 'very early' on prawn.

tactics.title: Fish the gaps a south-westerly swell has opened
tactics.lure_or_bait: White mussel, or redbait once the storms have set in
tactics.rig: 1/0 to 2/0 hook on 0.40 to 0.45 mm leader. Use a 1 to 2 oz sinker on a weak-link strop; 3 oz is the top end, only if the surge demands it.
tactics.retrieve: Search one gap or gully after another. Cast to the foam at the back of each, and move on after 15 minutes without a bite.
tactics.depth: On the bottom of gullies and reef gaps, 1 to 3 m
tactics.stand: Only on dry rock well above the reach of the swell, with a partner, never with your back to the sea. If the sea builds to rough, leave.
tactics.why: False Bay anglers say the SW swell gets spots 'working' and storms 'open up the gaps'. In the Eastern Cape, anglers rate cracker fishing good after two days of moderate south-west or west wind.

tactics.title: Crab or octopus bait in clear water
tactics.lure_or_bait: Red crab threaded on two hooks, or an octopus leg with the skin stripped at the end and bound with cotton
tactics.rig: Two 1/0 to 2/0 hooks in tandem on 0.40 to 0.45 mm, with a short sinker strop and a 1 to 2 oz sinker
tactics.retrieve: Cast to the reef edge and leave it. A pickup on crab 'is most likely a cracker', so wait for the run and lift firmly. Expect undersize fish and release them fast.
tactics.depth: On the bottom at the reef edge
tactics.stand: Beside a gully mouth, with clear water over mixed sand and reef
tactics.why: Sealine regulars say crackers 'take red crab or octopus in clear water', and that 'the way you thread your hooks through the crab is essential'.

tactics.title: Crab fly on calm, clear reef edges
tactics.lure_or_bait: Weighted crab pattern, size 2 to 1/0, or a shrimp pattern
tactics.rig: 9 ft rod, 8 or 9 weight, with intermediate or floating line and a 2 to 3 m leader of 0.40 mm fluorocarbon
tactics.retrieve: Cast ahead of a cruising fish, or near a group of galjoen where a cracker may be following. Let the fly sink to the bottom, then give short strips and long pauses. Release any galjoen you hook from 15 October to the end of February (closed season). Outside that window, galjoen have a 35 cm minimum and a bag of 2.
tactics.depth: On the bottom in 0.5 to 2 m
tactics.stand: On a low, dry rock, or wading the reef-sand edge only in flat or small sea, with the sun behind you
tactics.why: The Mission notes that big white musselcracker often follow groups of galjoen. The fly details are an estimate.

tactics.title: Softer bait when the water is cold
tactics.lure_or_bait: Sand prawn or white mussel rather than hard crab
tactics.rig: 1/0 to 2/0 hook on 0.40 to 0.45 mm, short trace, 1 to 2 oz sinker
tactics.retrieve: Fish slowly on the bottom and give the fish time
tactics.depth: On the bottom at the reef edge
tactics.stand: A sheltered gully that holds warmer water
tactics.why: Rock anglers report that 'often in cooler waters fish may prefer a softer bait', and on one Knysna trip sand prawn out-fished every conventional cracker bait.

legal.bag_note: 2 per day. Counts toward the aggregate of 10.
legal.note: A and B agree and both match R.959. No closed season. Not the same fish as the black musselcracker / poenskop (Cymatoceps nasutus), which is 50 cm and 1 per day.
legal.quote: White musselcracker (brusher, cracker) | Sparodon durbanensis | 60 cm | 2

white-musselcracker.review: Checked by an independent skeptic; 17 corrections applied
review_points: This contradicts itself. The only Cape-specific evidence in the profile (the Valsbaai thread, April 2019, SW swell starting to 'work' the spots) points to autumn and winter, when SW swells dominate, not to the Nov-Apr summer window. Summer in False Bay brings SE wind and flat sea, which the profile'

Cape evidence is thin and conflicting. A Sealine regular says 'Cape waters have no crackers' (Oct 2014), and Strandfontein locals report few. The one Cape record is a single small fish (Valsbaai, Apr 2019). Most tactic sources are from Mossel Bay, Knysna, Kanon (Gouritz), Struisbaai and Durban. 'Med

The cached readings of the article confirm only that musselcracker are mentioned, that they follow galjoen, and that they are in a 'next-up' list covered in print. They do not confirm a fly-caught musselcracker shown in the article. Every pattern, size, line and leader detail is an estimate.

The tactic steers anglers to galjoen shoals, and its peak window (Nov-Apr) overlaps the galjoen closed season (15 Oct to the end of Feb). A crab fly cast at a galjoen group will hook galjoen. With no warning, the page in effect sends anglers after a closed-season species.

Rough means waves over 1.8 m at the spot. Fishing gullies from rock ledges in that sea is the classic rock-angler drowning scenario. A 'stand well above the swell' note does not make it safe to rate rough-sea ledges as a good tactic.

This is conventional rock-and-surf tackle, presented on a light-tackle page. The profile itself notes big crackers die after long fights, and the species is Near Threatened, so pushing light gear at big fish is an ethics problem, and the heavy gear is out of scope. Most False Bay fish are juveniles

No source names musselcracker at Clovelly or Swartklip, and species text will show at every spot. Swartklip is on the Strandfontein-Macassar stretch, which a Cape Sealine poster says 'should only be visited in groups'. Recommending it with no safety note is a safety gap. Parts of the Fish Hoek shore
Not in the cited Wikipedia page, and no source given.
unverified: Temperature min, ideal and max are all estimates. No source gives thresholds, and the Mazeppa Bay (Transkei) 24 C report is no longer cited as support.

Peak months (March to August) are an estimate. They rest on one Valsbaai report from April 2019 and on False Bay's autumn and winter south-westerly swell season. Spawning August to January is sourced (Mann et al. 2014 via Wikipedia).

Condition weights are estimates. Dawn and dusk preference, occasional night feeding, and better fishing in moderate SW swell come from anglers' reports. Nothing supports the tide weights (pushing best), range, trend, clarity or wind weights.

Cape Town evidence is thin and conflicting: one small Valsbaai fish, few at Strandfontein, and one Cape regular saying there are no crackers. Most tactic sources are from Mossel Bay, Knysna, Kanon near Gouritz, Struisbaai, the Eastern Cape and Durban Bluff.
The size range for Cape Town shore fish (mostly undersize juveniles) is an estimate.
The fly tactic's pattern, size, line and leader are all estimates. The Mission article confirms only that big white musselcracker follow galjoen, not that one was caught on fly there.
The reviewer could not re-check the Sealine threads 7470, 91085, 7269, 101238 and 60034 (none was cached), so quotes from them are as the researcher reported.
The ORI/Mann 2013 species profile could not be reached (DNS failure).

white-steenbras.name: White steenbras
white-steenbras.season_note: Cape anglers catch them all year (Sealine Muizenberg thread: 'Steenbras: throughout the year'; Village Voice and ShowMe tables say 'All year'; Mattheys: 'caught almost year-round'). Mattheys says bigger fish move onto the sandbanks in winter, 'especially May, June and July'. Other Cape reports fall between April and August: Clifton 1st beach in mid-winter, Derdesteen in June, Blouberg to Melkbos in winter, and Jacita's reports for the False Bay beaches from Strandfontein to the Strand in May and June 2025. In False Bay most fish caught are undersized (District Mail). Adults spawn in late winter, July and August, off a few Transkei (Eastern Cape) estuaries (Bennett 1993b via Mann 2013, ORI), so the species does not spawn near Cape Town. There is no closed season (ORI). Juveniles recruit into Cape estuaries such as Zandvlei and Milnerton lagoon, which act as nurseries.

temp.basis: Estimate. The FishBase/AquaMaps modelled range (12.5 to 24.1 C, mean 15.7 C) was not re-verified, and ORI gives no temperature data. Angler evidence is anecdotal and mixed: one poster in a Sealine Table View thread (Feb 2024) says that when the water off Blouberg and 2de Steen is very cold, steenbras are the likely catch, and Jacita (16 May 2025) had steenbras active while kob were 'off the bite because the water is cold'. Others in the same Table View thread had no bites at all at 12 C and mostly blanks in cold water. The 12 C minimum rests on that no-bite report.

white-steenbras.habitat: Sandy surf beaches with scattered rock and rolling sandbanks. Fish hold in the deeper gutter in front of or beside a bank and move up into shallow water on the bank to feed. Mattheys: 'Don't be scared to fish shallow'. They also hold on sand edges beside reef: Fish Hoek bay (Sealine), the rocks at Derdesteen, the Strand reefs. The best-known Cape surf stretches are Derdesteen, Haakgat and Melkbos, Blouberg and 2de Steen, Clifton, Kommetjie Bay, Muizenberg to Sunrise and The Horses, and Strandfontein towards Macassar. The coast between the Eerste and Lourens river mouths is the Helderberg MPA, where no fishing is allowed. Adults range inshore to about 25 m (ORI); shore anglers find them feeding on shallow banks beside deeper gutters. Sub-adults tend to stay in the same stretch of surf. Juveniles live for 2 to 3 years in estuaries and lagoons such as Zandvlei and Milnerton lagoon, which are nurseries, and ORI notes they appear to feed on shallow banks at night there. These nurseries are not a place to target the species.
white-steenbras.diet: Bottom invertebrates taken from sand and reef: sand and mud prawns, bloodworm and other worms, crabs, mussels and small molluscs (FishBase; Two Oceans Aquarium; District Mail, which says they 'work prawns and worms' in surf zones and sandy flats). Anglers also catch them on red bait, white mussel, moonshine and wonderworm, and sometimes on sardine and chokka.
white-steenbras.typical_size: Most shore fish around Cape Town are juveniles and sub-adults of 30 to 55 cm, roughly 0.5 to 2.5 kg (estimate), which is under the 60 cm legal size. A 60 cm TL fish weighs about 2 to 3.4 kg: 3.4 kg on Bennett 1993a's length-weight equation, about 2.1 kg on Mehl 1973's (both via ORI). A big one is 8 to 10 kg or more: a 9 kg fish came from Soetwater, and fish over 1 m once came off the Strand reefs. Mattheys: 'we hardly ever see a double-digit steenbras in False Bay'. The largest recorded is 137.6 cm TL and 26.3 kg, the South African shore-angling record (ORI).
white-steenbras.handling: Endangered: listed regionally as Endangered (ORI, 2011) and on the IUCN Red List (2024 assessment per FishBase). WWF-SASSI Red ('Don't buy') and a no-sale species: catching one needs a recreational permit, and buying or selling one is illegal. DFFE recreational limits (R1111, Annexure 7): minimum size 60 cm, bag limit 1 per person per day, no closed season. Wikipedia says it is 'about to become a no keep species', so check the current DFFE regulations before keeping one. Half of white steenbras mature only at about 65 cm TL (ORI). A legal 60 cm fish has usually not yet spawned, so release it; releasing every fish is best for this species. Most fish caught near Cape Town are under the legal size, especially in the False Bay surf. Juvenile white steenbras are common in Zandvlei and Milnerton lagoon: these are nurseries for an Endangered species, so don't target them there, use circle hooks, and release any you catch in the water. The Zandvlei Trust asks that all indigenous fish caught there be released, and Zandvlei needs a standard fishing permit. Use circle hooks with the barb flattened. Unhook the fish in the water or keep it wet, handle it with wet hands or a wet cloth, never drag it over dry sand, and support big fish horizontally. Tag fish through ORI's tagging programme if you can. The spiny dorsal fin can prick; the teeth are no hazard. Collect bait (sand or mud prawn, bloodworm, mussel) only within your permit's daily limits and never in MPA restricted zones or the Helderberg MPA.

tactics.title: Dawn or dusk push into the gutter
tactics.lure_or_bait: Fresh sand prawn (2 to 3 threaded on) or a long, thin bloodworm or wonderworm bait about 8 to 10 cm long
tactics.rig: 9 to 10 ft rod rated to about 3 oz. Running sinker trace: 2 to 3 oz grapnel or bell sinker on a short sinker strop, swivel, then a 60 to 80 cm fluorocarbon snood of 0.40 to 0.45 mm (10 to 12.5 kg), with a 1/0 to 2/0 circle hook, barb flattened
tactics.retrieve: Cast to the near slope of the gutter and leave the bait still on a slightly slack line. Lift and drag it about a metre every 3 to 5 minutes. When a fish takes, let it load the rod and wind into it rather than striking (circle hook).
tactics.depth: On the bottom in 1 to 2 m of water, at the inside edge of the bank
tactics.stand: On the beach opposite the deepest gutter, where a rolling bank with scattered rock runs beside it. Cast short: the fish come up onto the flooding bank to feed.
tactics.why: Jacita (12 Aug 2025) says to fish 'on the push or turn of the tide', and (16 May 2025) reported the False Bay beaches fishing well 'especially on high tide'. Seaside Cottages says Strandfontein fishes best about two hours either side of high tide. Mattheys says steenbras feed shallow on the banks beside a deep gutter. The dawn and dusk timing is an estimate: no source gives a time-of-day pattern for steenbras.

tactics.title: Winter banks in a 1.2 to 1.8 m sea
tactics.lure_or_bait: Sand prawn, crab, red bait or mussel. Sardine or chokka strip as a backup.
tactics.rig: Light-tackle version: a soft 9 to 10 ft rod rated to about 3 oz, a 4000 to 5000 size reel with 20 lb braid and a 30 to 40 lb leader. Running sinker trace with a short sinker line and a 2 to 3 oz sinker (estimate), 10 to 12.5 kg fluorocarbon snood, 2/0 circle hook with the barb flattened. Mattheys's own 'lighter outfit' is a soft 12 to 14 ft rod rated 3 to 4 oz with 20 to 30 lb braid and a 40 to 50 lb braided leader, which is above this page's light-tackle limit.
tactics.retrieve: Leave the bait still. Fight with steady pressure and a soft drag, and don't pump hard, because the head-shakes pull hooks on braid.
tactics.depth: On the bottom of the gutter beside a rolling bank
tactics.stand: On the beach at the shoulder of a sandbank facing a deep gutter that runs in front of or along it, on a sandy beach with scattered rock. In a 1.2 to 1.8 m sea, fish from the sand and don't wade.
tactics.why: Mattheys (District Mail Helderberg): bigger fish move onto the sandbanks in May, June and July, and 'a 1,2 m to 1,8 m sea is perfect'. He also says they 'prefer feeding in calmer sea conditions, and cleaner water'.

tactics.title: Clear, calm water: scale right down
tactics.lure_or_bait: One long, thin bloodworm or 1 to 2 sand prawns kept small and natural. Moonshine or wonderworm if you have it.
tactics.rig: Light sliding trace on a 9 to 10 ft rod: 1 to 2 oz sinker running on the main line above a swivel, about 1 m of 0.30 to 0.35 mm fluorocarbon snood, size 1 to 1/0 circle hook
tactics.retrieve: Leave it still, or drag it very slowly along the bottom. Keep the drag light.
tactics.depth: On the bottom in the deepest water that still has some wash, 1 to 2.5 m
tactics.stand: On the beach where any white water is still working, such as behind a reef point or beside a rip. Stand back from the water's edge and keep a low profile.
tactics.why: The District Mail column recommends fresh bloodworm and prawn on a running sinker or light sliding trace, with 'a finesse approach in clear water'. Sealine's Muizenberg anglers say to keep the bait 'small and long'. Jacita (12 June 2025) tipped Strandfontein to the Strand for baardman and white steenbras in 0.8 to 1.2 m surf and named moonshine and wonderworm as the week's top baits. Mattheys warns steenbras are 'very fussy feeders especially in clean water and flat seas', so this is a way to get bites in poor conditions, not a peak time.

tactics.title: Low tide: bloodworm into the outer gutter off the flats
tactics.lure_or_bait: Fresh bloodworm, or a prawn and bloodworm combination
tactics.rig: 9 to 10 ft rod, 2 oz running sinker, 60 cm of 0.40 mm fluorocarbon snood, 1/0 circle hook with the barb flattened
tactics.retrieve: Leave it still. Rebait often, because sand crabs strip baits.
tactics.depth: On the bottom in the outer gutter beyond the low-tide bar
tactics.stand: At low tide, walk out onto the exposed flats in daylight or at dawn and cast to the outer gutter. Never wade above the knee or into a channel, and walk back before the push floods the gutters behind you. At night, fish from the dry beach only and never alone. Around Muizenberg, stay on the Muizenberg to Sunrise stretch east of Surfer's Corner: the St James restricted area along the coast to the west is a no-take zone.
tactics.why: In the Sealine Muizenberg thread, Alan Lloyd's general low-tide advice is 'don't be afraid of fishing low tide, just wade as far as you can and cast out a bloodworm', and Dafishking caught steenbras 'at nite in front of that flats on low tide'. Another poster warns 'just don't fish it alone at night'. Marthin (Sealine) recommends bloodworm for steenbras towards Muizenberg beach and says 'Low to push tide works best' at Melkbaai. The knee-deep limit and daylight-only wading are a safety rule added here, not from the sources.

tactics.title: After a blow: newly opened gutters in coloured water
tactics.lure_or_bait: A bigger, smellier combination bait: bloodworm or prawn tipped with chokka strip ('mixed grill'), or prawn with sardine
tactics.rig: 9 to 10 ft rod, 3 oz grapnel sinker to hold against side-pull (the top end for light tackle), 50 to 60 cm snood of 0.45 mm (shorter in strong water), 2/0 circle hook with the barb flattened
tactics.retrieve: Leave it still and rebait every 10 to 15 minutes to keep the scent fresh
tactics.depth: On the bottom of holes and gutters the swell has just opened
tactics.stand: On the first day the sea drops back after a strong north-westerly or south-easterly, walk the beach and fish from the sand into the gutters and holes the swell has opened: Swartklip after a south-easter, the beach beside Derdesteen after a north-west front. Stay off the rocks. On the False Bay side, don't fish between the Eerste and Lourens river mouths: that is the Helderberg MPA, a no-take zone.
tactics.why: Jacita (30 May 2025) describes northerly winds 'churning up the inshore seabed, opening gullies and flushing out bait', a general note for all species.
