Seaside Cottages says to fish Swartklip and Broken Road after a strong south-easter for kob, steenbras and rays. Sealine anglers rate a cold north-westerly day good at Derdesteen once the gutters open, and say sanded-up beaches need big seas to reopen. Jacita (16 May 2025): bloodworm and mixed grill were best for steenbras. Mattheys finds steenbras prefer cleaner water, so this is a secondary option.

tactics.title: Cold upwelled water (low confidence)
tactics.lure_or_bait: Small fresh bait: one bloodworm or a single sand prawn
tactics.rig: 9 to 10 ft rod, 2 oz running sinker, 0.35 to 0.40 mm fluorocarbon snood, size 1 to 1/0 circle hook
tactics.retrieve: Leave it still, and wait longer before moving or rebaiting
tactics.depth: On the bottom of the shallowest gutter with wash, where the water warms fastest
tactics.stand: On the Atlantic-side beaches (Derdesteen, 2de Steen, Melkbos, Blouberg), fish the push in the middle of the day when the shallow banks have warmed
tactics.why: One poster in a Sealine Table View thread says that when the water is very cold, steenbras are the likely catch, and Jacita (16 May 2025) had steenbras active while kob were off the bite in cold water. Others in the same Table View thread had no bites at 12 C and mostly blanks in cold water, so the evidence is mixed. The midday timing and the small bait are estimates.

tactics.title: Running sinker with prawn or worm in the nearest gutter
tactics.lure_or_bait: Fresh sand prawn, bloodworm or wonderworm. Mussel or red bait near rocks.
tactics.rig: 9 to 10 ft rod, 2 to 3 oz sinker on a running trace, 60 to 80 cm fluorocarbon snood of 0.40 to 0.45 mm, 1/0 to 2/0 circle hook with the barb flattened
tactics.retrieve: Leave it still, reposition every few minutes, and wind into the fish steadily rather than striking
tactics.depth: On the bottom, 1 to 2 m deep, at the edge of a gutter or a sand patch beside rock
tactics.stand: From the beach opposite the deepest gutter, or on the sand edge beside rocks (Fish Hoek bay, the sand beside Derdesteen rocks). Fish the two hours either side of high water, especially the push.
tactics.why: This is the standard Cape surf method for steenbras across Sealine, Jacita and District Mail. A Sealine angler caught a steenbras from Fish Hoek bay. Strandfontein is best fished about two hours either side of high tide (Seaside Cottages).

legal.bag_note: 1 per person per day
legal.note: A and B agree and both match R.959. No national closed season. Catch-and-release is encouraged but is not law. On the Cape shore, 'steenbras' usually means this species. Red (copper) steenbras, Petrus rupestris, is a different fish and has been PROHIBITED since R.959. West coast steenbras: 60 cm, 1 per day. Black steenbras (poenskop): 50 cm, 1 per day.
legal.quote: White steenbras (pignose grunter) | Lithognathus lithognathus | 60 cm | 1

white-steenbras.review: Checked by an independent skeptic; 27 corrections applied
review_points: A source exists and gives a narrower window. The ORI profile (Bennett 1993b) says 'Late winter, Jul-Aug', off a few Transkei estuaries. June is not supported. It has no effect locally, because the fish do not spawn near Cape Town.

The ORI length-weight equations give about 3.4 kg at 60 cm TL (Bennett 1993a) or about 2.1 kg (Mehl 1973), so 3.5 to 4 kg is too high. ORI also gives maximum recorded size as 1376 mm TL and 26.3 kg (SA shore-angling record), so 'about 1 m' understates the species.

ORI gives length at 50% maturity as 65 cm TL (n=601, Bennett 1993b). The 60 cm minimum size is therefore below maturity, and a just-legal fish is more likely than not still immature. Handling should say so and encourage releasing every fish, not only large females.
This number is invented and presented as fact. ORI says adults occur in the inshore marine environment to 25 m. Mattheys supports fishing shallow banks, but not a 3 m limit.

The Seaside Cottages page does not mention Clovelly. In the Sealine Fish Hoek thread, Enigma caught a steenbras 'from Fish Hoek bay', and named the rocks below Clovelly station only for kob, dassie and zebra.

No source gives a steenbras time-of-day pattern. Mattheys says nothing on time of day. Jacita's 'prime strike windows' was a tide note for one week (high tide about two hours before dawn and dusk) and covered all species. The only steenbras-specific timing evidence is a night catch at low tide at Mu

The report says high tides fell about two hours before dawn and dusk that week, so at dawn the tide was dropping. It was a note about that week's tide times, not a general rule for this species, and not about a pushing tide.

No catches were reported. The page says the beaches are 'prime time for targeting' baardman and white steenbras, and 'Moonshine and Wonderworm' is a general top bait not tied to steenbras. 0.8 to 1.2 m is 'small' or 'moderate' in the engine's vocabulary, not 'flat'. Mattheys also says steenbras are
unverified: All four temperature numbers (min 12, ideal 14 to 19, max 23 C) are estimates. The FishBase/AquaMaps modelled range of 12.5 to 24.1 C was not re-verified, ORI gives no temperature data, and the angler evidence is mixed.

All five light weights are estimates; no source gives a time-of-day pattern for adult steenbras. ORI says estuarine juveniles feed on shallow banks at night and the one adult timing report is a night low-tide catch at Muizenberg, which is why night was raised. A lab study (Kandjou and Kaiser 2014) found juveniles more active by day.
Peak months May to July rest mainly on one tackle-shop column (Mattheys 2023) plus scattered winter forum reports.
Sea weights for flat (0.55) and rough (0.3) are estimates. Only the moderate peak (1.2 to 1.8 m, Mattheys) and Mattheys's warning about clean water and flat seas are sourced.
Tide weights for low (0.7) and dropping (0.6) are estimates. Pushing and high come from Jacita notes that cover several species; low is backed by Muizenberg and Melkbaai forum posts.
flow 0.55, range (springs 0.85, neaps 0.75), trend (falling 0.85, steady 0.85, rising 0.65) and wind (calm 0.8, breeze 1, strong 0.55) are all estimates.
Clarity weights: Mattheys says cleaner water is preferred, but anglers report fishing well in churned water after blows. The clear 0.85 versus coloured 0.7 balance is an estimate.
The cold-water tactic is low confidence; its midday timing and small-bait advice are estimates.
The light-tackle rigs (9 to 10 ft rods, 2 to 3 oz sinkers, 30 to 40 lb leader) are scaled down from Mattheys's 12 to 14 ft outfit and are estimates.
Sub-adult weight band (0.5 to 2.5 kg for 30 to 55 cm) is estimated from the ORI length-weight relation, not measured.
No Cape Town-area record of white steenbras on fly or lure was found; recorded fly and lure catches are from Langebaan, De Mond and the upper Breede, outside this page's area.
Current 2026 regulations: 60 cm and 1 per person per day are confirmed in DFFE R1111 Annexure 7. Wikipedia says a no-keep listing is imminent; no gazette notice was found.
The IUCN 2024 assessment date comes from FishBase and was not re-checked.
Not re-checked: the Zandvlei Trust 'murky water' quote and the capeflyfishing blog.
Whether the Broken Road fishing spot lies inside the Helderberg MPA could not be confirmed, so it is not suggested as a stand.

white-stumpnose.name: White stumpnose
white-stumpnose.season_note: You can catch them all year. Adults spawn from September to March. In winter they move offshore into deeper water, and Langebaan fish spend midwinter out in Saldanha Bay (Wikipedia). The summer peak months are an estimate based on that pattern, a Melkbos surf report from February 2025 (white stumpnose caught with cob and elf) and a Kalk Bay night catch in March 2012. A Kalk Bay regular's comment that the wall fishes best from October to April is about the wall in general (mostly elf and maasbanker), not this species. Older False Bay writing (Horne 1955) says the opposite for the shallows: 'when warm water comes to False Bay white stumpnose leave the shallows and do not return till the following winter.' So the engine should go by water temperature more than the calendar. Summer suits the cold West Coast and Table Bay side. In False Bay, cooler spells are better. Zandvlei is named as a nursery for two species of stumpnose. Milnerton Lagoon was historically a stumpnose spot and probably also holds juveniles. Most fish in both are undersize. White stumpnose are now only occasional at Kalk Bay.

temp.basis: estimate. Based on the water this species is caught in around the Cape: West Coast, Langebaan/Saldanha and Table Bay inshore water is about 11 to 18 C, and False Bay shallows can reach 20 to 22 C in late summer. Horne 1955 says white stumpnose leave the False Bay shallows when warm water arrives. They move offshore into deeper water in winter (Wikipedia). A search summary of FishBase gave a modelled preferred range of 14.5 to 26.4 C. That figure is global and modelled, and too warm to use for the Cape shore. No measured feeding-temperature limits were found.

white-stumpnose.habitat: Adults shoal over sand near small reefs and rocky outcrops, along harbour walls, and in gullies and holes beside surf-zone sandbanks. In summer they range from the surf zone down to about 50 m, and in winter they go deeper, to about 120 m (Wikipedia). In lagoons they use the tidal channels and the sand beside them. A Langebaan tracking study (Attwood et al. 2007, seen only as a search summary) reported fish moving along deep channels, mostly at night and at twilight. Juveniles use estuaries, bays, surf zones, seagrass beds and coastal lagoons as nurseries. Zandvlei is named as a nursery for 'two species of stumpnose'. Its mouth is often closed in summer, so tide effects there apply only when it is open. Stumpnose were historically a main target at Milnerton Lagoon.
white-stumpnose.diet: A bottom feeder on crustaceans and molluscs. Large adults crush clams, mussels and snails. Prey also includes sand prawn, crabs, amphipods and worms. Juveniles eat amphipods, isopods, ostracods and filamentous algae, plus some detritus. Baits that match this diet: white mussel (it turned small pecks into solid knocks at Kalk Bay), sand prawn and worms such as bloodworm. Use bought bait in the nature reserves.
white-stumpnose.typical_size: This is an estimate: most shore fish around Cape Town are probably 20 to 30 cm (about 0.2 to 0.5 kg). Most fish in Zandvlei and Milnerton Lagoon are juveniles under the 25 cm limit. A good fish is 35 to 40 cm (about 1 to 1.5 kg). A big one is 45 to 50 cm. The published maximum is about 60 cm TL. Females mature at about 22 cm FL, and males at about 15 to 24 cm FL (Wikipedia).
white-stumpnose.handling: IUCN Vulnerable. WWF-SASSI red ('Don't buy') because stocks are overfished across most of the range. A search summary of the SANBI assessment says beach-seine stocks at Hout Bay, Blouberg and Melkbos have collapsed. Anglers need a recreational fishing permit. The minimum size is 25 cm TL and the bag limit is 10 per person per day (WWF-SASSI page). Check the current DFFE regulations. Do not confuse it with Cape stumpnose (R. holubi). That species has a different size and bag limit and is common in the same estuaries. White stumpnose have sharp dorsal and anal spines and strong crushing teeth, so hold the fish from behind the head with wet hands. It nibbles and can swallow small hooks: use small circle hooks or strike early. If a fish is deep-hooked, cut the line instead of digging the hook out. Release undersize fish quickly at the waterline. At Zandvlei, release every white stumpnose. The Zandvlei Trust says catch and release of indigenous species is required by law there (confirm with the City of Cape Town reserve rules). Zandvlei also needs a standard fishing permit, and livebait is illegal there. Zandvlei and Milnerton Lagoon (Table Bay Nature Reserve) are nature reserves, so use bought bait rather than pumping prawn unless the reserve rules allow it. Never use a small white stumpnose as livebait.

tactics.title: Night high tide off the harbour wall with white mussel
tactics.lure_or_bait: White mussel (fresh or frozen) threaded up the hook. Sand prawn or a thin chokka strip as backups. If you only get small pecks, switch to white mussel.
tactics.rig: Size 1 to 1/0 thin-wire hook (a circle hook is better for release) on a 60 to 80 cm, 0.30 to 0.35 mm fluorocarbon snood. A 1 to 2 oz running sinker stopped above a swivel. 2 to 4 kg mono or 10 to 15 lb braid on a 7 to 9 ft light rod.
tactics.retrieve: Cast, let the bait settle and keep the line just tight. Lift and drag it about 30 cm every minute or two. Ignore the first pecks and strike on a solid knock.
tactics.depth: On the bottom, on the clean sand at the foot of the wall or 10 to 30 m out from it.
tactics.stand: On the harbour wall or breakwater, in flat or small seas only. Cast along the outside of the wall onto sand, not into the boulders. At Kalk Bay, fish from the lighthouse arm and cast towards Muizenberg, parallel to the main road. Watch for sudden surges over the Kalk Bay wall, and stand back from the edge in the dark. Fish from the harbour only: St James, just towards Muizenberg, is a no-take zone.
tactics.why: Kalk Bay, March 2012: a night session that fished best 'especially on the high tide'. Switching to white mussel turned small bites into 'hard knocks' and a white stumpnose. The same thread says it was the first one seen come out there 'in a long time', when earlier years gave bags full, so expect them only occasionally now. Another fish in that thread was probably a Cape stumpnose. A Langebaan tracking study reportedly found them moving mostly at night and at twilight, but only a search summary of it was seen.

tactics.title: Small surf: mussel, prawn or worm in a gully beside a sandbank
tactics.lure_or_bait: White mussel, sand prawn or bloodworm. All three are equal options. Use a small, neat bait.
tactics.rig: Size 1 to 1/0 thin-wire or circle hook on a 60 cm, 0.28 to 0.33 mm snood. A 1 to 2 oz grapnel or pyramid sinker on a short sinker trace so the bait lies on the sand. 3 to 5 kg line on a 9 to 10 ft light rod. Fish it only in small surf. In moderate surf this sinker will not hold, so move to sheltered water instead.
tactics.retrieve: Cast to the edge of the bank or the mouth of the gully and hold. Drag back about a metre every few minutes to search.
tactics.depth: On the bottom in gullies, holes and along the inside edge of the sandbank, 1 to 3 m deep.
tactics.stand: On the beach, facing a gully, hole or rip beside a sandbank, ideally where sand meets low reef. Melkbos is the one Cape surf report. Other Atlantic-side beaches with sand and low reef are an estimate.
tactics.why: Melkbos, February 2025: white stumpnose came out of the surf with cob and elf over about a week. The post gives no bait, tide, light or water colour, so the bait choice follows the diet (molluscs, crustaceans and worms). Earlier advice that they prefer coloured water and bloodworm came from Port Elizabeth anglers, so it is not used here.

tactics.title: Cold water: fish deeper and slower
tactics.lure_or_bait: White mussel or sand prawn, small and fresh, in a neat small bait.
tactics.rig: Size 1 hook on a 60 cm, 0.30 mm snood with a 2 to 3 oz running sinker so you can reach deeper water. 3 oz is the top end for light tackle. 3 to 5 kg line on a 9 to 10 ft light rod.
tactics.retrieve: Cast and leave it static. Move it only every 5 minutes or so.
tactics.depth: The deepest sand you can reach: the bottom of a channel, the end of a harbour arm or a deep gully.
tactics.stand: At the end of the breakwater, or on a point beside the deepest water, in flat or small seas only. In lagoons, fish the deep channel near the mouth. At Zandvlei, release every fish.
tactics.why: Adults move offshore into deeper water in winter, and Langebaan fish spend midwinter in Saldanha Bay. Any fish that stay inshore will be in the deeper water.

tactics.title: Warm water: only at dawn, dusk and night
tactics.lure_or_bait: White mussel, sand prawn or bloodworm.
tactics.rig: Size 1 to 1/0 hook on a 60 to 80 cm, 0.30 mm snood with a 1 to 2 oz running sinker. 3 to 4 kg line on an 8 to 9 ft light rod.
tactics.retrieve: Slow drag and pause. Fish the change of light and into the dark.
tactics.depth: On the bottom in the deeper water beside structure, not the hot shallows.
tactics.stand: On a harbour wall or a rock ledge over deeper sand, in flat or small seas only, rather than shallow beaches or warm vlei flats.
tactics.why: Horne (1955): 'When warm water comes to False Bay white stumpnose leave the shallows and do not return till the following winter.' Fishing in low light follows the Kalk Bay night catch. Reports that the tracked fish moved at night and at twilight are unverified.
sources: Attwood et al. 2007 tracking note (search summary only, unverified)

tactics.title: Rough sea: move to sheltered water
tactics.lure_or_bait: White mussel or sand prawn.
tactics.rig: Size 1 hook on a 60 cm, 0.30 mm snood with a 1 to 2 oz running sinker. Sheltered water does not need more lead. Use 3 to 4 kg line on an 8 to 9 ft light rod.
tactics.retrieve: Static, with an occasional drag.
tactics.depth: On the bottom on sand in the calm water.
tactics.stand: Inside the harbour basin, well back from the outer wall, or in a sheltered lagoon channel out of the swell. Do not fish the outer harbour wall or any rocks in a big swell: sudden surges come over the Kalk Bay wall. If nowhere is sheltered, stay off the water. At Zandvlei, release every fish.
tactics.why: White stumpnose pick at bait on sand near structure, which is easiest to fish in calm water. A big swell makes a light bait unfishable and the walls and rocks dangerous. Saying that big swell scatters the fish is an estimate.

tactics.title: Light running sinker with mussel or prawn on sand by structure
tactics.lure_or_bait: White mussel or sand prawn. Bloodworm or a thin chokka strip are alternatives.
tactics.rig: Size 1 to 1/0 thin-wire or circle hook on a 60 to 100 cm, 0.28 to 0.35 mm fluorocarbon snood, with a short sinker line so the hook line is about three times longer. A 1 to 2 oz running sinker. 3 to 4 kg line on a light 8 to 9 ft rod.
tactics.retrieve: Cast onto clean sand and keep in touch with the bait. Drag slowly every minute or two and wait for a firm knock before striking.
tactics.depth: On the bottom, on sand beside reef, harbour walls, channel edges or weed.
tactics.stand: Wherever sand meets structure: a harbour wall, a gully beside low reef, or the edge of a lagoon channel. Dusk into the night, dawn, and a rising or high tide are probably best. In Zandvlei and Milnerton Lagoon most fish are undersize. Release every fish at Zandvlei, and expect tide effects there only when the mouth is open.
tactics.why: White stumpnose feed on the bottom, on molluscs and crustaceans over sand near reef. At Kalk Bay one was taken at night on white mussel on the high tide. A Langebaan angler caught four on a running rig with a short sinker line and a hook line about three times longer.

legal.bag_note: 10 per day. It counts toward the aggregate of 10 and on its own fills it.
legal.note: A and B agree. The R.959 gazette and brochure Table 4 both give 25 cm. The acts.co.za consolidation leaves the size cell blank; that is a transcription gap, so do not use that copy.
legal.quote: White stumpnose | Rhabdosargus globicebs | 25 cm | 10

white-stumpnose.review: Checked by an independent skeptic; 22 corrections applied
review_points: These quotes come from Port Elizabeth surf anglers. aquadementia refers to 'anne avenue' (Summerstrand, PE) and to grunter in warm water, and Upcoming Star says 'here in and around pe'. This is Eastern Cape advice transferred to Cape Town. The same poster also says 'cant really target them specifica

This is standard medium surf tackle, not light tackle. It is also oversized for a small-mouthed picker whose Cape shore fish are mostly 20 to 30 cm. It also conflicts with the profile's own advice to use small, thin-wire hooks.

In the thread, 'they fussy feeders so small hooks and thin diameter hook snoods is ideal' was written about steenbras ('steenies'), by a PE poster. It is not about white stumpnose. The only white stumpnose rig detail (a short sinker line with the hook line three times longer) comes from Langebaan, w

The profile treats release as advice only. The Zandvlei Trust says 'Catch and release of indigenous species such as Leervis is required by law' at Zandvlei. White stumpnose is indigenous, so release there appears to be mandatory.

Zandvlei Estuary Nature Reserve and Milnerton Lagoon / Table Bay Nature Reserve are protected reserves. No cited source confirms that bait collection is allowed there, and the Zandvlei Trust page says nothing on bait rules. The tactic also sends anglers to target a Vulnerable, overfished species in

The Sean Mills page says all three lagoons are 'best fished from a boat', and all three are outside the one-hour radius. For the in-range waters on the same page (Milnerton Lagoon and Sandvlei), white stumpnose is NOT listed. No evidence was found of white stumpnose taken on fly from the shore withi

The Langebaan fish were caught on a bait rig with a short sinker line, not on a lure, at a lagoon outside the radius. No source shows white stumpnose taking soft plastics or a dropshot anywhere in the Cape. Calm, clear daytime is a very common condition, so the panel would often show an unsupported
This is a Ski-Boat magazine article about boat fishing: anchoring behind the Strandfontein tidal-pool wall, or the surf line out to 15 m from a boat. It is boat by-catch, not shore evidence.
unverified: Water temperature limits (min 11, ideal 13 to 18, max 21 C) are estimates. No measured feeding-temperature data was found.

Weights for sea state, wind, pressure trend, tidal range and clarity are estimates. The tide weights rest on one Kalk Bay report ('especially on the high tide'). The clarity weights are estimates: the coloured-water preference in the earlier draft came from Port Elizabeth anglers, not the Cape.

Light weights are estimates. The night and twilight tracking claim (Attwood et al. 2007) was seen only as a search summary, and the Wikipedia page has no time-of-day detail. The only Cape light evidence is one Kalk Bay night session.
flow 0.45 is an estimate. The fish use tidal channels in lagoons but are also caught on still sand beside harbour walls, so they get a moderate preference for moving water.

Peak months (Oct to Apr) are an estimate. They rest on winter offshore dispersal (Wikipedia), one Melkbos report (Feb 2025) and one Kalk Bay catch (Mar 2012). The Kalk Bay 'Oct to Apr' comment is about the wall in general. Horne (1955) says white stumpnose leave the False Bay shallows when warm water arrives and return in winter. One search summary said line boats caught them in False Bay shallows at night from May to October, but no page confirmed it.
The October and February spawning peaks in Saldanha Bay (Attwood et al. 2010) are unverified: the abstract URL is cut short. Wikipedia confirms only September to March spawning.
Tracking details from Attwood et al. 2007 (deep-channel movement, night and twilight activity, 9 to 15 km in 12 days, daily commuting to favourite sites) come from a search summary only.
Typical shore size (20 to 30 cm, big fish 45 to 50 cm) is an estimate from published maximums and size at maturity, not from Cape catch records.
Regulations: the 25 cm TL minimum and 10 per person per day come from the WWF-SASSI page. Check them against the current DFFE recreational regulations.

Zandvlei release rule: the Zandvlei Trust says catch and release of indigenous species is required by law. Confirm this with the City of Cape Town reserve rules. Whether bait may be collected in the Zandvlei and Milnerton (Table Bay Nature Reserve) reserves is not confirmed.
That Milnerton Lagoon is a white stumpnose nursery is inferred. Only Zandvlei is named as a stumpnose nursery in the sources.
The collapse of beach-seine stocks at Hout Bay, Blouberg and Melkbos comes from a search summary of the SANBI Red List page, which returned 403 when fetched.
No source shows white stumpnose caught on lures or flies from the Cape shore. The dropshot and fly tactics were removed for that reason.
The surf tactic's stands beyond Melkbos are an estimate. The Strand and Kommetjie 'stumpnose' mentions do not name the species.

yellowtail.name: Yellowtail
yellowtail.season_note: Shore yellowtail around Cape Town is a summer fishery. FG Tackle (Strand) puts the main season at November to May, and Upstream Fly Fishing runs its yellowtail trips from October to April. Sealine posters name January and February as the best months at Rooikrans. In winter the shoals mostly move to the West Coast islands and offshore banks (Dassen Island, Harold's Bank off Cape Point), where only boats reach them. Arrivals are driven by wind and water over several days. A south-easter that has blown for at least three days pushes warm surface water and fish deep into False Bay: Cole names Simon's Town, Glencairn, Fish Hoek Bay and towards Muizenberg, without saying whether from shore or boat. A westerly or south-westerly then brings clean blue water back onto the Point, and fish come closer inshore a few days after a north-wester. Fish are 'there one day and gone the next'. Yellowtail are caught off the Kalk Bay harbour wall only occasionally (Sealine); the south-easter link there is inferred from the harbour's general summer pattern. At Blouberg the only report found is a 2017 sighting of fish busting a few hundred metres out, and no shore catch from Blouberg or Melkbos was found, so rate Blouberg as a rare, opportunistic chance. Glencairn appears only as a general area in Angler Publications; no source names the quarry rocks specifically.

temp.basis: Min 13 C: Donavan Cole, Angler Publications ('prefer warmer water of 15 C and upwards... times when the fish can be caught in water as cold as 13 C'). FG Tackle says 14 C, with big fish down to 12 C. Ideal_lo 16 C: Sealine Cape Point thread ('Anything less than 16 is dodgy... Less than 14 dont bother with spinning'), and FG Tackle says 'try and find 17 C or higher'. Ideal_hi 21 C is an estimate: Cape inshore water rarely goes above about 21 to 22 C. Max 24 C is an estimate taken from the top of FishBase's 18 to 24 C range; KZN writing says the fish leave in the hottest months. No Cape-specific source gives an upper limit.

yellowtail.habitat: A fast-swimming schooling fish of the open water. From the shore it is caught only where deep, clean, blue water comes right up to the rocks. The classic spot is the Rooikrans ledges on the False Bay side of Cape Point, which Sealine calls 'possibly THE best spot for spinning for yellowtail from shore'. Kleinkrans, between Rooikrans and Buffels Bay, and the ledge below the lighthouse are harder to reach. All of these are inside the Cape Point gate and outside the no-take zones (see handling). In summer after south-easters fish also come in along the False Bay west shore. There, the rocks along the railway line between Glencairn Beach and Simon's Town station lie outside both the Boulders no-take zone and the Jager's Walk to Glencairn Beach closed area. Sunny Cove and the Fish Hoek station rocks lie inside that closed area, so they are not recommended (see handling). The end of Kalk Bay harbour wall gives the odd fish and sits next to the St James no-take zone. Yellowtail follow shoals of baitfish along kelp edges and current lines off points. They feed near the surface early in the day. FG Tackle, writing for ski-boat anglers, says they sound to about 30 to 40 m mid-morning, which is out of shore range, and come up again mid-afternoon. Rare on the open beaches of Table Bay.
yellowtail.diet: A generalist predator. In Dunn's 2014 UCT study (samples from Cape Infanta on the South Coast to Lamberts Bay on the West Coast), small pelagic fish were the main prey, followed by crustaceans. Cape writers name sardine (pilchard), maasbanker, anchovy and tiny lanternfish, plus squid (chokka). FishBase says 'small fish, squid and crustaceans'. When the fish are on small bait they ignore large lures (Angler Publications).
yellowtail.typical_size: Shore fish in False Bay are usually 2 to 5 kg (Angler Publications). Fish up to about 10 to 12 kg are 'not uncommon', and the odd 20 kg fish comes off Rooikrans (Sealine 2007). FG Tackle says False Bay fish rarely reach 10 kg. Size at 50% maturity is about 55 cm fork length for females and 58.5 cm for males (Dunn 2014).
yellowtail.handling:
Recreational permit required. Bag limit is 10 per person per day, with no minimum size (WWF-SASSI; FG Tackle 'as per ORI'). WWF-SASSI lists line-caught yellowtail as green, Best Choice. Dunn (2014) found about 41% of the catch was below size at maturity, so release fish under about 60 cm fork length and keep only what you will eat. Trebles in a thrashing yellowtail can easily end up in the angler's hand. Change trebles to single inline hooks, and control the fish's head with a lip grip or wet hands before unhooking. Yellowtail is the top end of light tackle: Rooikrans regulars use at least 19 to 25 kg line and a gaff, and FG Tackle recommends 11 to 12 ft rods, so a 10 ft rod with PE3 braid is the minimum, not a comfortable margin. Shore anglers on the high ledges use a long gaff. Gaff only fish you intend to keep, and land fish for release by hand or with a lip grip in a gully. If you keep a fish, bleed it and chill it.
SAFETY: the Rooikrans and Kleinkrans ledges are steep and dangerous in swell, and anglers have died there. When the swell is big, the ledges are too dangerous: fish a sheltered spot or stay home.
ACCESS: Rooikrans, Kleinkrans, Buffels Bay, Bordjiesrif and the lighthouse ledge are inside the Cape of Good Hope section of Table Mountain National Park. It charges an entry fee and has gate hours, about 06:00 to 18:00 from October to March and 07:00 to 17:00 from April to September (check SANParks). In the peak months sunrise is before the gate opens and sunset after it closes, so at these spots be at the gate when it opens and leave in time for closing. Dusk there is out of reach.
NO-TAKE ZONES (Table Mountain National Park MPA, 2004 gazette): Paulsberg, from Venus Pool (Bordjiesrif) north to Smitswinkel Point; St James, from the Kalk Bay tidal pool to the St James tidal pool, so do not cast north from the end of the Kalk Bay harbour wall; Boulders, from Rocklands to Seaforth in Simon's Town; Castle Rock, from Miller's Point to Partridge Point; Cape of Good Hope, from Scarborough to Hoek van die Bobbejaan on the Atlantic side. Rooikrans, Kleinkrans, Buffels Bay and the Bordjiesrif ledges south of Venus Pool lie outside these zones.
CLOSED AREA: MLRA Regulation 10(f)(ii) closes the sea for 500 m out from the high-water mark, from Jager's Walk (south of Fish Hoek Beach) to the northern boundary of Glencairn Beach. That covers Sunny Cove and the railway rocks along that stretch. It is unclear whether this 1998 closure still applies to rod-and-line anglers, so do not fish there until DFFE or SANParks confirms that you may. The rocks between Glencairn Beach and Simon's Town station lie outside both this area and the Boulders zone.

tactics.title: Dawn spin through the bust
tactics.lure_or_bait: Long, thin white or green surface plug or chisel-nose plug of about 40 to 60 g (for example a Seal Point plug), or a 40 to 60 g keel spoon
tactics.rig: 9 ft 6 in to 10 ft rod casting about 30 to 60 g, 5000-size reel, PE3 braid, 1.5 m of 0.6 mm (about 50 to 60 lb) leader, single inline hooks in place of trebles, firm drag. This is the top end of light tackle: FG Tackle recommends 11 to 12 ft rods.
tactics.retrieve: Get the lure in the water as soon as birds work or fish bust. Cast past the school and pull the lure fast and straight through the feeding fish. Do not drop it on their heads. Keep the rod high so a plug skips or wakes, and keep winding to your feet because fish follow right in.
tactics.depth: Surface to 1 m
tactics.stand: On the deep-water tip of the ledge or point closest to the working birds, in place at first light. At spots inside the Cape Point gate, the gate opens after sunrise in summer: be at the gate when it opens, get onto the ledge as soon as you can, and expect to take turns on small platforms.
tactics.why: Cole: 'Earlier is usually better'. The feeding birds 'usually disperse mid morning and the fish will go off the bite'. He favours plugs that are 'white or green in a long thin shape' and says to 'cast over the school and then pull your lure straight through the frenzy'. Sealine Rooikrans regulars use a white chisel-nose plug or a keel spoon.

tactics.title: Onshore wind pushing warm water in
tactics.lure_or_bait: Compact 40 to 60 g lure that casts into the wind: a keel spoon, a CID Shiverstick 45 g, or a 40 to 50 g casting jig
tactics.rig: 9 ft 6 in to 10 ft rod casting about 30 to 60 g, 5000-size reel, PE3 braid, 1.5 m of 0.6 mm (about 50 to 60 lb) leader, single inline hooks, firm drag. Top end of light tackle.
tactics.retrieve: Long casts. Count down 3 to 5 seconds, then wind fast with sweeps of the rod tip. Vary the speed until a fish follows.
tactics.depth: Upper 3 m
tactics.stand: The deep-water end of a ledge facing into the wind, where warm surface water and bait are being pushed against the shore. Fish only when yellowtail are showing (birds working, fish busting); otherwise move on.
tactics.why: Built on the False Bay pattern: 'The strong SE winds will also push the fish deep inside the bay... catches can be made from Simonstown, Glencairn, Fish Hoek Bay and towards Muizenberg' (Cole; shore or boat not stated). Sealine advice is to wait until a south-easter has blown 'for at least 3 days' and to fish the train line 'only when the tail are present'. The sources describe a wind that has blown for days. This rule reads only the current wind and the water temperature, so treat it as a rough guide. It fits best on the False Bay west shore, where the south-easter is onshore. Yellowtail are caught off the Kalk Bay wall only occasionally (Sealine).

tactics.title: Offshore breeze and clean blue water
tactics.lure_or_bait: 40 to 60 g slim casting jig or spoon (for example a CID Casting Sprat 90 mm or an Old Cape Secret spoon), or a white chisel-nose plug when fish are on top
tactics.rig: 9 ft 6 in to 10 ft rod casting about 30 to 60 g, 5000-size reel, PE3 braid, 1.5 m of 0.6 mm (about 50 to 60 lb) leader, single inline hooks, firm drag. Top end of light tackle.
tactics.retrieve: Cast along the blue-water edge. Count down, then wind fast. If nothing shows, alternate fast winding with short pauses and rod-tip lifts.
tactics.depth: Surface to 5 m
tactics.stand: A deep-water ledge or point with the wind off the land behind you flattening the water in front. Cast along the edge of the clean blue water.
tactics.colour: Pink, blue or green over silver
tactics.why: 'A westerly wind is the favoured wind for catching them around the point' (Cole). FG Tackle: after a south-easter, 'This SW wind is the magic hand that moves the warmer, clean blue oceanic water back against the shore'. A Sealine poster says fish 'come closer into shore' a few days after a north-wester. These were written for the False Bay side of Cape Point, where a westerly blows off the land. The temperature gate keeps this rule off cold upwelling days, when a south-easter blows offshore on the Atlantic side.

tactics.title: Mid-morning lull: count down a casting jig
tactics.lure_or_bait: 40 to 60 g heavy keel spoon or slim casting jig
tactics.rig: 9 ft 6 in to 10 ft rod casting about 30 to 60 g, 5000-size reel, PE3 braid, 1.5 m of 0.6 mm (about 50 to 60 lb) leader, single inline or assist hook. Top end of light tackle.
tactics.retrieve: A long shot. Cast as far as you can off the deep side and let the lure sink for about a 10 to 20 second count (an estimate; shorten it after a snag on kelp). Bring it back with fast wind-and-lift strokes, changing speed every few turns.
tactics.depth: Mid-water to as deep as the ledge allows (about 5 to 15 m, an estimate)
tactics.stand: The deepest corner of the ledge or point, where the bottom drops away fastest and current runs past
tactics.colour: Pink, black or grey over silver, blue or green
tactics.why: FG Tackle: 'More often than not, fish will sound around mid-morning and sit at a depth of 30-40m only to rise mid-afternoon again', and 'Dropping your spoon/lure down and varying retrieve rates often raises fish where there were seemingly none.' That advice was written for casting from ski-boats. Fish at 30 to 40 m are usually out of reach from the shore, so expect little. Try it only where very deep water runs right up to the rocks. Cole adds that when fish are feeding 'on tiny lantern fish or maasbankers... you will need to throw the smallest lure your tackle can handle'.

tactics.title: Afternoon rise on a stickbait
tactics.lure_or_bait: Floating or sinking stickbait or a long white popper, 40 to 60 g
tactics.rig: 9 ft 6 in to 10 ft rod casting about 30 to 60 g, 5000-size reel, PE3 braid, 1.5 m of 0.6 mm (about 50 to 60 lb) leader, single inline hooks, firm drag. Top end of light tackle.
tactics.retrieve: Fast walking or splashing action on top. If fish follow and refuse, switch to a straight fast wind just under the surface.
tactics.depth: Surface
tactics.stand: The deep-water tip of the ledge or point. Watch for birds coming back to the water late in the day. Inside the Cape Point gate, leave in time for closing, which is before sunset.
tactics.why: FG Tackle notes fish rise again mid-afternoon after sounding. Cole: 'Plastic surface poppers/plugs will also get a lot of action when targeting surface feeding fish.' The light weighting for overcast days is an estimate.

tactics.title: Fly on a calm morning when they bust in range
tactics.lure_or_bait: 1/0 to 3/0 synthetic Clouser Minnow (SF blend wing), white, or olive over white
tactics.rig: 9 ft 10 to 12 wt rod, intermediate or fast-sinking line, 1.5 m of 30 to 40 lb fluorocarbon tippet, strong drag. All of this is an estimate: the source gives no rod or line weight.
tactics.retrieve: Cast to the edge of the bust. Count down 5 to 10 seconds, then strip fast, one arm's length at a time, without stopping.
tactics.depth: Surface to 3 m
tactics.stand: A low but safe ledge, well above the wash, with deep water in front and clear room behind for the backcast, away from crowded spinning platforms
tactics.why: A long shot, adapted from a boat method. The Mission's Cape Point yellowtail took 'a simple 1/0 synthetic Clouser Minnow with an SF blend wing' on a countdown and an 'arm length at a time' strip. That fish came to a charter boat after being teased up with Kona squids. The Mission also says 'few of these fish have been reported caught on foot', so only try this when fish come within about 25 m.

tactics.title: Clean-water spin from a deep-water point
tactics.lure_or_bait: 40 to 60 g white or green chisel-nose plug, keel spoon or slim casting jig (CID Shiverstick 45 g / Casting Sprat 90 mm type). Downsize to the smallest you can cast when fish are on small bait.
tactics.rig: 9 ft 6 in to 10 ft rod casting about 30 to 60 g, 5000-size reel, PE3 braid, 1.5 m of 0.6 mm (about 50 to 60 lb) leader, single inline hooks, firm drag. This is the top end of light tackle: FG Tackle recommends 11 to 12 ft rods for False Bay, and Rooikrans regulars use at least 19 to 25 kg line.
tactics.retrieve: Search with long fan casts and a fast steady wind, with an occasional pause and lift. Scan constantly for diving birds and nervous water, and cast at once when they show.
tactics.depth: Surface to 5 m
tactics.stand: The deep-water tip of the ledge or point where clean blue water meets the rocks and current runs past, well above the wash
tactics.colour: White or green. Pink is a common choice for lipped plugs.
tactics.why: Combines Cole's Cape Point advice (fast lures, match the bait size, clean blue water) with FG Tackle's False Bay shore tackle ('PE3 in the False Bay region'), scaled down to a 10 ft rod for this page's light-tackle limit.

yellowtail.review: Checked by an independent skeptic; 25 corrections applied
review_points: The Venus Pool boundary does not rest only on a forum post: the gazetted coordinates (cached) confirm it. The bigger problem is that the profile leaves out the no-take zones that touch the spots it recommends. The St James restricted zone runs from the Kalk Bay tidal pool, right beside the Kalk Bay

The cached MLRA Regulation 10(f)(ii) sets a closed area 500 m seaward of the high-water mark, from a 090 degree line off Jager's Walk (south of Fish Hoek Beach) to the northern boundary of Glencairn Beach. Its opening words ban 'fishing or collecting any fish' there except under a permit. That stret

Rooikrans, Kleinkrans, Buffels Bay, Bordjiesrif and the lighthouse ledge all lie inside the Cape Point gate. Sealine posters say 'the gate opens at 6'. From memory (the SANParks page returned 403), the gate is open 06:00 to 18:00 from October to March and 07:00 to 17:00 from April to September. Sunr

This is unsafe. It recommends fishing ledges in swell above 1.8 m, at high tide, when wash over the ledges is at its worst. The cited sources say only that the Rooikrans ledges are dangerous in big swell and that anglers have died there. None supports fishing them in rough seas. The rig (PE4, 0.7 mm

Cole's chokka drift with a 9/0 hook and 1 m trace is a boat method ('mainly used by commercial boats', according to the cached summary). No source reports shore yellowtail taken on bait in coloured water, and both sources say fish rarely feed, or catches fall to nothing, in green or brown water. A 9

FG's sounding and 'varying retrieve rates' advice is written for casting from offshore ski-boats (cached FG summary). Speed and slow-pitch jigs are vertical jigging lures for boats. A shore angler cannot reach fish at 30 to 40 m. The sink count and the 5 to 15 m depth have no source but are presente

wind_rel is relative to each spot, but the sources describe compass winds with a time lag: SE 'for at least 3 days', then fish come in 'a few days' after a NW or SW. At Table Bay and Atlantic spots, the summer onshore wind is W to NW and offshore is the SE (cold upwelling; Cole says the SE cools wat

The engine shows the tactics panel at every spot where yellowtail rates, so a user at Blouberg or Melkbos would be told to stand on the Rooikrans ledges. Stand text should describe a position at the current spot.
unverified: light weights: dawn and the mid-morning drop-off are sourced (Cole, FG Tackle). The night (0.1), day-dull (0.65) and dusk (0.6) values are estimates. At spots inside the Cape Point gate, dawn in the peak months and dusk all season fall outside gate hours. A species-level weight cannot show this, so the engine needs a gate-hours mask for those spots.

sea weights (flat 0.8, small 1, moderate 0.75) are estimates. rough is set to 0 as a safety veto, because nearly all shore yellowtail water is rock ledges, where the sources report deaths in big swell.
tide weights and spring/neap range are estimates. A Sealine poster said yellowtail respond to wind and water temperature more than to tide.
flow 0.7 is an estimate, based on fish holding on current-swept deep points.
pressure trend weights are estimates. Sources describe a sequence of SE winds followed by SW or NW winds, not pressure itself.
wind strength weights are estimates. Strong south-easters bring fish into False Bay, but no source rates strength at the time of fishing.

The two wind tactics use spot-relative wind_rel as a stand-in for compass winds that act over days (SE for at least 3 days, then W, SW or NW). They are gated by water temperature and month but are only a rough guide away from the False Bay west shore and the east side of Cape Point. A 72-hour wind-direction input or a spot restriction would need an engine change.
ideal_hi 21 C and max 24 C are estimates resting on FishBase's 18 to 24 C range and KZN writing, not on Cape-specific data.
Cape Point gate hours (about 06:00 to 18:00 October to March, 07:00 to 17:00 April to September) are from memory. The SANParks page returned HTTP 403 during review.

MLRA Regulation 10(f)(ii) (Jager's Walk to Glencairn Beach, 500 m seaward): it is unresolved whether this 1998 closure still binds rod-and-line shore anglers. Sealine posters fish there, but the profile does not recommend it until DFFE or SANParks confirms.
Cole's False Bay places (Simon's Town, Glencairn, Fish Hoek Bay, towards Muizenberg) are not stated to be shore catches.
Kalk Bay harbour wall: yellowtail are only occasional there (Sealine). The south-easter link is inferred from the harbour's general summer pattern.
Glencairn quarry rocks: no source names this exact spot for yellowtail.
Blouberg: no confirmed shore catch was found. The only report is a 2017 sighting of fish busting a few hundred metres out.
Buffels Bay: shore yellowtail there is implied (Kleinkrans lies between Rooikrans and Buffels Bay; FG Tackle lists Buffels Bay as a yellowtail area) but no source documents it directly.
Release size of about 60 cm FL is derived from Dunn's maturity sizes (55 to 58.5 cm FL). It is a suggestion, not a legal limit.

Shore lure weights (40 to 60 g) and the 9 ft 6 in to 10 ft rod are estimates set by this page's light-tackle limit. Sources name lure models but not shore casting weights, apart from the CID Shiverstick at 45 g. FG Tackle recommends 11 to 12 ft rods, so the 10 ft rod is below what local shops advise.
The mid-morning jig tactic's sink count (10 to 20 s) and depth (5 to 15 m) are estimates. FG's sounding advice was written for ski-boats.
The fly tactic adapts a boat method to the shore, and its rig is an estimate. Shore yellowtail on fly is described as almost never achieved.

zebra.name: Zebra (wildeperd)
zebra.season_note: Present all year. The species is described as sedentary, and juveniles as very sedentary on shallow reefs (IUCN, via Wikipedia). An unopened Rhodes study of juvenile sparids at Schoenmakerskop reportedly re-sighted zebra on 53% of observation days. False Bay is the western end of its range (WWF-SASSI; The Mission), so around Cape Town it is a False Bay fish, scarce or absent on the colder Atlantic side. It is rarer and harder to catch than blacktail (The Mission). It spawns August to December, with an October peak in the Eastern Cape (IUCN, via Wikipedia). Winter is not a poor time: a 1971 Eastern Cape note says zebra 'are usually caught when the water temperature is low', and the dated catches there are from May and July (DSAE). The April to November peak is an estimate. It rests on that cool-water note, the run-up to and peak of spawning, and the calmer, cleaner water that often comes after the south-easter season ends. False Bay water is usually warmest in late summer (February to March), and those months are left out of the peak. No Cape catch statistics were found. Local reports: wildeperd and dassies at low tide off the Glencairn Quarry, Simon's Town (Sealine, September 2010); dassie, zebra and kob from the rocks below Clovelly station (Sealine, November 2009); zebra off Strand beach in the evenings (Helderberg Basin blog, 2009); zebra at Silversands, Betty's Bay (Sealine, 2012).

temp.basis: estimate. A warm-temperate South African endemic whose range stops at False Bay, so it is scarce where inshore water stays below about 12 to 13 C (the Atlantic seaboard). Cape Town fish come from False Bay, which runs about 13 to 21 C through the year. A 1971 Grocott's Mail angling note (DSAE 'zebra' entry) says zebra 'are usually caught when the water temperature is low', and the dated Eastern Cape catches are from May and July. So the ideal band sits in the cool-to-middle part of the False Bay range, and cool water is not scored as poor. No measured temperature preference was found.

zebra.habitat: Rocky shore. It holds in the wash of intertidal flats, banks, gullies, holes and the surf of small bays (The Mission). Adults range from the surf zone down to about 120 m. Juveniles are very sedentary on shallow reefs, in gullies, tidal pools and estuary mouths, and the species as a whole is described as sedentary (Wikipedia, citing the IUCN assessment by Mann et al. 2014). An unopened Rhodes study of juvenile sparids at Schoenmakerskop reportedly re-sighted zebra on 53% of observation days. A south-east coast study, seen only in a search summary, reportedly saw adults in the intertidal zone only at high tide. The one Cape report has wildeperd at low tide off the Glencairn Quarry ledges. Around Cape Town the reported spots are the rocks below Clovelly station, the Glencairn Quarry ledges at Simon's Town, Strand beach in the evenings, and Silversands at Betty's Bay. Swartklip and the Strand reefs are untested for zebra. Zandvlei Trust recalls wildeperd as an occasional surprise catch at the Orient Road spot in years past. Release any caught at Zandvlei, as the Trust asks for all indigenous fish.
zebra.diet: A specialist bottom feeder. Adults eat mainly polychaete worms and amphipods. Juveniles eat amphipods, polychaetes and harpacticoid copepods (Mann and Buxton 1992, Koedoe 35(2), Tsitsikamma). FishBase also lists fish, molluscs, crustaceans and worms. For bait this points to worms (bloodworm, pencil bait or wonderworm) and small crustaceans (sand prawn), with mussel as a local option, not fish baits.
zebra.typical_size: Most shore-caught fish are 20 to 30 cm (roughly 0.2 to 0.5 kg), and many are under the 30 cm legal minimum. A good one is 35 to 40 cm (about 1 to 1.5 kg). The species reaches 60 cm TL, but 30 cm is the common size (FishBase; Wikipedia). Half are mature at 28 cm FL, at about 6 years old.
zebra.handling: No-sale recreational species. You need a recreational fishing permit. Minimum size 30 cm TL, bag limit 5 per person per day (WWF-SASSI; MLRA regulations Annexure 7, as amended by R.959 of 23 November 2012), within the overall limit of 10 fish per person per day. Confirm the current DFFE regulations before keeping any. It grows slowly, matures late (about 6 years) and lives to 33 years (FishBase). The species is sedentary, so a gully can be fished out. Release undersize fish quickly: wet hands, little handling, back into the same gully. Short-shank or small circle hooks make unhooking easier. It has the spiny dorsal and anal fins typical of sea bream. Freshly caught fish give off a strong, unpleasant smell (FishBase; Wikipedia). IUCN Least Concern. Closed areas: no fishing or bait collection in the Helderberg MPA, between the Eerste River mouth (Macassar) and the Lourens River mouth (Strand), 500 m seaward. From the Lourens mouth to the Gordon's Bay breakwater only shore angling is allowed. The Table Mountain National Park no-take areas in False Bay are St James, Boulders, Castle Rock (Miller's Point to Partridge Point) and Paulsberg. Cape of Good Hope, from Scarborough to Hoek van die Bobbejaan, is also no-take. A 2009 local guide says fishing is not allowed on Strand beach during the day, so check the current by-law. At Silversands, check the Betty's Bay MPA zoning before fishing. Shore fishing on the False Bay coast is best done in a group. Macassar, Monwabisi and Strandfontein have repeated safety warnings.

tactics.title: Pushing tide into the gullies
tactics.lure_or_bait: Bloodworm or pencil bait threaded up the shank and over the eye, or a sand-prawn tail. Keep the bait about thumbnail size. Wonderworm is a fallback.
tactics.rig: #1 to #4 short-shank bait hook (Chinu or Ringer pattern) on a 30 to 40 cm trace of 0.30 to 0.35 mm fluorocarbon. A 1 to 2 oz ball or star sinker running above a swivel. 6 to 8 kg mono, or 0.14 to 0.18 mm braid with a mono leader, on a 9 to 10 ft light rock rod.
tactics.retrieve: Lob it into the back of the gully where the wash spills in. Keep a tight line and lift and drag the sinker half a metre every minute or so ('scratching'). Strike on a firm double knock, because zebra pick at baits and strip them.
tactics.depth: On the bottom where sand meets rock at the gully edge, 1 to 3 m deep
tactics.stand: On a dry, raised ledge beside a gully mouth, not on the front rocks taking the swell. Cast into the foam line inside the gully.
tactics.why: A south-east coast study (not opened) reportedly saw adults in the intertidal zone only at high tide. Around Cape Town, the one report has them at low tide off the Quarry ledges, so treat the flood as one good window, not the only one. They eat mostly worms and amphipods and have small mouths, so a small worm bait on a small hook works best.

tactics.title: Unweighted drift-line in a quiet gully
tactics.lure_or_bait: Unweighted bait: a whole bloodworm, a black or white mussel, or a sand prawn. Two hooks with a different bait on each is worth trying.
tactics.rig: #2 to #4 hook on 0.25 to 0.30 mm fluorocarbon tied straight to the main line. No sinker; the bait is the only weight. A 7 to 9 ft light rod with 4 to 6 kg line.
tactics.retrieve: Let the surge carry the bait naturally into the gully and down the rock face. Take up slack only, and strike on a steady pull. This stops working once the water is moving hard.
tactics.depth: Slowly sinking through 0.5 to 3 m, settling at the base of the gully wall
tactics.stand: On the side of the gully where the wash moves away from you, so the bait drifts into the hole
tactics.why: A Sealine member described drift-lining at the Glencairn Quarry as 'no sinker, drop shot type fishing', using the bait as the weight, and warned it 'won't work too well in moving water'. This was general advice for the Quarry ledges, not zebra-specific; the thread's species were roman, hottentot, wildeperd and dassies. A natural, slow-sinking bait suits a wary fish that picks at its food.

tactics.title: Low-tide ledge at the Quarry
tactics.lure_or_bait: Two baits at once: mussel on one hook, and wonderworm, bloodworm or a sliver of chokka on the other. Redbait if you have it.
tactics.rig: Two-hook dropper rig: #2 hooks on 15 cm droppers of 0.30 mm fluorocarbon, 30 cm apart, with a 1 to 2 oz sinker at the bottom on a weak link for snags. 9 to 10 ft light rod.
tactics.retrieve: Drop it into the deeper holes off the ledge edge and hold it still. Lift slowly to check the baits every few minutes, and re-bait often because blacktail strip baits fast.
tactics.depth: Bottom of the holes and channels just off the ledge, 2 to 5 m
tactics.stand: On the front ledge exposed at low tide, only in a flat or small sea, after watching a few sets come through. Fish straight down into the deeper water and move back as the tide pushes in.
tactics.why: At the Glencairn Quarry (Simon's Town) anglers reported 'Wildeperd and Dassies on low tide', and one advised that an afternoon high tide 'would've been too high'. He suggested two hooks with different baits.

tactics.title: Pink shrimp fly in clear wash
tactics.lure_or_bait: Steve Austin fly: a Crazy Charlie-type shrimp with a pink crystal-flash body, pink thread and gold dumbbell eyes, optionally pink legs and a tan calf-fur wing. Size #6 to #8 is an estimate.
tactics.rig: 5 to 7 weight rod, floating line, 9 ft leader tapered to 0.20 to 0.25 mm fluorocarbon
tactics.retrieve: Suggested, not from the source: cast past the gully edge and let the dumbbell eyes take the fly to the bottom, then make short 5 to 10 cm twitches with long pauses.
tactics.depth: Bouncing the bottom of gullies and sand patches 0.5 to 2 m deep
tactics.stand: On a low ledge or sand edge where you can see into the gully, in a flat or small sea. Keeping low and back from the edge in clear water is sensible (estimate).
tactics.why: The Mission names the Steve Austin as its wildeperd fly on a 5 to 7 weight outfit with a floating line and 9 ft leaders, and calls zebra 'rare and more difficult to catch' than blacktail. Fly size, retrieve and stand are estimates.

tactics.title: Dropshot a scented worm off a ledge
tactics.lure_or_bait: 2 to 3 inch scented soft worm, e.g. Berkley Gulp! Sandworm in natural, camo or pink. Tipping the hook with a small piece of real bloodworm helps.
tactics.rig: #4 to #6 dropshot hook nose-hooked 30 to 40 cm above a 7 to 14 g dropshot weight, on a 0.25 mm fluorocarbon leader. Light 2 to 4 kg spinning outfit.
tactics.retrieve: Lower it straight down off the ledge or make a short cast along it. Keep the weight still and shake the rod tip gently. Work very slowly, moving a metre only after a minute without a touch.
tactics.depth: 30 to 40 cm off the bottom, in 2 to 6 m along the base of the ledge
tactics.stand: On a deep-water ledge such as the Glencairn Quarry front, working parallel to the rock face, in a flat or small sea
tactics.why: This is an extrapolation, not a reported Cape method. Zebra are specialist worm feeders, and scented worm imitations take other small sea bream. A dropshot holds the bait in the strike zone without snagging in kelp and rocks.

tactics.title: Stained wash once the sea has dropped
tactics.lure_or_bait: A sand prawn and bloodworm combination, a bit bigger than usual so it gives off scent in the coloured water
tactics.rig: #1 to #1/0 short-shank hook on a 30 cm trace of 0.35 mm fluorocarbon. A 2 to 3 oz star sinker running above a swivel to hold in the surge; that is the top end of light tackle, so use the lightest that holds. 9 to 10 ft light rock rod.
tactics.retrieve: Cast to the edge of the foam where the wash drains back out of a gully. Leave it longer than in clear water so the scent can spread. Lift it only to stop it washing into snags.
tactics.depth: Bottom, 1 to 3 m, at the downstream edge of the foam patch
tactics.stand: Well back on a high, dry rock above the gully, never on wet front rocks in a moderate sea. Not for rough seas.
tactics.why: Estimate. A 1971 Eastern Cape zebra report noted the water was 'a good fishing colour', which suggests some colour helps. No source says zebra feed more boldly in stained water, so the clarity weighting is an estimate.

tactics.title: Dusk bait session on the sand-and-reef edge
tactics.lure_or_bait: Bloodworm or sand prawn
tactics.rig: #1 to #2 short-shank hook, 0.30 to 0.35 mm fluorocarbon trace, 1 to 2 oz sinker on a running swivel. Add a glow bead above the hook for the last light. 9 to 10 ft light rod.
tactics.retrieve: Hold it still on the bottom along the edge where sand meets reef or rock. Lift and reposition every few minutes. Pack up as the light goes.
tactics.depth: Bottom, at the sand and reef edge, 1 to 3 m
tactics.stand: On the beach beside a sandy gutter that runs along rock or reef, with a group. At Strand, stay out of the Helderberg MPA, the no-take stretch between the Eerste River mouth (Macassar) and the Lourens River mouth (Strand).
tactics.why: A 2009 Helderberg local guide says Strand beach anglers 'target Kob, White Steenbras, Sharks, Zebra' during the evenings, and that fishing there is not allowed during the day. Dusk is also a common feeding time for sea bream that hold to cover by day (estimate). No zebra report was found from Swartklip or the Strand reefs.

tactics.title: Light bait in the gully wash
tactics.lure_or_bait: Bloodworm, pencil bait, sand prawn or mussel. Collect bait yourself only within your permit's limits, and never inside an MPA no-take zone.
tactics.rig: #1 to #4 short-shank hook on a 30 to 40 cm trace of 0.30 mm fluorocarbon, with a 1 to 2 oz running sinker. 9 to 10 ft light rock rod.
tactics.retrieve: Cast into the foam at the back of a gully and scratch it slowly along the bottom. Strike on a firm pull, not on the first pecks. Release undersize fish at once.
tactics.depth: Bottom, 1 to 3 m, at the sand and rock edge
tactics.stand: On a safe, dry ledge beside a gully with moving white water, casting into the wash rather than out to sea
tactics.why: Zebra live in the wash of gullies and holes, the species is described as sedentary, and it feeds on worms and amphipods. A small worm bait in the gully is the most consistent method.

zebra.review: Checked by an independent skeptic; 19 corrections applied
review_points: This is overstated. The Rhodes source was seen only in a search result, and its title is about JUVENILE sparids. The opened sources (Wikipedia, citing IUCN) say only that juveniles are 'very sedentary' and that the species is 'sedentary'. No opened source describes adults returning to the same gully

These weights favour a study that was never opened (seen in a search summary: adults in the intertidal only at high tide) over the only Cape-specific report. That report, from the Glencairn Quarry in 2010, says wildeperd were caught 'on low tide' and that the afternoon high tide 'would've been too h
This is stated as fact but comes only from an unopened search summary. The Mann & Buxton abstract cited for this tactic says nothing about tide.
The Koedoe abstract has no seasonal comparison. The claim may be in the full PDF, but it was not verified, and it is cited as fact twice.

This contradicts the profile's own temperature source. DSAE quotes Grocott's Mail 1971: 'Zebras are usually caught when the water temperature is low'. The dated DSAE catches are in May and July (winter). No source supports reduced feeding in cold water.

There is no zebra report from Swartklip or from the Strand reefs. The Helderberg blog refers to Strand BEACH (sand) in the evenings. Angler Publications mentions the Strand reefs only for kob on paddle-tails. The profile's own unverified list admits the Swartklip gap.

The profile leaves out the Helderberg MPA, a no-take zone with no bait collection, running from the Eerste River mouth at Macassar to the Lourens River mouth at the Strand, 500 m seaward. It lies right between the Swartklip and Strand spots this profile sends people to. It also leaves out Paulsberg
The rule contradicts itself on safety. The engine will show this tactic at night for spots the text says to leave after dark.
unverified: temp: min 12, ideal 13 to 18, max 22 C are all estimates. No measured temperature preference was found, only the range ending at False Bay and a 1971 Eastern Cape note that zebra are usually caught when the water temperature is low.
All condition weights (light, sea, tide, flow, range, trend, clarity, wind) are estimates based on how gully sea bream generally behave. No source quantifies them.

Tide weights (low 0.85, pushing 1, high 0.85, dropping 0.8) are an estimate that balances two signals: a Sealine report of wildeperd at low tide off the Glencairn Quarry ledge, and an unopened south-east coast study (search summary only) that saw adults in the intertidal only at high tide.
Clarity weights (clear 0.75, coloured 0.85) are an estimate. The only support is a 1971 Eastern Cape line about 'a good fishing colour'.

peak_months April to November are an estimate: the 1971 cool-water note and May and July catch dates (Eastern Cape), the August to December spawning period, and calmer autumn water. The warmest False Bay months (December to March) are left out. There are no Cape catch statistics.
spawn_months 8 to 12 come from Eastern Cape data (Mann, via Wikipedia). SAIAB calls it a winter spawner off KZN. Timing in False Bay is not documented.

Site fidelity: only 'sedentary' (species) and 'very sedentary' (juveniles) are sourced. The Rhodes Schoenmakerskop study of juvenile sparids (53% re-sighting) was seen only in a search result. No opened source describes adults returning to the same gully.
A seasonal diet shift (more amphipods in winter) was claimed from Mann & Buxton 1992 but is not in the abstract. The full paper was not opened, so the claim was removed.
typical_size for shore fish (20 to 30 cm, good fish 35 to 40 cm) is an estimate. Only the species' common and maximum lengths are sourced.
The dropshot scented-worm tactic is an extrapolation from diet and related sea bream. No Cape source reports it for zebra.
Fly tactic: only the Steve Austin pattern, the 5 to 7 weight rod, the floating line and the 9 ft leader are from The Mission. Fly size, retrieve, take behaviour and stand are estimates.
The unweighted drift-line advice from the Quarry thread was general advice for that spot, not given for zebra.
Hook sizes, trace diameters and sinker weights in the bait tactics are estimates sized for a small-mouthed 20 to 40 cm sea bream. No source gives a zebra-specific hook size.
No zebra report exists from Swartklip or the Strand reefs. Both were removed as named spots; the Strand record is from the beach, in the evenings.
The ban on daytime fishing at Strand beach comes from a 2009 blog. The current municipal by-law was not checked.
The Zandvlei wildeperd record is a recollection of past catches at the Orient Road spot, not a current report and not placed at the mouth.

The ORI/SAAMBR linefish profile (Mann 2013) could not be opened (DNS failure on oceanographicresearchinstitute.org). Biology was taken from FishBase, Wikipedia (citing the Mann et al. 2014 IUCN assessment) and the Mann & Buxton 1992 abstract.

The bag limit of 5 and minimum size of 30 cm come from WWF-SASSI and the MLRA Annexure 7 text (2012 amendment). No 2025 or 2026 DFFE notice was checked. The Helderberg MPA zoning comes from cached research records, not a DFFE notice opened here.
